Hypothesis: Electrostatic-frustration-confined mineralization (EFCM) can be made quantitative and falsifiable for CsPbBr3 formation inside an anionic, CO2-philic porphyrin–Zr MOF by explicitly operating in a parameter window where fixed pore charge is not Debye-screened (low ionic strength, weakly coordinating counterions, high-solvent dielectric) and by engineering spatially segregated pore “repulsion pockets” (fixed sulfonates) and “halide-trapping zones” (neutral H-bond donors). In this regime, a coupled Poisson–Boltzmann (PB) electrostatics + classical nucleation theory (CNT)/growth model predicts a measurable increase in the nucleation barrier for Br−-rich Pb–Br complexes near sulfonated pockets, forcing nucleation to occur only at energetically permitted loci and arresting growth at sub-10 nm domain sizes due to an electrostatic + confinement-limited chemical potential. These ultrasmall CsPbBr3 domains exhibit (i) increased accessible interfacial specific surface area within preserved porosity, (ii) pore-field-induced exciton Stark shifts and band-edge modulation that can be independently verified by operando electroabsorption and quasi-Fermi level splitting (QFLS), and (iii) directional charge transfer to framework-embedded metalloporphyrin CO2-reduction sites (Co/Fe) driven by field-assisted band bending and short donor–acceptor distances, yielding dual-mode CO2 sensing (optical/electrical) and enhanced CO2 reduction. The approach explicitly overcomes reviewer-identified weaknesses by: (a) predefining screening-resistant electrostatic operating conditions and acceptance criteria from PB–CNT predictions; (b) incorporating control MOFs that decouple confinement from electrostatics (neutral polar analog and ion-paired/charge-blocked anionic analog); (c) resolving the Br− repulsion vs halide trapping tension via spatial zoning and direct in-pore anion mapping plus ion-migration assays; and (d) attributing CO2 reduction unambiguously through operando perovskite integrity tracking and charge-transfer directionality (spectroelectrochemistry with internal standards, TPV/photovoltage, and isotope labeling).
Plan: A. Quantitative electrostatics + nucleation model (falsifiable upfront)
A1. Measure framework fixed-charge density (σfixed) and counterion population.
- Prepare A-PorZr-MOF films/powders in defined counterion forms (H+, Na+, TBA+; see controls below).
- Quantify sulfonation degree and fixed charge per linker via: digestion 1H NMR + IC (SO3−), elemental analysis (S/Zr), and acid–base titration (for H+ form). Convert to σfixed (C·m−2) using crystallographic surface area per channel (from refined unit cell).
- Measure mobile counterion occupancy by exchanging with 15N-labeled TBA+ or Na+ and quantifying uptake by ICP-MS/IC; confirm distribution by ToF-SIMS depth profiling on films.
A2. Define screening-resistant operating window using PB.
- Use solvent dielectric εr for DMF/DMSO mixtures measured by dielectric spectroscopy; incorporate into PB.
- Set ionic strength I from precursor speciation (measured by conductivity + ion chromatography of free Br−) rather than nominal salt concentration.
- Compute Debye length λD = (εrε0kT/2NAe2I)1/2 and require λD ≥ 0.3–1.0 nm (predefined go/no-go for field persistence in 1.5–3.0 nm pores).
- PB outputs: potential profile ψ(r), field E(r), and ion distributions for each σfixed/counterion/I.
A3. Couple PB to CNT/growth to predict domain size vs σfixed (acceptance criteria).
- Use PB-derived electrostatic work term ΔGelec added to CNT nucleation barrier: ΔG* = (16πγ3/3(Δμeff)2) + ΔGelec, where Δμeff includes confinement and solvent activity; γ extracted from literature/fit using neutral-pore control.
- Predict nucleation rate J ∝ exp(−ΔG*/kT) and expected nucleation density inside pores; integrate with a diffusion-limited growth model with electrostatic exclusion length (from PB) to estimate steady-state domain radius Rpred.
- Acceptance criteria (pre-registered): (i) monotonic decrease of R (or increase of nucleation density with arrested growth) with increasing σfixed at constant pore size; (ii) collapse of this trend when λD < 0.2 nm (high I) or when charges are ion-paired/blocked.

B. MOF architecture: electrostatic pockets + separate halide-trap zones (resolving tension)
B1. Primary target MOF (A-PorZr-MOF): mixed-linker, channelized, sulfonated porphyrin–Zr framework.
- Node: Zr6O4(OH)4 clusters.
- Linkers:
  (i) Tetratopic porphyrin linker (TCPP-derived) bearing peripheral sulfonates (target 0%, 25%, 50%, 75% sulfonation series; avoid 100% initially for crystallinity risk).
  (ii) Short ditopic linker (e.g., 2,5-dihydroxyterephthalate or biphenyl-4,4′-dicarboxylate tuned by length) to enforce 1D channels; target pore diameter 1.5–3.0 nm (validated by NLDFT from Ar/Kr adsorption + PXRD refinement).
- Spatial zoning to decouple functions:
  • “Repulsion pockets”: sulfonates oriented toward channel interior.
  • “Halide-trap zones”: incorporate neutral urea/amide substituents on the *ditopic* linker (not on sulfonated porphyrin) so halide binding occurs at distinct axial positions away from initial nucleation pockets. This is engineered by selecting ditopic linkers with pendant urea groups projected toward inter-channel windows rather than the primary channel centerline.
B2. Metalloporphyrin catalytic sites.
- Metalate a controlled fraction (10%, 30%, 60%) of porphyrins with Co(II) (primary) and Fe(II) (secondary) post-synthetically under conditions that preserve Zr–carboxylate connectivity.
- Keep remaining free-base porphyrins as optical reporters/energy transfer references.

C. Risk-mitigated MOF synthesis strategy (explicit go/no-go + fallback)
C1. Go/no-go metrics for “novel” MOF.
- Must meet simultaneously: (i) PXRD crystallinity with Rietveld fit to target topology; (ii) BET/Kr area ≥ 1200 m2·g−1 after activation; (iii) CO2 Henry constant enhanced vs neutral analog by ≥2×; (iv) film integrity (no cracking) for 200–800 nm oriented films.
C2. Fallback target if novel topology fails.
- Use a known robust Zr-porphyrin framework topology that tolerates functionalization (e.g., a PCN-224-like or MOF-525-derived porphyrin–Zr lattice) but introduce anionic character via (i) partial sulfonation capped at 25–50% and/or (ii) mixed-linker insertion of sulfonated monotopic modulators anchored to Zr6 nodes. This preserves crystallinity/porosity while still enabling σfixed tuning.
- Maintain the same control suite and EFCM protocol so mechanistic testing remains valid even if topology changes.

D. Electrostatic-frustration confined mineralization (EFCM) with explicit screening controls
D1. Precursor speciation and ionic-strength control (key to reviewer concern).
- Use PbBr2 with controlled bromide activity: generate PbBrx(2−x) complexes using minimal added bromide; quantify free Br− by IC.
- Maintain low I during pore loading: avoid excess salts; target conductivity corresponding to I ≤ 5–20 mM (tuned to achieve λD threshold from PB).
- Solvent: DMF:DMSO ratio tuned (e.g., 7:3 to 9:1) to balance εr, viscosity, and precursor solubility; dielectric measured.
D2. Mineralization protocol.
- Step 1: load Pb–Br precursor into activated MOF films under vacuum-assisted infiltration.
- Step 2: introduce A-site cations (Cs+ and FA+) by pulse-feeding: early pulses Cs+ only (rigid nuclei), later limited FA+ to y = 0–0.2 (precomputed tolerance factor window) to relieve strain without forming FA-rich bulk phases.
- Step 3: trigger crystallization by antisolvent vapor diffusion (e.g., toluene/ethyl acetate) with temperature ramp (e.g., 20→60 °C) while monitoring in situ GIWAXS.
- Variables: σfixed series (0–75%), counterion (H+, Na+, TBA+), and ionic strength I.
D3. Hard controls to decouple confinement vs electrostatics (mandatory).
- Control C1 (neutral polar analog): same topology/pore size but replace sulfonates with neutral, similarly polar groups (e.g., sulfones or oligo-ether substituents) to preserve polarity/CO2 affinity without fixed charge.
- Control C2 (charge-blocked anionic): same sulfonated MOF but ion-pair sulfonates with bulky, poorly dissociating cations (e.g., TBA+ or polymeric quaternary ammonium) to collapse ψ(r) while retaining sterics/polarity; verify by reduced zeta/streaming potential and PB inputs.
- Control C3 (external perovskite): deposit CsPbBr3 on MOF surface (no confinement) with identical precursor chemistry.

E. Direct verification of spatial zoning, Br− behavior, and ion migration
E1. In-pore anion/cation mapping (addressing tension and screening).
- ToF-SIMS depth profiles on films (Br−, Pb+, Cs+, FA fragments, sulfonate S− signals) before/after mineralization.
- Angle-resolved XPS with gentle sputter to track Br/Pb gradients; compare across σfixed and charge-blocked controls.
- If available: resonant X-ray scattering at Br edge or synchrotron nano-IR mapping to localize halide interactions with urea/amide zones.
E2. Ion migration assays under bias.
- Apply bias-stress in device geometry; monitor halide migration signatures via time-dependent EIS (Warburg element emergence) and Kelvin-probe surface potential drift.
- Correlate with presence/absence of urea/amide zones (a second internal control: urea-free sulfonated MOF).

F. Band-edge alignment and charge-transfer directionality (beyond UPS/KPFM)
F1. Operando spectroelectrochemistry with internal standards.
- Use Co-porphyrin redox (Co(II/I)) as an internal potential marker; track formation of Co(I) under illumination with applied bias while simultaneously monitoring perovskite bleach (TA) and MOF porphyrin absorption changes.
- Compare across σfixed series and charge-blocked control to isolate field-induced band bending.
F2. QFLS/photovoltage corroboration.
- Measure transient photovoltage (TPV) and/or open-circuit photovoltage in photoelectrochemical configuration; extract QFLS shifts upon CO2 dosing to connect dielectric/electrostatic modulation to energetics.
F3. Electroabsorption (Stark) spectroscopy.
- Quantify field-induced spectral shifts in perovskite exciton/absorption; compare with PB-predicted E(r) magnitudes to close the modeling–measurement loop.

G. CO2 sensing and CO2 reduction: attribution-safe workflow
G1. CO2 sensing (optical + electrical) with mechanistic correlation.
- Optical: ratiometric PL (porphyrin emission as reference vs perovskite PL) under controlled CO2 (0–1 bar) and humidity (10–80% RH).
- Electrical: photoconductance/impedance in interdigitated electrode geometry; extract response time constants.
- Mechanistic tie-in: correlate response magnitude with (i) CO2 uptake (Henry constant) and (ii) Stark shift changes under CO2 (dielectric modulation), across σfixed and control series.
G2. CO2 reduction (photoelectrochemical) with operando integrity checks.
- Use gas-tight cell; quantify products by GC/IC; confirm carbon source via 13CO2.
- Operando perovskite integrity: GIWAXS/PXRD snapshots, XANES of Pb/Br environment if feasible, and post-run ToF-SIMS/XPS for halide depletion.
- Misattribution prevention: run dark controls, porphyrin-only MOF controls, and deliberately decomposed perovskite control to fingerprint decomposition-product activity.

H. Predefined decision points (go/no-go) tied to the quantitative model
H1. Electrostatic frustration viability.
- Go if: (i) measured σfixed and I give λD ≥ 0.3–1.0 nm; (ii) domain size (PDF/STEM) decreases with σfixed in sulfonated MOFs but not in neutral polar or charge-blocked controls.
- No-go/adjust if: high I collapses trends; mitigation: reduce I, change counterion to weaken screening, or switch to lower-ionic-strength precursor chemistry.
H2. Charge transfer directionality.
- Go if: Co(I) formation rate (TA/EPR) increases with σfixed and is suppressed in charge-blocked control at matched porphyrin loading and perovskite amount; TPV/QFLS indicates improved charge separation.

Primary characterization suite (mapped to claims):
- Confinement/domain size: synchrotron PDF + STEM-EDX/EELS tomography + in situ GIWAXS.
- Electrostatics: streaming potential (films), zeta (powders), dielectric spectroscopy (solvent), electroabsorption (Stark).
- Charge transfer: transient absorption, time-resolved EPR (Co(I)), IMPS/EIS.
- Br− zoning/migration: ToF-SIMS, AR-XPS, bias-stress EIS.
- CO2 function: adsorption isotherms + sensing calibration + 13CO2 product attribution.
Feasibility: 1) Quantitative electrostatics addresses screening risk directly. The proposal no longer assumes Coulomb repulsion dominates under all precursor conditions: λD and PB-derived fields are computed from measured σfixed, εr, and ionic strength (from conductivity/IC), and frustration is only claimed within a predefined screening-resistant window (λD ≥ 0.3–1.0 nm). The PB→CNT/growth model yields explicit, falsifiable predictions (domain radius vs σfixed; collapse under charge-blocking or high I), converting the central premise into a testable mechanism rather than an assertion.

2) Controls decouple confinement, polarity, and electrostatics. Two hard controls—(i) a neutral-but-polar, pore-size-matched analog and (ii) a charge-blocked (ion-paired) anionic analog—separate geometric confinement from fixed-field effects. This directly addresses reviewer concerns that size control or band shifts could arise from polarity, surface states, or stoichiometry rather than fixed charge.

3) The Br− repulsion vs halide trapping tension is resolved by spatial zoning plus verification. By placing fixed sulfonates in defined “repulsion pockets” and neutral urea/amide donors in separate “trap zones” (on a different linker family/position), the design can simultaneously (a) raise nucleation barriers for Br−-rich complexes at specific loci and (b) immobilize mobile halides during operation away from nucleation sites. In-pore anion mapping (ToF-SIMS/AR-XPS) and bias-stress migration assays provide direct evidence that these functions occur in distinct regions.

4) Band alignment is corroborated operando with internal standards, not inferred from UPS/KPFM alone. Operando spectroelectrochemistry uses the metalloporphyrin redox couple as an internal energetic reference while tracking Co(I) formation under illumination; TPV/QFLS and Stark spectroscopy then link electrostatics to energetics and charge separation. This multi-modal approach reduces ambiguity from surface states and trapped ions common in porous films.

5) Synthetic risk is mitigated with explicit go/no-go metrics and a robust fallback topology. High sulfonation is recognized as structurally risky; therefore, sulfonation is introduced as a graded series (0–75%) with crystallinity/porosity benchmarks, and a fallback to a known stable Zr-porphyrin topology (functionalized to introduce anionic character without framework collapse) preserves the mechanistic testbed even if the “novel” framework underperforms.

6) CO2 reduction attribution is protected against perovskite photocorrosion artifacts. Operando integrity checks (GIWAXS/PXRD snapshots, post-run halide mapping, decomposition fingerprint controls) plus 13CO2 labeling prevent misassignment of activity to decomposition products or porphyrin-only pathways. Directionality of charge transfer is specifically tied to Co(I) kinetics and its dependence on σfixed/charge-blocking, providing a causal chain from electrostatics → charge-transfer property → catalytic outcome.

Collectively, the revised plan turns the electrostatic-frustration concept into a parameterized, model-validated, control-supported mechanism with clear acceptance criteria, while retaining the original concept chain: Coulomb repulsive force → confined CsPbBr3 domain formation → bandgap/band-edge modulation → improved charge-transfer property into porphyrin-MOF CO2-reduction sites → dual-mode CO2 sensing and enhanced CO2 reduction.
final_critique: The strongest aspect is the explicit falsifiability: measuring σfixed, εr, and ionic strength to parameterize PB, then using PB-derived fields to modify nucleation barriers and predict domain size trends with rigorous controls. This directly addresses the usual non-falsifiable “electrostatics in pores” problem. However, several mechanistic links remain under-specified quantitatively. (i) The PB→CNT coupling is plausible but the electrostatic term ΔGelec is not derived in a physically traceable way for charged, multicomponent precursors (PbBrx species, Cs+/FA+), nor is there a clear mapping from PB ion profiles to the actual nucleating species chemical potential/activity inside the pore. (ii) The Debye-length go/no-go is necessary but not sufficient in highly coordinating solvents (DMF/DMSO): specific ion pairing/adsorption to Zr6 nodes and sulfonates can dominate over mean-field screening, potentially invalidating PB assumptions and shifting the mechanism from “field frustration” to “site-specific complexation.” (iii) The “tolerance factor” node in the required concept chain is only weakly connected: FA pulsing is proposed, but no explicit metric ties tolerance factor (or lattice strain) to nucleation/growth arrest versus electrostatics. (iv) The CO2 reduction causality chain still risks ambiguity because CsPbBr3 in polar media is metastable; even with operando checks, partial halide loss or Pb(0)/PbOx formation could contribute to photoactivity and band-edge shifts, requiring more stringent discriminants than proposed (e.g., quantitative mass balance of halide and Pb speciation over time). Overall: technically sophisticated and control-aware, but the central quantitative bridge from PB fields to nucleation thermodynamics and to the tolerance-factor element needs deeper, explicitly parameterized derivations and orthogonal validation of PB’s applicability under the chosen chemistries.

original_chain: Durability -> Low-valent metal-containing MOF -> Chemical stability -> Pyridine 2,6-dicarboxylic acid -> Nitrite -> In situ surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy
concept_chain: In situ surface-enhanced infrared absorption spectroscopy
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A pydc-built MOF can be made nitrite-durable—not by assuming nitrite is “benignly adsorbed,” but by engineering (i) a chelation-locked, inner-sphere nitrite adduct at a low-valent node that is kinetically reversible and sterically prevented from μ-bridging/ligand displacement, and (ii) an intrapore SEIRA readout that is provably node-local rather than solution- or antenna-surface-dominated. Mechanistically, pyridine-2,6-dicarboxylate (pydc) enforces a rigid N,O,O donor pocket that (a) increases the reorganization penalty for μ-1,3 nitrito bridging and for carboxylate dissociation that nucleates hydrolysis, and (b) tunes the node redox potential so that nitrite binding proceeds primarily by fast, reversible η1 coordination (diagnostic νas/νs(NO2) splitting) rather than net electron transfer (NO formation, nitrito→nitrato oxidation, or M(II)→M(III) drift). This durability claim will be tested with a de-risked ‘passivated internal-antenna SEIRAS’ architecture: plasmonic Au nanoantennas will be rendered chemically inert (ultrathin Al2O3 by ALD) yet SEIRA-active, then trapped inside the MOF by post-synthetic infiltration/size-exclusion rather than speculative periodic lattice templating. If the central claim is correct, operando intrapore SEIRAS (with rigorous bulk-subtraction and distance/field validation) will show (1) reversible ν(NO2) features that isotope-shift with 15NO2− without concurrent growth of hydrolysis bands (ν(M–OH), ν(COOH)), and (2) no online NO/NO2 evolution and minimal node oxidation in parallel operando XAS/EPR, correlating with ≤1% metal leaching and ≤5% porosity loss under defined nitrite/pH stress.
Plan: DE-RISKING PACKAGE (mandatory go/no-go before full durability mapping)

Gate 0 — Choose a realizable pydc framework + explicit redox-control window
0.1 Node choice (tightened): start from an Fe(II)–pydc framework with demonstrated aqueous persistence (or a closely related Fe(II)–pyridinedicarboxylate topology) rather than Cu(I)/Co(I) as the first target. Rationale: Fe(II) offers (i) strong pydc chelation, (ii) Mössbauer/EPR/XAS discriminability, and (iii) better synthetic accessibility under anaerobic conditions.
0.2 Redox control plan: all operando flow experiments conducted in an anaerobic glovebox-assembled loop (≤1 ppm O2; O2 measured inline with an optical O2 probe). Feed solutions are degassed (freeze–pump–thaw ×3 or Ar sparge) and include a defined redox buffer pair chosen to be IR-silent in the nitrite window (e.g., low-mM Fe(II)/Fe(III) couple in a chelator-free form if compatible, or a sulfite/bisulfite micro-additive only if it does not react with nitrite; final selection by preliminary compatibility screen). Go/no-go metric: operando XANES edge position (or Mössbauer Fe(II) fraction) must remain ≥90% Fe(II) over 2 h at pH 7 with 1 mM nitrite before proceeding.

Gate 1 — Antenna incorporation strategy that is realizable (abandon “periodic lattice positions”)
1.1 Antenna type: Au nanorods (longitudinal plasmon in mid-IR-supporting SEIRA) or Au nanospheres (simpler) with a conformal 1.5–3.0 nm Al2O3 shell deposited by ALD (trimethylaluminum/H2O) to passivate Au against nitrite adsorption/redox while retaining near-field enhancement. Acceptance: Al2O3 thickness by TEM/EELS within 1.5–3.0 nm; no exposed Au by XPS (Au surface signal attenuated; Al–O present).
1.2 Surface handle for MOF affinity (on top of Al2O3): graft carboxylate-terminated phosphonate or silane (e.g., 3-(triethoxysilyl)propylsuccinic anhydride hydrolyzed) onto Al2O3 to promote physical retention/compatibility without creating a nitrite-active metal surface.
1.3 Incorporation route (post-synthetic infiltration + size-exclusion trapping):
  a) Synthesize MOF crystals or membranes first (no nanoparticles present during solvothermal growth).
  b) Solvent-exchange into a low-surface-tension carrier (ethanol/acetone) then infiltrate antenna@Al2O3 dispersion under mild vacuum/pressure cycling to drive particles into meso-/macro-defects and accessible channels.
  c) Lock-in/trap by a brief secondary growth (“healing layer”) of the same MOF from dilute precursor to narrow pore apertures and prevent leaching of antennas while minimizing pore blocking.
1.4 Quantitative acceptance criteria for antenna incorporation:
  - Loading: 0.05–0.5 wt% Au relative to MOF (ICP-MS after digestion), targeting enough hotspots while limiting pore blockage.
  - Dispersion statistics: cryo-FIB-SEM + TEM tomography on ≥3 regions; nearest-neighbor distance distribution reported; acceptance = no aggregates >200 nm; ≥80% of antennas isolated or in clusters with inter-antenna gaps ≥10 nm (to avoid conductive coupling/reshaping) and ≤100 nm (to maintain hotspot density).
  - Porosity retention: N2 sorption (or Ar at 87 K) shows ≥80% BET area retained vs pristine MOF; PXRD crystallinity ≥90% peak intensity retention; membrane permeability drop ≤30% vs pristine.
  - Stability of antenna shape: TEM before/after pH cycling (4–10) and 100 mM nitrite for 2 h shows aspect ratio change <10% and no coalescence.

Gate 2 — Optical/SEIRAS geometry + proof the signal is intrapore and node-proximal
2.1 Measurement geometry (explicit): ATR-SEIRAS using a Ge ATR element (high refractive index; shallow penetration) with a defined incident angle (e.g., 60°) in a microfluidic flow cell. The MOF membrane (10–30 µm) is pressed against the ATR crystal; flow channel height 50–150 µm; flow rate 0.1–1.0 mL min−1. Effective evanescent penetration depth targeted ~0.2–1.0 µm (frequency-dependent), ensuring the probed volume is dominated by the membrane region adjacent to the ATR crystal.
2.2 Bulk nitrite absorption management:
  - Use differential referencing: acquire background under identical ionic strength/pH without nitrite, then introduce nitrite and compute ΔA.
  - Maintain short optical path in the flowing solution (ATR) rather than transmission through millimeters of liquid.
  - Concentration staging: validate at 10 µM–10 mM first; only proceed to 100 mM if ΔA from bulk in control (no MOF) is ≤20% of the MOF+antenna ΔA in the ν(NO2) window after subtraction.
2.3 Field-localization validation using internal standards:
  - Introduce a nonreactive, size-matched IR reporter that partitions into pores but does not bind nodes strongly (e.g., deuterated acetonitrile or a deuterated aromatic) and quantify enhancement vs (i) MOF without antennas and (ii) antenna@Al2O3 dispersed outside the membrane.
  - Acceptance: apparent enhancement factor ≥10× for the pore-partitioning reporter in MOF+antenna relative to MOF-only under identical loading.
2.4 Distance-to-antenna estimate (model + experiment):
  - Build a simple electromagnetic decay model (I ∝ exp(−d/ℓ), ℓ ~ 5–20 nm depending on antenna) to estimate the fraction of node sites within effective enhancement distance based on antenna loading and dispersion statistics.
  - Validate experimentally by comparing SEIRA intensity of a node-binding ligand (e.g., pyridine) vs a non-binding pore occupant at matched pore concentrations.

Gate 3 — Decisive redox-discrimination (nitrite binding vs redox chemistry)
3.1 Isotope assignments:
  - Use 15NO2− to shift νas/νs(NO2) and confirm nitrite-derived bands.
  - Use H2^18O during hydrolysis-challenge steps to label M–^18OH / carboxylate protonation-related bands (and to distinguish node hydrolysis products vs nitrite-only signatures).
3.2 Coupled operando detection:
  - Online MS (or DEMS if electrochemical control is added later) sampling the headspace/effluent for NO (m/z 30), NO2 (m/z 46), N2O (m/z 44 with isotopic patterns) during nitrite exposure.
  - Parallel operando XAS (Fe K-edge) in a flow-through capillary cell on a subset of conditions to quantify oxidation-state drift.
  - Optional EPR to detect NO–metal or Fe(III) signatures if formed.
3.3 Acceptance (binding-dominant regime required to proceed):
  - Online MS shows NO/NO2 signals ≤5% of a calibrated positive-control reaction (Fe(II) salt + nitrite in solution) at matched nitrite/pH.
  - XANES indicates ≤10% net oxidation of Fe(II) during 2 h exposure at target conditions (pH 6–8; up to 10 mM nitrite for initial mapping).

Gate 4 — Antenna-chemistry confound controls (mandatory)
4.1 Antenna-only porous control: embed the same Au@Al2O3 antennas into an inert porous matrix (e.g., mesoporous silica membrane with similar thickness) and run identical nitrite flow; any ν(NO2) features define the antenna-local background.
4.2 Blocked-node MOF control: an isostructural/high-connectivity analogue where open metal sites are capped (post-synthetically with a strongly bound, IR-distinct capping ligand) to suppress node nitrite binding; if ν(NO2) persists strongly, it indicates non-node contributions.
4.3 MOF without antennas: confirms that enhancement (not chemistry) is needed to resolve intrapore kinetics.

FULL STUDY (only after gates pass)
Step A — Durability mapping under controlled stress
A.1 Stress matrix: nitrite 10 µM→100 mM; pH 4, 6, 8, 10; ionic strength 0.1–1.0 M; optional co-stress trace O2 (controlled 1–10 ppm).
A.2 Kinetic extraction: global fitting of ν(NO2) bands + framework markers (ν(COO−), ν(COOH), ν(M–OH)) to a reversible-binding + irreversible-degradation model; report k_ads, k_des, k_deg with confidence intervals.

Step B — Ex situ correlation to structure/chemistry
B.1 PXRD/PDF for crystallinity/local disorder; BET/uptake to quantify pore retention.
B.2 Metal leaching by ICP-MS; linker loss by HPLC/LC-MS.
B.3 Node speciation: Mössbauer (Fe) and EXAFS (coordination change), cross-correlated to operando spectral signatures.

Decision criteria for confirming the hypothesis
- Operando: ν(NO2) responds reversibly to washout (≥90% recovery of band area within defined time), with no monotonic growth of ν(M–OH) or ν(COOH) beyond a small threshold (e.g., <10% of ν(COO−) area).
- Redox: NO/NO2 evolution below thresholds and ≤10% node oxidation during mapped conditions.
- Materials: after a defined accelerated test (e.g., 10 mM nitrite, pH 6–8, 24 h), ≤1% metal leaching and ≤5% pore loss; PXRD ≥90% crystallinity retention.

Fallbacks (pre-specified)
- If Fe(II) oxidizes unavoidably: move to a high-valent but pydc-based node (Fe(III) or Zr) strictly as a spectroscopy-validation platform for intrapore SEIRAS first, then return to low-valent with electrochemical potential control (conductive support + potentiostat) as Phase II.
- If antenna loading blocks pores: reduce loading to 0.01–0.05 wt% and increase SEIRA integration time; alternatively use smaller Au nanospheres (10–20 nm) with the same Al2O3 passivation.
Feasibility: This revision explicitly de-risks the two hardest parts identified by reviewers: materials integration and signal attribution.

1) Antenna incorporation is now realizable and quantified: instead of claiming crystallographically periodic placement (high-risk), antennas are inserted post-synthetically by infiltration and trapped by a controlled “healing” regrowth step. Passivated Au@Al2O3 prevents nitrite chemistry on the antenna surface and mitigates reshaping/sintering. Success is judged by explicit thresholds: 0.05–0.5 wt% loading, ≥80% BET retention, no aggregates >200 nm, and <10% antenna shape change after pH/nitrite cycling.

2) SEIRAS physics is addressed with an explicit ATR geometry and validation plan: a Ge ATR element (defined angle, flow-channel dimensions) minimizes bulk solution path length; differential referencing and bulk-only controls constrain subtraction at high nitrite. Field localization is proven using pore-partitioning internal standards and an antenna-only porous control, coupled to a distance/coverage model based on measured dispersion statistics (tomography).

3) Binding vs redox is decisively separated: 15NO2− assigns nitrite bands; H2^18O labels hydrolysis products; online MS quantifies NO/NO2/N2O; operando XAS (and Mössbauer/EPR as needed) quantifies node oxidation-state drift. Predefined acceptance thresholds (≤10% oxidation; NO/NO2 ≤5% of a positive control) prevent over-interpreting IR-only data.

4) Low-valent risk is reduced by starting with Fe(II) (instrumentally trackable and more synthetically plausible than Cu(I)/Co(I) MOFs in water) and by adding explicit oxygen-scrubbing metrics and go/no-go criteria for valence persistence during flow.

5) Controls now isolate every confound flagged: (i) antenna-only porous matrix, (ii) blocked-node MOF, (iii) MOF without antennas, plus isoreticular linker/node comparisons. Together, these controls allow unambiguous assignment of ν(NO2) kinetics to intrapore node coordination rather than boundary layer absorption or antenna surface chemistry.

These changes keep the original concept chain intact (pydc chelation → low-valent durability toward nitrite → intrapore operando SEIRAS) while providing engineering realism and discriminating mechanistic tests aligned with established MOF stability principles (strong chelation/rigidity improving chemical resilience) and with state-of-the-art operando discrimination strategies (IR + MS/XAS/EPR; isotope labeling).
final_critique: This is unusually strong in methodological engineering: it replaces the previously high-risk premise of periodic antenna placement with a quantitatively gated infiltration/trapping workflow, and it anticipates the dominant SEIRAS failure modes (bulk nitrite subtraction, antenna-surface nitrite chemistry, and near-field localization) with explicit geometry, acceptance thresholds, and orthogonal operando validation (MS + XAS/EPR + isotopes). The main scientific vulnerability is the central mechanistic claim that pydc rigidity and redox tuning will *generically* suppress nitrite-driven μ-bridging/carboxylate displacement and net redox chemistry at Fe(II) nodes in water. As written, it asserts outcomes (reorganization penalties, preference for fast reversible η1 binding, limited electron transfer) without a sufficiently concrete node model: Fe(II) MOFs span high-spin/low-spin, variable open-site density, and diverse secondary building units; these details control nitrite linkage isomerism, propensity for NO formation, and hydrolytic instability. The redox-buffer plan is also under-specified and carries nontrivial chemical risk (e.g., sulfite/bisulfite are not inert to nitrite under some conditions; Fe(II)/Fe(III) couples may introduce competing complexation or catalysis). Finally, the infiltration/healing step may systematically bias the SEIRA readout toward defect-rich, antenna-adjacent regions, so ‘node-local’ may still not equate to ‘representative of the bulk MOF’; the proposal partially addresses this with tomography and controls, but not with a quantitative linkage between sampled fraction and overall durability metrics.

original_chain: Ni(II) -> Sorption capacity -> Secondary building unit -> X-ray crystallography -> Desolvation -> Kinetics
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A cationic Ni(II) MOF built from a deliberately *controllably labile* dinuclear Ni2(μ2-OH)(carboxylate)3(pyridyl)2 SBU will achieve higher oxoanion sorption capacity (qmax) and faster uptake kinetics (reduced t90) when activated by a crystallography-guided *partial* desolvation protocol that generates a quantified fraction of open/weakly ligated axial Ni sites while retaining accessible pore connectivity. The mechanistic claim is explicitly falsifiable: (i) partial desolvation creates an “open-site population” (axial vacancy fraction, fvac) that increases the intrinsic anion-exchange rate constant (kex) via transient inner-sphere coordination to Ni and cooperative outer-sphere H-bonding to μ2-OH; (ii) any desolvation-induced unit-cell contraction can either increase or decrease intracrystalline mobility depending on whether the *accessible pore volume and pore limiting diameter* (PLD) are preserved—therefore transport acceleration is predicted only within an activation window defined by simultaneously high fvac and non-degraded connectivity metrics (PLD/accessible volume from zeo++/PLATON); and (iii) the observed rate enhancement will be attributable to a shift in the rate-determining step only if independently measured mobility (ionic conductivity/PFG-NMR tracer diffusion) increases and the uptake activation energy decreases in the partially desolvated state. This refined framework avoids overclaiming “electrostatic potential gradients” and instead ties contraction/desolvation to measurable structure descriptors (fvac, PLD, accessible pore volume) and independent mobility/activation-energy observables, while explicitly stress-testing the under-coordinated Ni/μ2-OH node against aquation, hydrolysis, and Ni leaching across pH 4–9 and competitive anion backgrounds.
Plan: Step 1 — Resolve SBU stoichiometry/charge balance and engineer controlled lability (pre-registered chemistry).
1.1. Target node and charge accounting (explicit): synthesize a cationic framework containing Ni2(μ2-OH)(O2CR)3(Lpy)2 cores where (a) three carboxylates are bridging (net −3), μ2-OH contributes −1, and Ni2 contributes +4; the resulting SBU core is charge-neutral before axial ligation, while *framework cationicity* is introduced by using a net-cationic linker set (e.g., incorporating a quaternized pyridinium-bearing ditopic linker as a fraction of Lpy) or by embedding cationic pendant groups on the linker backbone. Counteranions (SO4^2−/HSO4−) are incorporated in channels during synthesis for ion exchange.
1.2. Design for lability without catastrophic undercoordination: enforce a square-pyramidal/octahedral Ni environment in the as-synthesized state with axial positions occupied by labile neutral ligands (H2O/MeOH/DMF), and tune axial lability by (i) selecting pyridyl donors that are less labile than solvent yet do not occupy both axial sites, and (ii) sterically biasing one axial site to be weakly bound (longer Ni–Osolv) as determined by SCXRD.
1.3. Phase generation: prepare (i) mm-scale single crystals for SC–SC tracking and (ii) microcrystalline fractions with narrow particle-size cuts (e.g., 0.5–1 μm; 2–5 μm; 10–20 μm by controlled synthesis/sieving) for kinetic discrimination.
1.4. Baseline characterization (pre-activation): SCXRD (node geometry, solvent occupancy, counterion location/occupancy), PXRD (phase purity), ICP-OES/MS (Ni content), CHNS/combustion, TGA-EGA (solvent identity/amount), and FT-IR.

Step 2 — Crystallography-guided partial desolvation activation (CG-PDA) with quantitative structural descriptors (mandatory directive #4).
2.1. SCXRD-derived pore/connectivity metrics: from each refined SCXRD model compute pore limiting diameter (PLD), largest cavity diameter (LCD), accessible surface area, and accessible pore volume using zeo++ (probe radii pre-registered: 1.4 Å for H2O; 2.0–2.4 Å to bracket oxoanion effective sizes) and cross-check with PLATON SQUEEZE/VOID analyses.
2.2. Humidity-programmed activation: use DVS-controlled a_w steps (e.g., 0.95 → 0.75 → 0.50 → 0.30 → 0.20) at fixed temperature (e.g., 298 K) with equilibration criteria defined by mass change rate (<0.01% min−1 over 30 min). Collect in situ variable-humidity PXRD to track unit-cell parameters.
2.3. SC–SC tracking with fragility mitigation: limit SCXRD to a pre-registered maximum of 3–4 states per single crystal (as-synthesized; two intermediate a_w points; final chosen activation state) and replicate across ≥5 crystals; implement low-dose data collection, crystal mounting that maintains humidity (capillary with mother liquor vapor), and mosaicity/twinning checks.
2.4. Define activation window by quantitative, dual descriptors:
  • Structural window: fvac (fraction of Ni axial sites vacated from SCXRD occupancies + EXAFS coordination numbers) ≥ 0.25 while PLD and accessible pore volume remain ≥ 90% of the solvated state (zeo++).
  • Stability window: Ni loss during water exposure/uptake test ≤ 0.5% of total Ni per cycle (ICP of supernatant) and ligand loss below LOQ by LC-UV/LC-MS.
Only states satisfying both are advanced to full sorption/kinetics campaigns.

Step 3 — Independent transport/mobility quantification vs structural contraction (mandatory directive #1; replaces “electrostatic gradient” claim).
3.1. Ionic mobility metric A (preferred): electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) on oriented single-crystal aggregates or pressed pellets with controlled orientation if feasible.
  • Prepare oriented beds (align 1D channel axis via mild magnetic alignment if crystals are anisotropic, or by sedimentation alignment on patterned substrates).
  • Measure ionic conductivity in aqueous electrolyte (background ionic strength fixed) for solvated vs partially desolvated vs fully desolvated states, extracting bulk resistance and activation energies from temperature-dependent EIS (e.g., 288–318 K).
3.2. Ionic mobility metric B (if feasible): PFG-NMR tracer diffusion using a suitable NMR-active oxoanion analog (e.g., 19F-containing tracer such as BF4−/PF6− for cationic channel environments, or 77Se for selenate where instrument access allows). Report Dtracer with error bars; compare across activation states.
3.3. Temperature-dependent uptake: perform uptake kinetics at ≥3 temperatures (e.g., 288/298/308 K) and extract apparent activation energies (Eapp) under conditions where film transport is minimized (see Step 4). A decrease in Eapp concurrent with increased mobility supports the transport-acceleration claim; an increase indicates pore constriction dominates.

Step 4 — Falsifiable, hierarchical kinetics mechanism package (mandatory directive #2).
4.1. Experimental design for discriminating limitations:
  • Particle-size series: run identical uptake experiments on at least three size fractions (0.5–1 μm; 2–5 μm; 10–20 μm). Intracrystalline diffusion control predicts characteristic time ∝ L^2; exchange-limited predicts weak size dependence.
  • Stirring-rate series: vary external mass transfer (e.g., 200/600/1000 rpm) at constant particle size to test film diffusion; film-limited rates scale with stirring.
  • Concentration series: vary initial oxoanion concentration to probe site-limited saturation and rate dependence.
4.2. Single-crystal uptake imaging (spatiotemporal):
  • Use μXRF/EDS line scans (and/or confocal Raman mapping if anion has signature bands) along the crystallographic channel axis during partial uptake times to detect diffusion fronts/gradients.
  • Fit concentration profiles to 1D diffusion-reaction models to extract Deff and kex with confidence intervals.
4.3. Model hierarchy and selection (pre-registered): fit datasets to a nested set of mechanistic models rather than generic pseudo-order fits:
  • M1: external film diffusion + instantaneous sorption (mass-transfer coefficient kf).
  • M2: intraparticle diffusion in 1D channels (Deff) with boundary film term.
  • M3: diffusion + finite exchange reaction at sites (Deff + kex).
  • M4: dual-population sites (open Ni sites + noncoordinating ion-exchange sites) with distinct kex values and capacities.
Select models by AIC/BIC with bootstrapped confidence intervals; report parameter identifiability (profile likelihood) and goodness-of-fit to both time traces and spatial profiles.

Step 5 — Sorption capacity/selectivity tied to structural state.
5.1. Oxoanion targets: SeO4^2− and HAsO4^2−/H2AsO4− with pH-controlled speciation; optional ReO4− as a monovalent geometric analog to decouple charge effects.
5.2. Isotherms: collect equilibrium isotherms for each activation state at fixed ionic strength (e.g., 1–10 mM background electrolyte) and specified pH (e.g., 6.5–7.5 for environmentally relevant). Fit with Langmuir/Freundlich *only as descriptive*, while mechanistic interpretation uses site counts from SCXRD/EXAFS.
5.3. Competition: test Cl−, NO3−, HCO3−, SO4^2−, PO4^3− at environmentally relevant ratios; quantify selectivity coefficients and capacity retention.

Step 6 — Mechanism-specific structural validation (binding mode + node integrity).
6.1. Guest-validated structures: SCXRD (where feasible) of loaded crystals from within activation window to identify inner-sphere Ni–O(oxoanion) binding versus outer-sphere μ2-OH hydrogen bonding; quantify occupancies and disorder.
6.2. XAS/EXAFS operando and post-mortem: Ni K-edge XANES/EXAFS on (i) solvated, (ii) partially desolvated, (iii) loaded, and (iv) cycled samples to quantify Ni coordination number changes and rule out conversion to Ni(OH)2/NiOOH signatures.
6.3. Leaching/ligand release package (mandatory directive #3):
  • Operando Ni leaching: ICP-OES/MS of supernatants vs time during uptake at pH 4, 6.5, 9 and with competitors.
  • Ligand release: LC-UV/LC-MS quantification of linker fragments in supernatants.
  • Acceptance criterion: within the activation window, cumulative Ni loss ≤0.5% per cycle and no increasing trend over ≥10 cycles.

Step 7 — Controls to establish causality.
7.1. Control A (non-labile Ni): isoreticular Ni MOF with saturated axial positions (e.g., strongly bound axial ligands or a node topology that lacks accessible axial sites) to isolate the effect of open-site creation.
7.2. Control B (no μ2-OH): same topology but μ2-O replaced/absent (synthetic analog), isolating H-bond relay contribution to capacity/kinetics.
7.3. Control C (contraction without open sites, if accessible): a framework that contracts under desolvation but maintains fully coordinated Ni, to decouple contraction effects from site creation.

Pre-registered success/failure outcomes (falsifiable).
• Success requires simultaneous: (i) partially desolvated state shows increased mobility (higher conductivity or higher Dtracer) and lower Eapp than solvated state; (ii) kinetics show size-scaling consistent with increased Deff and/or increased kex depending on state; (iii) qmax increases relative to fully desolvated (accessibility restored) without unacceptable Ni/ligand loss.
• Failure modes are informative: if contraction reduces PLD/accessible volume and mobility drops, uptake slows—this directly falsifies any universal “contraction accelerates transport” narrative and will redirect to linker/SBU redesign to maintain PLD while creating fvac.
Feasibility: 1) Literature-anchored rationale with tightened claims: High-capacity oxoanion capture by cationic Ni(II) MOFs via ion exchange is validated (Asset 1), but this proposal adds a quantitative, state-resolved activation variable rather than assuming activation is benign. SBU geometry controlling sorption behavior is well-established (Asset 2), and SC–SC, desolvation-linked kinetic acceleration via channel transport is plausible (Asset 4) but here is reframed into measurable pore/connectivity and mobility metrics (zeo++/PLATON + EIS/PFG-NMR + temperature-dependent kinetics), directly addressing reviewer concern (i).
2) Node stoichiometry and aqueous stability are treated as first-class risk items: charge balance is explicitly engineered (counteranions in channels; framework cationicity via linker design), and the under-coordinated/open-site concept is constrained to an activation window bounded by quantified Ni/ligand leaching thresholds across pH 4–9 and competitors, with EXAFS to rule out Ni hydroxide/oxyhydroxide formation (addresses concern (ii) and mandatory directive #3).
3) Kinetics are made diagnostic and falsifiable: instead of relying on pseudo-order fits, the plan pre-registers discriminating experiments (particle size, stirring rate, temperature dependence, single-crystal spatial profiling) and a hierarchical diffusion–reaction model selection workflow with confidence intervals and identifiability checks (addresses concern (iii) and mandatory directive #2).
4) SCXRD fragility is mitigated and de-risked: the SC–SC program limits the number of humidity states per crystal, uses replication, and moves the activation-window definition away from PXRD peak width to quantitative structural (fvac, PLD, accessible volume) and stability (Ni loss per cycle) descriptors tied to function, satisfying mandatory directive #4 and addressing concern (iv). Even if some crystals fail, the microcrystalline kinetics/mobility and post-mortem structural probes still deliver the mechanistic package.
5) Clear decision points: The proposal is structured with go/no-go criteria (activation window thresholds, mobility increase requirement, leaching limits). This ensures that if partial desolvation constricts pores or destabilizes Ni nodes, the mechanism is rejected early and the design is iterated (e.g., linker sterics to preserve PLD, alternative counteranions, or reduced open-site fraction) rather than forcing an overconfident narrative.
final_critique: The proposal is unusually rigorous and falsifiable, with good separation of structural, transport, and reactivity contributions. The strongest elements are (i) pre-registered activation-window criteria linking fvac and connectivity to function, (ii) hierarchical diffusion–reaction model selection with identifiability checks, and (iii) explicit stability/leaching acceptance criteria across pH and competitors. Score deductions are driven by several technical risks and some under-specified feasibility points: (1) Quantifying fvac by SCXRD solvent occupancies is intrinsically fragile—partial occupancy of disordered axial solvent and counterions can be highly model-dependent, and EXAFS coordination numbers may not uniquely resolve “vacancy” versus substitution by anions/water during handling; the plan needs tighter operando control to prevent rehydration artifacts. (2) The EIS plan is ambitious for MOF powders/pellets in aqueous electrolyte; separating true intracrystalline ion mobility from interparticle/contact resistances and electrode polarization is nontrivial, and “oriented aggregates” is not yet a concrete, proven method in this context. (3) PFG-NMR tracer diffusion choices (BF4−/PF6−) may be chemically incompatible with a strongly anion-exchanging, water-exposed cationic Ni MOF (competitive binding, hydrolysis, or poor relevance to oxoanions); 77Se is elegant but may be impractical. (4) The proposed control B (no μ2-OH) may be synthetically unrealistic while preserving topology and Ni2 node identity; similarly, control C (contraction without open sites) may be difficult to realize without changing many confounders. (5) The core synthetic premise—creating framework cationicity via a “fraction of quaternized pyridinium-bearing ditopic linker” while retaining crystallinity/SC–SC behavior and stable Ni2(μ2-OH) nodes—may be the dominant risk and is not yet supported by a contingency plan (e.g., post-synthetic quaternization vs mixed-linker solvothermal routes vs cationic metalloligands).

original_chain: Cobalt nanoparticle -> 1 M KOH -> Active site -> Al-PMOF -> Electrolysis -> CO selectivity -> Electron transfer
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A cobalt-nanoparticle/Al-PMOF hybrid with deliberately shortened inter-site electron-transfer distance and a built-in hydroxide-excluding secondary coordination sphere will increase CO selectivity during CO2 electrolysis in 1 M KOH by (i) accelerating inner-sphere electron transfer to *COOH/*CO on interfacial Co–Nx/porphyrin-adjacent sites while (ii) locally suppressing water/proton access and *H coverage that drives HER. Methodological adaptation: instead of embedding metal nanocrystals randomly in Al-PMOF (Ag@Al-PMOF precedent), we will (a) pre-install a periodic, crystallographically defined array of Co-binding pockets in Al-PMOF via mixed-linker porphyrin–carboxylate nodes and (b) confine Co nucleation to these pockets to form sub-3 nm Co nanoparticles electronically wired through π-conjugated porphyrin linkers, while (c) post-synthetically grafting quaternary-ammonium (cationic) substituents on pore walls to create a Donnan-exclusion layer that enriches CO2/HCO3− and repels OH−/H2O near the Co surface. This combined structural/electrostatic secondary-sphere design will bias the interfacial microkinetics toward *COOH formation and rapid *CO desorption, improving CO selectivity relative to non-wired Co NPs or ungrafted Co@Al-PMOF.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select an Al-PMOF topology compatible with porphyrinic linkers (TCPP-like) and high alkaline tolerance; synthesize phase-pure Al-PMOF thin films on conductive substrates (carbon paper or Au-coated glass) using solvothermal growth to preserve electrical contact (mirroring the Ag@Al-PMOF “pristine interface” requirement).
1.2 Implement mixed-linker design: co-assemble (i) TCPP (tetrakis(4-carboxyphenyl)porphyrin) for π-conductive pathways and (ii) a ditopic carboxylate linker bearing a protected tertiary amine (later quaternized) to enable post-synthetic electrolyte gating. Target a defined porphyrin spacing comparable to the shortest-distance MOFs in Asset 2 (≈10–12 Å) to minimize electron-hopping distance.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Site-programmed Co anchoring: metallate a controlled fraction of porphyrin macrocycles with Co(II) (Co–porphyrin) while leaving the remainder metal-free to maintain electronic communication and avoid overbinding CO. This creates periodic coordination “docking sites” for Co nucleation.
2.2 Constrained nucleation of Co nanoparticles: infiltrate Co precursor (e.g., Co(acac)2 or Co(NO3)2) and a mild reductant (NaBH4 vapor-phase or solvothermal polyol reduction) under conditions that favor nucleation at Co–porphyrin/adjacent carboxylate pockets. Use pore-size and coordination guidance to cap NP growth (goal: 1–3 nm) and maximize interfacial perimeter. Avoid full MOF pyrolysis (unlike Asset 1) to preserve Al-PMOF porosity and the designed secondary sphere.
2.3 Electrostatic secondary-sphere gating: deprotect tertiary amines and quaternize (e.g., MeI or (CH3)3O+BF4−) to form fixed cationic sites on pore walls. This is the key adaptation for alkaline operation: create local Donnan partitioning that reduces OH− activity and water availability at the Co surface while stabilizing CO2-derived anions (HCO3−/CO32−) and increasing CO2 residency in pores.
2.4 Build a series of controls to deconvolute mechanisms: (i) Co NPs on carbon without MOF, (ii) Co NPs in Al-PMOF without porphyrin wiring, (iii) Co NPs in porphyrinic Al-PMOF without quaternization, (iv) Ag@Al-PMOF benchmark (Asset 3 style), and (v) porphyrinic Al-PMOF with Co–porphyrin but no Co NPs.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structural and interfacial verification: PXRD for crystallinity; SEM/TEM/HAADF-STEM to confirm NP size and confinement; XPS/XANES/EXAFS to quantify Co oxidation state and Co–N/Co–O coordination; N2 sorption/CO2 sorption to track porosity changes after NP formation and quaternization.
3.2 Electron-transfer and active-site metrics: electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and potential-step chronoamperometry to extract charge-transfer resistance and apparent electron-transfer rate; operando Raman/FTIR to track *COOH/*CO signatures on Co and porphyrin environments; quantify electrochemically active surface area (ECSA) and correlate with inter-site distance (Asset 2 logic applied to electrocatalysis).
3.3 CO2RR performance in 1 M KOH: gas chromatography for CO/H2; calculate Faradaic efficiency (FECO), partial current density for CO, and stability (≥20 h). Compare against controls at matched geometric current density.
3.4 Mechanistic falsification tests: (i) vary quaternary-ammonium density to map OH− exclusion vs FECO, (ii) isotopic experiments (H2O/D2O; 13CO2) to separate proton-coupled electron transfer from mass-transfer effects, (iii) measure local pH proxies (SECM or pH-sensitive fluorescent probes in MOF films) to validate microenvironmental modulation.
3.5 Model-guided interpretation: DFT on Co–NP/porphyrin edge models to compute *H, *COOH, *CO binding energies with and without proximal cationic groups; microkinetic modeling to relate altered adsorption energetics and local activities (CO2, OH−) to FECO trends.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 3 demonstrates that embedding metal nanocrystals in Al-PMOF creates a charge-transfer-capable interface that suppresses HER and enhances CO selectivity; Asset 2 shows catalytic rates increase as inter active-site distances shrink, supporting a design that intentionally minimizes electron-transfer distance through porphyrin-rich architectures; alkaline-stable Co nanoparticle electrocatalysis in 1 M KOH is well-established (Asset 1), providing operational compatibility.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal uses MOF-specific levers (mixed-linker crystallographic site programming, post-synthetic modification, and secondary-sphere electrostatics inside permanent porosity) rather than generic nanoparticle optimization. Co nucleation is constrained by coordination pockets and pore geometry; electron transfer is mediated by π-conjugated porphyrin linkers; ion-partitioning is engineered via fixed charges—a classical coordination-polymer strategy to control local chemical potentials.
3. Comparative Advantage: Relative to random Co NP deposition, the adapted Al-PMOF provides (i) higher density of electronically wired interfacial active sites (reduced electron-transfer resistance), (ii) suppressed HER via hydroxide/water exclusion and reduced *H coverage, and (iii) improved morphological stability against sintering by confinement (as observed for Ag@Al-PMOF vs bare Ag). This should yield higher FECO and sustained performance in harsh 1 M KOH than ungated MOF hybrids or conventional Co catalysts.
final_critique: This is a technically sophisticated and largely coherent proposal that demonstrates strong command of MOF chemistry, electrochemical CO2RR, and secondary-sphere design. The engineering resolution is high: mixed-linker Al-PMOF synthesis, controlled Co–porphyrin metallation, confined NP growth, and post-synthetic quaternization are all actionable and grounded in known techniques. Logical consistency is strong but not flawless: the proposal occasionally over-aggregates effects (electron-transfer acceleration, OH− exclusion, CO2 enrichment) without clearly prioritizing which step is rate- or selectivity-determining under 1 M KOH, where CO2 availability and carbonate equilibria dominate. The Donnan-exclusion argument for simultaneously repelling OH− while enriching HCO3−/CO32− near negatively charged Co surfaces is plausible but would benefit from a more explicit thermodynamic or transport-based justification. Evidence grounding is solid and stays within the chemistry/MOF/electrocatalysis domain, with appropriate use of Assets 1–3. Rationale quality is high: the proposal genuinely adapts MOF-specific levers rather than repackaging generic nanoparticle optimization. Minor score deductions reflect mechanistic overreach rather than lack of feasibility.

original_chain: Mesopore volume -> Phase separation -> Nafion -> Water stability -> MOF-802 -> Dehumidification -> MOF-802
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding MOF-802 nanocrystallites within a Nafion-derived, phase-separated ionomer will improve cyclic dehumidification only if (A) ionomer/interfacial mesoporosity is deliberately created and remains percolated for vapor access and (B) MOF-802’s intrinsic adsorption sites remain accessible and hydrolytically stable under repeated humidity swings. We therefore hypothesize a dual-architecture, dual-function mechanism: (1) **Interfacial/ionomer mesopores (5–30 nm)** are generated by a controlled secondary mesophase separation (evaporation-gradient casting + ionic-domain-selective porogen), producing continuous water-transport highways to MOF surfaces; this reduces external mass-transfer resistance and suppresses kinetic hysteresis caused by slow polymer-domain diffusion. (2) **Interfacial sulfonate–Zr6 coordination is tuned to be anchoring (stabilizing) rather than poisoning (blocking)** by controlling defect density and sulfonate activity: moderate coordination at particle exteriors immobilizes crystallites and decreases Zr leaching/hydrolysis, while excess coordination (or overly defective nodes) would block pore apertures and destabilize the node. We will explicitly separate and quantify (A) mesoporosity located in Nafion/interfacial regions from (B) any true mesoporosity inside MOF-802. Mechanistically, any *true* MOF mesoporosity (if present) is expected to arise only from defect-engineering plus confined reorganization under casting/solvent activity (analogous to phase-separation/crystallization coupling in hierarchical MOFs), and will be independently verified by contrast-matched scattering, gas-sorbate selection, and positron/PFG-NMR methods. Performance gains will be demonstrated by fitting transient DVS data to a **dual-resistance transport model** (MOF uptake kinetics + membrane diffusion), showing a shifted rate-limiting step relative to controls rather than a mere increase in total capacity.
Plan: 1) Materials synthesis and parameterization (explicit defect and size control)
- **MOF-802 nanocrystallites**: synthesize 50, 100, 150 nm targets via modulated solvothermal routes (formic vs acetic acid modulators; modulator:Zr molar ratios spanning low/medium/high) to generate a controlled defect series.
- Quantify node defect proxies prior to compositing: TGA-derived missing-linker estimates (mass-loss comparison), 1H NMR of digested samples for modulator incorporation, BET/CO2 uptake for micropore accessibility.
- Pre-disperse MOF-802 in alcohol/water mixtures compatible with Nafion casting (e.g., lower alcohols + controlled water fraction) using standardized sonication energy and dispersant-free protocols to avoid pore-blocking surfactants.

2) Composite architecture: inducing secondary phase separation while preserving MOF accessibility
- **Nafion selection (IEC variation)**: prepare membranes from multiple IEC grades (or equivalent EW grades) spanning lower to higher ionic content to systematically tune hydrophilic-domain volume fraction and cluster spacing.
- **Casting with controlled evaporation gradients**: use a leveled doctor-blade or casting knife with programmable temperature/airflow to set at least three evaporation-rate regimes (slow/medium/fast). Record mass-loss vs time to parameterize solvent removal kinetics.
- **Transient porogen localized in ionic domains**: add PEG (Mw ~2 kDa) at a controlled wt% range (e.g., 0, low, medium, high) selected to preferentially partition into hydrophilic regions; after film formation, extract PEG by solvent exchange (water/alcohol sequence) until washings show no PEG by TOC or 1H NMR.
- **Loading and particle-size mapping**: fabricate a structured matrix across MOF loading (e.g., low/medium/high) and particle size (50/100/150 nm) to map phase-separation length scales against mesoporosity and kinetics.

3) Mandatory control matrix (causality and attribution)
- **Nafion-only** ± PEG (quantifies polymer/PEG-derived mesoporosity and transport changes without MOF).
- **MOF-802 in non-ionic fluoropolymer analog** (same casting/PEG protocol; isolates “polymer void mesoporosity” without sulfonate anchoring).
- **Nafion with neutralized sulfonates** (e.g., Na+ form) ± PEG (suppresses sulfonate–Zr coordination; tests necessity of anchoring chemistry).
- **IEC series** (at fixed MOF size/loading and fixed PEG and evaporation regime) to connect ionic-domain geometry to pore formation and kinetics.
- **PEG-free casts** for every MOF/Nafion condition (separates native Nafion phase separation from induced mesoporosity).

4) Pore attribution strategy: explicitly separating (A) ionomer/interfacial mesopores vs (B) MOF-internal mesopores
- **Sorbate selection and normalization**:
  - Use **CO2 sorption (273 K)** to preferentially probe MOF microporosity/accessibility in composites (minimizes polymer diffusion barriers relative to N2 at 77 K).
  - Use **water vapor sorption isotherms** (multiple RH steps) to probe operational porosity and hydrophilic-domain behavior.
  - Use **careful mass and volume normalization**: report uptake per (i) total composite mass, (ii) MOF mass fraction (ash-corrected if needed), and (iii) geometric membrane volume to decouple capacity from porosity location.
- **Contrast-matched SANS/SAXS**:
  - Conduct SAXS on dry and humidified samples to extract ionic-cluster spacing and mesophase length scales.
  - Use SANS with contrast variation (D2O/H2O swelling; and/or deuterated solvent swelling where feasible) to localize scattering from water-filled ionomer pores vs MOF domains; fit to multi-population models (ionomer clusters vs larger mesopores vs particle form factor).
- **Positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS)**:
  - Quantify sub-nm to few-nm free-volume elements in polymer domains (distinguishes polymer free volume evolution from MOF micro/mesopore claims).
- **PFG-NMR water diffusivity**:
  - Measure effective water self-diffusion coefficients in membranes at controlled hydration (e.g., at fixed RH) to determine whether induced mesoporosity increases transport and whether MOF loading creates tortuosity penalties.

5) Interfacial chemistry and “anchoring vs poisoning” discrimination (mandatory direct readouts)
- **XPS**: track S 2p and Zr 3d binding-energy shifts vs controls (neutralized Nafion; non-ionic fluoropolymer) to confirm sulfonate–Zr coordination; quantify surface atomic ratios to detect sulfonate enrichment at MOF interfaces.
- **FTIR/Raman**: monitor sulfonate asymmetric/symmetric stretching changes indicative of coordination; compare H+ vs Na+ Nafion to separate acid/base effects.
- **Zr K-edge EXAFS (fitting)**:
  - Compare pristine MOF-802, MOF-802 physically mixed with Nafion (no casting), and cast composites.
  - Fit first-shell Zr–O and higher-shell features to detect node distortion, additional Zr–O–S contributions, or loss of framework order.
- **Leaching assays (ICP-MS)**:
  - During humidity swing cycling, periodically collect condensed water (or extraction medium) and quantify Zr to directly measure hydrolytic degradation; correlate leaching with coordination signatures and defect level.

6) Humidity-cycling durability and structural integrity
- **Humidity swing protocol**: repeated cycling (e.g., 10–90% RH at fixed temperature) with controlled dwell times to stress adsorption/desorption.
- Track **PXRD** peak retention (crystallinity), **N2/CO2 accessibility changes**, and **EXAFS/XPS changes** pre/post cycling to determine whether anchoring stabilizes or accelerates collapse.

7) Dehumidification performance and kinetic/transport model (operationalizing “cooperative kinetics”)
- **Dynamic vapor sorption (DVS)**: perform step-change RH experiments (adsorption and desorption) at multiple RH windows relevant to dehumidification; extract transient mass uptake curves.
- **Dual-resistance model fitting**:
  - Represent uptake as coupled processes: (i) membrane-scale diffusion through ionomer/interfacial mesopores (effective diffusivity, Deff) and (ii) MOF adsorption kinetics (lumped kinetic constant or LDF parameter, kMOF).
  - Fit transients across thicknesses (prepare at least two membrane thicknesses) to separate diffusion-limited vs adsorption-limited regimes.
  - Use model selection to demonstrate the composite reduces diffusion resistance (higher Deff) without decreasing kMOF via pore blocking.
- **Benchmarking**: compare against pristine MOF-802 beds (powder) and Nafion-only membranes with identical casting history to isolate geometry and polymer effects.

8) Decision logic and go/no-go criteria
- If CO2-accessible microporosity per MOF mass decreases while XPS/EXAFS indicates strong Zr–O–S formation, conclude “poisoning”; mitigate by lowering IEC, switching to Na+ form during casting then re-acidifying post-cast, or reducing defect density.
- If water diffusivity (PFG-NMR) increases and DVS fitting shows Deff increases while MOF microporosity is retained, conclude mesoporous transport benefit is real and not an artifact.
- If contrast-matched scattering shows mesopore population is primarily in ionomer/interfacial regions with no change in MOF internal porosity, revise the claim to “interfacial mesoporosity-enabled kinetics” (still valuable) and avoid overstating hierarchical MOF porosity.

Feasibility: 1) Physical plausibility with explicit attribution: Hierarchical porosity can arise from phase separation coupled to crystallization/reorganization in MOFs (toolbox precedent), but in a polymer composite the dominant new mesoporosity is more likely interfacial/ionomer-derived. This proposal is feasible because it treats these as separable hypotheses and installs mandatory attribution methods (contrast-matched SANS/SAXS, PALS, CO2 vs N2/water sorption, PFG-NMR) to avoid conflating polymer voids with MOF-internal mesopores.

2) Anchoring vs poisoning is testable and controllable: Sulfonate–Zr interactions are chemically credible, yet can either stabilize particles or block apertures/alter nodes—especially in defect-rich Zr6 clusters. We directly quantify coordination (XPS/FTIR/EXAFS) and couple it to functional accessibility (CO2 micropore uptake per MOF mass) and stability (ICP-MS Zr leaching + PXRD). The defect series provides a mechanistic lever to identify the “safe window” where anchoring improves hydrolytic stability without aperture blockage.

3) Kinetics is operationalized into measurable parameters: Instead of asserting “cooperative kinetics,” we will fit RH-step DVS transients to a dual-resistance model to extract membrane Deff and MOF adsorption kinetics (kMOF). Thickness-variation and control membranes isolate whether observed rate gains derive from reduced polymer diffusion resistance (expected from induced mesoporosity) versus changes in intrinsic MOF uptake.

4) Causality is ensured by a factorial design and mandatory controls: A structured matrix over PEG content, evaporation rate, MOF loading, particle size, and IEC—plus PEG-free, non-ionic fluoropolymer, and neutralized-sulfonate controls—ensures any mesoporosity and performance changes can be causally assigned to (i) secondary phase separation, (ii) ionic-domain chemistry, and (iii) MOF interfacial anchoring rather than uncontrolled casting artifacts.

5) Application relevance: Zr-based MOFs (including MOF-802-class) are established water-stable adsorbents for dehumidification; Nafion provides robust phase-separated ionic domains that can be engineered into transport pathways. The composite geometry is inherently scalable (solution casting) and the evaluation uses dehumidification-relevant humidity swings and working-capacity metrics.
final_critique: The proposal is unusually strong in causal attribution and mechanistic falsifiability: it anticipates the key confound (polymer voids being misassigned as MOF hierarchy) and installs appropriate discriminants (contrast-variation scattering, PALS, CO2 vs N2/water sorption normalization, and PFG-NMR). The anchoring/poisoning axis is also treated as an experimentally resolvable continuum with direct readouts (XPS/EXAFS) and functional correlates (CO2-accessible microporosity per MOF mass; Zr leaching). Score deductions stem from (i) under-specified quantitative targets/acceptance windows (e.g., required mesopore connectivity/percolation metric; acceptable sulfonate coordination extent; required Deff and kMOF shifts to claim success), (ii) some methodological risk that PEG and casting solvent history alter Nafion morphology and water uptake hysteresis in ways not captured by the proposed dual-resistance model (which may be non-identifiable without independent Deff priors), and (iii) limited clarity on how ‘true MOF-internal mesoporosity’ would be unambiguously proven in a polymer-confined environment beyond indirect scattering/sorption signatures (i.e., risk of over-interpreting broadened pore-size distributions and interfacial void scattering as internal MOF changes).

original_chain: Organic ligand -> Magnetic resonance imaging -> 1,2,4,5-benzenetetracarboxylic acid -> Magnetic resonance imaging -> In situ growth -> Metal-organic framework -> Proton-coupled electron transfer
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A Ti8O8-cluster MOF shell (MIL-125 family) grown in situ on magnetic nanocores (Fe3O4 or MnFe2O4) can increase MRI relaxivity primarily by modulating water access/exchange to the core’s dipolar field (“shell-gated outer-sphere/second-sphere mechanism”), while a reversible Ti(IV)↔Ti(III) proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) process provides an orthogonal, stimulus-responsive switch that measurably changes hydration dynamics (water residence time τM, local diffusion, and proton exchange) rather than being claimed as a dominant paramagnetic relaxer itself. To de-risk structural feasibility and causality, PM-BTC (pyromellitate) will be introduced only within the experimentally defined phase-admissible window where it is demonstrated to act as (A) a true framework co-linker in a mixed-linker MIL-125(PM-BTC/BDC) phase or (B) a controlled defect-capping/cluster-terminating ligand that increases –COOH/–COO−/μ-OH density without destroying MIL-125 topology. The central mechanistic claim is tightened to: (i) shell thickness and porosity determine whether water transport to the core is diffusion-limited, setting a quantitative optimal thickness regime; (ii) PM-BTC-derived acidic/protic sites (true incorporation or defect-capping) increase bound/interfacial water fraction and accelerate proton exchange, shifting NMRD/temperature-dependent relaxometry signatures consistent with increased second-sphere contribution; (iii) biologically relevant redox couples (ascorbate/GSH vs O2/H2O2) reversibly modulate Ti oxidation state in buffered aqueous media, changing hydrophilicity/μ-OH population and thus τM and water diffusion through the shell. MRI improvements will be attributed to the magnetic core (dominant r2, potentially r1 at small cores/fields) with the MOF acting as a tunable “hydration gate”; Ti(III) paramagnetism will be treated as a secondary, quantifiable contribution and explicitly separated by controls.
Plan: Phase I — Prove what PM-BTC does in Ti8O8-node MIL-125 chemistry (free-standing first)
1) Free-standing phase map (mandatory de-risking)
  1.1 Baseline synthesis: Prepare MIL-125(BDC) microcrystals and nanocrystals under a fixed reference condition (Ti(OiPr)4 in DMF, controlled H2O eq, modulator = benzoic acid or acetic acid; 110–130 °C, 12–24 h). Verify MIL-125 topology by high-quality PXRD (indexing + Rietveld against a MIL-125 reference model), SEM/TEM, and N2 sorption (where stable).
  1.2 PM-BTC incorporation screen: Systematically vary PM-BTC:BDC in the linker feed (0, 2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50 mol% in feed) at constant total linker concentration. For each composition: (i) collect PXRD and attempt Rietveld refinement; (ii) quantify crystallinity and unit-cell changes; (iii) record FTIR (carboxylate νas/νs; –COOH vs –COO− signatures) and Raman (Ti–O modes) to detect coordination-mode changes.
  1.3 Decisive “true incorporation vs capping/adsorption” tests (with mass balance):
    • Quantitative digestion NMR: Digest in DCl/DMSO-d6 (or HF-free Zr analog not applicable here; for Ti-MOF use acidic DMSO protocols validated for MIL-125), quantify BDC and PM-BTC integrals with an internal standard, and close the mass balance (ligand in product + ligand in mother liquor/washes). Report PM-BTC incorporation fraction vs feed fraction.
    • Solid-state NMR: ^13C CP/MAS to resolve distinct carboxylate environments; if available, ^1H–^13C HETCOR to link –COOH/–COO− environments to aromatic carbons. Use these spectra to distinguish lattice-incorporated carboxylates (narrower, symmetric environments) from surface-adsorbed species (broader, multiple environments).
    • Competitive wash/desorption control: Subject products to stringent solvent exchange (DMF→EtOH→water) and mild base wash (carbonate buffer, pH ~9, short exposure) to remove weakly bound PM-BTC; re-run digestion NMR/FTIR. Persistence indicates incorporation/strong defect binding.
  1.4 Define the “admissible window”: Identify the maximum PM-BTC content that retains MIL-125 diffraction and porosity. If MIL-125 collapses above a threshold, formally restrict the shell design to: (A) mixed-linker MIL-125 only below that threshold, and/or (B) PM-BTC as a deliberate defect-capper/surface ligand (quantified) rather than a lattice co-linker.
  1.5 If MIL-125(PM-BTC/BDC) cannot be obtained as a single phase: pivot (predefined contingency) to a MIL-125(BDC) lattice with PM-BTC introduced post-synthetically as defect-capping ligand via ligand-exchange at missing-linker sites; quantify exchanged amount by digestion NMR and monitor PXRD invariance.

Phase II — Build core@shell only after phase rules are established
2) Magnetic core synthesis and surface programming
  2.1 Synthesize monodisperse Fe3O4 and MnFe2O4 cores (10–20 nm) by thermal decomposition; confirm size and superparamagnetism (TEM, DLS, VSM).
  2.2 Ligand exchange to catechol-anchored, carboxyl-terminated stabilizer (dopamine-PEG-COOH or catechol-PEG-phosphate): ensure (i) colloidal stability in DMF/EtOH/H2O, (ii) strong Ti(IV) chelation for heterogeneous nucleation. Verify by FTIR/XPS (catechol binding), zeta potential, and stability under solvothermal conditions.

3) In situ growth of Ti-MOF shells with thickness targets tied to diffusion physics
  3.1 Growth regime selection: Use low supersaturation (slow Ti precursor addition; reduced total Ti concentration) to suppress homogeneous nucleation. Run time-series growth to obtain shells of nominal thickness 2, 5, 10, 15, 25 nm.
  3.2 Shell thickness “non-diffusion-limited” target (predefined): Aim for ≤10–15 nm as the primary design window. Rationale: water diffusion time across shell tD≈L^2/D; with L=10 nm and D~(1–2)×10^-9 m^2/s, tD~50–100 ns, which is short relative to typical relaxation correlation times; thicker shells (≥25 nm) will be tested but are expected to introduce diffusion limitation and reduced gating responsiveness.
  3.3 Composition implementation based on Phase I outcome:
    • If true mixed-linker MIL-125(PM-BTC/BDC) is admissible: synthesize shells at PM-BTC incorporation levels (measured, not feed) of e.g., 0, ~3, ~8, ~15 mol%.
    • If PM-BTC functions as defect-capper: first grow MIL-125(BDC) shells with controlled defectivity (via modulator/Ti:linker ratio), then introduce PM-BTC by post-synthetic defect-capping (aqueous/EtOH conditions that do not etch the core), quantify capping amount.
  3.4 Defect engineering with quantitative metrics:
    • Use modulator (acetic/benzoic acid) to tune missing-linker density; quantify by digestion NMR (linker:Ti ratio), TGA (organic:inorganic ratio), and acid/base titration of accessible –COOH/μ-OH (potentiometric titration).

Phase III — Explicit relaxivity model, parameter extraction, and mechanistic proof
4) Structural and interfacial characterization (shell on core)
  4.1 TEM/HAADF-STEM + EDS/EELS: confirm conformal shell, thickness distribution, and Ti localization.
  4.2 PXRD: verify MIL-125 reflections retained after shell growth; compare to free-standing references.
  4.3 Quantify hydration and water mobility:
    • Water vapor sorption (bound vs mobile uptake signatures) and DSC of hydrated samples (freezing/melting depression to estimate confined water fraction).
    • Fast field-cycling (FFC) relaxometry of water protons in suspensions to generate NMRD profiles (0.01–20+ MHz) for mechanistic fitting.

5) Relaxivity mechanism: fit to a gated-access model and set measurable targets
  5.1 Model statement (what is being claimed): Total relaxivity of core@shell is modeled as r_i = r_i,core·A(L,ϕ,τD) + r_i,SS + r_i,Ti(III), where A is a water-access factor governed by shell thickness L, porosity/tortuosity ϕ, and diffusion time τD; r_i,SS is second-sphere/outer-sphere contribution from protic sites; r_i,Ti(III) is an optional, measured term.
  5.2 Extract τM and access parameters:
    • Temperature-dependent r1/r2 (e.g., 10–50 °C) combined with NMRD fitting to distinguish diffusion-limited vs exchange-limited regimes.
    • H2O/D2O isotope substitution: quantify the change in r1 and r2 and compare to proton-exchange models; a significant KIE supports second-sphere/proton exchange contributions.
  5.3 Predefined success criteria:
    • Demonstrate a thickness-dependent maximum in relaxivity (or access factor) consistent with a gating model (optimal ≤10–15 nm; decline at ≥25 nm).
    • Demonstrate that increasing quantified protic-site density (titration-accessible –COOH/μ-OH) shifts NMRD/temperature dependence consistent with enhanced second-sphere contribution, not merely increased surface area.

Phase IV — Biologically relevant redox switching with cycling and stability
6) Define and execute reversible aqueous redox protocol (no strong organometallic reductants)
  6.1 Redox couples and conditions (buffered, physiological):
    • Reduction: ascorbate (AscH−, 1–10 mM) and/or glutathione (GSH, 1–10 mM) in PBS/HEPES at pH 7.4; optional anaerobic control to maximize reduction.
    • Oxidation: dissolved O2 (air-saturated buffer) and/or low mM H2O2 as an oxidative trigger (carefully controlled to avoid core oxidation artifacts).
  6.2 Monitor Ti(IV)/Ti(III) switching and reversibility:
    • EPR to quantify Ti(III) (g~1.94-type signals) with subtraction controls (bare cores; core@MIL-125 without Ti(III); Fe/Mn background).
    • XPS Ti 2p and Ti L-edge XAS on free-standing and core@shell samples (collect identical references to avoid misassignment).
    • Multi-cycle protocol: at least 5 cycles (reduce→wash→oxidize→wash) while measuring (i) Ti(III) fraction, (ii) r1/r2 at fixed field(s), (iii) PXRD retention, (iv) DLS/zeta stability.
  6.3 Leaching and integrity under cycling:
