- Pore-protection control: optionally pre-load a removable, weakly bound pore filler (e.g., low MW alcohol or volatile amine) during shell growth to reduce ligand ingress; remove post-growth under mild vacuum/solvent exchange.
3.3 Shell continuity vs pore occlusion—quantitative pass/fail metrics (mandatory):
- Micropore retention: CO2 uptake at 298 K retained ≥70% after shelling; N2 BET retained ≥65%; NLDFT pore-size distribution peak position shift ≤0.1 nm.
- Kinetic accessibility: CO2 uptake half-time (t1/2) increase ≤2× versus unshelled Ni-core at the same particle size.
- Shell continuity/percolation: four-probe conductivity of pressed pellets/films increases by ≥10× relative to Ni-core (or reaches ≥10−5 S cm−1, whichever is more stringent).
- Structural integrity: cross-sectional TEM/EDX/EELS shows a continuous Ni-rich shell with thickness 5–20 nm and no evidence of pore mouth plugging (supported by unchanged micropore PSD and uptake kinetics).

Step 4 — Interfacial energetics and directional charge-transfer verification (explicit plan)
4.1 Band/work-function measurements:
- UPS and valence-band XPS on (a) Ni-core, (b) Ni3(HITP)2 reference film, (c) core@shell to determine work function and valence band maxima.
- Optical gap estimates: diffuse reflectance UV–vis (Tauc) for core and shell-containing samples.
- Mott–Schottky (electrochemical) for flat-band potentials where applicable (shell film on conductive substrate; core@shell composite electrode).
4.2 Directional transfer experiments (mandatory evidence set):
- Operando EIS under chopped illumination on core@shell vs Ni-core and Ni3(HITP)2 controls (same geometric area and Ni loading) to show reduced charge-transfer resistance and altered capacitance consistent with carrier accumulation in the shell.
- Kelvin probe/ surface photovoltage (SPV) mapping on single crystals before/after shelling to detect illumination-induced potential gradients consistent with junction formation.
- Selective quenching controls: apply an insulating ultrathin ALD overlayer (e.g., 1–2 nm Al2O3) on the shell as a “blocked interface” control; activity drop without major adsorption change supports interfacial charge/ROS role.

Step 5 — Remediation-relevant performance evaluation (beyond benzyl alcohol)
5.1 Mechanistic probe reaction (kept but reframed): Photocatalytic aerobic oxidation of benzyl alcohol → benzaldehyde as a ROS/charge-transfer diagnostic only. Run in water-rich conditions (e.g., 90:10 H2O:MeCN) and report quantum yield proxies, selectivity, and ROS scavenger dependence.
5.2 True contaminant classes (mandatory):
(A) Cr(VI) reduction/immobilization: Evaluate Cr(VI) → Cr(III) under visible light and/or mild bias in buffered water. Quantify by diphenylcarbazide UV–vis for residual Cr(VI), total Cr by ICP, and solid-phase Cr(III) association by XPS/EXAFS where feasible.
(B) Organic micropollutant degradation: Select at least one representative pollutant (bisphenol A or sulfamethoxazole) and quantify removal kinetics by LC-MS/HPLC.
5.3 Realistic water matrices (mandatory): Perform tests in (i) pH 6.8–7.4 buffer, (ii) 10 mM bicarbonate and 10–50 mM chloride, (iii) with NOM surrogate (e.g., 2–10 mg L−1 humic acid). Track performance loss and diagnose radical scavenging by NOM.
5.4 Contaminant-relevant endpoints (mandatory):
- Mineralization: TOC (and/or COD) reduction over time for organic pollutant runs.
- Byproduct/toxicity-adjacent: LC-MS screening for transformation products plus a standardized bioassay (e.g., Microtox luminescence inhibition) on treated vs untreated water.
- Durability/leaching: ≥10 cycles; Ni leaching by ICP-MS (target <1% of total Ni per cycle; cumulative <5% over 10 cycles) and post-mortem PXRD/XPS.

Step 6 — Benchmarking against literature anchors and internal controls
6.1 Benchmarks: Compare against (i) Au/UiO-66-NH2 (benzyl alcohol oxidation benchmark per Asset 1 logic), (ii) representative standalone Ni 2D MOF (Ni3(HITP)2 film/powder), and (iii) Ni-core without shell. Normalize rates per BET area, per exposed Ni (chemisorption titration where possible), and per absorbed photon flux.
6.2 Decoupling proof: Demonstrate that adsorption capacity primarily tracks the core (pre/post shell with preserved microporosity) while redox kinetics/photocurrents primarily track the shell (conductivity/operando EIS/SPV), establishing functionally separated domains rather than a mixed/blocked interface.
Feasibility: 1) Interface feasibility (addressing epitaxy/continuity skepticism): The proposal constrains shell formation to a surface-confined, low-supersaturation growth regime with explicit thickness targets (5–20 nm) and hard acceptance metrics for continuity (≥10× conductivity increase) and non-occlusion (≥70% CO2 uptake retained; PSD invariance). Cross-sectional TEM/EDX provides direct evidence of conformal coverage; uptake kinetics (t1/2) ensures that “porosity retained” is not merely static but remains accessible.

2) Energetics feasibility (addressing “redox-decoupled” ambiguity): Rather than assuming alignment, the plan directly measures work functions/valence bands (UPS/VB-XPS), optical gaps, and flat-band potentials (Mott–Schottky) for core, shell, and heterostructure, then corroborates directional transfer with operando EIS under illumination and SPV/Kelvin probe mapping. The ALD-blocked interface control is a stringent falsification test: if activity persists unchanged, the claimed interfacial charge/ROS pathway is rejected.

3) Core performance plausibility (addressing Ni-for-Cu uncertainty): Ni-for-Cu exchange is treated as an experimentally testable variable with explicit pass/fail thresholds for retained BET/micropore volume and CO2 uptake. The plan anticipates that metal exchange could reduce open-metal-site density or change polarity; therefore, adsorption claims are only advanced if the quantified porosity/uptake criteria are met, and the proposal includes comparative isotherms (CO2, H2O) and zeta potential to capture polarity changes.

4) Remediation credibility (addressing “model reaction” overreach): Benzyl alcohol oxidation is repositioned as a mechanistic ROS probe, while performance claims are anchored to (i) Cr(VI) reduction and (ii) a real organic micropollutant in buffered, ion-containing, NOM-containing waters. Reporting TOC/COD and toxicity-adjacent assays converts the study from selective organic synthesis to environmental treatment metrics.

5) Materials precedent and risk management: Asset 4 supports structure-preserving Cu→Ni transmetallation in oxamate 3D frameworks with improved stability/sorption. Asset 3 supports the rationale for conductive 2D MOF layers as charge-transport skins. The main technical risk—shell blocking—has built-in decision gates (porosity/kinetics thresholds) and alternative mitigation (pore-protection during growth, thinner shell, reduced cycles) while preserving the original concept chain (SCSC Ni core + conductive Ni-2D shell + adsorption/redox domain separation).
final_critique: This is an unusually well-resolved MOF heterostructure proposal with explicit decision gates, quantitative pass/fail criteria, and falsifiable mechanistic claims. Engineering resolution is very strong: SCSC transmetallation, surface-confined 2D MOF growth, cross-sectional compositional mapping, operando EIS/SPV, and realistic water-matrix remediation tests are all state-of-the-art and articulated with actionable parameters. Logical consistency is also high: the redox-decoupling hypothesis is not merely asserted but operationalized through energetics measurements and interface-blocking controls. Minor logical risk remains in the assumption that Ni3(HITP)2 will maintain conductivity and structural integrity under prolonged aqueous, ROS-generating conditions; while acknowledged via durability tests, the proposal still leans on literature robustness that is not universal. Evidence grounding is solid: the proposal stays firmly within coordination chemistry, MOF physics, sorption, and environmental catalysis, though the breadth of techniques slightly exceeds what is strictly necessary to prove the central claim. Rationale quality is high, as the work directly addresses a known bottleneck in MOF remediation (trade-off between adsorption capacity and redox activity) via a creative spatial-separation strategy rather than incremental optimization. Overall weaknesses are limited to feasibility risk aggregation (many hard gates) and the possibility that shell conductivity thresholds may be difficult to meet reproducibly on particulate samples.

original_chain: Reusability -> Surface area -> Capping linker installation -> Actinide integration -> Pore aperture -> Zr-MOF -> Mechanical contraction -> Iodine
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Installing photodimerizable “molecular staples” as ditopic capping linkers inside a Zr-MOF will create an iodine-triggerable, fatigue-resistant aperture gate that preserves high surface area while enabling reversible mechanical contraction and subsequent actinide integration. Methodological adaptation: instead of monotopic defect-capping or simple linker exchange, we will (i) generate a Zr6-node MOF with deliberately positioned, paired open Zr–OH sites, (ii) coordinate a rigid anthracene-9,10-dicarboxylate staple (AnDC) in a half-bound state at these paired sites, and (iii) lock/unlock the staple by single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SCSC) [4+4] photodimerization/thermal cycloreversion. Mechanism: iodine adsorption forms charge-transfer complexes (I2···π) at anthracene units, increasing local polarizability and aligning adjacent anthracenes; subsequent light-driven dimerization converts two flexible π-surfaces into a covalent cycloadduct that shortens the effective linker span and increases node-to-node constraint, producing a predictable unit-cell contraction and narrowing of pore apertures. The covalent ‘stapled’ state suppresses iodine diffusion/leaching and reduces adsorption-induced amorphization, enabling high reusability. After iodine cycling, remaining open Zr–OH sites and staple-adjacent oxygen donors provide high-affinity, inner-sphere coordination pockets for actinide(IV) binding (Th4+/U4+ surrogates), while the gated aperture limits hydrolysis and mitigates actinide migration, enhancing retention.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Choose a robust Zr6-node topology that tolerates SCSC transformations (UiO-68 or PCN-57-type) but with larger windows than UiO-66 to accommodate internal staple installation without surface-area collapse.
1.2 Create spatially paired open Zr–OH sites by controlled missing-cluster defect engineering (stoichiometric deficiency + modulator selection) and post-synthetic hydroxylation; map defect pair distribution by pair distribution function (PDF) analysis and modulation-dependent synthesis matrices.
1.3 Synthesize the photostaple ligand: anthracene-9,10-dicarboxylic acid (AnDC) and an electronically tuned derivative (e.g., 2,6-difluoro-AnDC) to shift CT strength with iodine and tune dimerization kinetics.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 ‘Half-binding’ staple installation: expose activated MOF crystals to substoichiometric AnDC under mild conditions that favor coordination to one carboxylate end per staple (monocarboxylate coordination), leaving the second CO2H poised within a pocket near an adjacent open Zr–OH. Verify half-bound state by in situ DRIFTS (νas/νs(COO−) splitting) and solid-state 13C NMR.
2.2 SCSC locking: irradiate crystals with near-UV (365–405 nm) to induce intrapore anthracene–anthracene [4+4] photodimerization between neighboring staples (or between two half-bound anthracenes positioned by defect pairing), converting a dynamic gate into a covalent brace. Track SCSC retention by single-crystal XRD where possible and by in situ synchrotron PXRD (peak shifts without broadening).
2.3 Iodine capture and contraction protocol: expose both unlocked and locked states to I2 vapor at controlled activity; quantify uptake gravimetrically and by I K-edge XANES to distinguish physisorbed I2 vs CT-bound I2/I3−. Measure mechanical contraction by variable-pressure in situ PXRD and dilatometry on pressed pellets; correlate with window size changes via in situ PALS (positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy) or gas-probe sorption (Ar at 87 K + kinetic sieving probes).
2.4 Reversibility cycle: regenerate by mild heating or vacuum; switch gate state by thermal cycloreversion (for tuned anthracene dimers) or by a second photochemical protocol (wavelength-selective) to return to the unlocked state; repeat for ≥20 cycles.
2.5 Actinide integration after cycling: introduce Th4+ as a primary surrogate, then U4+ (or non-redox surrogate Ce4+) under rigorously anhydrous conditions to avoid node hydrolysis; target inner-sphere binding at remaining Zr–OH/open sites adjacent to staples. Optionally, convert captured iodine to polyiodide to pre-polarize binding pockets before actinide dosing.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Porosity/aperture: BET/DFT pore size distributions (Ar/CO2), PALS, and diffusion measurements (QENS or uptake kinetics with probe molecules) to quantify aperture gating and transport penalties.
3.2 Structural/mechanical: in situ PXRD under iodine loading/unloading to quantify unit-cell strain; nanoindentation/AFM modulus mapping on crystals to test whether stapling reduces adsorption-induced plasticity; compare locked vs unlocked.
3.3 Chemical state of iodine: Raman (I3−/I5− signatures), XPS (I 3d), and I K-edge XANES/EXAFS to establish CT complexation vs polyiodide formation; spatial mapping by X-ray fluorescence microscopy.
3.4 Actinide incorporation/retention: ICP-MS for loading, Th/U L3-edge XANES/EXAFS for coordination environment, and leach testing in relevant brines; quantify whether gated apertures reduce actinide release. Include radiation-stability surrogates (electron/UV irradiation) to assess staple robustness.
3.5 Benchmarking: compare against non-stapled parent Zr-MOF and a non-photoreactive aromatic dicarboxylate control (e.g., biphenyl-4,4′-dicarboxylate) to isolate the effect of the photostaple adaptation on contraction, reusability, and actinide retention.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Zr-MOFs support SCSC post-synthetic transformations without loss of crystallinity, and anthracene photodimerization is a well-established solid-state reaction that produces measurable geometric contraction. Iodine readily forms charge-transfer complexes with π-rich aromatics, enabling an adsorption-driven alignment/templating effect that can bias intrapore photochemistry. Actinide(IV) ions show strong affinity for oxygen-donor environments, and Zr6-node hydroxyl sites provide robust inner-sphere binding motifs compatible with high chemical stability.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal leverages coordination-polymer defect positioning to preorganize reactive organic units, then uses a covalent, stimulus-switchable transformation (photodimerization/cycloreversion) as a chemically encoded mechanical actuator. This is a molecular-level design adaptation (not a simple modulator/capping strategy) that directly couples pore-aperture control, adsorption-induced strain management, and post-use actinide docking within the same Zr-MOF scaffold.
3. Comparative Advantage: Relative to conventional iodine-adsorbing MOFs that suffer pore collapse, iodine leaching, or irreversible framework strain, the stapled gate introduces a reversible, covalently locked mechanical state that resists fatigue and maintains surface area across cycles. The same gated architecture creates protected, high-affinity oxygen-rich pockets that improve actinide retention and suppress migration/leaching, enabling a single material to function sequentially for iodine capture and actinide integration with superior reusability.
final_critique: This is a highly sophisticated and unusually well-integrated proposal that demonstrates deep command of Zr-MOF chemistry, defect engineering, solid-state photochemistry, and f-element coordination. The central adaptation—using paired Zr–OH defects to preorganize half-bound anthracene staples that can be covalently locked/unlocked via SCSC photodimerization—is conceptually strong and technically ambitious. The iodine-triggered alignment mechanism via I2···π charge-transfer is plausible and well-motivated, and the link between covalent stapling and reduced adsorption-induced amorphization is logically consistent with known MOF fatigue mechanisms. Minor deductions arise from (i) the optimistic assumption that defect pairs can be generated with sufficient spatial regularity to ensure high-yield intrapore photodimerization across bulk crystals, and (ii) the limited discussion of competing iodine chemistries (e.g., irreversible polyiodide growth) that could interfere with clean reversibility or cycloreversion. Additionally, while the actinide-integration concept is sound, the transition from iodine-conditioned pores to reproducible inner-sphere An–O/Zr–OH binding pockets would benefit from clearer thermodynamic prioritization versus framework hydrolysis pathways.

original_chain: Sodium acetate -> Coordinative interaction -> Particle size -> Mixed-ligand MOF -> Pore accessibility -> Polymorphic nanocrystallite -> Contrasting agent for MRI
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Sodium acetate can be repurposed from a simple coordination modulator into a transient, bidentate “kinetic fuse” that deliberately generates and then partially redissolves acetate-bridged polymorphic nanocrystallites during mixed-ligand MOF growth, yielding hierarchical (micro+meso) particles with size control and persistently higher pore accessibility. Mechanistically, acetate competes for metal coordination sites and temporarily caps/bridges SBUs (slowing ligand exchange and biasing metastable polymorphs); a programmed acetate activity gradient (time-dependent acetate speciation and removal) triggers controlled redissolution–recrystallization (nanofusion), stitching nanocrystallites into a single porous entity while leaving a regulated defect/mesopore network that improves water access and accelerates inner-sphere/outer-sphere interactions of encapsulated Mn(II) or Gd(III) MRI centers, thereby increasing relaxivity without sacrificing framework integrity.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a robust node chemistry compatible with mixed ligands and water stability: Zr6O4(OH)4 (UiO-type) or M3O (MIL-101-type) for pore stability; choose Mn(II) (or Gd(III) chelate as a guest) as the MRI-active component to avoid free-ion release.
1.2 Design a mixed-ligand pair that enables (i) high connectivity for robustness and (ii) local hydrophilicity for water exchange: primary linker = terephthalate (BDC) or aminoterephthalate (BDC-NH2); secondary linker = a shorter/different pKa carboxylate (e.g., fumarate) to tune node coordination dynamics and defect chemistry.
1.3 Define acetate programming space: sodium acetate concentration (0–500 mM), water/DMF ratio, temperature, and timed “acetate quench” (e.g., dilution into acetate-free solvent or mild acidification to shift acetate/HOAc and weaken bridging).

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Seeded, gradient-modulated solvothermal growth: initiate nucleation at high acetate activity to force small particle size and promote acetate-bridged metastable nanocrystallites (polymorphic nanocrystallites) via competitive coordination and surface capping.
2.2 Trigger perturbation-assisted nanofusion without templates: at a defined conversion (monitored by in situ turbidity or aliquot PXRD), execute an acetate activity drop (rapid dilution or controlled HOAc addition) to induce partial redissolution of the metastable nanocrystallites followed by oriented attachment/recrystallization into a fused hierarchical particle. Maintain mixed-ligand feed during the fusion window to lock in heteroleptic composition as the thermodynamic phase forms.
2.3 Post-synthetic MRI-center incorporation with coordination control:
- Option A (safer, robust): load a kinetically inert Gd(III) chelate (e.g., DOTA-like) into the hierarchical pores; use secondary-sphere hydrogen-bonding (NH2 or fumarate-rich regions) to retain the chelate while preserving water access.
- Option B (higher interaction, more mechanistic): introduce Mn(II) via node-adjacent binding at defect sites created by acetate modulation (coordinatively unsaturated sites), then cap with benign ligands (e.g., phosphate/imidazole) to prevent leaching while keeping inner-sphere water exchange.
2.4 Particle-size locking and colloidal stabilization: finalize by washing to remove acetate, then apply minimal polymer/PEGylation only if needed for dispersion, ensuring it does not occlude mesopores.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structural polymorph and fusion verification: time-resolved PXRD (polymorph evolution), HRTEM/SAED (nanocrystallite fusion/oriented attachment), SEM (size distribution), and PDF analysis if needed to capture short-range order during metastable phases.
3.2 Pore accessibility quantification beyond BET: N2/Ar sorption for micro/mesopore distribution (NLDFT), dye uptake kinetics (size-exclusion panel), PFG-NMR diffusometry of water/contrast-relevant probes, and in situ water vapor sorption to correlate hydrophilicity with diffusion.
3.3 Defect/coordination-state mapping: FTIR/solid-state NMR to detect acetate remnants and linker ratios; XPS/XAS/EPR (for Mn) to confirm coordination environment; ICP-MS for metal content and leaching.
3.4 MRI performance and mechanism tests: measure r1/r2 relaxivities vs particle size and mesopore fraction; perform temperature- and field-dependent relaxometry to distinguish inner-sphere vs outer-sphere contributions; correlate relaxivity with (i) water diffusivity, (ii) defect density, and (iii) accessibility metrics.
3.5 Controls and comparisons: (i) same mixed-ligand MOF without acetate programming, (ii) acetate present but no programmed quench, (iii) monoligand analogs, and (iv) template-derived mesoporous MOF benchmark to demonstrate comparative advantage.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Coordination modulation with acetate is established to control crystallization kinetics, particle size, and defectivity via competitive binding and altered linker deprotonation; acetate-bridged intermediates are known to generate alternative growth pathways. Perturbation-assisted nanofusion demonstrates that kinetic control plus redissolution of polymorphic nanocrystallites yields hierarchical porosity and enhanced accessibility without templates.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The adaptation is a chemistry-native kinetic program: sodium acetate is not merely an additive but an actively scheduled coordination competitor that engineers metastable intermediates and a redissolution–recrystallization window. Mixed-ligand selection is used to tune ligand-exchange kinetics, node lability, and hydrophilicity, making pore accessibility a designed outcome rather than a byproduct.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with (a) conventional modulated syntheses, the programmed acetate gradient adds a controllable fusion step that reliably introduces mesoporosity while maintaining microporous order; compared with (b) template/surfactant mesostructuring, it avoids pore blocking and scale-limiting template removal; compared with (c) simply shrinking particles for accessibility, hierarchical pores improve intraparticle diffusion and water access at constant or larger particle sizes, increasing MRI relaxivity through mechanistically targeted enhancement of water exchange near paramagnetic centers and improved retention/loading of agents without sacrificing framework stability.
final_critique: This is a technically ambitious and largely well-founded proposal that goes well beyond standard modulation strategies. The engineering resolution is high: the acetate programming, fusion trigger, mixed-ligand choice, and MRI-center incorporation are described with actionable experimental levers and appropriate analytical validation. Logical consistency is strong but not flawless: while acetate-bridged metastable polymorphs and redissolution–recrystallization are individually plausible, the proposal assumes—without sufficient risk analysis—that their coupling will reliably yield oriented attachment rather than uncontrolled Ostwald ripening or defect over-amplification, particularly in Zr-based systems with low node lability. Evidence grounding is solid and domain-appropriate, though the MRI relaxivity enhancement mechanism is somewhat extrapolated from accessibility metrics rather than anchored to quantitative water-exchange models (e.g., Solomon–Bloembergen–Morgan parameters). The rationale is creative and addresses a real bottleneck (accessibility vs. stability) with a chemistry-native solution, but it would benefit from clearer boundary conditions under which the kinetic fuse concept is expected to fail or succeed.

original_chain: Competitive adsorption -> Gas adsorption -> Coulombic forces -> Solvothermal method -> Zn(NO3)2·4H2O -> Piezo-mechanical response
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A permanently cationic Zn–azolate MOF can be engineered into an “ionic-lattice electret” only if its counterion is not freely mobile (DC conductor) nor rigidly pinned (mechanically inert), but instead resides in a metastable, bistable anion-binding pocket that allows Å-scale, reversible intra-pore relocation under small elastic strain (0.5–2%) while suppressing long-range diffusion. Under uniaxial compression, shear-enabled linker rotations and node distortions bias the occupancy of two nearby anion microstates (A/B) separated by ~1–3 Å, producing a measurable, fast (elastic-timescale) change in internal electrostatic potential ΔV at adsorption sites. This ΔV selectively stabilizes quadrupolar/polarizable adsorbates (CO2) over weakly interacting gases (N2/CH4) by increasing the electrostatic component of adsorption free energy, yielding a falsifiable, a priori predicted selectivity modulation (target ≥10% in IAST/breakthrough) that is temporally correlated with the fast electromechanical signal and decoupled from slow conductive artifacts. The design overcomes the reviewers’ concerns by (i) replacing ‘immobilized yet redistributable nitrate’ with a mechanically addressable but diffusion-suppressed NO3− in a defined pocket; (ii) establishing quantitative electromechanical and adsorption coupling predictions before synthesis (ΔxNO3− → ΔV → ΔΔGads → ΔSselectivity); (iii) using blocking-electrode, humidity-controlled, guard-electrode protocols to isolate true fast polarization from Maxwell–Wagner/electrode polarization and triboelectric effects; and (iv) employing a realistic synthetic fallback based on post-synthetic quaternization of a known Zn–azolate framework (phase-identified, porosity-gated) to ensure access to the targeted ionic topology.
Plan: Step 0 — Quantitative, falsifiable pre-synthesis predictions (mandatory gates)
0.1 Define the mechanically accessible strain window and modulus targets
- Target elastic uniaxial strain: ε = 0.5%, 1.0%, 2.0% on pellet/monolith without fracture.
- Target framework compliance: effective Young’s modulus 0.5–5 GPa (tunable via mixed-linker ‘slip-plane’ fraction) so that ε is achievable under <50–200 MPa applied stress.

0.2 Build a coupled multiscale model: (mechanics → ion shift → electrostatics → adsorption)
- Periodic DFT (or DFTB if needed for screening) on a representative unit cell fragment containing: Zn–N node, tethered imidazolium, and anion-binding pocket.
- Compute two local minima for NO3− in pocket states A and B (Δx = 1–3 Å), with an energy offset ΔE0 ≤ 2–5 kJ·mol−1 to permit stress biasing but prevent thermal wandering.
- Apply cell deformation (ε = 0.5–2%) and compute the stress-dependent free-energy bias ΔE(ε) between A/B and the expected occupancy shift: pB/pA = exp[−ΔE(ε)/kT].
- Electrostatic mapping: calculate ΔV(ε) at identified adsorption hotspots (e.g., near pore-facing imidazolium/anion pair) using DFT-derived charge density or fitted point charges; output ΔV in mV–V.
- Adsorption energetics: compute ΔΔGads(ε) = ΔGads,CO2(ε) − ΔGads,CO2(0) and analogues for N2/CH4 via (i) DFT binding energies with quadrupole interaction decomposition and/or (ii) GCMC using stress-dependent electrostatic potential grids.
- Translate into selectivity prediction under IAST: predict ΔS = S(ε)/S(0) for CO2/N2 and CO2/CH4 at 298 K, 0.1–1 bar.

0.3 Set minimum detectable electromechanical benchmark from the model
- Convert predicted net polarization change to an expected charge density on pellet faces: ΔP (C·m−2) from dipole moment change per unit volume (DFT) and A/B occupancy shift.
- Define detection threshold: ΔQmin = 10 pC per cycle (instrument-limited, to be verified) implying ΔPmin ≈ ΔQmin/A where A is electrode area.
- Go/no-go Gate G0: proceed to synthesis only if model predicts (i) ΔΔGads,CO2 − ΔΔGads,N2/CH4 ≥ 0.25–0.5 kJ·mol−1 at ε ≤ 2% (sufficient for ~10% selectivity shift at 298 K), and (ii) ΔQcycle above ΔQmin with fast component τfast < 1 s.

Step 1 — Ion-pair motif redesign: diffusion-suppressed, mechanically addressable nitrate pocket
1.1 Replace ‘mobile nitrate in pores’ with a defined, bistable anion pocket
- Incorporate tethered H-bond donors adjacent to the pore-facing imidazolium: urea/thiourea or bis-amide motif (two N–H donors) positioned to bind NO3− in two geometrically nearby orientations.
- Architectural target: a “cationic cleft” comprising (imidazolium C2–H + urea/amide N–H donors) creating two metastable binding poses A/B separated by 1–3 Å along a shear direction.
- Design rule: NO3− binding enthalpy strong enough to suppress translational diffusion (activation barrier for hopping between pockets > 20–30 kJ·mol−1), but A/B interconversion barrier moderate (5–15 kJ·mol−1) to allow elastic-strain biasing without requiring humidity.

1.2 Linker specification (two-function linker: framework-forming + pocket-forming)
- Primary azolate for Zn–N framework: imidazolate/benzimidazolate core for ZIF-like stability.
- Pendant group: (i) quaternizable imidazole to form tethered imidazolium; (ii) appended urea/amide arm within 3–6 Å of the imidazolium to make the pocket.
- Mixed-linker compliance: 10–30% longer, rotatable azolate linker (e.g., benzimidazolate with flexible spacer) to create shearable sublattices (‘slip-plane’ concept) while maintaining connectivity.

Step 2 — Realistic synthetic route with explicit fallback and phase/porosity gates
2.1 Primary route (preferred): post-synthetic quaternization of a known Zn–azolate framework
- Rationale: avoids crystallization disruption from pre-installed permanent cations.
- Choose a Zn–azolate framework with pendant imidazole (neutral) groups pointing into pores (literature-known ‘functionalized ZIF’ families or mixed-linker ZIF analogues).
- Synthesize solvothermally from Zn(NO3)2·4H2O and the azolate linkers under standard ZIF conditions with careful base control.
- Post-synthetic quaternization: alkylate pendant imidazoles (e.g., MeI/MeOTf alternatives) to create tethered imidazolium sites without collapsing topology; immediately exchange to NO3− via controlled nitrate treatment (mild, aqueous-alcoholic) to set the counterion.

2.2 Secondary route (direct ionic synthesis): cationic-linker solvothermal assembly
- Conduct solvothermal assembly in DMF/MeOH with controlled water activity; minimize strong bases that promote anion exchange.
- Use Zn(NO3)2·4H2O as Zn source; maintain nitrate excess to suppress replacement by coordinating solvent anions.

2.3 Phase identification and porosity go/no-go gates
- Gate G1 (phase): PXRD match to targeted topology or reproducible new phase; reject dense nonporous phases.
- Gate G2 (porosity): N2(77 K) and CO2(195 K) uptake confirming permanent porosity; reject samples with collapsed uptake.
- Gate G3 (counterion placement): NO3− confirmed by IR (ν3), ion chromatography of digests, and elemental analysis; check for unintended anions.

Step 3 — Prove ‘metastable but not diffusive’: impedance + solid-state NMR metrics
3.1 Variable-T impedance spectroscopy with blocking electrodes
- Use sputtered Au (or Pt) blocking electrodes; implement guard-ring electrode geometry to suppress leakage currents.
- Measure ε′(ω), ε″(ω), and σ(ω) from 10−2 to 10^6 Hz at controlled RH (0%, 20%, 50%) and 298–343 K.
- Extract DC conductivity σDC and relaxation times. Success criteria: σDC low enough that electrode polarization dominates only at very low frequencies; fast polarization feature persists under dry conditions.

3.2 Solid-state NMR to quantify anion motion (diffusion vs local hopping)
- 15N (nitrate) and/or 2H (if deuterated urea/amide) relaxation to estimate motion timescales.
- If feasible, pulsed-field gradient NMR on digested/liquid analogs is not applicable; instead use T1/T2 and line-shape analysis for site exchange.
- Success criteria: evidence for local two-site exchange (A↔B) without signatures of long-range diffusion.

Step 4 — Tightened electromechanical protocol to isolate true fast polarization from artifacts
4.1 Pellet/monolith fabrication and electrode architecture
- Prepare dense porous monoliths/pellets with reproducible thickness; apply sputtered Au electrodes on both faces; use guard electrode and insulating collar to control fringe fields.
- Environmental control: sealed chamber with controlled RH (0–50%) and temperature (298 K).

4.2 Time-domain and frequency-domain separation of fast elastic vs slow conductive effects
- Quasi-static compression with defined stress ramp rates; record charge under open-circuit and short-circuit conditions.
- Apply dynamic mechanical excitation (0.1–100 Hz) and measure current phase relative to strain.
- Define ‘fast electret-like’ component as in-phase (or fixed phase) with strain at frequencies where ionic conduction cannot follow; define slow drift as conductive.

4.3 Artifact controls (mandatory)
- Inert pellet control: same pelletizing and electrodes but inert porous solid of similar modulus (e.g., neutral ZIF analogue) to quantify triboelectric/contact charging baseline.
- Electrode material reversal: Au vs carbon vs Pt to test electrode-dependent electrochemistry.
- Kelvin probe or surface potential mapping pre/post cycling to detect contact charging.
- Load under vacuum/inert gas to define baseline; then repeat under CO2/N2/CH4 to test adsorbate-coupled signal.

Step 5 — Stress-biased adsorption with explicit decoupling from pore-volume effects
5.1 Measure stress-dependent single-component adsorption isotherms
- CO2, N2, CH4 at 298 K under controlled applied uniaxial stress corresponding to ε = 0, 0.5, 1, 2% (calibrated mechanically).
- Correct for simple void-volume reduction by independent measurement of pellet thickness/porosity change under load and by using the rigid-lattice control.
- Extract Qst(ε) via multi-temperature isotherms or microcalorimetry if available.

5.2 Mixed-gas breakthrough with a piston-loaded fixed bed
- CO2/N2 and CO2/CH4 mixtures at 298 K under: (i) zero load, (ii) constant load, (iii) cyclic load.
- Compare measured selectivity shifts to IAST predictions generated from stress-dependent single-component fits.

5.3 Competitive adsorption under humid/polar interferents (NH3/H2O)
- Guided by NH3 competitive adsorption literature: test humid CO2/N2 with controlled RH and ppm–% NH3.
- Use DRIFTS to differentiate NH3 proton-transfer/H-bonding vs nitrate pocket interactions; quantify capacity loss and recovery when toggling stress.

Step 6 — Operando mechanistic verification: ion-pocket response under stress
6.1 Operando DRIFTS under compression
- Monitor nitrate ν3 band splitting/shift (pocket occupancy change), imidazolium/urea N–H shifts (anion H-bonding changes), and CO2 bands (electrostatic stabilization signature).
- Correlate spectral changes with the fast electromechanical component, not slow drift.

6.2 In situ PXRD under compression
- Track reversible lattice distortions and any peak broadening indicative of plastic deformation; verify elastic reversibility within ε ≤ 2%.

Step 7 — Controls that directly test causality (electrostatics vs mechanics)
7.1 Neutral analogue control
- Same topology/linker backbone but without quaternization (no tethered imidazolium; no NO3− pocket). Expect: minimal fast electromechanical signal and minimal stress-dependent selectivity.

7.2 Counterion polarizability/mobility control
- Replace NO3− with a less H-bond accepting, less coordinating anion (e.g., BF4−) only if it can be installed without framework collapse.
- Prediction: reduced ΔV and reduced stress-coupled selectivity modulation.

7.3 Rigid-lattice control
- Same ionic chemistry but 0% compliant linker fraction. Prediction: smaller ε-induced A/B bias, smaller ΔQfast, and smaller ΔS.

Step 8 — Quantitative success criteria (go/no-go)
- Electromechanical: reproducible fast component with ΔQcycle ≥ model-predicted threshold and stable over 10^4 cycles; σDC sufficiently low that response persists under dry conditions.
- Adsorption: ΔSselectivity ≥ 10% for CO2/N2 or CO2/CH4 at ε ≤ 2% with matching sign/magnitude to the pre-synthesis model.
- Mechanistic: correlated nitrate-pocket spectral signature (DRIFTS/NMR) with fast electromechanical response and adsorption modulation; absence of similar behavior in neutral/rigid controls.
- Stability: PXRD/porosity retention and nitrate retention post-cycling.
Feasibility: Mechanistic plausibility with falsifiable predictions: The revised concept eliminates the internal contradiction of ‘immobilized yet redistributable nitrate’ by specifying a diffusion-suppressed, bistable anion pocket. This directly addresses reviewer concern (i) by targeting local A↔B hopping (Å-scale) rather than long-range NO3− migration that would produce DC conduction and humidity-driven drift. The mandatory pre-synthesis model translates realistic strains (0.5–2%) into quantitative ΔV at adsorption sites and ΔΔGads for CO2 vs N2/CH4, setting minimum detectable ΔQ and minimum selectivity modulation thresholds; the project can therefore fail fast (Gate G0) if the computed coupling is too small, addressing concern (iv).

Electromechanical signal discrimination: The protocol now uses blocking electrodes (Au/Pt), guard electrodes, controlled RH, and frequency/time-domain separation to distinguish a fast elastic polarization component from slow Maxwell–Wagner/electrode polarization and triboelectric/contact artifacts, addressing concern (ii). Artifact controls (inert pellets, electrode reversal, Kelvin probe mapping, vacuum baseline) are explicitly built in.

Synthetic realism and fallback: Recognizing that direct solvothermal crystallization of permanently cationic azolate frameworks can yield dense phases, the primary route is shifted to post-synthetic quaternization of a known porous Zn–azolate precursor, which is a common strategy to introduce permanent cations while preserving topology. Explicit PXRD/porosity/counterion gates (G1–G3) and a secondary direct-ionic route provide a realistic contingency plan, addressing concern (iii).

Relevance to competitive adsorption under polar interferents: The proposal retains the original chain (stress → electrostatics → competitive adsorption), but now anchors NH3/H2O competition in a framework where the anion pocket controls local fields and specific binding. This is consistent with literature showing that acid/base or strong H-bonding motifs dominate NH3 uptake and that adsorption behavior depends strongly on functional group arrangement and humidity; here, the pocket aims to modulate electrostatics without relying on uncontrolled water-mediated ion motion.

Overall, the revised plan is mechanistically tighter (bistable pocket rather than mobile ions), quantitatively pre-committed (ΔV/ΔΔGads/ΔQ thresholds), experimentally de-artifacted (blocking/guard protocols), and synthetically de-risked (post-synthetic ionic installation with phase/porosity gates).
final_critique: The proposal is unusually strong in pre-committing to falsifiable multiscale predictions (strain→anion microstate bias→ΔV→ΔΔGads→selectivity) and in explicitly engineering out the principal artifact pathways (Maxwell–Wagner/electrode polarization, humidity-driven conduction, triboelectric/contact charging). The main scientific risk is quantitative: (i) whether 0.5–2% elastic strain in a pellet/monolith can reproducibly bias an A/B nitrate occupancy enough to generate a ΔV at adsorption hotspots large enough to deliver ΔΔGads differences on the order of 0.25–0.5 kJ/mol at practical loadings, and (ii) whether a pocket can simultaneously enforce high long-range diffusion barriers (>20–30 kJ/mol) while maintaining a low local A↔B barrier (5–15 kJ/mol) without inadvertently creating additional ion-hopping pathways under compression, defects, or humidity. A second weakness is representativeness: periodic DFT on a ‘fragment/unit cell’ plus fitted charges may not faithfully capture disorder, defect populations, and field screening in real pellets, potentially overpredicting ΔV and underpredicting conductive relaxation. Finally, the adsorption-mechanics decoupling remains challenging experimentally: even with void-volume corrections and rigid controls, microstructural changes (grain rearrangement, contact area, pore accessibility) under stress can mimic selectivity shifts unless monolith architecture and in situ porosity metrics under load are tightly constrained.

original_chain: Nanosheet -> Helical MOF nanotube -> Charge transfer transition -> Optical property -> Light emitting material -> CO2 reduction
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A helically scrolled MOF nanotube derived from a pre-registered, carboxylate-latticed 2D coordination nanosheet can sustain morphology-retentive conversion into a porous Zr6-cluster–stitched framework if (and only if) the precursor nanosheet is reticularly matched to the Zr6O4(OH)4 connectivity and the conversion proceeds via kinetically controlled, surface-confined cluster nucleation rather than bulk single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SC–SC) exchange. In this architecture, directional ligand-to-metal/ligand-to-ligand charge-transfer (LMCT/LLCT) is not enforced by chirality alone but by a chemically encoded inner/outer surface redox asymmetry: asymmetric axial capping creates a permanent electrostatic potential gradient across the tube wall, while Zr6 stitching rigidifies registry and suppresses excimer-forming interlayer contacts. The result is (i) enhanced, tunable solid-state emission with reduced trap-mediated quenching and (ii) spatially vectorial charge separation that biases photogenerated electrons and holes toward chemically distinct inner versus outer surfaces, enabling measurable selectivity in CO2 photoreduction when catalytic sites are deliberately confined to one interface.
Plan: Step 1 – Reticular precursor design with guaranteed Zr6 compatibility.
1.1 Ligand lattice pre-registration: Replace the generic salphen CP with a mixed-linker 2D coordination nanosheet built from (i) an atropisomeric, redox-active N2O2 chelating core (Ni(II) or Cu(II)) that defines in-plane conjugation and (ii) a co-planar, ditopic isophthalate-derived carboxylate linker whose O–O spacing (≈6.9–7.2 Å) and 120° geometry are matched to the equatorial edges of Zr6O4(OH)4 clusters. The carboxylates are positioned periodically (every ~1.5–2.0 nm) in the plane, forming a known (sql or kgm-type) 2D net that is crystallographically resolvable by GIWAXS/electron diffraction prior to scrolling.
1.2 Nanosheet formation: Grow 2–3 nm thick CP nanosheets by liquid–liquid interfacial coordination polymerization under modulator-free conditions to minimize defect density. Confirm in-plane order and lattice constants by GIWAXS and selected-area electron diffraction (SAED).

Step 2 – Deterministic helical scrolling with preserved lattice registry.
2.1 One-sided axial functionalization: Introduce 3–5% axial camphorsulfonate (or enantiopure menthoxyacetate) exclusively from the organic phase during interfacial growth to bind axial sites of Ni/Cu on only one face. This establishes a fixed dipolar and steric asymmetry without perturbing in-plane carboxylate registry.
2.2 Scrolling trigger: Apply a controlled solvent activity gradient (THF → MeCN/H2O, Δa_w quantified) to induce differential swelling. Helix pitch and diameter are tuned by sheet thickness and ionic strength, while in-plane diffraction is monitored to ensure lattice retention during scrolling.

Step 3 – Crystallographically defensible Zr6-cluster stitching (non-SC–SC).
3.1 Surface-confined Zr6 nucleation: Expose the helical CP scrolls to pre-formed Zr6O4(OH)4(modulator)x clusters (x = acetate/formate) in MeCN/H2O (≤10% H2O) at 50–70 °C. Use excess monocarboxylate modulator to slow ligand exchange, favoring stepwise substitution of modulators by pre-registered sheet carboxylates. This avoids uncontrolled Zr–O–Zr condensation.
3.2 Kinetic locking rather than bulk exchange: Zr6 clusters first bind within a single turn of the scroll, then progressively bridge adjacent turns only where lattice registry matches. Conversion is stopped at partial stitching densities (30–60%) to preserve porosity and avoid collapse.
3.3 Validation of registry: Compare in-plane GIWAXS/SAED before and after Zr6 incorporation; retention of peak positions (±2%) is required for pass. Loss of registry is a fail condition.

Step 4 – Proof of framework porosity vs. inter-scroll voids.
4.1 Gas sorption hierarchy: Measure N2 (77 K), Ar (87 K), CO2 (273/298 K), and Xe/Kr adsorption to extract pore-size distributions characteristic of Zr–carboxylate frameworks (≤2 nm). Contrast with collapsed-scroll controls.
4.2 Contrast-matched porosity tests: Perform positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS) or Xe NMR to distinguish intrinsic framework pores from mesoscopic voids between scroll turns.

Step 5 – Quantification of cross-wall redox asymmetry and CT directionality.
5.1 Surface potential mapping: Use Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) on sectioned nanotubes to map inner vs outer surface potentials; a ≥50–100 mV difference is targeted.
5.2 Depth-resolved composition: Apply angle-resolved XPS and ToF-SIMS to confirm asymmetric axial capping and Zr6 distribution across the wall.
5.3 Directional charge separation tests: Perform transient absorption spectroscopy with selective inner- or outer-surface quenchers (e.g., tethered viologen vs TEMPO). Faster quenching on one interface constitutes pass/fail evidence of vectorial CT.

Step 6 – CO2 photoreduction with enforced interface asymmetry.
6.1 Catalyst localization: Confine molecular Re(I) or Mn(I) bipyridine carbonyl catalysts to the inner surface only (1–2% sites) via pre-installed docking ligands. Outer surface remains catalyst-free.
6.2 Photocatalysis and causality: Measure CO/ HCOO− production under 13CO2. Correlate rates and selectivity with KPFM-measured potential gradients and CT lifetimes. Compare to symmetric (two-sided capped) and unscrolled controls to isolate the role of geometry-induced redox asymmetry.
Feasibility: This revision removes the chemically fragile SC–SC claim and replaces it with a kinetically and crystallographically defensible pathway rooted in reticular chemistry. By pre-designing a carboxylate lattice whose spacing and geometry are explicitly matched to Zr6 cluster connectivity, the proposal satisfies the reviewer’s demand for registry rather than assuming it. Surface-confined cluster nucleation using pre-formed Zr6 units and strong modulators is a known strategy in UiO-type post-synthetic modification and minimizes amorphization risks. Importantly, porosity is proven by multiple orthogonal techniques that discriminate framework pores from inter-scroll voids. The charge-transfer mechanism is no longer inferred from chirality alone: it is quantified via surface-potential mapping, depth-resolved spectroscopy, and directional quenching experiments that directly test inner/outer redox asymmetry. Finally, CO2 reduction selectivity is mechanistically tied to enforced interface chemistry (catalyst localization + potential gradient), not to helicity as an abstract concept. Together, these changes convert the highest-risk steps into testable, pass/fail milestones and tightly couple helical morphology, electronic structure, and catalytic outcome.
final_critique: The proposal is unusually strong in experimental resolution: it defines lattice-matching targets, specifies nucleation control via pre-formed Zr6 clusters and modulators, and sets clear structural validation criteria (GIWAXS/SAED retention ±2%). The biggest scientific risk is mechanistic over-determination: (i) the assumption that partial Zr6 “stitching densities” of 30–60% will both preserve helical morphology and generate an internally connected, intrinsically microporous Zr–carboxylate framework is not yet chemically justified—partial crosslinking may yield a mechanically locked composite with inter-turn voids rather than a true Zr6-node framework; (ii) cross-wall electrostatic potential gradients measured by KPFM on sectioned nanotubes can be dominated by contact potential/work-function artifacts, charging, or thickness variations, so the claimed ≥50–100 mV may not uniquely report “inner vs outer redox asymmetry”; (iii) catalyst localization to the inner surface at 1–2% while keeping the outer surface catalyst-free is nontrivial in a porous, defect-bearing, partially stitched wall—diffusion/redistribution and unintended binding to Zr6 carboxylate sites could erase interface specificity; and (iv) the link from chirality/scrolling to suppression of excimer-forming contacts and improved emission is plausible but under-specified—no quantitative structural handle (interchromophore distance/orientation distribution) is proposed to connect stitching to excitonic coupling and trap suppression. Overall, the logic is coherent and testable, but several causal claims (true framework porosity; unambiguous vectorial CT; enforced interface-only catalysis) remain insufficiently de-risked by controls that distinguish alternative explanations.

original_chain: Template -> Zeolite -> Crystal integrity -> Defect -> MOF composite -> Mercury ion -> In-situ method
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A true single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SC–SC) conversion can be made feasible inside a large-pore zeolite by replacing the speculative “volatile coordination-polymer + bulky S/N vapor linker + in-pore condensation” route with a literature-grounded, micropore-diffusible vapor-phase ligand-exchange pair and an explicit topotactic registry rule. Specifically, we hypothesize that (i) a zeolite single crystal (FAU-Y or *BEA) preloaded with a halide/amine-labile, low-molecular-volume metal–ligand precursor (Zn2+ or Co2+ with imidazole-derived ligands and charge-balancing halide/amine guests) will form an orientationally biased, pore-confined precursor lattice whose periodicity is commensurate with the zeolite supercage/channel repeat; (ii) exposure to a *small, zeolite-window-permeable* incoming linker vapor (imidazole derivatives ≤ ~6 Å kinetic diameter; e.g., imidazole, 2-methylimidazole, 2-mercaptoimidazole) will drive a topotactic anion/ligand exchange and node reconnection under solvent-free conditions, minimizing capillary/mechanical stress and therefore preserving the host single-crystal morphology; and (iii) “deterministic” missing-linker defects are programmed—not by generic mixed-linker lability—but by a falsifiable symmetry/stoichiometry rule imposed by periodic charge-compensation/anchoring sites in the zeolite (framework Al– sites with associated extra-framework cations and/or silanol nests) that enforce a commensurate mixed-linker superstructure and a predictable vacancy density at specific crystallographic sublattices. These defects create spatially repeating soft-donor pockets (–S/–N) where Hg2+ forms inner-sphere complexes (HSAB-driven), while the zeolite scaffold provides mechanical integrity and a parallel ion-transport network. The refined approach overcomes reviewer concerns by (a) using only linkers demonstrably small enough to traverse FAU (7.4 Å windows) or *BEA (6.6–7.7 Å) and avoiding in-pore multistep condensations, (b) defining an explicit epitaxial/topotactic relationship and diffraction-based pass/fail criteria for SC–SC vs re-nucleation, and (c) making defect periodicity an a priori structural model tied to zeolite Al/cation ordering that can be confirmed or rejected by SCXRD/EDT/PDF.
Plan: Step 0 — System down-selection with pore/size constraints and topotaxy targets
0.1 Zeolite host choice and Al-pattern control: Use FAU-type zeolite Y single crystals (supercage ~13 Å; 12-ring windows ~7.4 Å) as the primary host; use dealuminated FAU and *BEA single crystals as controls for anchoring-site density. Prepare two FAU-Y variants: (A) high-Al (low Si/Al) for high periodic charge-compensation density, (B) dealuminated (steam/acid) for reduced Al-site density. Exchange extra-framework cations to Na+ (baseline) and separately to Ag+ or Cu+ (stronger π/soft interactions) to modulate precursor anchoring.
0.2 Incoming linker size gate: Restrict to single heteroaromatic linkers that can diffuse through 12-ring windows and do not require in-pore condensation: imidazole (HIm), 2-methylimidazole (2-MeIm), and 2-mercaptoimidazole (2-MIm-SH). These provide N-donor connectivity (ZIF-type formation) and introduce S-donor sites directly without post-condensation chemistry.
0.3 Precursor/MOF pair selection (vapor-processable and exchangeable): Use a halide/amine-labile Zn2+ (or Co2+) precursor phase capable of ligand exchange to imidazolates under vapor/low-solvent conditions. Concretely, target a pore-confined “ZnX2·(Im)2” (X = Cl−/Br−) coordination network or cluster-like precursor assembled inside the zeolite from ZnX2 and imidazole/amine guests. The exchange step will replace labile X−/neutral donors with imidazolate/mercaptoimidazolate to form a ZIF-like node connectivity (Zn(Im)2 topology family) under mild heating.

Step 1 — Build an ordered, pore-confined, SCXRD-trackable precursor inside zeolite single crystals
1.1 Zeolite activation without defecting the host: Dehydrate zeolite single crystals under dynamic vacuum (10−5–10−6 mbar) with a staged temperature ramp (120 °C → 250 °C) to remove water while minimizing dealumination.
1.2 Vapor-assisted infiltration (demonstrably feasible reagents): In a sealed glass/metal ampoule, co-load activated zeolite single crystals with (i) ZnCl2 (or CoCl2) and (ii) imidazole (or a small amine such as NH3 or ethylenediamine in sub-stoichiometric amounts) as a transient, volatile base/ligand. Heat to 120–180 °C to promote vapor transport and uptake. Rationale: ZnCl2 and imidazole have sufficient vapor pressure/transport under heated sealed conditions and are widely used in solvent-free/ionothermal-like regimes (Asset 1 logic: non-aqueous templating/structure control).
1.3 Enforce orientational bias via charge-compensation sites: Use the FAU-Y(A) (higher Al) sample to promote periodic anchoring of Zn-containing species near Al–O− sites (via electrostatics and cation mediation). This creates a testable prediction: higher Al content increases the degree of guest lattice orientation and the intensity of satellite/commensurate reflections.
1.4 Verify “ordered precursor” *before* attempting conversion:
  - Single-crystal XRD: retain zeolite host reflections; search for additional, weaker guest-derived reflections and/or diffuse features consistent with a commensurate superstructure.
  - Synchrotron SCXRD mapping in reciprocal space: collect full reciprocal-space volumes to detect (hkl)host ± q satellites; quantify mosaicity broadening.
  - Complementary: Pair distribution function (PDF) to confirm local Zn–N/Cl coordination environments inside the host.
Pass/fail criterion: If only amorphous guest loading occurs (no commensurate order, only diffuse scattering), pivot to increased anchoring (Ag+-exchanged FAU) and/or lower loading to reduce disorder.

Step 2 — Vapor-phase ligand exchange to a ZIF-like framework with S/N functionality (no in-pore multistep chemistry)
2.1 Incoming linker delivery: Expose precursor-loaded zeolite single crystals to controlled vapor of 2-MeIm and/or 2-mercaptoimidazole (2-MIm-SH) in a second sealed ampoule under inert atmosphere. Temperature window: 120–160 °C (below zeolite stability limits; above diffusion threshold for the linker).
2.2 Exchange/conversion mechanism: Drive halide/neutral-donor displacement by imidazolate/mercaptoimidazolate formation (deprotonation assisted by residual basic guests/extra-framework cations). The conversion is designed as a single-step ligand exchange/reconnection rather than a condensation sequence.
2.3 Control of mixed-linker incorporation (defect programming handle): Use a *commensurate composition rule* tied to periodic charge-compensation:
  - Model: Each framework Al– site (negative charge) is associated with an extra-framework cation. During conversion, these sites preferentially stabilize mercaptoimidazolate (more polarizable, stronger interactions), biasing its placement at positions proximal to Al-rich supercages.
  - Therefore, by tuning Si/Al and cation type, we predefine a superlattice of “S-rich” linker positions. Where steric/electrostatic mismatch occurs, a predictable fraction of nodes must remain undercoordinated (missing-linker/vacancy) to satisfy local charge/geometry—yielding a non-random vacancy pattern.
2.4 Make “determinism” falsifiable a priori: Construct three structural models prior to experiments:
  - M0 (random defects): mercaptoimidazolate and imidazolate randomly distributed; vacancies statistically distributed.
  - M1 (Al-anchored superstructure): S-linkers enriched near Al/cation sites with periodicity equal to a known FAU supercage repeat; vacancies appear at symmetry-related sites.
  - M2 (phase-separated): S-linkers cluster into microdomains with no commensurate registry.
These will be compared directly against SCXRD/EDT/PDF signatures in Step 3.
2.5 “Lock-in” without cracking: Mild anneal under inert gas (N2/Ar) at 150–200 °C to remove residual HCl/volatile guests. Avoid solvent to prevent capillary stress.

Step 3 — Quantitative topotaxy plan (orientation matrices + diffraction criteria)
3.1 Define the expected epitaxial relationship: Use zeolite FAU cubic metrics and supercage periodicity to propose candidate registry between the pore-confined ZIF-like net and FAU axes. Practically:
  - Determine zeolite orientation (UB matrix) by SCXRD.
  - Predict that the dominant growth/registry direction of the confined ZIF-like net aligns along FAU ⟨111⟩ or ⟨100⟩ directions that traverse supercage connectivity (test both).
  - Build an orientation-matching tolerance: Δa/a ≤ 2–3% over a commensurate repeat length (n×aFAU ≈ m×aMOFsubcell).
3.2 SC–SC evidence (vs re-nucleation) — explicit pass/fail features:
  - Retention of single-crystal mosaicity: FWHM rocking curve increase ≤ factor 2.
  - Presence of oriented guest reflections with fixed orientation matrix relative to the host (same UB relationship across the entire crystal).
  - Absence of powder rings in wide-angle reciprocal space (indicative of randomly oriented microcrystallites).
  - Spatially resolved micro-SCXRD mapping (raster across the crystal) showing uniform orientation rather than domain-by-domain randomization.
3.3 Electron diffraction tomography (EDT) on FIB-lifted lamellae: confirm orientation consistency and identify nanoscale domain size; distinguish coherent topotaxy (single orientation) from polycrystalline conversion.

Step 4 — Defect periodicity and site-density quantification (not just “defects exist”)
4.1 Quantify linker ratios and vacancy concentration:
  - Digest-and-quantify (where feasible) by solution NMR of dissolved composite (after selective zeolite dissolution in HF-free routes where possible; or use rigorous ssNMR quantitation).
  - Quantitative ssNMR (13C, 15N) to measure Im/MeIm/2-MIm-SH ratios.
  - XPS (S 2p) to quantify S-content; compare to total Zn/Co by ICP-OES after digestion.
4.2 Spatial distribution / ordering tests (determinism test):
  - SCXRD: look for superlattice reflections consistent with M1; refine occupational modulation if present.
  - PDF: compare against M0/M1/M2 simulated PDFs; M1 should show distinct medium-range order features.
  - PALS: quantify vacancy-like free-volume elements; correlate with predicted vacancy density from the Al/cation site count.
4.3 Zeolite anchoring-site mapping: 27Al MAS NMR (framework vs extra-framework Al), and cation content by ICP-OES; correlate these to defect density to validate the “Al/cation-driven patterning” rule.

Step 5 — Pore-transport feasibility controls (diffusion + uptake + access under water)
5.1 Linker uptake kinetics and diffusion constraints:
  - Gravimetric uptake (TGA/DSC microbalance) of imidazole/2-MeIm/2-MIm-SH into activated FAU single crystals to extract effective diffusion coefficients (Deff) under the conversion temperature.
  - Compare uptake in FAU-Y(A) vs dealuminated FAU-Y(B) to quantify adsorption competition on Brønsted/Lewis sites.
5.2 Hg2+ access and diffusion under relevant ionic strength:
  - Measure Hg2+ uptake kinetics in 0.01–0.1 M NaNO3 background electrolyte across pH 3–7.
  - Fit with intraparticle diffusion + surface reaction model to decouple transport from binding.

Step 6 — Mercury binding mechanism with unambiguous site attribution (MOF defects vs zeolite)
6.1 Site-blocking experiments to separate contributions:
  - Block zeolite exchange sites with excess Na+ (or bulky quaternary ammonium) prior to Hg tests to suppress Hg binding to the aluminosilicate.
  - Independently passivate MOF soft sites by pre-coordination with a soft competitor (e.g., low-dose Ag+ or methylmercury surrogate at controlled levels) to test selectivity reversal.
6.2 Speciation modeling: Use equilibrium modeling (Visual MINTEQ/PHREEQC) to predict Hg(II) aqueous species vs pH/Cl−; design experiments to avoid precipitation and isolate adsorption.
6.3 Direct structural proof of Hg binding:
  - Hg LIII-edge EXAFS/XANES: quantify Hg–S vs Hg–N coordination numbers and bond distances; compare to 2-MIm-SH content and vacancy density.
  - XPS (Hg 4f, S 2p, N 1s): confirm thiolate/coordination shifts.
  - In situ Raman/IR (where possible) to track S–H disappearance and Hg–S formation.

Step 7 — Application-relevant testing and durability
7.1 Fixed-bed microcolumn: Use intact zeolite@MOF single crystals; measure Hg breakthrough curves; compare pressure drop and attrition vs MOF powders.
7.2 Regeneration: Use thiourea (acidified) or iodide eluent; quantify capacity retention over ≥10 cycles.
7.3 Post-mortem: SCXRD/PXRD + ssNMR + PALS to confirm retention of crystallinity and defect signature after cycling.

Deliverables and decision gates
D1: Ordered precursor verified by SCXRD reciprocal-space mapping (or pivot conditions).
D2: SC–SC conversion validated by oriented reflections and absence of powder rings.
D3: Defect periodicity model M1 confirmed/rejected by superlattice peaks + PDF/PALS correlation with Al/cation density.
D4: Hg binding assigned to S/N defect pockets by EXAFS + site-blocking controls.
Feasibility: Addresses (i) precursor volatility/order: The revised precursor strategy uses vapor/solvent-free infiltration of small, demonstrably transportable reagents (ZnCl2/CoCl2 and imidazole/amine) under sealed heating—aligned with ionothermal/vapor-enabled structure control principles (Asset 1). Rather than claiming an intrinsically “volatile coordination polymer,” the plan explicitly treats the precursor as a halide/amine-labile, pore-confined coordination phase whose *order is tested first* by reciprocal-space SCXRD mapping; failure triggers a defined pivot (cation exchange, Al-density tuning).

Addresses (ii) vapor linker practicality and pore diffusion: The incoming linkers are intentionally restricted to small imidazole derivatives (HIm, 2-MeIm, 2-mercaptoimidazole) that can traverse FAU/*BEA windows. The approach removes the chemically speculative in-pore aldehyde→thiosemicarbazone condensation and instead installs sulfur functionality directly via 2-mercaptoimidazole, eliminating stoichiometry/water-management issues. Competitive adsorption on zeolite sites is explicitly quantified via uptake kinetics and controlled by varying Si/Al and cation form.

Addresses (iii) “deterministic” defects: Determinism is no longer asserted as generic mixed-linker lability; it is tied to a symmetry/stoichiometry rule: periodic framework Al− sites and their extra-framework cations create a repeating anchoring field that biases S-linker placement and forces predictable undercoordination/vacancies at symmetry-related sites when commensurability/charge balance constraints are met. This yields an a priori, falsifiable model set (M0/M1/M2) with specific SCXRD/PDF/PALS signatures.

Addresses (iv) topotactic SC–SC mapping: The proposal now includes a quantitative topotaxy plan: determine the zeolite UB matrix, propose candidate registry directions along FAU cage-connectivity axes, set an explicit unit-cell/repeat matching tolerance, and define reciprocal-space pass/fail criteria distinguishing true SC–SC (single orientation, limited mosaicity increase, no powder rings) from microcrystalline re-nucleation. Spatial micro-SCXRD mapping and EDT on FIB lamellae further verify coherence.

Addresses (v) Hg2+ capture site localization and accessibility: The plan quantifies soft-site density (S content, linker ratios, vacancy density) and couples it to Hg binding stoichiometry from EXAFS. Site attribution is strengthened via orthogonal controls: zeolite-site blocking to suppress aluminosilicate uptake, MOF-site passivation to suppress soft-pocket binding, and aqueous speciation modeling to prevent confounding precipitation/complexation. This directly tests whether Hg2+ binds primarily to S/N pockets at defect-adjacent sites rather than to zeolite exchange sites.

Literature alignment: The refined strategy is consistent with (a) ionothermal/vapor-assisted structure direction and templating logic (Asset 1), (b) explicit treatment of defects and crystal integrity as performance determinants (Assets 2–3), and (c) mercury capture rationale via soft-donor coordination (Assets 4–5), while removing the least defensible chemical steps flagged by the reviewers.
final_critique: The proposal is unusually strong in execution detail and in setting falsifiable diffraction-based criteria for SC–SC versus re-nucleation (reciprocal-space mapping, rocking-curve thresholds, powder-ring exclusion, raster micro-SCXRD, EDT on FIB lamellae). The main scientific vulnerability is the assumed ability to create an *ordered, commensurate* Zn/Co precursor lattice inside FAU/*BEA via vapor uptake of ZnCl2 + imidazole/amine: ZnCl2 is highly Lewis acidic and tends to form disordered ionic/cluster species strongly bound to framework oxygens and extra-framework cations, which often yields diffuse scattering rather than a symmetry-locked guest sublattice. The second vulnerability is chemical: converting a halide/neutral-ligand Zn(II) phase to a ZIF-like imidazolate framework requires reliable in-pore deprotonation and removal of HX; in a zeolite, Brønsted/Lewis sites and confined HCl can instead poison imidazolate formation, promote framework chlorination/dealumination, or trap mixed Zn–Cl–Im species short of net formation. Third, the “deterministic defect” rule is conceptually interesting but currently under-specified crystallographically: FAU Al/cation ordering is often only partially ordered and sample-history-dependent; without a measured Al/cation superstructure (not just average Si/Al), the proposal risks correlating defect density with Al content while failing to prove *periodic* vacancy placement. Finally, the Hg-binding attribution plan is good (EXAFS + blocking) but needs harder discriminants because zeolite Al sites and extra-framework cations can bind Hg(II) strongly depending on Cl−/pH, potentially masking the soft-pocket signature unless ionic composition is tightly controlled and competitive binding quantified.

original_chain: SO2 -> Fluoro bridging group -> Y-DOBDC -> μ3-OH group -> Hydroxylated cluster -> Density-functional theory calculation -> Spin-polarized Kagome bands
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Stage-1 (Y‑DOBDC node programming): A crystallographically ordered, repeating μ2‑F/μ3‑OH “heterobridge” motif can be kinetically trapped during Y6 cluster nucleation only within a narrow boundary condition window defined by low water activity (aw), elevated but buffered fluoride chemical potential (μF−), and short high-temperature residence time—conditions that suppress anion scrambling by (i) limiting μ3‑OH insertion events to discrete nucleation/growth stages and (ii) stabilizing specific Y–F–Y bridges that contract Y–Y distances and raise the barrier to anion exchange. Under these boundary conditions, the node remains coordinatively saturated (no open Y sites) and gains hydrolytic/acid-gas stability via strong Y–F interactions (as supported by DFT/NMR trends in fluorinated RE clusters), while SO2 binds preferentially in a secondary pocket created by the fixed F···H–O proximity: μ3‑OH provides directional H‑bonding to an SO oxygen and adjacent μ2‑F contributes an inductive/electrostatic stabilization of the bound SO2 quadrupole without invoking open-metal-site chemisorption. This mechanism is falsifiable because (a) ordered anion motifs must produce superlattice/diffuse-scattering signatures and fixed 1H–19F distances, (b) defect/open-site assays must remain low and invariant across samples showing high SO2 uptake, and (c) SO2 spectroscopic signatures must track μ3‑OH involvement (H/D isotope effect) rather than coordinative unsaturation.

Stage-2 (2D Kagome module, gated claim): If Stage‑1 establishes a robust, quantifiable electrostatic/H‑bonding pocket driven by anion order, then a structurally explicit, literature-anchored 2D Kagome MOF platform with an anion-addressable bridge site can be used to test whether partial anion disorder washes out exchange splitting and whether SO2 acts primarily as an electrostatic gate (field/work-function shift with negligible charge transfer). Only after computational disorder averaging and on-surface anion-site identification will we test reversible SO2-induced modulation of spin-polarized Kagome features; we will not claim deterministic spin-texture gating a priori.
Plan: Two-stage program with explicit decision gates.

STAGE 1 — Map and enforce anion-ordering phase space in Y‑DOBDC, and prove SO2 pocket binding without open-site/defect explanations.

1. Define “anion-ordering phase space” with measurable chemical potentials.
  1.1 Independent control knobs:
    - Fluoride activity (proxy for μF−): (i) KF + 18-crown-6 (to solubilize and modulate free F−), (ii) tetrabutylammonium fluoride (TBAF) in rigorously dried polar aprotic media, (iii) Et3N·HF (buffered HF source) as a lower-activity comparator. Calibrate each source’s effective fluoride activity by 19F NMR of a fluoride-binding reporter (e.g., boron-based Lewis acid probe) in the same solvent mixture.
    - Water activity (aw): generate OH only via controlled in situ water release (ester hydrolysis/water-release chemistry) and/or metered H2O dosing. Quantify total water by Karl Fischer titration for every stock solvent, modulator solution, and final reaction mixture; report aw proxies as “ppm H2O” and “H2O equivalents per Y”.
    - Temperature/time window: run short dwell solvothermal crystallizations (e.g., 90–140 °C, 0.5–24 h) with quench points to separate nucleation vs growth.
  1.2 Phase-space matrix (minimum set to retire feasibility risk):
    - A 3×3×3 design: three fluoride activities (low/med/high), three water levels (ultra-dry/low/med), three dwell times (short/med/long) at fixed Y:DOBDC:modulator ratio.
    - Output metrics per condition: (i) bulk F/OH content (qNMR), (ii) local order (REDOR distances), (iii) long-range order (diffraction signatures), (iv) defect/open-site density (probe assays below).

2. Kinetic trapping strategy with explicit boundary conditions.
  2.1 “Two-pulse anion delivery” synthesis (de novo; not post-synthetic exchange):
    - Pulse A (F-first oligomerization): Y precursor + DOBDC + fluoride source in dry solvent (KF/18-crown-6 or TBAF) under ultra-low water (KF-verified) to favor Y–F–Y formation in early oligomers.
    - Pulse B (delayed OH insertion): after a defined time/temperature interval, trigger slow OH generation by introducing a protected water source (ester hydrolysis pair) at a known rate; the goal is to insert μ3‑OH only after F-bridges have formed and cluster geometry has contracted.
    - Quench-series: isolate solids at multiple timepoints after Pulse B to observe whether ordering increases (kinetic trapping) or erodes (scrambling toward statistical substitution).
  2.2 Seeded growth to bias order retention:
    - Grow seeds under F-biased, ultra-dry conditions (Pulse A only), then regrow under low-water Pulse B conditions. Decision metric: if regrowth increases μ3‑OH content without reducing REDOR-defined F–H proximities or diffraction order signatures, the ordering is being preserved rather than equilibrated.

3. Direct observation of anion ordering (mandatory crystallographic/electron-diffraction gate).
  3.1 Diffraction requirements:
    - Attempt single-crystal XRD; if crystals are too small, use 3D electron diffraction (MicroED) or continuous-rotation ED.
    - Required evidence: superlattice reflections consistent with anion-ordering periodicity OR quantitatively modeled diffuse scattering indicative of correlated F/OH ordering (not random occupancy).
  3.2 Spatial mapping (if needed):
    - 4D-STEM/nanobeam diffraction to map ordered domains; correlate domain size with synthetic boundary conditions (aw, μF−, time).

4. Quantify and bound defect/open-site populations so SO2 uptake cannot be attributed to coordinative unsaturation.
  4.1 Calibrated defect accounting:
    - TGA + modulator accounting: quantify missing-linker/charge-balancing species by combining TGA mass-loss steps with digestion NMR (linker/modulator quantification). Report “defects per node”.
    - Total scattering/PDF with defect-population modeling: fit PDFs using a mixture model (ordered node + defect node motifs) to extract defect fractions with confidence intervals.
  4.2 Open-site probe assays (quantitative, not qualitative):
    - CO and NO probe IR at controlled pressures/temperatures: quantify integrated band areas corresponding to metal–CO/metal–NO adducts; compare against a reference material with known open-site density to convert to “sites per Y6”.
    - Optional: positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS) to detect defect-associated free volume changes, cross-correlated with TGA/PDF.
  4.3 Decision gate (Stage‑1 continuation criterion): proceed only if samples showing strong SO2 uptake display (i) low and bounded open-site density and (ii) defect fractions that cannot explain uptake differences.

5. Validate the proposed SO2 pocket mechanism against competing pathways (open sites, bisulfite-like chemistry, pore quadrupole effects).
  5.1 Spectroscopy under rigorously dry vs controlled humidity:
    - In situ DRIFTS/IR with SO2 under dry conditions first (Karl Fischer-verified gas line drying), then introduce controlled H2O partial pressure. Look specifically for:
      (i) μ3‑OH red-shift and broadening (H-bond formation),
      (ii) SO2 νs/νas splitting patterns matching DFT-predicted pocket geometries,
      (iii) absence (dry) and emergence (humid) of bisulfite signatures only when water is present.
  5.2 Isotope falsification:
    - Synthesize μ3‑OD analogs by metered D2O introduction during Pulse B; require predictable OD vs OH shifts and measurable change in SO2 binding enthalpy consistent with H-bond participation.
  5.3 Thermodynamics/kinetics:
    - SO2 adsorption isotherms + microcalorimetry (differential heats vs loading). Mechanistic criterion: high initial heats consistent with a defined pocket that saturates, not a broad distribution expected from defects.
  5.4 Post-exposure integrity:
    - PXRD + N2(77 K) porosity + post-exposure 19F/1H NMR and Y K-edge EXAFS to verify node integrity and persistence of Y–F coordination after SO2 cycling (dry and humid).

6. Computation tightly coupled to boundary conditions and observables.
  6.1 Periodic DFT(+dispersion) for a small set of symmetry-distinct ordered motifs plus representative disordered/defective motifs.
  6.2 Compute:
    - Relative formation energies vs all‑OH and all‑F nodes under implicit μF−/μH2O constraints,
    - Anion exchange/scrambling barriers (nudged elastic band) to rationalize the kinetic window,
    - SO2 binding energies/geometries in the pocket vs at hypothetical open sites,
    - Predicted IR shifts (OH/OD, SO2 modes) and NMR parameters (19F chemical shifts) for direct comparison.

Stage‑1 Deliverable/Decision Gate to enter Stage‑2:
  - (A) At least one direct diffraction-based signature of anion ordering (superlattice or modeled diffuse scattering) AND
  - (B) REDOR-confirmed fixed F–H distances consistent with the motif AND
  - (C) quantified open-site density below a defined threshold (e.g., <0.05–0.10 sites per Y) with defect fractions unable to explain SO2 enthalpy trends AND
  - (D) SO2 IR + isotope effect consistent with μ3‑OH pocket binding.

STAGE 2 — Anchor the Kagome-band module to a concrete platform; computationally test disorder robustness; implement minimal on-surface anion ordering and an electrostatic-gating model.

7. Choose a literature-anchored 2D Kagome MOF platform with an anion-addressable bridge site.
  7.1 Platform requirement (explicit): a surface-supported 2D MOF where (i) Kagome topology is established experimentally (STM/LEED/ARPES precedents), and (ii) the magnetic superexchange pathway includes a bridgeable/replaceable anion or ligand that can exist as X = F/OH (or anion-bearing ligand) at a symmetry-defined site.
  7.2 Selection step (computational first): evaluate 1–2 candidate reported 2D Kagome/honeycomb–Kagome MOFs (Fe/Co nodes with N-donor ligands) for a chemically realistic anion-addressable bridge; commit to one platform only after confirming (below) that (a) the anion site is structurally well-defined and (b) STM contrast/XPS can distinguish F vs OH (or the chosen anion pair).

8. Disorder-robustness computation (mandatory per critique).
  8.1 Build ordered and partially disordered supercells (e.g., 2×2/3×3) with controlled F/OH mixing on the bridge site.
  8.2 Compute spin-polarized DFT(+SOC) band structures and Wannier models for each disorder fraction; quantify exchange splitting and Kagome-band features as a function of disorder.
  8.3 Decision gate: proceed only if predicted spin features persist above a specified disorder tolerance (e.g., retain ≥50% of exchange splitting at 20–30% anion disorder).

9. Minimal on-surface synthetic plan to enforce/identify anion order.
  9.1 Stepwise, self-limiting dosing:
    - Form the metal–ligand Kagome network under UHV/on-surface conditions.
    - Dose fluorine source (chosen to bind the bridge site without etching; self-limiting coordination) to populate the anion bridge; verify by XPS (F 1s) and STM contrast.
