Specifically: (i) MB remains cationic over pH 3–11; therefore maximum electrostatic driving force is expected when the composite surface is net negative (pH > pHPZC), augmented by π–π interactions with BDC linkers and possible interactions with defect-associated –OH/H2O at Zr6 nodes. (ii) RB exists predominantly as a cation/zwitterion in acidic-to-neutral conditions and undergoes deprotonation of its carboxyl group toward higher pH; thus RB adsorption is predicted to peak near the pH where (1) the MOF surface is not strongly negative enough to repel any anionic fraction and (2) coordination/H-bonding at defect/open Zr sites is maximized while aggregation/size-exclusion is minimized. (iii) Defect density and linker functionalization (–SO3H vs –NH2) shift pHPZC and the density/type of Lewis/Brønsted sites; therefore, by predefining target pHPZC windows and defect levels, the pH of maximum uptake for MB vs RB can be predicted before adsorption experiments.

The proposal explicitly decouples (A) defect density (missing-linker/open Zr sites), (B) intracrystalline mesoporosity, and (C) hot-pressing by a factorial design with matched MOF loading and geometry and by intracrystalline-mesopore validation controls that rule out interparticle void artifacts. Transport enhancement under mixed dyes will be tested by extracting kf (film mass transfer) and Deff (intraparticle diffusion) from flow breakthrough curves using an advection–dispersion + linear driving force (LDF) / pore-diffusion framework, thereby directly verifying whether hierarchical pores increase Deff rather than merely increasing accessible mass or altering external surface area.
Plan: A. Experimental design to orthogonalize variables (mandatory 2×2×2 matrix, matched loading and geometry)

A1. Define factors and levels (minimum 8 conditions; all grown on identical PUF coupons).
- Factor 1: Hot-pressing (P): unpressed (P0) vs pressed (P1).
- Factor 2: Mesoporosity (M): non-hierarchical microporous UiO-66 (M0) vs verified intracrystalline hierarchical UiO-66 (M1).
- Factor 3: Chemistry/defect state (C): low-defect UiO-66-H (C0) vs high-defect + functionality (C1) using either UiO-66-NH2 or UiO-66-SO3H (implemented as two parallel 2×2×2 matrices if resources allow; at minimum choose one functionality and vary defect level within it).

A2. Matching constraints (applied to all 8 conditions).
- MOF mass loading matched within ±5% (TGA-based), achieved by tuning growth cycles/precursor concentration; if necessary, do multiple short growth cycles to converge on target loading.
- Geometric dimensions matched (thickness and area) within ±3%; compression ratio recorded.
- Report adsorption normalized as q (mg/gMOF) and Qv (mg/cm3 monolith) for all tests.

B. Synthesis and decoupling strategy: separately control defects vs intracrystalline mesopores

B1. PUF scaffold standardization.
- Use open-cell PUF with cell size 100–500 µm; cut to standardized coupons (e.g., 2 cm × 2 cm × 3 mm).
- Clean: Soxhlet in ethanol (6 h) then water (2 h), dry at 60 °C.
- Surface activation: O2 plasma (e.g., 50 W, 5 min) to introduce –OH/–COOH; verify by XPS (increase in O/C ratio) and contact angle.

B2. Baseline conformal UiO-66 growth (common backbone).
- Zr precursor: ZrCl4 or ZrOCl2·8H2O; linker: BDC (or 2-aminoterephthalate / sulfo-BDC for functional series).
- Solvothermal in DMF with controlled water content; target thin conformal crystallite layer that does not occlude PUF macropores.
- Use identical growth time/temperature across factorial set, then adjust cycles to match loading.

B3. Defect engineering (C factor) decoupled from mesoporosity (M factor).
- Defect control lever: monotopic acid modulator (formic/acetic acid) at defined modulator:Zr ratios to create missing-linker defects/open Zr sites.
- Low-defect (C0): low modulator ratio (e.g., 10–30 equiv vs Zr), aim for near-stoichiometric UiO-66.
- High-defect/functional (C1): higher modulator ratio (e.g., 80–150 equiv vs Zr) to increase missing-linker density; for functionality choose UiO-66-NH2 or UiO-66-SO3H (fixed linker identity across the matrix) and hold modulator constant within that matrix so “defect level” is the controlled subfactor.
- Quantify defects: (i) digestion 1H NMR (linker:modulator incorporation), (ii) acid-base titration of node –OH/–OH2, and (iii) pyridine-IR for Lewis/Brønsted site density.

B4. Intracrystalline mesoporosity (M1) with evidence-based synthesis rather than surfactant-only claims.
- Preferred route to reduce co-variation: a controlled “linker labilization/etching” or “coordination modulation + selective etch” approach that generates mesopores within crystallites after crystallization, rather than relying solely on surfactant templating during nucleation.
  (i) First grow defect-defined UiO-66 (from B3).
  (ii) Post-synthetic mesopore creation: mild, time-limited etching (e.g., aqueous acetic acid or buffered salt solution) calibrated to introduce 5–20 nm intracrystalline mesopores while retaining PXRD crystallinity.
- Non-hierarchical control (M0): identical defect state but no etching step.

B5. Intracrystalline mesopore validation controls (mandatory).
- TEM/HRTEM on isolated crystallites removed from PUF (gentle sonication to detach a representative fraction).
- N2 sorption with hysteresis analysis (e.g., type IV with H1/H2 features) and NLDFT pore size distribution; report micropore volume (Vmicro) and mesopore volume (Vmeso).
- Artifact control: mechanically grind/densify detached MOF powder; re-run N2 sorption. If mesoporosity collapses disproportionately upon grinding, it suggests interparticle void contribution; intracrystalline mesopores should persist (within experimental variance).
- Complementary: SAXS (if available) to evidence mesostructural length scales independent of interparticle packing.

C. Hot-pressing as interphase engineering with explicit acceptance criteria and failure diagnostics

C1. Hot-press process window (P1).
- Temperature: bracket around PUF softening but below degradation (e.g., 120, 140, 160 °C).
- Pressure: 0.5, 2, 5 MPa; dwell 1–10 min; use a design-of-experiments sub-study on one representative sample to select a single “validated press condition” that meets acceptance criteria below.
- Architecture option: symmetric pressing (uniform thickness) for the factorial matrix; graded/asymmetric pressing reserved as an optional extension after mechanistic validation.

C2. Acceptance criteria (must be met for a pressed sample to be considered valid).
- PXRD: retain UiO-66 crystallinity (no new amorphous halo beyond baseline composite).
- Microporosity retention threshold: Vmicro(pressed) ≥ 80% of Vmicro(unpressed) for the same chemistry/mesoporosity level (measured on detached MOF fraction or crushed composite, same protocol).
- Macropore percolation: micro-CT or mercury porosimetry indicates connected macropore network retained (no catastrophic closure).

C3. Failure diagnostics (mandatory).
- Polymer occlusion/penetration: DSC to detect PUF thermal transitions shift; FTIR mapping or ToF-SIMS depth profiling to detect polyurethane signatures on MOF surface post-press.
- Leaching: ICP-OES of Zr in effluent during flow tests and after regeneration; define “minimal leaching” as below a pre-set threshold (e.g., <0.5% of total Zr per cycle).
- Shedding: gravimetric mass loss and turbidity/particle count in effluent.

D. Quantitative, a priori pH/charge/speciation predictions and verification

D1. Predict dye speciation/charge vs pH.
- MB: treat as cationic across pH 3–11 (dominant MB+).
- RB: compute distribution of cationic/zwitterionic/anionic forms using reported pKa values (carboxyl deprotonation and any relevant equilibria); generate predicted net charge vs pH and expected size/aggregation tendency window.

D2. Predict composite surface charge crossover.
- For each MOF chemistry/defect level, predict a pHPZC window based on functional group acidity (–SO3H lowers pHPZC; –NH2 raises pHPZC) and defect-associated –OH/–OH2.
- Pre-register predictions: expected pHPZC order and anticipated pH of maximum electrostatic attraction for MB and RB.

D3. Verify pHPZC/zeta potential experimentally.
- Measure zeta potential vs pH (3–11) for detached MOF-coated fragments or crushed composite in electrolyte (e.g., 1–10 mM KCl). Extract pHPZC (zeta = 0).
- Compare measured pHPZC to pre-registered predictions; update only after reporting deviation.

E. Adsorption and transport testing with parameter extraction (batch + flow)

E1. Batch isotherms and kinetics (controls for intrinsic affinity).
- Single-dye isotherms for MB and RB at multiple pH values selected around predicted optima and across pH 3–11.
- Fit Sips (heterogeneous Langmuir) and report qmax, affinity constants; normalize per gMOF and per cm3 monolith.
- Kinetics: fit pseudo-second-order plus intraparticle diffusion model, but treat these as empirical descriptors only.

E2. Flow-through breakthrough experiments (primary mechanistic test).
- Fixed-bed or membrane-flow cell with controlled superficial velocity; record C/C0 vs time and compute dynamic capacity.
- Model: advection–dispersion with film mass transfer (kf) and intraparticle uptake via LDF (kLDF) related to Deff and particle/crystallite length scale; include axial dispersion term.
- Fit breakthrough curves to extract kf and Deff (or kLDF) for each factorial condition.
- Falsifiable criterion for “hierarchical transport advantage”: at matched loading and chemistry, M1 must show statistically significant higher Deff (or kLDF) than M0; if only capacity increases without Deff increase, the diffusion-bottleneck claim is rejected.

E3. Mixed-dye competition (binary MB/RB; optional ternary with an anionic dye).
- Run mixed feeds at environmentally relevant ionic strength (NaCl 0–0.5 M).
- Quantify selectivity factors and competitive dynamic capacities; assess whether hierarchical samples preserve Deff under competition.

F. Reuse and robustness
- Regeneration: pH swing and/or ethanol/salt rinse; define regeneration protocol and measure capacity retention.
- Mechanical: compression cycling and abrasion; correlate shedding/leaching with press condition.
- Target benchmark: ≥10 cycles with <15% capacity loss, Zr leaching below threshold, and no significant loss of Vmicro beyond acceptance criterion.

G. Reporting and decision gates
- Gate 1: mesoporosity validity—only M1 samples with TEM-confirmed intracrystalline mesopores and grinding-invariant mesopore signatures proceed to transport claims.
- Gate 2: pressing validity—only P1 samples meeting Vmicro retention and polymer-occlusion diagnostics proceed to performance comparisons.
- Gate 3: mechanism—transport model parameters (Deff/kf) must support hierarchical diffusion enhancement independent of loading; otherwise revise hypothesis toward accessibility/loading effects.
Feasibility: 1) Addresses defect–mesoporosity conflation with orthogonal controls: The plan separates defect creation (modulator-controlled missing linkers/open Zr sites quantified by digestion NMR, titration, and pyridine-IR) from mesopore formation via a post-synthetic, time-limited etching step. Intracrystalline mesoporosity is not assumed; it is validated by TEM, sorption hysteresis/DFT, and a grinding control that discriminates interparticle voids from true intracrystalline mesopores.

2) Quantitative pH/charge predictions prevent post hoc interpretation: Dye speciation (MB fixed cationic; RB pH-dependent charge) is computed before experiments. Composite pHPZC is predicted based on functional groups/defects and then measured via zeta potential vs pH. Uptake maxima are pre-registered as functions of (pH − pHPZC) and RB net charge fraction; disagreement becomes a clear falsification pathway and points to alternative mechanisms (e.g., aggregation, coordination dominance, or size exclusion).

3) Hot-pressing risk is managed with explicit acceptance criteria and diagnostics: Pressing is treated as a controlled interphase modification with a defined process window and hard go/no-go metrics: PXRD retention, ≥80% micropore volume retention, macropore connectivity retention, and polymer-occlusion checks (DSC/FTIR mapping/ToF-SIMS). This directly addresses the reviewer concern that hot-pressing could collapse pores or occlude MOF surfaces.

4) Transport claims are directly testable via parameter extraction rather than qualitative kinetics: Breakthrough curves under controlled flow are fit to an advection–dispersion + film transfer + intraparticle diffusion/LDF model to extract kf and Deff. Because MOF loading and geometry are matched across the factorial matrix, increases in Deff can be attributed to hierarchical pore architecture rather than higher loading. This makes the diffusion-bottleneck hypothesis falsifiable.

5) Prior art supports the core concept while the revised design improves rigor: Literature demonstrates Zr-MOF–PUF composites can remove MB/RB with strong pH dependence and benefit mechanically from hot-pressing, and that hierarchical UiO-66 can dramatically improve adsorption rates/capacities for bulky organics by alleviating mass-transfer constraints. The revised proposal strengthens this foundation by enforcing factorial controls, mesopore validation, and mechanistic modeling needed for reviewer-level confidence and reproducibility.
final_critique: The proposal is unusually rigorous in decoupling defect density, mesoporosity, and hot-pressing, and in pre-registering pH/speciation expectations against measured pHPZC—this strongly supports falsifiability. The main technical risk is that the post-synthetic etch step will intrinsically co-vary with defect chemistry (missing-linker density, linker functional group hydrolysis stability, and node lability), making “M” not fully orthogonal to “C” unless etch severity is re-optimized per chemistry while holding mesopore metrics constant (which is nontrivial). The diffusion-model inference is directionally correct, but identifiability is not guaranteed: kf, axial dispersion, LDF rate constants, and an ill-defined characteristic length (crystallite vs agglomerate vs coating thickness on PUF struts) can trade off in fits, especially if the MOF is a thin conformal layer rather than discrete pellets. The plan also under-specifies how crystallite size distribution and coating thickness will be measured/controlled across conditions—both directly enter Deff extraction and could masquerade as a “hierarchical pore” effect. Finally, hot-pressing diagnostics focus on micropore retention and polymer occlusion, but do not explicitly quantify interfacial shear strength/adhesion or changes in macropore tortuosity that could dominate hydraulic performance and breakthrough behavior.

original_chain: Electrophoretic deposition -> Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy -> X-ray diffraction -> Porous carbons -> Electrocatalytic activity -> Metal-organic framework
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Orientationally programmed electrophoretic deposition (OP‑EPD) of high–aspect-ratio NU‑1000-type MOF platelets onto 3D carbon paper can be made quantitatively reliable by using a shear-dominant alignment regime (with optional magnetic assist only after susceptibility is measured) to achieve a target out-of-plane texture (Herman’s orientation factor f ≥ 0.6). This alignment will primarily create through-plane electronic percolation pathways ("c-axis highways") for Marcus-type redox hopping in oxidatively doped NU‑1000 films, lowering the through-plane film resistance (Rfilm,⊥) measured by EIS/4‑probe geometries. The proposal explicitly decouples electronic benefits from ionic transport: platelet alignment will be engineered to preserve (or improve) ionic access by enforcing inter-platelet mesoporosity via spacer/glue selection and wetting control; if ionic tortuosity increases, the mechanistic claim is constrained to electronic transport only. After conversion, ‘orientation retention’ is defined as (i) morphological texture retention (lamellae/platelet-stack alignment across thickness) and (ii) catalytic phase texture (any statistically significant preferred orientation of Ni2P nanocrystallites relative to the electrode normal). The conversion sequence (confined metal loading + shrinkage-managed carbonization + low-temperature phosphidation) is designed to preserve (i) even if (ii) is partial; the go/no-go criterion is that aligned-MOF electrodes yield measurably lower through-plane electronic resistivity and/or lower charge-transfer resistance (Rct) after conversion versus randomly oriented controls at identical loading and porosity. Mixed-linker ‘hopping enhancer’ chemistry is retained only if topology/habit and reversible oxidative doping are experimentally verified (PXRD + digestion NMR + GIWAXS texture + EIS-derived Dhopping); otherwise, the redox-hopping claim is restricted to a MOF-stage mechanistic validation rather than a required driver of final Ni2P@C kinetics.
Plan: Step 0 — De-risking overview (explicit go/no-go gates)
G0.1 Alignment gate: demonstrate f ≥ 0.6 (GIWAXS/SAXS azimuthal integration) at film thickness 2–10 μm on carbon paper without cracking/delamination.
G0.2 Transport gate: show that alignment decreases through-plane electronic resistivity (ρ⊥) by ≥10× vs random, while ionic permeability (electrolyte uptake and symmetric-cell ionic resistance) is not degraded by >2×; otherwise constrain claims to electronic transport only.
G0.3 Texture inheritance gate: after conversion, demonstrate preserved morphological texture (cross-sectional SEM/TEM + tomography) and a statistically significant anisotropy difference (aligned-derived vs random-derived) in either electronic transport (ρ⊥/ρ∥) or EIS-extracted Rct at identical catalyst mass and porosity.

Step 1 — MOF platelet synthesis, charge programming, and mixed-linker verification
1.1 Platelet NU‑1000 analogue synthesis (baseline, no mixed-linker): synthesize Zr6O4(OH)4-based NU‑1000-type platelets using pyrene tetracarboxylate (H4TBAPy) under modulated solvothermal conditions tuned for high aspect ratio (e.g., benzoic/acetic acid modulator; low water activity; targeted lateral size 1–5 μm, thickness 50–200 nm). Quantify habit by SEM/TEM and AFM (thickness distribution).
1.2 Surface charge/adhesion: post-synthetically install phosphonate anchoring at node-termini using phenylphosphonic acid (PPA) or 4-carboxyphenylphosphonic acid under conditions that cap terminal –OH/H2O without collapsing pores. Quantify incorporation via P 2p XPS, ICP (P:Zr), and FTIR (P–O stretches). Target zeta potential ≤ −30 mV in chosen EPD solvent.
1.3 Optional mixed-linker ‘hopping enhancer’ (only if topology/habit survives): introduce 5–15 mol% electron-donating pyrene-derived tetratopic analogue (e.g., alkoxy/alkyl substituted) during synthesis.
   • Go/no-go: (i) PXRD matches NU‑1000 topology within peak shifts/broadening limits; (ii) digestion 1H NMR gives linker ratio within ±2 mol% of feed; (iii) platelet habit retained (aspect ratio within 20% of baseline).

Step 2 — Quantified alignment physics and OP‑EPD cell design
2.1 Alignment strategy selection (shear-first, magnetic optional):
   A) Shear-dominant alignment (primary): use a Couette or parallel-plate shear cell integrated with EPD electrodes.
      • Geometry: electrode gap 2–5 mm; working electrode = carbon paper (Toray-type) mounted as stationary plate; counter electrode = Pt mesh; shear imposed by a rotating inner cylinder (Couette) or oscillating plate.
      • Shear rates: start 200–2000 s−1 (viscosity-adjusted with 1–5 wt% PVP or PMMA-free viscosity modifiers that do not adsorb strongly), guided by rotational Peclet number Pe_r = (γ̇/Dr). For platelets with Dr ~ 0.1–10 s−1 (to be measured by DLS/rotational diffusion estimates), target Pe_r ≥ 10 for deterministic alignment.
      • Quantitative check: measure viscosity η and compute hydrodynamic aligning torque scaling τhydro ~ η γ̇ V (V = platelet volume). Confirm alignment kinetics by time-resolved SAXS (if available) or ex situ GIWAXS after defined shear times (e.g., 10, 30, 60 s).
   B) Magnetic alignment (optional assist, not assumed): only pursued after measuring magnetic susceptibility anisotropy Δχ of Co-doped platelets (SQUID/VSM). Required condition for feasibility is that magnetic energy Umag = (Δχ V B^2)/(2μ0) exceeds thermal energy by factor ≥5 (Umag ≥ 5kBT). If unmet at B ≤ 1 T (practical lab magnets), magnetic alignment is dropped.
2.2 OP‑EPD parameters (pulsed field to reduce polarization/cracking):
   • Solvent: MeCN or EtOH/MeCN mixtures with controlled ionic strength; add 0.1–0.5 mM TBAPF6 (or analogous) to stabilize current without collapsing double layer.
   • Field: 20–150 V cm−1 square-wave; duty cycle 20–40%; frequency 10–200 Hz; deposition time 30–300 s to reach 2–10 μm.
   • Temperature control: 20–25 °C to keep η constant (affects alignment).
   • Target: uniform mass loading (e.g., 0.3–1.0 mg cm−2) quantified gravimetrically and by ICP (Zr).
2.3 Orientation lock-in without pore occlusion:
   • Replace speculative “nanoglue” with two screened options and a rejection criterion:
     (i) Vapor-phase diacid crosslinking (e.g., oxalic/succinic vapor) targeting node-node bridging at sub-monolayer coverage.
     (ii) <3 wt% silica from TEOS vapor infiltration followed by low-temp (≤120 °C) condensation.
   • Go/no-go: N2 sorption (powder analogues) shows ≤15% BET loss; electrolyte uptake (Step 3) not reduced >20%.

Step 3 — Orientation metrics (in situ/ex situ) with explicit targets
3.1 GIWAXS/GIWAXS-azimuthal analysis on films: collect 2D patterns and compute Herman’s orientation factor f from azimuthal intensity of (00l) (MOF) or equivalent reflections.
   • Target: f ≥ 0.6 for aligned; f ≤ 0.2 for random.
3.2 2D SAXS (or USAXS) for mesoscale lamellae alignment: quantify anisotropy of scattering to confirm platelet-stack alignment (morphological texture), not only crystallographic.
3.3 Cross-sectional electron diffraction mapping: prepare FIB cross-sections; collect nano-beam electron diffraction (NBED) / SAED along thickness to map local orientation distribution and identify misorientation gradients.

Step 4 — Transport mechanism decoupling (electronic vs ionic)
4.1 Through-plane electronic conductivity/resistivity:
   • Build a through-plane test stack: Au-coated flat punch contacts on top of MOF film on carbon paper; apply defined pressure; measure I–V and extract ρ⊥. Compare to in-plane interdigitated electrode measurements (ρ∥) on insulating substrates with transferred films.
4.2 Redox-hopping validation (MOF-stage mechanistic test, not assumed to drive final catalyst):
   • Perform oxidative doping in TBAPF6/MeCN; quantify mixed-valency via CV and in situ UV–vis–NIR (polaron band).
   • EIS under controlled potentials to extract apparent Dhopping and compare aligned vs random (expect Dhopping,⊥ >> Dhopping,∥ if c-axis oriented, consistent with NU‑1000 anisotropy literature).
   • Deliverable: correlation between f and Rfilm,⊥ (and/or Dhopping,⊥).
4.3 Ionic permeability/wetting and tortuosity:
   • Electrolyte uptake: gravimetric uptake and contact-angle measurements in target aqueous electrolyte (e.g., 1 M KOH).
   • Symmetric-cell ionic resistance: assemble two identical MOF-coated carbon papers facing each other with separator and electrolyte; EIS to estimate effective ionic resistance/tortuosity independent of faradaic kinetics.
   • Decision rule: if ionic resistance increases >2× with alignment at same thickness/loading, claims are narrowed to electronic benefits and mitigation is pursued (increase inter-platelet mesoporosity via sacrificial spacer in Step 2.3).

Step 5 — Controlled conversion to Ni2P@C with shrinkage/sintering suppression and defined ‘retention’ metrics
5.1 Confined metal loading to avoid sintering:
   • Prefer incipient wetness infiltration using Ni(NO3)2 (±Co(NO3)2) in minimal solvent, targeting 5–15 wt% Ni relative to MOF-derived carbon yield.
   • Optionally pre-anchor Ni2+ via phosphonate sites (chelation) to reduce migration.
   • Verify spatial distribution pre-pyrolysis by STEM-EDS on microtomed sections.
5.2 Shrinkage-managed carbonization:
   • Two-step pyrolysis under Ar: 300–350 °C (1–2 h, slow ramp 1 °C min−1) to carbonize organics while preserving morphology; then 650–750 °C (0.5–1 h) to improve conductivity but limit platelet collapse. Only pursue 800–900 °C if morphology retention is verified at 750 °C.
   • Add sacrificial spacer option (screened): co-infiltrate a removable salt (e.g., NaCl nanoparticles) or polymer microspheres to template mesopores; remove post-carbonization by water wash. Go/no-go by SEM/TEM showing preserved inter-platelet voids.
5.3 Low-temperature phosphidation:
   • NaH2PO2 upstream in tube furnace; 300–350 °C for 1–2 h under Ar/H2 to form Ni2P while minimizing sintering.
5.4 Define and measure orientation retention:
   (i) Morphological retention: quantify lamellae alignment from cross-sectional SEM/TEM + 3D FIB-SEM tomography (orientation distribution of platelet-like features; target: aligned-derived maintains ≥70% of pre-pyrolysis texture parameter).
   (ii) Crystallographic texture (if present): 2D GI-XRD of Ni2P; compute texture coefficient differences vs random-derived. Not required for success if (i) and transport anisotropy persist.

Step 6 — Electrocatalysis with causality controls
6.1 Electrocatalytic testing (choose primary reaction to match catalyst):
   • HER/OER in 1 M KOH (consistent with Ni2P literature). Report η10, Tafel slope, TOF proxies, ECSA-normalized activity, and 50–100 h stability.
6.2 Operando-relevant EIS:
   • EIS at catalytic potentials to extract Rct and mass-transport elements; correlate Rct with (a) post-conversion ρ⊥ and (b) morphological texture parameter.
6.3 Mandatory control matrix (aligned vs random at each stage):
   • MOF films: aligned OP‑EPD vs random EPD vs solvothermal film (if feasible).
   • Converted catalysts: aligned-derived Ni2P@C vs random-derived Ni2P@C at identical Ni loading and carbon mass.
   • Spacer/glue control: with vs without spacer/glue at fixed f.
   • Mixed-linker control: only if Step 1.3 passes, otherwise omitted.

Deliverables and timelines (high-level)
D1 (Months 1–3): Achieve reproducible alignment (f targets) and quantify torque feasibility (Pe_r and/or Umag criterion).
D2 (Months 3–6): Electronic/ionic decoupling dataset (ρ⊥, ρ∥, uptake, symmetric-cell EIS) establishing what alignment improves.
D3 (Months 6–12): Post-conversion texture retention proof (tomography + GI-XRD) and aligned vs random performance delta in HER/OER with operando EIS linkage.
Feasibility: 1) Alignment physics is de-risked by making shear the primary alignment mechanism with explicit, measurable control parameters (cell geometry, γ̇ range) and a quantitative criterion (Pe_r ≥ 10) rather than assuming magnetic alignment. Magnetic alignment is treated as optional and gated by a SQUID/VSM-derived Δχ and an Umag/kBT threshold at practical B fields.

2) The electron-vs-ion transport critique is addressed by explicitly separating claims and measurements: (i) through-plane electronic resistivity/conductivity (ρ⊥) using dedicated geometries and (ii) ionic permeability/tortuosity using electrolyte uptake + symmetric-cell EIS. The project only asserts reduced “ionic blocking” if ionic metrics improve or remain comparable; otherwise, the mechanistic statement is constrained to electronic percolation improvements, preventing conflation.

3) Texture inheritance is redefined from a vague “crystallographic registry” to two measurable constructs: morphological texture retention (platelet/lamellae alignment across thickness) and any Ni2P crystallographic texture (2D GI-XRD). Because high-temperature steps can erase crystallographic texture, the conversion protocol is intentionally shrinkage-managed (≤750 °C unless proven safe) and sintering-suppressed (confined loading + low-T phosphidation + optional sacrificial spacers). Success is judged by a statistically significant aligned-derived vs random-derived anisotropy in transport/EIS and/or performance, not by peak ratios alone.

4) Mixed-linker doping and redox-hopping are retained but no longer a weak causal leap: topology/habit preservation is required by PXRD + digestion NMR + morphology metrics, and redox-hopping measurements are framed as a MOF-stage mechanistic validation (consistent with NU‑1000 anisotropic Dhopping literature) rather than an assumed determinant of the final Ni2P@C catalyst unless a clear empirical correlation is observed.

5) Overall, each weak link has a go/no-go experiment and a fallback path (drop magnetic alignment; constrain ionic claims; accept morphological—rather than crystallographic—retention; drop mixed-linker doping) that preserves the proposal’s core chain (OP‑EPD → quantified texture → transport/EIS → controlled conversion → electrocatalysis) while aligning with known behavior of NU‑1000 films and MOF-derived phosphide@carbon electrodes.
final_critique: Methodologically, the proposal is unusually well-engineered: it specifies measurable alignment targets (Herman’s f), a physically grounded alignment regime (shear with Pe_r gating), and a control matrix that directly tests causality (aligned vs random at identical loading/porosity). The strongest feature is the explicit decoupling of electronic vs ionic transport using dedicated through-plane resistivity geometries and symmetric-cell ionic resistance—this addresses a frequent conflation in textured-electrode claims. Deductions are primarily due to (i) incomplete risk accounting for carbon-paper heterogeneity: local pore architecture and roughness can dominate apparent texture/ρ⊥ and complicate GIWAXS interpretation unless spatially resolved mapping/replicates are built in; (ii) potential ambiguity in the central transport mechanism: “c-axis highways” and Marcus hopping in oxidatively doped NU-1000 films is plausible but may be difficult to isolate from contact resistance, grain-boundary effects, and percolation via carbonized binder/glue after conversion; (iii) conversion-stage texture inheritance may be dominated by shrinkage, capillary collapse, and Ni2P nucleation kinetics, making the link between pre-conversion crystallographic texture and post-conversion Rct tenuous unless rigorous normalization (true porosity, Ni2P particle size distribution, carbon conductivity, wettability) is enforced; and (iv) some metrology is ambitious for the timeline (time-resolved SAXS under shear, 3D FIB-SEM tomography with statistically meaningful ODF extraction) and may become the rate-limiting deliverable.

original_chain: Etching process -> Hollow structure -> Estradiol -> Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy -> TbFe-MOF
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A TbFe-MOF can be transformed into a single-crystal-derived hollow architecture via a redox-neutral, spatially gated “transmetallation–demetallation Kirkendall hollowing” (TD-KH) process, in which the Fe-carboxylate sublattice is selectively de-coordinated in the interior by a slowly diffusing, high-affinity Fe-chelator while the Tb-carboxylate shell is simultaneously reinforced by post-synthetic Tb–O bond reformation. Mechanistically, the hollowing is driven by (i) unequal cation/ligand mobility across the crystal (Kirkendall vacancy coalescence into a void) and (ii) differential bond lability (Fe–O(carboxylate) being kinetically more labile than Tb–O under the chosen chelation/pH window). The resulting hollow Tb-enriched shell presents higher accessible Lewis-acid Tb(III) sites and shorter ion-transport pathways, decreasing baseline charge-transfer resistance (Rct) and increasing interfacial capacitance. Upon estradiol exposure, phenolic/OH coordination to Tb(III) and H-bonding/π interactions within the porous shell produce a pronounced, quantifiable increase in Rct (and change in constant-phase element, CPE), enabling an amplified EIS readout versus solid TbFe-MOF. The methodological adaptation is a chemistry-selective hollowing route that avoids oxidative linker cleavage entirely: a chelator-driven, diffusion-controlled, sublattice-selective demetallation coupled to shell re-metallation to lock crystallinity and create a robust hollow TbFe-MOF for impedance sensing.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Rational TbFe-MOF selection/design: Choose a mixed-metal carboxylate MOF topology that tolerates partial metal exchange without linker loss (e.g., a MIL-88/MIL-53-like Fe-carboxylate motif coexisting with Tb-carboxylate connectivity, or a MOF-on-MOF heterostructure where a Tb-rich outer region is grown over an Fe-rich core). Target micron-scale single crystals to enable diffusion gradients and Kirkendall void formation.
1.2 Establish a Tb-enriched shell / Fe-enriched core without etching: Use a two-stage growth (core–shell MOF-on-MOF). Stage A: crystallize an Fe-rich MOF core using terephthalate (BDC) or substituted BDC to ensure robust carboxylate connectivity. Stage B: epitaxially overgrow a TbFe mixed layer under Tb-favoring conditions (higher Tb:Fe feed, slightly lower modulator concentration) to bias Tb occupancy near the exterior.
1.3 Pre-calibrate bond lability window: In batch suspensions, screen chelators and conditions that preferentially complex Fe(III/II) over Tb(III) while preserving carboxylate linkers and crystallinity. Candidates: deferoxamine (DFO) or 1,10-phenanthroline derivatives for Fe, or EDTA/NTA under carefully buffered conditions (pH where Fe-chelation is strong but Tb-carboxylate remains intact). Select conditions with negligible linker leaching by HPLC/TOC.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 TD-KH hollowing (chelator diffusion gating): Disperse Tb-shell/Fe-core crystals in buffered aqueous/alcoholic medium containing the selected Fe-chelator at low concentration. Control the Damköhler number (reaction vs diffusion) by tuning chelator concentration, temperature, and crystal size so chelation occurs predominantly after inward diffusion, thereby initiating Fe removal in the interior and generating vacancy flux.
2.2 Kirkendall void formation control: Maintain a small outward flux of Fe-chelate complexes while Tb and carboxylate nodes remain comparatively immobile, causing vacancy supersaturation and coalescence into a central void. Stop the process at defined timepoints to map solid→yolk-shell→hollow transitions.
2.3 Shell locking via post-synthetic Tb reinforcement: After desired void fraction is reached, quench by chelator removal (dialysis/centrifugation) and perform a mild Tb(III) salt treatment (e.g., Tb(NO3)3 in ethanol/water with a weak base modulator) to re-coordinate any undercoordinated carboxylates and heal defects, increasing mechanical/electrochemical stability without adding insulating polymers.
2.4 Electrode integration tailored for EIS: Grow or deposit the hollow TbFe-MOF as a thin, percolating film on conductive substrates (glassy carbon or Au) using electrophoretic deposition or in situ solvothermal film growth to minimize grain-boundary resistance. Introduce a selective estradiol capture interface without thick binders: graft a sparse aromatic anchoring monolayer (e.g., 4-aminobenzoate or pyrene-carboxylate) to promote π-enrichment while leaving Tb sites accessible.
2.5 Impedance sensing protocol: Run EIS in a standard redox probe (ferri/ferrocyanide) and in probe-free electrolyte to separate faradaic (Rct) and capacitive contributions. Quantify estradiol-induced ΔRct and ΔCPE parameters across concentrations; optionally couple with differential pulse voltammetry to confirm estradiol interfacial accumulation.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structural and compositional proof of TD-KH: PXRD for crystallinity retention; SEM/TEM for hollow interior and shell thickness; FIB-SEM or electron tomography for 3D void verification; STEM-EDS line scans/mapping to confirm Fe depletion in the core and Tb enrichment in the shell.
3.2 Chemical speciation controls (to prove chelator selectivity, not linker loss): ICP-MS of supernatants vs time for Fe and Tb; LC/UV-Vis for chelated Fe complexes; HPLC/TOC to quantify linker leaching (must be minimal). Compare to controls lacking chelator and to single-metal Tb-MOF under identical conditions.
3.3 Defect/healing assessment: FTIR/Raman for carboxylate coordination modes; XPS for Tb/Fe surface ratios; BET/N2 sorption for accessible porosity changes; nanoindentation/AFM (if films) to verify shell mechanical robustness after reinforcement.
3.4 Electrochemical mechanism mapping: Fit EIS to a Randles or transmission-line model appropriate for porous films to extract Rct, CPE(Q,n), and Warburg elements. Correlate baseline Rct with shell thickness/void fraction and correlate estradiol response with Tb surface density (XPS/ICP) and accessible porosity.
3.5 Analytical performance and selectivity: Determine LOD, linear range, and repeatability in buffer and spiked matrices (wastewater/serum). Test interferents (estrone, estriol, bisphenol A, phenol) to validate Tb-centered phenolic coordination selectivity. Include regeneration studies (mild chelator-free rinse or pH swing) to demonstrate reversible binding and sensor reuse.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Selective demetallation and post-synthetic metal exchange are well-established in MOF chemistry, including stability differences between rare-earth carboxylate coordination and transition-metal carboxylates. Kirkendall-type hollowing is a known solid-state diffusion phenomenon; here it is implemented through controlled sublattice metal removal rather than oxidative linker destruction, enabling void formation while retaining the organic backbone.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): TbFe-MOF inherently contains two metals with distinct coordination kinetics/thermodynamics. The TD-KH method exploits this bimetallic coordination asymmetry: Fe is selectively mobilized by chelation to create vacancy flux, while Tb stabilizes the residual carboxylate network and can be used to heal/lock the shell post-hollowing. This leverages coordination chemistry (metal–ligand lability, chelation thermodynamics, post-synthetic re-metalation) as the primary design axis.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to oxidative/radical etching, TD-KH is redox-neutral and avoids uncontrolled linker scission, improving reproducibility and preserving functional binding motifs. Compared to simple templating, the void is generated intrinsically by diffusion/coordination kinetics, yielding tunable shell thickness and composition gradients (Tb-rich exterior) that directly enhance estradiol preconcentration and maximize EIS sensitivity through larger, more specific ΔRct signatures at constant mass loading.
final_critique: This is an unusually detailed and conceptually sophisticated proposal that demonstrates strong command of bimetallic MOF chemistry, diffusion-controlled transformations, and impedance-based sensing. The TD-KH mechanism is logically constructed and internally consistent, with appropriate attention to bond lability, chelation thermodynamics, and Kirkendall vacancy physics. Validation strategies are rigorous and well-matched to the claims. Minor score deductions arise from (i) practical uncertainty around maintaining single-crystal integrity during extensive Fe removal in micron-scale crystals, particularly for MIL-88/MIL-53-like frameworks known to be flexible, and (ii) the assumption that Tb–carboxylate re-metalation will uniformly 'heal' defects without inducing amorphization or phase segregation, which is plausible but not yet strongly evidenced. Additionally, the estradiol–Tb coordination mechanism, while reasonable, would benefit from more quantitative binding justification relative to competing phenolics.

original_chain: Heterojunction -> Mass ratio -> Hydrothermal method -> Catalysis -> Fresh water productivity -> MOF topological modification
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A topologically reprogrammed, single-phase MOF-derived intraframework heterojunction—created by hydrothermal cation-exchange to generate spatially segregated bimetallic nodes (n-type Ti-rich oxo nodes juxtaposed with p-type Cu-rich redox nodes) inside a robust Zr-fumarate framework—will maximize pervaporation fresh water productivity at an optimal Cu:Ti:MOF mass ratio because (i) node-to-node band-offset within the same continuous pore network forms a built-in field that biases proton/water-wire transport (Grotthuss-type hopping) while electrostatically penalizing hydrated ion entry, and (ii) topology-preserving linker “rewiring” (mixed-linker fumurate/sulfonated-fumarate) creates a percolating hydrophilic sublattice that maintains crystallinity yet increases water uptake and connectivity without introducing nonselective voids. The productivity maximum occurs when Cu/Ti node domains percolate (maximizing internal junction density) but remain below the threshold where excessive redox/oxo clustering collapses micropore continuity or increases salt leakage.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Choose a hydrolytically robust parent MOF topology: start from UiO-66-family Zr-fumarate (fumarate as short linker to maximize pore wall polarity and stability). Target: fcu net with high water stability.
1.2 Define the topological modification goal as “mixed-linker rewiring” rather than defect creation: synthesize Zr6O4(OH)4 nodes with a controlled fraction (0, 10, 20, 30 mol%) of sulfonated fumarate (fumarate-SO3H) co-linker to create a hydrophilic, ion-repelling sublattice while preserving fcu connectivity.
1.3 Define intraframework heterojunction components as node-localized redox/oxo centers: Cu(II) (electron-accepting/redox-active, can create hole-rich sites under hydration) and Ti(IV) (oxo/hydroxyl-rich, electron-donating n-type character when partially hydrolyzed). The junction is internal (node-domain juxtaposition), not MOF@oxide.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Topology-preserving mixed-linker MOF synthesis (baseline):
- Solvothermal formation of Zr-fumarate / fumarate-SO3H mixed-linker MOFs using ZrCl4, fumaric acid, and sodium sulfofumarate (or sulfonated fumarate precursor) with acetic acid as crystallization modulator. Optimize to obtain phase-pure fcu crystals (PXRD) with controlled linker ratios (digest NMR).
2.2 Methodological adaptation (structurally novel): hydrothermal, spatially programmed cation-exchange to create intraframework bimetallic-node domains and internal heterojunctions.
- First exchange: Hydrothermal Ti installation. Suspend activated mixed-linker MOF in aqueous Ti precursor that favors node-binding (e.g., Ti(IV) lactate or Ti(IV) citrate complex, mildly acidic pH 3–4) in a Teflon-lined autoclave at 80–120 °C. Aim: partial substitution/coordination at node –OH/H2O sites forming Ti–O–Zr bridging/hydroxo grafts without nucleating TiO2.
- Second exchange: Hydrothermal Cu installation with spatial bias. Re-suspend Ti-modified MOF in aqueous Cu(II) acetate with chloride-free conditions; use a short hydrothermal pulse (60–100 °C) and exploit sulfonate-rich regions (from fumarate-SO3H) to preferentially coordinate Cu(II) near those linkers (electrostatic/chelation bias), generating Cu-rich nano-domains juxtaposed to Ti-rich domains within one crystal.
- Mass ratio programming: prepare a composition library by varying (a) Ti loading (0–15 wt% as Ti), (b) Cu loading (0–15 wt% as Cu), and (c) sulfonated-linker fraction (0–30 mol%). Determine actual mass ratios by ICP-OES (Zr/Ti/Cu) plus digest 1H NMR for linker ratio.
2.3 Membrane construction emphasizing junction utilization (not filler blending artifacts):
- Grow an oriented, sub-micron MOF thin film directly on a porous polymer support (e.g., PAN or PES) via seeded secondary growth to avoid polymer-filler interfacial voids.
- Post-synthetic hydrothermal exchanges (Ti then Cu) are performed on the already-grown MOF film to ensure junctions reside inside the selective layer.
- Optionally apply a nanometric PVA “gutter” layer only on the feed side to enhance mechanical integrity while keeping the MOF film as the primary selective pathway.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Confirm topology retention and mixed-linker rewiring:
- PXRD + Rietveld/Le Bail to confirm fcu net retention after exchanges.
- Digest 1H NMR to quantify fumarate vs fumarate-SO3H incorporation.
- Pair distribution function (PDF) or EXAFS (Zr K-edge, Ti K-edge, Cu K-edge) to verify Ti–O–(Zr) grafting and Cu coordination environments without oxide nanoparticle formation.
3.2 Prove intraframework heterojunction formation (spatially segregated node domains):
- STEM-EDS/EELS mapping across single crystals/film cross-sections to visualize Ti- and Cu-enriched nanodomains.
- Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) on films under controlled humidity to detect internal potential gradients consistent with built-in fields.
- Water-vapor sorption + in situ IR/Raman to quantify hydrogen-bond network strengthening and sulfonate hydration.
3.3 Mechanistic linkage to selective water transport and salt exclusion:
- Measure water self-diffusion in films by PFG-NMR (or QENS) vs composition; correlate with KPFM-derived potential gradients.
- Measure salt uptake (NaCl, MgCl2) by ion chromatography after equilibration; expect minimized uptake at optimized Cu/Ti and sulfonate fraction.
- Streaming potential/zeta potential of films in saline to quantify Donnan exclusion enhancement from sulfonate sublattice plus junction field.
3.4 Desalination performance and productivity maximum:
- Pervaporation of synthetic seawater (3.5 wt% NaCl) and high-salinity brine (10–20 wt% NaCl) at controlled temperature; record flux, salt rejection, and compute fresh water productivity.
- Identify the optimum in productivity vs Cu:Ti:MOF mass ratio and sulfonated-linker fraction.
- Controls: (i) parent Zr-fumarate film, (ii) mixed-linker only (no metals), (iii) Ti-only, (iv) Cu-only, (v) same total metal loading but reversed exchange order to test spatial programming, (vi) films deliberately forced to form TiO2/CuO nanoparticles (alkaline hydrothermal) to show that nanoparticle formation degrades selectivity relative to intraframework junctions.
3.5 Stability testing:
- 200 h continuous pervaporation with periodic saline cycling; track PXRD, ICP leaching (Ti/Cu), and performance retention.
- Chloride tolerance and anti-fouling tests (humic acid, SDS) to evaluate robustness of junction chemistry under realistic feeds.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: (a) Mixed-linker strategies are established to tune MOF pore polarity and charge while preserving topology, enabling rational transport control. (b) Hydrothermal/post-synthetic metalation and cation exchange at node –OH sites is a known route to install new functionalities in robust Zr-MOFs without collapse, and internal charge separation (built-in fields) is a validated mechanism in heterojunction-enabled transport/catalysis. (c) Mass-ratio optima are empirically common in heterojunction systems because interfacial density and percolation compete with blockage/aggregation; here the analogous parameter is internal junction density vs pore continuity.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal is MOF-native: it uses topological modification via mixed-linker “rewiring” of the coordination network and node-specific post-synthetic hydrothermal exchange to create an intraframework heterojunction. The junction is not an external oxide coating or physical mixture; it is encoded at the coordination-polymer node/linker level, aligning with coordination chemistry design principles.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to conventional MOF/oxide heterocomposites or defect-rich fillers, the single-phase intraframework heterojunction (i) eliminates nonselective interfacial voids (selective layer is a continuous MOF film), (ii) maximizes junction density per unit transport path because junctions reside inside pores, (iii) provides a tunable electrostatic/field-driven selectivity lever (Cu/Ti distribution + sulfonate sublattice), and (iv) offers a clean mass-ratio optimization axis (Cu:Ti loadings) directly tied to a mechanistic proxy (KPFM potential gradients, PFG-NMR diffusion), enabling a defensible productivity maximum rather than empirical trial-and-error.
final_critique: This is a highly sophisticated and largely well-constructed proposal that demonstrates deep familiarity with Zr-MOF chemistry, mixed-linker topology control, and post-synthetic node modification. The strongest aspects are (i) the insistence on single-phase intraframework heterojunctions rather than composites, (ii) explicit mass-ratio programming tied to a mechanistic proxy (junction density vs pore continuity), and (iii) an unusually rigorous validation suite (EXAFS/PDF, KPFM, PFG-NMR). Score deductions arise from two areas. First, the electronic-structure argument (n-type Ti vs p-type Cu nodes, band offsets, built-in fields) is conceptually appealing but only semi-quantitative; no explicit discussion of Fermi-level alignment, defect states, or hydration-induced redox equilibria is provided, leaving ambiguity as to whether the field strength is sufficient to measurably bias proton/water-wire transport over nanometer scales. Second, the hydrothermal cation-exchange selectivity and spatial segregation (Cu-rich vs Ti-rich domains) relies heavily on sulfonate bias and kinetic control, but lacks a clear thermodynamic or kinetic model to demonstrate that domain formation, rather than statistical node decoration, will dominate across a film. These gaps do not invalidate feasibility but slightly weaken logical closure.

original_chain: CH4 -> Mg(OH)2 -> Catalytic activity -> Step-by-step crystal growth -> Cavity size
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that brucite Mg(OH)2 nanoplates can be converted, via a dissolution–reprecipitation process that preserves external platelet morphology (quasi-topotactic “shape/registry retention”), into a *hollow, single-crystal-dominant Mg2(dobdc) (Mg-MOF-74) rod-SBU framework* whose 1D channels and engineered internal cavity cooperatively increase (i) CH4 uptake/confinement near open Mg2+ sites and (ii) density of Mg–O–Mg linkages (μ2-O/μ2-OH bridged motifs within the Mg-oxo rod) that are implicated in electrocatalytic CH4→formate in Mg-MOF-74 (Asset 1). Mechanistically, the proposal addresses reviewer concerns by (a) targeting an *established* Mg–O rod SBU (MOF-74 family) formed specifically by dobdc-type ligation (2,5-dihydroxyterephthalate), rather than a generic ‘Mg-oxo-MOF’; (b) explicitly treating the conversion as interface-controlled dissolution–reprecipitation with strain management, not ideal topotaxy; (c) quantifying hollowing through coupled transport–reaction kinetics (Mg2+ flux out, linker flux in, acid-controlled Mg(OH)2 dissolution rate, and MOF precipitation rate), yielding a calibrated mapping from dosing/acidity/temperature to shell thickness and void diameter; and (d) using operando and isotopic controls to prove Mg–oxo rod nodes are generated and are the locus of CH4 activation rather than Mg(OH)2/MgO degradation products.

Catalytic pathway: We retain electrochemical CH4 oxidation to formate (Asset 1) but redesign around a chemically credible electrode architecture where the MOF supplies adsorption/activation sites and the conductive scaffold supplies electron transport; we will explicitly suppress OER, perform 13CH4 labeling, and close Faradaic carbon and charge balances to validate true CH4-to-formate conversion.
Plan: Step 0 — Define the structural target and success criteria (pre-registered):
0.1 Target framework: Mg2(dobdc) (Mg-MOF-74; dobdc4− = 2,5-dioxido-1,4-benzenedicarboxylate; from 2,5-dihydroxyterephthalic acid, H4dobdc). Target SBU/topology: infinite Mg–O rod (…Mg–O–Mg…) with open Mg2+ sites after activation; known 1D channels (~11 Å) and proven CH4→formate electrocatalysis (Asset 1).
0.2 Structural go/no-go metrics: (i) PXRD match to Mg-MOF-74 (phase purity ≥90% by Rietveld), (ii) Mg K-edge EXAFS consistent with MOF-74 rod coordination (no dominant Mg(OH)2 signature), (iii) N2 sorption (BET and micropore volume within literature range for Mg-MOF-74; reduced but retained porosity acceptable for hollow shells), (iv) hollow morphology (TEM/tomography) with shell thickness/void diameter quantified with ≤10% dispersion.

Step 1 — Mg(OH)2 nanoplate precursor engineered for controlled interfacial conversion:
1.1 Synthesis: hydrothermal precipitation to obtain hexagonal brucite Mg(OH)2 nanoplates (target lateral size 200–800 nm; thickness 20–80 nm) with dominant (001) basal facets.
1.2 Characterization: PXRD (texture/orientation), AFM for thickness distribution, HRTEM/SAED to establish single-crystal platelet registry, and zeta potential vs pH to guide interfacial growth conditions.
1.3 Strain-management design: apply a thin, labile Mg-carboxylate “primer layer” by brief exposure to dilute H4dobdc (or benzoate) at pH where Mg(OH)2 partially dissolves (see Step 2). This seeds heterogeneous nucleation of MOF-74 on the platelet surface to reduce random homogeneous nucleation (polycrystallinity risk).

Step 2 — Quasi-topotactic, morphology-retaining conversion to Mg-MOF-74 hollow shells (dissolution–reprecipitation with kinetic control):
2.1 Chemistry window (operationalized): Use a buffered solvothermal mixture (DMF/EtOH/H2O) with controlled acidity (acetic acid or formic acid; target pH* in the 4.8–6.2 range in mixed solvent, calibrated by acid equivalents and confirmed by titration in matched solvent). Rationale: low enough to dissolve Mg(OH)2 at a measurable rate, but high enough to avoid bulk etching/collapse and to favor surface-confined MOF precipitation.
2.2 Stepwise dosing protocol (explicit parameters to be mapped):
- Temperature program: 60 °C nucleation hold (0.5–2 h) → 90–110 °C growth (2–12 h).
- Linker dosing: pulse addition of H4dobdc (e.g., 4–10 pulses over growth period) to maintain supersaturation near the interface while minimizing homogeneous nucleation.
- Mg2+ activity control: optional addition of Mg(NO3)2 (low mM) as “background Mg” to smooth Mg2+ gradients and reduce cracking (tested systematically).
2.3 Hollowing mechanism and kinetic model (quantitative):
Model the process as a moving-boundary (Stefan-type) problem where Mg(OH)2 dissolution at the inner interface supplies Mg2+ that diffuses outward through the growing MOF shell while H4dobdc diffuses inward; MOF precipitation occurs where ionic product exceeds Ksp-like threshold for Mg2(dobdc).
Measured/fit parameters:
- k_diss(pH,T): Mg(OH)2 dissolution rate constant (from ICP of Mg in supernatant vs time under identical conditions).
- D_linker,eff and D_Mg,eff through shell: effective diffusivities (from time-resolved uptake experiments using labeled linker analog or conductivity/ICP gradients; complemented by SAXS/TEM timepoints).
- k_precip(T, [linker], [Mg2+]): interfacial precipitation rate (fit to shell-thickness growth curves).
Deliverable: a calibrated relationship: shell thickness (δ) and void radius (R_void) as functions of acid equivalents, linker pulse concentration, and time/temperature; report as contour maps and predictive regression/physics-informed model.
2.4 In situ / time-resolved tracking (mandatory proof of control):
- Time-resolved SAXS to follow hollowing (core-to-shell electron density change) and shell thickening.
- In situ synchrotron PXRD during conversion to track disappearance of Mg(OH)2 reflections and emergence/growth of Mg-MOF-74 peaks; extract crystallite size/strain.
- Optional liquid-cell TEM for qualitative validation of hollowing trajectory (with beam-dose controls).
2.5 Spatial composition/registry mapping across timepoints (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% conversion):
- STEM-EDS/EELS line scans across platelets to confirm Mg/O/C distribution and core depletion.
- Electron diffraction/4D-STEM orientation mapping to test “single-crystal-dominant” retention vs polycrystalline shell formation.

Step 3 — Definitive validation of Mg–O rod SBU / Mg–oxo–Mg motifs and exclusion of degradation artifacts:
3.1 Local structure spectroscopy:
- Mg K-edge XANES/EXAFS on timepoints and final material; fit coordination numbers/bond distances against references: Mg(OH)2, MgO, and authentic Mg-MOF-74.
- Total scattering Pair Distribution Function (PDF) to capture short-range Mg–O–Mg correlations characteristic of rod SBU even if long-range order is imperfect.
3.2 Porosity and open-metal-site confirmation:
- Activation: solvent exchange (MeOH) then vacuum anneal (e.g., 150–200 °C, optimized to avoid collapse).
- Gas sorption: N2 (77 K) and CH4 isotherms; derive isosteric heat (Qst) to quantify strengthened CH4 binding with open Mg sites.
- In situ DRIFTS with CH4 (and CD4 control) to probe adsorption signatures; correlate with open-site density.
3.3 Post-synthesis controls:
- Prepare non-hollow Mg-MOF-74 (conventional solvothermal) and “collapsed shell” control (over-etched) to decouple chemistry vs architecture.

Step 4 — Electrochemical CH4→formate catalysis redesigned for credibility and mass-balance closure:
4.1 Electrode integration (conductivity explicitly addressed):
- Grow/immobilize hollow Mg-MOF-74 shells onto a conductive scaffold (carbon cloth, CNT paper, or graphene aerogel). Use one of:
  (i) electrophoretic deposition of MOF onto carbon cloth with minimal insulating binder, or
  (ii) in situ growth/anchoring using a polydopamine or carboxylated-carbon interlayer to improve adhesion.
- Add conductive additive only as needed (e.g., 5–15 wt% carbon black) and keep constant across samples.
4.2 Electrolyte/potential window and OER suppression:
- Use near-neutral bicarbonate electrolyte (e.g., 0.5–1.0 M KHCO3) to buffer pH and stabilize carboxylate frameworks; quantify Mg leaching vs pH.
- Perform potential screening (e.g., 1.2–1.8 V vs RHE) while monitoring OER current; implement rotating disk/flow-cell to manage gas transport.
- Compare CH4-saturated vs Ar/N2 control; include O2-free conditions.
4.3 Product quantification and isotopic proof:
- Use 13CH4 feed and quantify 13C-formate by quantitative 1H/13C NMR (with internal standard) and/or ion chromatography; confirm isotopologue by LC–MS if needed.
- Report full Faradaic efficiency with carbon mass balance: formate, CO/CO2 (GC), and any liquid oxygenates.
- Kinetic isotope effect: compare CH4 vs CD4 to test C–H cleavage involvement at rate-determining step.
4.4 Operando/after-action identification of active site and stability:
- Operando XAS (Mg K-edge) if feasible or quasi-operando freeze-quench XAS to verify Mg remains in MOF-74-like coordination under bias.
- Post-mortem PXRD, PDF, and N2 sorption to quantify crystallinity/porosity retention.
- ICP-MS of electrolyte to quantify Mg leaching; correlate any activity spikes with degradation signatures.
- Compare to benchmarks: Mg(OH)2 electrode, MgO, conventional (non-hollow) Mg-MOF-74, and hollow shell with blocked pores (polymer infiltration) to directly test the cavity/confinement hypothesis.

Milestones / decision points:
M1 (Months 1–4): Achieve phase-pure Mg-MOF-74 formation on platelets; establish time-resolved PXRD/SAXS hollowing curves.
M2 (Months 4–8): Quantitative cavity-control map (acid/linker/temperature → δ and R_void) + EXAFS/PDF proof of rod SBU.
M3 (Months 8–12): Electrochemical CH4 oxidation with 13CH4-formate detection and closed mass balance; stability verified (≤5–10% Mg leaching over test window; retained PXRD pattern).
If M3 fails (e.g., no 13C-formate beyond background), pivot within-scope to thermal/photocatalytic CH4 activation using the same hollow Mg-MOF-74 architecture and identical isotopic/KIE validation, while preserving the central structure–confinement–site-density hypothesis.
Feasibility: 1) Structural target is chemically grounded (addresses critique i): Mg2(dobdc) (Mg-MOF-74) is explicitly selected because dobdc-type ligation is known to generate the Mg–O rod SBU with open Mg2+ sites after activation; this is the same Mg-based framework implicated in electrocatalytic CH4→formate activity (Asset 1). The proposal no longer claims an unspecified ‘Mg-oxo-MOF’; it targets a defined topology/SBU and uses EXAFS/PDF/PXRD to verify Mg–O–Mg rod formation.

2) Conversion realism and crystallinity risk management (addresses critique ii): We do not assume perfect topotaxy from brucite to MOF. Instead, we engineer a quasi-topotactic, morphology-retaining dissolution–reprecipitation pathway by (a) seeding heterogeneous nucleation on Mg(OH)2 surfaces (primer layer), (b) controlling Mg2+ gradients and minimizing homogeneous nucleation via pulsed linker dosing, and (c) explicitly measuring strain/crystallite orientation evolution via in situ synchrotron PXRD and 4D-STEM orientation mapping. Intermediate timepoint mapping (STEM-EDS, SAED, XAS) provides decisive evidence for whether single-crystal-dominant shells are achieved or whether polycrystallinity occurs, with clear go/no-go criteria.

3) ‘Precise cavity control’ is operationalized quantitatively (addresses critique iii): Hollowing is treated as a coupled transport–reaction problem with measurable parameters (Mg(OH)2 dissolution rate vs acidity/temperature, effective diffusivities through the shell, precipitation kinetics). In situ SAXS/PXRD and time-resolved TEM provide direct, calibrated shell/void growth trajectories, yielding a predictive map from dosing/acidity/temperature to geometry (δ, R_void), rather than a qualitative assertion.

4) Catalysis plan is chemically and analytically defensible (addresses critique iv): Because Mg nodes are not intrinsically redox-active conductors, the electrode is redesigned so the MOF supplies adsorption/activation sites while a conductive scaffold supplies electron transport; electrolyte and potential windows are specified, OER competition is explicitly monitored, and products are quantified with 13CH4 labeling plus Faradaic and carbon mass balance closure. Operando/quasi-operando structural probes and rigorous post-mortem analyses (PXRD/PDF/sorption, Mg leaching by ICP) ensure that any observed activity is assigned to intact Mg-MOF-74 hollow shells rather than degradation to Mg(OH)2/MgO.

5) Alignment with literature assets and core concept chain: Asset 1 supports that Mg-MOF-74 contains the relevant Mg–oxo rod motifs correlated with CH4→formate electrocatalysis and that Mg(OH)2 is comparatively inactive, directly motivating the conversion strategy. Asset 2 supports that stepwise growth plus selective etching/inhomogeneous robustness can produce hollow MOFs with enhanced catalytic performance; here, we implement the analogous concept but add the missing quantitative kinetics and definitive structural proof demanded by the reviewers.
final_critique: The structural target (Mg-MOF-74) and verification package (Rietveld + Mg K-edge EXAFS/PDF + sorption + tomography) are strong and unusually rigorous. The main scientific risk is the central claim of “single-crystal-dominant hollow shell” formation from brucite: dissolution–reprecipitation will, in most cases, generate polycrystalline MOF-74 domains because MOF nucleation is linker-controlled and crystallographic registry between brucite (layered hydroxide) and MOF-74 (rod SBU) is not naturally commensurate. The proposal acknowledges non-ideal topotaxy, but still stakes mechanistic and performance arguments on registry/strain management without defining quantitative acceptance criteria for ‘single-crystal-dominant’ beyond qualitative orientation mapping. Second, the hollowing kinetic model is plausible but under-specified in the one place it must be predictive: the precipitation thermodynamics/kinetics of Mg2(dobdc) in DMF/EtOH/H2O with modulator acids. A Ksp-like threshold is asserted, but Mg-MOF-74 formation is not a simple salt precipitation; it depends on linker deprotonation/coordination equilibria, solvent composition, and modulator competition, so fitted parameters may not transfer across conditions, weakening the promised contour-map “design rules.” Third, the electrocatalysis plan is improved (mass balance, 13CH4), but the mechanistic premise that Mg–O–Mg motifs at Mg2+ sites mediate multi-electron CH4-to-formate under anodic bias remains high-risk: (i) Mg2+ is not redox-flexible, (ii) OER competition in the stated 1.2–1.8 V vs RHE window is severe, and (iii) any observed formate can still arise from carbon corrosion, electrolyte impurities, or linker oxidation unless additional controls (blank carbon cloth under identical bias; quantified organic leaching/oxidation) are explicitly pre-registered. Finally, stability criteria (≤5–10% Mg leaching) may be incompatible with sustained anodic operation in bicarbonate at elevated potentials for a carboxylate MOF; framework dissolution/defect formation could dominate and confound ‘active site’ attribution despite post-mortem PXRD retention.

original_chain: FT-IR spectroscopy -> Regeneration -> Coprecipitation method -> Phosphate -> Phosphorus
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A coprecipitation-derived, spatially segregated Fe3O4@Zr-MOF core–shell sorbent will enable high-capacity phosphate capture and low-chemical regeneration by enforcing a reversible inner-sphere binding mechanism: phosphate will bind predominantly to Zr6-oxo node defect sites as Zr–O–P bridges during uptake, while a redox-triggered, local pH/ligand microenvironment generated at the Fe3O4 core under mild stimuli (low-voltage electro-Fenton/H2O2 or weak chelator wash) will selectively weaken Zr–O–P linkages without collapsing the framework, enabling phosphorus recovery as concentrated phosphate and sustaining performance over many cycles. Mechanistically, (i) high-affinity Zr(IV)–phosphate coordination at engineered missing-linker sites provides selectivity and capacity, (ii) the coprecipitated magnetite core provides rapid separability and a controllable interfacial chemical potential that accelerates desorption, and (iii) the core–shell architecture prevents Fe leaching and preserves MOF crystallinity by isolating redox chemistry from Zr–carboxylate bonds. FT-IR spectroscopy will be used operando/ex situ to track formation and removal of P–O–Zr/Fe bands and to quantify regeneration completeness via band deconvolution.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a water-stable Zr-MOF platform with accessible Zr6 nodes and known phosphate affinity (UiO-66 family or MOF-808). Prepare a mixed-linker formulation to introduce controlled defect density: use terephthalate (BDC) plus a monocarboxylate modulator (formate/acetate) to create missing-linker sites while retaining topology.
1.2 Define phosphate speciation conditions relevant to remediation/regeneration (pH 6–8 for adsorption; regeneration screens at pH 9–11 carbonate or 10–50 mM citrate/EDTA alternatives). Prepare competitive anion matrices (SO4^2−, HCO3−, Cl−, NO3−, SiO3^2−) and natural organic matter (humic acid) challenge solutions.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Methodological adaptation—coprecipitation to enforce core–shell segregation and interfacial anchoring:
  a) Coprecipitate Fe3O4 nanoparticles (10–30 nm) from Fe(II)/Fe(III) salts (1:2) under N2 at 70–80 °C by base addition, but perform coprecipitation in the presence of a thin polydopamine (PDA) priming layer (dopamine self-polymerization at pH ~8.5) to supply catechol/amine anchors.
  b) Grow a Zr-MOF shell directly on Fe3O4@PDA via solvothermal synthesis: ZrCl4 (or ZrOCl2·8H2O) + BDC (and defect-inducing modulator) in DMF/H2O with controlled water content to favor nucleation on PDA rather than in bulk. Target 20–80 nm shell thickness by varying precursor concentration and time.
  c) Post-synthetic node activation to maximize phosphate-accessible sites while maintaining robustness: solvent exchange (EtOH/H2O), then mild thermal activation (120–150 °C) to open Zr–OH/H2O sites; optionally introduce a small fraction of phosphonate-free, basic pendant groups (e.g., amino-BDC) to promote electrostatic preconcentration without competing with Zr sites.
2.2 Phosphate capture testing:
  a) Measure kinetics and isotherms at pH 6–8; quantify capacity and selectivity under competing ions.
  b) Use magnetic separation to demonstrate process intensification (fast solid–liquid separation without filtration).
2.3 Regeneration adaptation—stimulus-assisted desorption while preserving the Zr framework:
  a) Baseline regeneration: carbonate wash (Na2CO3/NaHCO3, pH 10–11) vs. mild chelator wash (citrate 10–50 mM, pH 7–9) to identify lowest chemical demand.
  b) Redox-assisted regeneration (core-enabled): apply low H2O2 dose (0.5–5 mM) with brief low-voltage electrostimulation (or aeration) to activate Fe3O4 surface cycling; the goal is to generate transient interfacial OH−/reactive species that disrupt Zr–O–P bridging locally, accelerating desorption at lower bulk pH/chemical concentration.
  c) Capture recovered phosphorus: precipitate eluate as struvite (MgNH4PO4·6H2O) or Ca-phosphate by controlled addition of Mg2+/NH4+ or Ca2+; evaluate purity and mass balance.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structural integrity and phase analysis across cycles: PXRD (MOF crystallinity), TEM/EDX mapping (core–shell retention; P distribution), BET/porosity, and ICP-OES (Zr/Fe leaching).
3.2 Mechanistic verification using FT-IR spectroscopy as the primary chain-end tool:
  a) Identify adsorption signatures: growth of ν(P–O) bands (1000–1100 cm−1) and emergence/shift consistent with inner-sphere Zr–O–P; monitor changes in Zr–OH/μ3-OH region and carboxylate symmetric/asymmetric stretches to detect unwanted linker displacement.
  b) Regeneration tracking: quantify reduction of phosphate bands after regeneration; apply peak deconvolution to separate free/outer-sphere phosphate vs. bridged phosphate; correlate with desorbed phosphate concentration.
  c) Complementary: XPS (P 2p chemical state; Zr 3d shifts), zeta potential vs pH to link electrostatics, and optional in situ ATR-FTIR during adsorption/desorption to capture reversible binding kinetics.
3.3 Performance metrics: capacity retention over ≥20 cycles, regeneration efficiency (% desorbed), chemical consumption per gram P recovered, and selectivity coefficients in complex matrices; compare to non-magnetic Zr-MOF and to Fe3O4–ZIF-8 analogs to isolate the effect of Zr-node binding + core-enabled regeneration.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Zr(IV)-oxo clusters form strong inner-sphere complexes with phosphate (Zr–O–P), underpinning high selectivity (supported by Zr-MOF phosphate binding literature). Magnetic MOF composites show high recyclability and fast separation, and prior work demonstrates coprecipitation as a robust route to embed Fe3O4 for regeneration-ready adsorbents. FT-IR is well-established for diagnosing phosphate binding modes through ν(P–O) evolution and metal–oxygen–phosphorus bridging signatures.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal leverages MOF node chemistry (defect-engineered Zr6 clusters) as the primary binding motif while using a coprecipitated magnetic core purely as a physical handle and controllable interfacial stimulus source. The core–shell design is a supramolecular/architectural adaptation that preserves coordination-polymer integrity by spatially separating redox-active iron from Zr–carboxylate nodes.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with Fe3O4–ZIF-8 phosphate sorbents, Zr-node binding offers higher thermodynamic selectivity for phosphate and improved hydrolytic stability; compared with plain Zr-MOF powders, the magnetic core enables rapid separation and, critically, a lower-chemical-demand regeneration via interfacial stimulus-assisted desorption. Operando/ex situ FT-IR provides a direct, cycle-by-cycle mechanistic readout of P-binding and removal, enabling rational optimization of defect density and regeneration conditions rather than empirical trial-and-error.
final_critique: This is a technically sophisticated and well-articulated proposal with strong command of Zr-MOF chemistry, phosphate coordination mechanisms, and composite material design. Engineering resolution is high: synthesis, defect control, shell thickness tuning, regeneration chemistries, and analytical validation are all specified at an actionable level. Logical consistency is strong but not flawless—the central assumption that mild Fe3O4-mediated redox or electro-Fenton conditions can selectively weaken Zr–O–P bonds without perturbing Zr–carboxylate coordination is plausible but under-justified thermodynamically and kinetically. Evidence grounding is solid and stays within the chemistry/MOF domain, though the reliance on FT-IR deconvolution as a primary quantitative regeneration metric risks overinterpretation without stronger corroboration from P mass balances and operando controls. The rationale is compelling and non-trivial, addressing the genuine bottleneck of chemical-intensive regeneration in Zr-based phosphate sorbents via an architectural rather than compositional innovation.

original_chain: Heavy metal removal -> Adsorption capacity -> Carbon dioxide -> Humidity -> Selectivity -> Adsorptive Separation
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A humidity–CO2-gated, spatially segregated dual-domain MOF composite can improve *competitive selectivity* for soft heavy metals (Pb(II), Cd(II), Cu(II)) **without relying on net bulk acidification**, by operating in a narrowly defined speciation window where (i) amine sites reversibly bind CO2/H2O as ammonium bicarbonate to modulate surface charge and ion-pairing, and (ii) thiol/oxo capture sites retain sufficient deprotonation to enable inner-sphere complexation. The key mechanistic refinement is that CO2 does not universally enhance adsorption: instead, selectivity gains are predicted only when bicarbonate formation increases local ionic strength and electrostatic screening at the amine-rich shell—thereby suppressing outer-sphere uptake of hard background cations—*while carbonate complexation of Pb/Cd/Cu remains subdominant* and thiol pKa shifts do not fully quench soft-donor binding. By explicitly modeling and measuring carbonate speciation, thiol protonation, and transport across a defined amine-shell thickness, the system is designed to function as a true two-stage adsorptive architecture rather than a mixed bed. Regeneration is hypothesized to be feasible because binding at thiol sites is dominated by reversible inner-sphere coordination (ΔGads moderated by protonation state and competition), not irreversible precipitation or oxidation-driven trapping, and because CO2 removal collapses ammonium bicarbonate, reducing electrostatic stabilization of metal–surface complexes under low-ionic-strength wash.
Plan: 1. **Pre-registered speciation and surface-complexation modeling (boundary conditions first):**
1.1 Develop a PHREEQC-based aqueous speciation model including Pb(II)/Cd(II)/Cu(II) carbonate complexes, background Na+/Ca2+/Mg2+ (10–50 mM), and humic acid complexation.
1.2 Couple this to a surface complexation model with explicit equilibria for (a) amine ↔ ammonium ↔ ammonium bicarbonate, (b) thiol ↔ thiolate (including pKa shifts under electrostatic fields), and (c) metal–thiolate and metal–Zr–oxo complexes. Parameterize with literature constants and refine using titration data (see 3.2).
1.3 Use the model to map a design space (pH 5–7.5, pCO2 0–0.2 atm, ionic strength 1–50 mM) identifying regions where CO2 is predicted to enhance vs diminish Pb/Ca and Cd/Mg selectivity. This map pre-defines all experimental operating points.

2. **MOF synthesis with quantified site densities:**
2.1 Amine-gated shell: UiO-66 mixed-linker MOF (terephthalate/2,5-diaminoterephthalate) synthesized to a target amine density of 2–3 mmol –NH2 g−1 MOF, verified by acid–base titration and elemental analysis.
2.2 Thiol capture domain: UiO-66 post-synthetically thiolated via diazotization–thiolation, targeting 1–1.5 mmol –SH g−1 MOF. Thiol accessibility quantified by Ellman’s reagent and XPS S 2p fitting.

3. **Architectural assembly and validation (core–shell, not mixed):**
3.1 Sequential dip-coating/ultrasonication deposition on melamine sponge or ceramic monolith: inner thiol-MOF first, followed by outer amine-MOF shell.
3.2 Define shell thickness (5–50 µm) by controlling coating cycles; verify spatial segregation via FIB-SEM/EDS cross-sections, ToF-SIMS depth profiling, and micro-CT for connectivity.
3.3 Quantify transport: measure effective diffusivity of Pb(II) and Ca2+ through the amine shell using time-lag experiments; calculate Damköhler numbers to demonstrate staged capture rather than equilibrium mixing.

4. **Operando verification of CO2 gating under aqueous flow:**
4.1 Use 13CO2-labeled humid gas to condition the sorbent; perform operando ATR-FTIR in flow to track bicarbonate/carbonate bands on amine sites during water exposure.
4.2 Quantify bicarbonate loading (mmol g−1) and amine protonation via combined FTIR integration and ex situ 13C ssNMR.
4.3 Measure zeta potential and local pH (fluorescent probes) as a function of gating state; compare against model predictions.

5. **Adsorption, selectivity, and controls:**
5.1 Conduct single and competitive isotherms (Pb/Cd/Cu vs Ca/Mg/Na) under CO2-gated, N2-gated (matched ionic strength), and carbonate-free conditions.
5.2 Include hard controls: amine-only MOF, thiol-only MOF, physically mixed amine+thiol MOFs, and spatially segregated composites.
5.3 Report capacities normalized strictly to *active MOF mass* (excluding support), with independent mass balance by digestion/ICP-OES.

6. **Regeneration and reversibility tests:**
6.1 Measure isosteric heats of adsorption (temperature-dependent isotherms) for Pb(II) under gated vs ungated states.
6.2 Perform competitive elution with CO2-off switching (dry N2) and ≤0.05 M benign electrolyte; track desorption kinetics and mass balances.
6.3 Monitor thiol oxidation and reversibility over ≥20 cycles using S K-edge XANES and XPS; correlate any oxidation with capacity loss.

7. **Fixed-bed demonstration:**
7.1 Run continuous-flow columns using operating points validated by modeling; generate breakthrough curves and fit with Thomas/Yoon–Nelson models incorporating effective diffusivity.
7.2 Compare performance against ZIF-coated sponges and single-function MOFs under identical matrices.
Feasibility: This revised plan directly addresses reviewer concerns by constraining claims to a quantitatively defined speciation regime rather than assuming universal CO2 benefit. Carbonate competition is explicitly incorporated and tested via carbonate-free and matched-ionic-strength controls, ensuring that observed selectivity changes arise from gating chemistry rather than pH or salinity artifacts. The core–shell architecture is no longer inferred but validated through cross-sectional imaging and transport analysis, with shell thickness and diffusivity linked to Damköhler numbers to prove staged capture. Thiol chemistry risks are mitigated by (i) direct measurement of thiol pKa and oxidation state, (ii) thermodynamic validation of reversible binding via isosteric heats, and (iii) regeneration protocols grounded in competitive desorption rather than assumed lability. Capacity targets are reframed as conditional outcomes tied to measured site densities and accessibility, with strict normalization to active MOF mass to avoid inflation.
