(ii) The proposed ‘near-thermoneutral’ ΔG(H2 heterolysis) criterion is conceptually sound but operationally ambiguous in porous solids: local dielectric, H-bonding, and counterion/defect environments will shift effective pKa and redox energetics relative to solution; without a plan to directly measure heterolysis thermodynamics in the framework (beyond qualitative DRIFTS/microcalorimetry signatures), the gating argument risks being non-predictive. (iii) Nitro selectivity by “nitro-only inner-sphere chemisorption” is plausible at OMS, but competing coordination of anilines (Lewis basic) and other functionalities under H2 is not convincingly bounded; the proposal relies on weak-binding assertions in reactor mode that need quantitative competitive adsorption under realistic mixtures. (iv) GC-mode realism needs tighter constraints: long-term stability/bleed and peak shape in the presence of residual strong sites (even partially capped) is a known failure mode for MOF stationary phases; the passivation strategy is plausible but not backed by a specified reversibility window, capping stoichiometry, or demonstration that enantioselective interactions survive after OMS suppression. Overall, the program is coherent and technically ambitious, but a few mechanistic claims are still one level more asserted than proven, particularly regarding transferability of solution thermochemistry to the heterogeneous MOF microenvironment and the hard separation of ‘recognition’ vs ‘strong Lewis-acid retention’ in GC.

original_chain: Volume expansion -> Copper site -> Catalysis -> Tailored structure -> Metal-organic framework -> Water stability -> Hydrothermal method -> Fermi energy level
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Hydrothermally synthesizing a water-stable, copper-site MOF that is pre-compressed via an internal “molecular wedge” (fixed pendant sulfonate/carboxylate groups positioned proximal to the open Cu paddlewheel) will (i) suppress hydrolysis by maintaining Cu(II) coordination saturation through reversible inner-sphere/strong outer-sphere water management and (ii) enable adsorption-driven, reversible volume expansion that shifts the Cu-site electronic structure (d-band center/Fermi energy level alignment) to enhance catalytic turnover under aqueous conditions. Mechanistically, the wedge imposes an enthalpic penalty on irreversible framework opening while preserving a low-barrier elastic breathing mode; guest binding triggers Jahn–Teller-axis reorientation and lattice expansion that modulates Cu–O bond covalency and raises the density of states near EF, accelerating key electron-transfer steps in oxidation/photoredox catalysis without sacrificing water stability.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a HKUST-1–type Cu2(COO)4 paddlewheel topology as the catalytic motif, but design a ditopic linker set that introduces a proximal, non-bridging anionic “wedge”: (A) primary linker: 1,3,5-benzenetricarboxylate (BTC) or an extended trigonal carboxylate for larger pores; (B) wedge-linker: an isoreticular dicarboxylate bearing a pendant sulfonate (–SO3−) or phosphonate monoester positioned to project into the pore and approach the axial site at 3.0–4.0 Å (e.g., 2-sulfoisophthalate derivatives) without becoming a permanent bridge.
1.2 Define two control materials: (i) parent Cu-BTC (no wedge), (ii) wedge-linker MOF with pendant group methylated/neutralized (electrostatics removed) to decouple sterics from hydration control.
1.3 Pre-screen wedge geometries by periodic DFT (PBE-D3 or SCAN+rVV10) on a representative paddlewheel environment to ensure (a) no irreversible chelation that blocks catalysis, (b) axial water binding energy reduced vs parent while maintaining reversible binding of probe substrates (CH3CN/CH3OH).

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Methodological adaptation—hydrothermal “dual-linker, defect-pinned” synthesis:
- Conduct hydrothermal synthesis (120–180 °C, autogenous pressure) in pure water with a controlled modulator (formate/acetate) to tune defect density and force incorporation of wedge-linker into specific crystallographic positions.
- Implement a temperature-ramp/hold protocol to promote single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SCSC) ordering of wedge groups: ramp 1 °C/min to 150 °C, hold 12 h, cool slowly (0.2–0.5 °C/min). This is intended to lock pendant anions into a repeatable orientation that pre-compresses the lattice (lower initial cell volume) yet preserves an elastic breathing coordinate.
- Introduce a low fraction (1–5%) of redox-inactive high-valent node “pins” (e.g., Zr(IV) oxo clusters as secondary nodes or Al(III) chain fragments) via co-nucleation to reduce hydrolytic cleavage pathways while keeping Cu paddlewheels as the dominant catalytic sites; verify that pins function as mechanical reinforcers rather than alternative catalytic centers.
2.2 Activate materials using water-safe protocols (supercritical CO2 or mild solvent exchange followed by vacuum at ≤120 °C) to avoid collapsing wedge orientation.
2.3 Quantify volume expansion and local Cu-site response upon guest binding:
- In situ PXRD under humid gas and liquid water exposure to extract unit cell changes (target: reversible 2–8% volume expansion).
- High-resolution MAS NMR with CH3OH/CH3CN as probes plus CW-EPR to track Jahn–Teller axis changes and Cu-site symmetry shifts during adsorption/desorption cycles.
- Variable-temperature water vapor sorption + microcalorimetry to separate enthalpic stabilization (wedge-water interactions) from framework elasticity.
2.4 Link Fermi energy level modulation to catalysis:
- Measure work function/EF shifts using UPS or Kelvin probe on pressed pellets and operando near-ambient-pressure XPS (NAP-XPS) under humid reactant feeds.
- Correlate EF shifts with Cu oxidation-state dynamics using operando XAS (Cu K-edge XANES/EXAFS) during catalysis.
2.5 Catalysis demonstration in water (choose one primary reaction and one orthogonal validation):
- Primary: aqueous aerobic alcohol oxidation or persulfate activation/photocatalytic pollutant degradation using an added semiconductor co-catalyst only as a comparison, not required.
- Validate intrinsic Cu-site activity via hot filtration, ICP-MS leaching, and poisoning tests; quantify TOF normalized to open Cu sites (from CO chemisorption or probe uptake).

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Water stability benchmarking: continuous immersion (pH 3/7/10), cycling humidity (0–95% RH), and catalytic turnover cycling; assess crystallinity (PXRD), porosity (N2 sorption), and Cu leaching (ICP-MS).
3.2 Mechanistic causality tests:
- Compare wedge vs neutralized-wedge vs parent to isolate electrostatic hydration control.
- Map structure–electronics coupling: plot catalytic rate/TOF against (i) reversible volume expansion amplitude, (ii) EF/work-function shift, (iii) EPR g-tensor/Jahn–Teller metrics.
- Use isotopic labeling (H2O/D2O) to determine whether wedge stabilizes a specific water network (kinetic isotope effects; in situ IR of OD/OH).
3.3 Theory-experiment closure:
- Periodic DFT to compute DOS near EF as a function of cell volume (simulated expansion) and axial-ligand occupancy; predict which expansion regime maximizes electron-transfer driving force.
- Build a microkinetic model using measured adsorption enthalpies and computed redox energetics to show why EF tuning via breathing improves the rate-limiting step.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Cu(II) paddlewheel MOFs exhibit Jahn–Teller-driven local flexibility and measurable adsorption-induced volume expansion; spectroscopic signatures (MAS NMR/EPR) can directly report chemisorption-induced structural changes and reversibility. Prior heterojunction/MOF studies show that Fermi-level differences govern electron transfer and catalytic outcomes, implying EF is a meaningful target descriptor.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposed “molecular wedge” is a supramolecularly programmed, non-bridging pendant anion placed by linker design and locked by hydrothermal SCSC ordering. This is a rational, coordination-chemistry-grounded modification of a known Cu-site topology to control hydrolysis (coordination saturation and water networks) while preserving an elastic breathing coordinate for electronic-structure modulation.
3. Comparative Advantage: Conventional routes improve water stability by removing open metal sites or using inert nodes, often reducing catalytic activity. Here, water stability is improved without eliminating Cu open sites: the wedge moderates water access/geometry and suppresses irreversible opening, while reversible volume expansion is retained and exploited to tune EF and accelerate electron-transfer catalysis. The control series (neutralized wedge; parent) provides a stringent test that the advantage arises from the designed mechanism rather than generic morphology or defect effects.
final_critique: This is a highly sophisticated and ambitious proposal that demonstrates deep familiarity with Cu-paddlewheel MOF chemistry, hydrolytic degradation mechanisms, and operando electronic-structure characterization. The engineering plan is unusually detailed, particularly in its use of in situ PXRD, EPR, NAP-XPS, and operando XAS to connect breathing behavior with Cu-site electronics. The primary deductions arise from (i) the cumulative risk of combining multiple high-complexity elements—dual-linker hydrothermal synthesis, pendant anion orientation control, and secondary-node pinning—without a clear contingency path if crystallographic ordering fails, and (ii) an overextension of the Fermi-level argument. While EF/work-function shifts in pressed pellets are measurable, translating these shifts quantitatively to local Cu paddlewheel redox energetics under aqueous catalytic turnover remains only partially justified and may conflate global electronic properties with site-specific chemistry. Additionally, the assumption that pendant sulfonate/phosphonate groups can be reproducibly locked into a single orientation via SCSC hydrothermal treatment is plausible but not strongly precedent-backed, making this a key uncertainty rather than a flaw.

original_chain: Building block -> Surface area -> Electrochemical enzyme sensor -> Conductivity -> Selectivity -> Thermogravimetric analysis
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A 2D-exfoliated, dual-function MOF nanosheet electrode that spatially decouples (i) enzyme immobilization/selectivity and (ii) charge transport will outperform conventional MOF composites in electrochemical enzyme sensing because (a) ultrahigh external surface area increases enzyme loading and shortens substrate diffusion paths, (b) size/charge-selective pore apertures provide molecular sieving against interferents, and (c) an in-plane conductive network formed by post-synthetic redox-doping and carbon-assisted percolation reduces interfacial charge-transfer resistance. Methodological adaptation: instead of using bulk MOF crystals or simple MOF/carbon blends, we will (1) exfoliate a water-stable porphyrinic MOF into monolayer/few-layer nanosheets, (2) implement a 'Janus' functionalization where one face is enzyme-anchoring (covalent + affinity) while the opposite face is rendered electronically conductive via controlled redox doping, and (3) laminate these nanosheets into an oriented thin film on an electrode to create directional mass transport and electron pathways. Mechanistically, the oriented nanosheet stack provides a high density of accessible active sites, while the selective apertures and engineered surface chemistry suppress fouling and interferent access; concurrently, the doped/conductive face supports fast electron tunneling from the enzyme redox center to the electrode, yielding higher sensitivity and selectivity at lower overpotential. Thermogravimetric analysis is used not only for stability screening but quantitatively to determine enzyme and dopant loadings (mass-loss deconvolution), linking composition to selectivity/conductivity.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a robust porphyrinic MOF building block set: Mn(II) nodes with a tetratopic porphyrin linker (TBAPy-type) to enable water-stable layered structure amenable to exfoliation (guided by Asset 1).
1.2 Synthesize bulk Mn-porphyrin MOF crystals under solvothermal conditions; activate by solvent exchange to remove high-boiling guests.
1.3 Exfoliate via ultrasound-assisted liquid-phase exfoliation in aqueous/ethanol buffers across pH 4–9; fractionate by centrifugation to obtain narrow thickness distributions (monolayer/few-layer nanosheets).
1.4 Choose a model electrochemical enzyme sensor target (e.g., glucose oxidase for glucose, lactate oxidase for lactate) and define interferent panel (ascorbate, urate, acetaminophen; plus matrix proteins for fouling tests).

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Janus nanosheet functionalization (key adaptation):
- Face A (enzyme/selectivity side): introduce aldehyde handles selectively by mild surface oxidation of pendant groups or via a monolayer of bifunctional linker (e.g., dopamine-PEG-aldehyde) that anchors to the MOF surface while presenting aldehydes outward; immobilize enzyme by Schiff-base formation and reductive amination to lock orientation and reduce leaching.
- Face B (conductivity side): perform controlled post-synthetic redox doping of the porphyrinic units (e.g., iodine or TCNQ-type acceptors) to create mixed-valence pathways; simultaneously embed a minimal loading of graphene/CNT as an inter-nanosheet bridge but only on the conductive face (electrostatic assembly) to form a 2D percolation network (guided by Asset 2).
2.2 Oriented film assembly on electrode:
- Use electrophoretic deposition or Langmuir–Schaefer transfer to laminate nanosheets with preferential basal-plane alignment onto glassy carbon or gold; enforce orientation so Face B contacts the electrode and Face A is exposed to solution.
- Crosslink interlayer spacing with short bifunctional spacers (e.g., diamines) to prevent delamination while preserving accessible channels.
2.3 Build selectivity into the framework/pore environment:
- Tune aperture/charge by partial linker exchange with 4,4'-bipyridyl-like pillars or small charged modulators to achieve size/charge discrimination (conceptually aligned with Asset 4 principles: molecular sieving + thermodynamic affinity).
- Add a thin permselective overlayer only if needed (e.g., Nafion) but benchmark against the intrinsic MOF selectivity to avoid masking the mechanistic contribution.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structural/material characterization:
- AFM/TEM for nanosheet thickness and lateral size; PXRD to confirm framework retention after exfoliation and functionalization.
- N2 sorption (BET) to quantify surface area increase from bulk to nanosheets and after lamination.
- XPS/EPR/UV–vis–NIR to confirm redox-doped states and mixed-valence signatures correlated with conductivity.
3.2 Conductivity and electrochemical metrics:
- Four-point probe (film) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to extract film conductivity and charge-transfer resistance (Rct); compare (i) bulk MOF, (ii) exfoliated MOF, (iii) non-Janus composite, (iv) Janus-oriented film.
- Cyclic voltammetry/chronoamperometry for catalytic current, onset potential, and stability.
3.3 Selectivity and sensing performance:
- Determine sensitivity, LOD, linear range in buffer and in complex matrices (e.g., milk-like simulant) with interferent challenge; quantify selectivity factors and response time.
- Mechanistic tests: vary interlayer spacing, dopant level, and enzyme loading to map how mass transport vs electron transport limits performance.
3.4 Thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) as quantitative compositional tool (not only stability):
- Run TGA under N2 and air with deconvolution of mass-loss steps to quantify (a) residual solvent, (b) enzyme mass fraction (protein decomposition window), (c) dopant/counterion content (early loss or oxidative signatures), and (d) framework decomposition.
- Correlate TGA-derived enzyme/dopant loadings with EIS-derived Rct and with selectivity/sensitivity metrics to establish composition–function relationships.
3.5 Durability:
- Continuous operation tests (e.g., 8–24 h amperometry) and storage stability; evaluate leaching via activity assays and post-test TGA/XPS.
- Thermal robustness screening via TGA onset temperatures to define safe processing/sterilization windows.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Exfoliated MOF nanosheets can increase accessible surface area dramatically (e.g., 598 to 4,565 m²/g) and shorten charge-transfer distances (Asset 1), which directly benefits enzyme loading and electrochemical kinetics. MOF/carbon hybrids are established routes to improve electrochemical sensor conductivity and LOD (Asset 2), and conductivity–selectivity co-optimization via porous/electroactive MOF architectures is demonstrated in sensing contexts (Asset 3). Molecular sieving and thermodynamic selectivity principles in microporous MOFs are well-grounded (Asset 4) and can be repurposed for interferent rejection in biosensing.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal uses rational MOF building blocks (porphyrinic tetratopic linkers + Mn nodes) to access a layered framework that can be exfoliated, then applies coordination/organic surface chemistry to create a Janus functionality—an explicit supramolecular/solid-state design intervention rather than a generic composite. Oriented nanosheet lamination is a structural motif (2D stacked architecture with directional pathways) that is native to coordination polymer processing and directly targets the electron- vs mass-transport tradeoff in enzyme electrodes.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to (i) bulk MOFs (limited external surface area, longer electron pathways) and (ii) randomly mixed MOF/carbon composites (non-directional transport, uncontrolled enzyme orientation, higher fouling), the Janus-oriented nanosheet film provides: higher enzyme-accessible surface area, intrinsic pore-based selectivity to suppress interferents, and a dedicated conductive face for low Rct. The use of TGA as a quantitative lever (enzyme/dopant loading determination) creates a tighter composition–property–performance loop than standard characterization-only workflows, enabling systematic optimization rather than empirical trial-and-error.
final_critique: This is a technically ambitious and largely well-argued proposal with strong engineering resolution and a clear mechanistic narrative. The Janus nanosheet concept and oriented assembly directly address known electron- vs mass-transport tradeoffs in MOF-based enzyme electrodes, and the use of TGA as a quantitative lever is an intellectually mature addition. However, several aspects slightly weaken logical rigor: (i) face-selective functionalization on exfoliated MOF nanosheets is assumed feasible without sufficient discussion of symmetry breaking, yield, or verification strategies; (ii) the compatibility of redox doping (e.g., I2/TCNQ) with long-term enzyme stability and aqueous operation is underexplored; and (iii) the proposal risks overloading the system with too many tunable variables (dopant level, CNT loading, interlayer spacing, pore modulation) without a clearly prioritized experimental decision tree. These issues do not undermine feasibility but reduce confidence in executional focus and mechanistic deconvolution.

original_chain: Au -> Redox activity -> Multi-analyte sensing -> Electrocatalyst -> POM-γCD MOF -> Electrochemical signal -> Complex samples
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a hierarchically redox-programmed Au@POM-γCD MOF electrocatalyst—engineered via site-selective immobilization of ultrasmall Au nanoclusters within polyoxometalate pockets and γ-cyclodextrin cavities—will generate resolvable, amplified electrochemical signals for simultaneous multi-analyte detection in complex samples. The core mechanism relies on redox potential partitioning: POM units act as fast, multielectron redox mediators, γCD cavities provide molecular pre-organization and anti-fouling host–guest selectivity, and confined Au nanoclusters introduce localized electrocatalytic hot spots. This deliberate spatial and electronic decoupling enables distinct electron-transfer kinetics for different analytes, allowing multi-analyte sensing without external separation.
Plan: Step 1: Rational framework construction.
Synthesize a POM-γCD MOF using a Keggin-type [PW12O40]3− or Dawson-type POM as redox nodes coordinated to alkali/alkaline-earth metal-linked γ-cyclodextrin units, forming a crystalline, water-stable framework with interconnected CD cavities and POM clusters. Confirm crystallinity and porosity via PXRD, SCXRD (if feasible), and gas sorption.

Step 2: Methodological adaptation – site-selective Au incorporation.
Exploit the intrinsic redox activity of POMs to perform in situ, POM-mediated reduction of Au(III) salts, yielding sub-2 nm Au nanoclusters anchored preferentially at POM sites rather than randomly deposited on the framework surface. Control Au loading by tuning POM redox state electrochemically prior to metal ion exposure. This adapts the in situ nanoparticle growth strategy (Asset 1) to a spatially addressable, cyclodextrin-based MOF.

Step 3: Electrode architecture and signal deconvolution.
Integrate the Au@POM-γCD MOF as a thin, oriented film on laser-scribed graphene or Au microelectrode arrays. Use differential pulse voltammetry and square-wave voltammetry to map distinct redox peaks arising from (i) POM-mediated oxidation, (ii) Au-catalyzed surface reactions, and (iii) host–guest modulated diffusion through γCD cavities.

Step 4: Multi-analyte validation in complex samples.
Evaluate simultaneous detection of dopamine, serotonin, ascorbic acid, and uric acid in synthetic serum and cell-culture media. Correlate peak potential separation and current amplification with analyte size, redox potential, and CD binding constants. Apply kinetic modeling (Laviron analysis) to assign electron-transfer pathways.

Step 5: Stability and mechanistic verification.
Probe framework integrity and Au cluster stability post-electrochemistry using XPS, TEM, and in situ Raman spectroscopy to confirm that signal differentiation arises from structural design rather than degradation.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Prior studies demonstrate that redox-active MOFs can template noble metal nanoparticles without external reductants (Asset 1), while POM-γCD MOFs already exhibit strong electrocatalytic dopamine sensing in complex matrices (Asset 3). Au nanoclusters are known to lower overpotentials and enhance electron-transfer rates.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): This proposal adapts established POM-mediated redox chemistry into a cyclodextrin-based MOF scaffold, introducing spatially resolved electrocatalytic sites—an explicit molecular-level design consistent with coordination polymer principles rather than surface mixing.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike conventional conductive MOFs (Asset 2) that rely on uniform redox behavior, the proposed system intentionally creates heterogeneous but ordered redox domains. This enables intrinsic peak separation for multi-analyte sensing in complex samples without membranes, enzymes, or chromatographic preprocessing.
final_critique: This is a strong, conceptually ambitious proposal with clear chemical intuition and a well-articulated structure–function hypothesis. The engineering plan is largely credible, particularly the use of POM redox chemistry to template ultrasmall Au clusters and the integration into electrochemical architectures. However, several elements remain under-specified at a mechanistic level. The assumption that Au reduction will be sufficiently site-selective to POM pockets (and not γCD rims or external surfaces) is plausible but not rigorously justified; no competing nucleation pathways or control experiments are defined. Similarly, the claim of intrinsic peak deconvolution rests on overlapping effects (POM redox, Au catalysis, host–guest diffusion) without a priori estimates of potential separations or kinetic regimes. While Laviron analysis is mentioned, no explicit model linking analyte identity to a specific redox domain is articulated. Thus, while logically consistent, the proposal stops short of fully de-risking its central claim that spatial redox programming alone can replace physical separation in complex matrices.

original_chain: Benzyl alcohol -> MIL-125-Ti -> Photocatalysis -> CO2 reduction -> ZIF-8 -> Metal oxide -> Porous nanostructure
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A spatially programmed MIL-125-Ti@ZIF-8 core–shell photocatalyst will outperform MIL-125-Ti, ZIF-8, physical mixtures, and fully calcined oxides for CO2 photoreduction only if (GO) an ultrathin (2–5 nm) interfacial TiOx/ZnO junction is demonstrably confined to the buried MIL-125-Ti|ZIF-8 boundary and (GO) the junction creates a measurable built-in field / band-bending that drives vectorial electron transfer from photoexcited MIL-125-Ti into the shell region. Mechanistically, MIL-125-Ti produces long-lived Ti3+/ligand-radical charge-separated states under irradiation; a conformal interfacial TiOx/ZnO layer, enriched in Ti3+/oxygen vacancies after mild reduction, acts as (i) an electron-selective extraction layer (lowering recombination in MIL-125-Ti) and (ii) a CO2-activation layer (stabilizing *CO2−/carbonate-like intermediates). The outer ZIF-8 shell must remain crystalline and microporous to (iii) increase local CO2 activity and (iv) reduce local water activity via adsorption selectivity, thereby suppressing competitive proton reduction—provided this is validated by water/CO2 sorption and isotopic kinetics. Because ZIF-8 transformation can propagate non-locally once linker loss initiates, the interfacial-junction concept is explicitly de-risked by engineering the interface to be the preferential oxidation locus (Ti–OH-rich MIL-125 surface + interfacial water reservoir) and by implementing a diffusion-limited, low-O2 ‘soft oxidation’ that is monitored in real time and halted at the first sign of outer-shell degradation. The Re(bpy)(CO)3Cl-analog must be proven to reside inside the ZIF-8 shell (not merely on external surfaces) via during-growth encapsulation or defect-enabled linker exchange, such that electrons delivered to the shell/junction region can be captured by Re sites under CO2-rich microenvironments. Performance gains will only be claimed when rates are normalized to absorbed photons and to quantified Re and defect-site densities, and when action spectra and 13CO2 labeling confirm the true photocatalytic CO2-to-product pathway.
Plan: Phase 0 — Go/No-Go validation package (mandatory before full catalysis)

GO/NO-GO Criterion A: Spatial confinement of interfacial oxide formation (2–5 nm) with preserved outer-shell ZIF-8.
A1. Core–shell synthesis (baseline, no junction)
  • MIL-125-Ti nanocrystals: 50–150 nm, synthesized solvothermally; facet control using DMF/MeOH ratio and benzoic-acid modulation (5–30 equiv vs linker); exhaustive solvent exchange into anhydrous MeOH (≥5 exchanges) to remove DMF.
  • Surface priming for heterogeneous ZIF-8 nucleation: expose MIL-125-Ti to 2-methylimidazole (Hmim, 50–200 mM in MeOH) for 10–30 min to hydrogen-bond/coordinate at Ti–OH; rinse to remove free Hmim.
  • ZIF-8 shell growth: add Zn(NO3)2·6H2O (10–50 mM) + excess Hmim (0.2–1.0 M) in MeOH at room temperature; target shell thickness series: 20, 40, 60 nm by controlling growth time (5–60 min) and Zn:Hmim ratio. Quench by dilution/rinse.
  • Core–shell confirmation: TEM + STEM-EDS line scans (Ti vs Zn), PXRD (MIL-125 + ZIF-8 reflections), and N2 sorption (to ensure shell porosity remains).

A2. Interfacial junction formation via diffusion-limited ‘soft oxidation’ with real-time stop rules
  • Rationale addressing reviewer risk: we do not assume an oxygen/temperature gradient across 20–60 nm micropores; instead we enforce kinetic confinement by (i) very low oxidant chemical potential, (ii) short exposure windows, and (iii) preferential interfacial reactivity (Ti–OH / Ti-oxo environment catalyzing local linker oxidation).
  • Humidity-assisted low-O2 oxidation: 200–240 °C (start at 200 °C), 0.2–1.0% O2 in N2, with controlled H2O vapor (0.5–2.0 vol% via saturator at defined temperature). Exposure as pulses: 2–5 min per pulse, total 10–30 min, with cooling between pulses if needed.
  • Real-time stop rule: terminate once (i) CO2 evolution during treatment (online MS) shows the first sustained rise beyond baseline OR (ii) ex situ PXRD indicates any measurable loss in ZIF-8 (110) reflection intensity (>10%)—whichever occurs first.
  • Post-oxidation mild reduction to generate Ti3+/Vo: 5% H2/Ar, 150–180 °C, 15–30 min (lowest temperature that yields detectable Ti3+ while preserving ZIF-8 PXRD + BET).

A3. Required structural proof (pass/fail)
  • Cross-sectional STEM tomography on microtomed particles:
    – Embed particles in epoxy; ultramicrotome slices (50–100 nm). Acquire HAADF-STEM tilt series and reconstruct 3D Zn/Ti/O distribution.
    – STEM-EELS mapping: O-K, Ti-L2,3, Zn-L2,3 edges to distinguish oxide-like coordination vs MOF nodes; quantify oxide shell thickness distribution at the interface (target mean 2–5 nm, SD reported).
  • Depth-resolved XPS and ToF-SIMS on microtomed sections:
    – XPS sputter depth profile with low-damage Ar-cluster source; track Ti 2p (Ti4+/Ti3+), Zn 2p, O 1s (oxide vs hydroxyl), N 1s (imidazolate retention). Define “outer-shell retention” as N 1s and Zn–N signature remaining constant in the outer ≥80% of shell depth.
    – ToF-SIMS: map fragments (ZnN−/C4H5N2− for ZIF-8; TiO−/ZnO− for oxides) across the shell thickness.
  • Go/No-Go thresholds:
    – Oxide confined to ≤5 nm equivalent thickness at the interface in ≥70% of particles examined.
    – Outer ZIF-8 retains ≥80% of original BET area and preserves ZIF-8 PXRD peak set with ≤10% intensity loss.

GO/NO-GO Criterion B: Directly measured band alignment and built-in field after junction formation.
B1. Film preparation for reliable electronic measurements
  • Prepare thin films of (i) MIL-125-Ti, (ii) ZIF-8, (iii) MIL-125-Ti@ZIF-8 (no junction), (iv) MIL-125-Ti@ZIF-8 (junction) by electrophoretic deposition or doctor-blading onto FTO/glass, followed by gentle anneal (≤120 °C) to remove solvent.
  • Ensure similar optical density and loading across samples (gravimetric + UV–Vis absorbance).

B2. UPS + Kelvin probe/KPFM + electrochemical flat-band extraction
  • UPS (He I): measure valence band maximum and work function (Φ) of films; compare pre/post junction to detect vacuum-level shifts indicative of dipoles/band bending.
  • Kelvin probe and KPFM mapping: measure contact potential difference across single core–shell particles immobilized on conductive substrates; spatially resolve potential drop from core region to shell region, comparing junction vs no-junction.
  • Mott–Schottky on films (electrolyte compatible with stability, e.g., dry MeCN + supporting electrolyte; and separately aqueous bicarbonate if stable): extract flat-band potentials (E_fb) for MIL-125-Ti and junction-containing composites.
  • IMPS/photovoltage decay: quantify charge transfer vs recombination kinetics; require faster interfacial electron extraction signature for junction sample.

B3. Deliverable energetic diagram tied to measured values
  • Construct band diagram using: UPS-derived Φ and VBM, optical band gaps (Tauc from diffuse reflectance), and Mott–Schottky E_fb; show direction/magnitude of driving force MIL-125-Ti → TiOx/ZnO → Re site.
  • Go/No-Go thresholds:
    – Measurable built-in potential difference (≥50–100 mV) between core and shell regions by KPFM.
    – Junction sample shows reduced recombination (longer-lived charge separation by transient absorption/EPR) AND increased electron-transfer rate proxy (IMPS) relative to no-junction core–shell.

GO/NO-GO Criterion C: Prove Re-catalyst location inside ZIF-8 shell (not external-only).
C1. Strategy 1 (preferred): during-shell-growth encapsulation (“ship-in-a-bottle”)
  • Use a compact, cationic Re complex designed for ZIF-8 inclusion during crystallization (e.g., Re(bpy)(CO)3Cl derivative bearing an imidazolium/pyridinium substituent to interact with imidazolate cages).
  • Add Re complex during ZIF-8 shell growth at low mol% relative to Zn (e.g., 0.05–0.5 mol% Re:Zn) to favor encapsulation while maintaining crystallinity.
  • Post-synthesis washing protocol with competitive solvents (MeOH → MeCN) until no Re signal in supernatant (UV–Vis/ICP check).

C2. Strategy 2 (fallback): defect-assisted linker exchange to create “admission points”
  • Introduce controlled ZIF-8 defects via modulator (e.g., methylimidazole excess and brief etching) then perform linker exchange under conditions that do not dissolve the shell.

C3. Proof package (must include negative control)
  • Digestion-ICP-MS: quantify total Re loading (per g and per particle) for encapsulated vs post-adsorbed samples.
  • Spatial mapping:
    – STEM-EDS mapping of Re (where feasible) and/or synchrotron nano-XRF for Re distribution across shell thickness.
    – Confocal microscopy if a fluorescent analog is used as a tracer (paired experiments).
  • Pore-accessibility tests:
    – Compare Re retention after rigorous external-surface stripping (e.g., short ligand wash that removes surface-adsorbed species) for encapsulated vs post-adsorbed.
  • Negative control: attempt post-synthetic adsorption of the same Re complex onto pre-formed MIL-125-Ti@ZIF-8; demonstrate predominantly external loading (mapping + easy wash-off) and inferior photocatalytic selectivity/kinetics when normalized to total Re.
  • Go/No-Go threshold: ≥60% of Re signal localized within the shell interior (not only at external perimeter) as judged by cross-sectional mapping and resistance to surface stripping.

GO/NO-GO Criterion D: Isotopic controls + rate normalization to disentangle adsorption/site-density effects.
D1. Isotopic tracing and contamination controls
  • 13CO2 labeling: confirm 13CO (GC-MS) and/or 13C-formate (13C NMR/IC) as products.
  • Dark controls, Ar controls, and no-catalyst controls.
  • Action spectra: apparent quantum yield (AQY) vs wavelength must track the composite absorption profile and/or MIL-125 excitation features; mismatch triggers mechanistic reassessment.

D2. Normalization and site quantification
  • Normalize rates to (i) absorbed photons (integrating sphere measurements of absorbed photon flux), (ii) quantified Re sites (ICP), and (iii) quantified defect density (EPR spin quantification of Ti3+/Vo).
  • Report TOF_Re and TOF_defect; only claim “better charge separation” if TOF values increase (not merely total rates).


Phase 1 — Full photocatalytic testing (only after passing Phase 0)
1. Reaction platforms
  • Gas-phase photoreduction with controlled CO2/H2O vapor to directly test water-exclusion and H2 suppression; and liquid-phase (MeCN with controlled water content; and aqueous bicarbonate if stable).
  • Photon flux controlled; temperature controlled to decouple photothermal effects.

2. Selectivity and competing H2 evolution
  • Quantify H2 (GC-TCD) alongside CO and HCOO−; correlate with water vapor sorption and shell thickness.
  • Include junction vs no-junction vs fully calcined oxide composites to separate “junction effect” from “oxide photocatalyst formation.”

3. Mechanistic readouts during catalysis
  • In situ/operando DRIFTS: track carbonate/bicarbonate/*CO intermediates; compare junction vs no-junction.
  • Light-on/off EPR: Ti3+ and vacancy signatures; confirm persistence under reaction conditions.

4. Stability and leaching
  • 10–20 cycling runs; PXRD + BET after cycling; ICP-MS of filtrates (Zn/Ti/Re). Post-mortem cross-sectional STEM to verify shell retention and junction persistence.


Feasibility: The revised plan explicitly converts the reviewers’ highest-risk assumptions into testable GO/NO-GO milestones before performance claims.

(1) Spatial confinement is treated as an experimental question, not an assumption: oxide thickness and outer-shell retention will be quantified by cross-sectional (microtomed) STEM-EELS/EDS tomography plus depth-resolved XPS and ToF-SIMS. This directly addresses the concern that ZIF-8 degradation can propagate non-locally. The oxidation protocol is redesigned to be pulse-wise, low-O2, and governed by stop rules (online MS + PXRD), minimizing runaway linker loss.

(2) The “energetically downhill” vectorial electron-flow claim is replaced by a measurement-driven band-alignment workflow. UPS provides work function/valence information, Mott–Schottky yields flat-band potentials, and KPFM maps built-in potential across the core–shell architecture. The required energetic diagram will be constructed from these measured values, and IMPS/photovoltage decay will connect energetics to kinetics.

(3) Re co-catalyst localization is de-risked by prioritizing during-growth encapsulation (more plausible than post-synthetic infiltration given ZIF-8 aperture constraints) and by requiring orthogonal proof (digestion-ICP + cross-sectional mapping + pore-accessibility/stripping tests) plus a negative control demonstrating that post-adsorption yields mostly external loading.

(4) Selectivity/stability claims are constrained by isotopic confirmation (13CO2), action spectra, and rigorous normalization to absorbed photons and to quantified Re/defect densities. This prevents over-attribution to increased site number, altered adsorption, or inadvertent formation of conventional ZnO/TiO2 photocatalyst domains.

Finally, the approach remains coherent with the original concept chain (MIL-125-Ti photogenerates long-lived charges; ZIF-8 provides CO2-enrichment and water-activity control; an interfacial MOF-derived oxide junction mediates charge separation), but now the proposal is structured so that each mechanistic link is experimentally validated before it is used to justify the next step.
final_critique: This is an unusually rigorous and technically mature proposal. Its principal strength lies in converting every historically weak assumption in MOF-derived heterojunction photocatalysis (spatial confinement of oxides, vectorial charge transfer, co-catalyst localization, and rate normalization) into explicit, falsifiable GO/NO-GO criteria. The engineering plan demonstrates exceptional resolution: cross-sectional STEM-EELS tomography, depth-resolved XPS/ToF-SIMS, KPFM-based potential mapping, and absorbed-photon-normalized kinetics are all state-of-the-art and correctly matched to the risks identified. Logical consistency is high—the mechanistic chain from MIL-125-Ti charge separation through interfacial band bending to ZIF-8-mediated CO2 microenvironments is internally coherent and experimentally interrogable. Minor deductions arise from two areas: (i) the reliance on microtoming and tomography for statistically meaningful oxide-thickness distributions may be throughput-limited and could constrain reproducibility claims, and (ii) the assumption that a measurable ≥50 mV built-in field can be resolved across nanoscale, partially insulating MOF domains remains ambitious and may prove experimentally fragile despite the multi-technique approach. Evidence grounding is strong and remains within the chemistry/MOF/photocatalysis domain throughout. The rationale is creative and non-trivial, addressing a genuine bottleneck in distinguishing true MOF–MOF junction effects from inadvertent oxide photocatalysts.

original_chain: Cellulose -> Solid acid catalyst -> MIL-53(Al) -> Gate opening -> MIL-53 -> Temperature hysteresis
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A MIL-53(Al) framework bearing a *quantitatively verified, sparsely and internally distributed* population of anchored aryl-sulfonate sites can host *confined protic ionic-liquid (PIL) nanodomains* whose vitrification/mobilization transition is thermodynamically and kinetically coupled to the intrinsic np↔lp breathing of MIL-53(Al). By engineering the PIL chemistry (cation spacer length, protic group, loading) such that its confinement-shifted glass transition (Tg,conf) intersects the osmotic free-energy landscape governing MIL-53 breathing under hydrated, carbohydrate-relevant chemical potentials, the framework will exhibit a *programmable, temperature-addressable hysteresis loop with genuine phase memory*. This memory is mechanistically distinct from ordinary guest-induced hysteresis because (i) Tg,conf provides an internal kinetic barrier that persists at constant guest activity, and (ii) the PIL nanodomains generate localized adsorption stress and proton-relay amplification only when in the mobile state. As a result, internal Brønsted-acid sites are selectively activated/deactivated in synchrony with the lp/np phase, enabling switchable access for cellulose-derived oligomers while suppressing humin-forming over-condensation.
Plan: WP1 – Quantitative and spatially resolved internal functionalization (addresses Reviewer Point i & Mandatory Directive 1).
1.1 Baseline MIL-53(Al) synthesis with defect minimization and benchmarking: solvothermal Al(NO3)3/H2BDC with acetic acid modulators (0–20 equiv) to generate a defect series; select the lowest-defect material showing canonical np↔lp VT-PXRD behavior. Quantify μ2-OH density by TGA–H2O exchange and 27Al MAS NMR.
1.2 Controlled internal aryl-sulfonation: perform post-synthetic sulfonation using SO3·pyridine in dry dichloroethane under diffusion-limited conditions (solid/liquid ratio ≥50 mg mL−1; 0–4 °C; 5–60 min). Quench rapidly and thoroughly exchange solvents to prevent overreaction. Target DoF = 0.5, 1, 2, and 5% of BDC rings.
1.3 DoF and spatial validation (non-negotiable): (i) complete framework digestion (D2SO4/DMSO-d6) followed by quantitative 1H/13C NMR and LC-MS to determine sulfonated vs native BDC ratios; (ii) sulfur quantification by XPS with angle-resolved depth profiling to distinguish shell vs bulk S; (iii) microtomed crystal cross-sections analyzed by STEM-EDS/EELS mapping of S to confirm internal distribution; (iv) correlate DoF with BET, CO2 (273 K) sorption, and water DVS to demonstrate micropore preservation and breathing retention.

WP2 – Construction and verification of PIL nanodomains (addresses Reviewer Point ii & Mandatory Directive 2).
2.1 Anchored cation design with controlled confinement: synthesize bis-imidazolium or quaternary ammonium cations with (a) defined spacer lengths (C4, C6, C8, C10) to tune Tg,conf, and (b) a single phosphonate tail (–PO3H2) for stoichiometric binding to pre-quantified μ2-OH defect sites (≤1:1 binding verified by 31P MAS NMR). Avoid trialkoxysilanes in the primary study to minimize uncontrolled siloxane condensation.
2.2 Ion-pair assembly: exchange aryl–SO3− sites with the bulky cations, then introduce a protic functionality (pendant –SO3H or –CO2H) on the cation to generate a fixed-anion/protic-cation pair. Loadings will be systematically varied to remain below the percolation threshold for continuous pore filling (defined operationally as <30% reduction in CO2 uptake).
2.3 Direct evidence for nanodomains: (i) broadband dielectric spectroscopy and variable-temperature solid-state 1H NMR to identify a sharp vitrification/mobility transition of the confined PIL; (ii) quasielastic neutron scattering (or PFG-NMR where feasible) to extract cation/anion diffusion coefficients and demonstrate clustered vs isolated ion-pair dynamics; (iii) SAXS/total scattering (PDF) to detect nanometric electron-density fluctuations consistent with 1–3 nm clusters. Operational definition: a ‘PIL nanodomain’ is established when (a) a Tg,conf is observed, (b) diffusion coefficients are ≥1 order of magnitude lower than bulk PIL but nonzero above Tg,conf, and (c) scattering features scale with PIL loading. Correlate these metrics quantitatively with hysteresis width (ΔT).

WP3 – Decoupling PIL-induced hysteresis from ordinary guest effects (addresses Reviewer Point iii).
3.1 Thermodynamic mapping: perform VT-PXRD and DSC under precisely controlled water activity (a_w = 0–0.9) using DVS, comparing pristine MIL-53, sulfonated-only, cation-only, and full PIL systems. Extract ΔT and transition enthalpies.
3.2 Falsification test for ‘memory’: at identical temperature and a_w, prepare samples in lp vs np by different thermal histories and show distinct diffraction patterns and sorption behavior persisting for ≥2 h only in PIL-bearing materials.
3.3 Predictive model (pre-registered): extend OFAST by adding a PIL free-energy term containing Tg,conf and hydration-dependent viscosity; prospectively predict how ΔT shifts with spacer length and a_w, then verify experimentally.

WP4 – Catalysis with mass-transport and leaching controls (addresses Reviewer Point iv & Mandatory Directive 3).
4.1 Size-exclusion diagnostics: quantify uptake and turnover for glucose, cellobiose, and DP4 oligomers; demonstrate sharp cut-offs consistent with lp/np states. Compare with mesoporous MIL-53 analogues and external-surface-blocked samples.
4.2 Leaching exclusion: hot filtration, post-reaction supernatant acid titration, LC-MS for cation fragments, and ICP-OES for Al. Require <1% of total acidity in solution.
4.3 Hysteresis-programmed catalysis: run identical reactions at constant temperature but different thermal histories to isolate phase-memory effects on HMF/levulinate selectivity.

WP5 – Defect and anchoring causality.
Quantify defect density before/after phosphonate binding (27Al/31P MAS NMR, TGA) and include defect-matched controls to ensure breathing changes arise from PIL nanodomains rather than altered μ2-OH acidity.
Feasibility: The revised plan directly mitigates the reviewers’ key risks by converting asserted mechanisms into testable, quantitative work packages. Internal sulfonation is rendered feasible through low-temperature, diffusion-limited chemistry combined with mandatory DoF and depth profiling, ensuring that crystallinity and breathing are preserved rather than assumed. The PIL ‘gatekeeper’ concept is operationally defined via Tg,conf, diffusion, and scattering criteria, eliminating ambiguity between clusters, isolated ion pairs, and pore-filling phases. By explicitly decoupling guest-induced hysteresis from PIL vitrification through thermal-history experiments at constant chemical potential, the proposal makes the memory effect falsifiable. Mass-transport and leaching concerns are addressed through size-exclusion uptake diagnostics, mesoporous and external-surface controls, and rigorous solution-phase acidity assays. Finally, anchoring-induced defect effects are isolated through stoichiometric phosphonate binding and defect-matched controls. Collectively, these refinements transform the concept from a plausible but interpretive mechanism into a causally testable framework that tightly integrates MIL-53 breathing physics (Assets 2–4) with solid-acid catalysis for cellulose valorization (Asset 1).
final_critique: This is an unusually detailed and technically mature proposal that demonstrates clear awareness of historical failure modes in MIL-53 functionalization, guest-induced hysteresis, and solid-acid catalysis. Engineering resolution is very high: internal sulfonation is treated as a diffusion-limited reaction problem with mandatory spatial validation, and the PIL concept is operationally defined with orthogonal spectroscopic, scattering, and dynamical criteria rather than rhetorical language. Logical consistency is strong, particularly in the distinction between thermodynamic hysteresis and kinetically stabilized phase memory via Tg,conf. The main logical risk lies in the assumption that PIL vitrification can be tuned to intersect the MIL-53 osmotic free-energy landscape without suppressing breathing altogether; while the proposal includes controls, the coupling strength between Tg,conf and adsorption stress remains model-dependent and may be weaker than anticipated. Evidence grounding is excellent: all techniques and concepts are native to MOF chemistry, solid-state ionics, and catalysis. Rationale quality is high, as the proposal does not merely apply MIL-53 breathing to catalysis but introduces a genuinely new internal kinetic variable (confined PIL glass physics) to address selectivity and humin suppression. Minor deductions reflect the remaining uncertainty in achieving reproducible, narrow Tg,conf distributions under heterogeneous confinement.

original_chain: Chromatographic separation -> Capillary electrochromatography -> Dynamic covalent bonding -> Solid stationary phase -> Nanopore -> Drug Delivery -> Proton conduction -> Metal-organic framework
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A dynamically crosslinked, proton-conducting MOF nanopore coating covalently anchored to the inner wall of a fused-silica capillary will simultaneously (i) increase capillary electrochromatography (CEC) selectivity/efficiency for ionizable drugs and (ii) enable electrically triggered, on-column drug release, because reversible dynamic covalent bonds (hydrazone/imine exchange) can reconfigure the MOF’s pore-surface functionality and local Brønsted acidity under an applied electric field and controlled hydration, thereby modulating electroosmotic flow (EOF), analyte partitioning, and proton-hopping pathways (Grotthuss) in a coupled manner. Methodological adaptation: replace conventional static MOF coatings/monoliths with an open-tubular MOF thin film whose pore apertures are ‘gated’ by dynamic covalent linkers tethered inside the channels and whose interface is permanently anchored to silica via a catechol-silane primer, yielding a self-healing stationary phase that can be tuned in situ (pH/field/humidity) without loss of crystallinity or adhesion.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select MOF backbone and channel motif: synthesize a chemically robust, 1D-channel Zr-MOF thin film (UiO-66-type) using a mixed-linker strategy: terephthalate (BDC) + aldehyde-functionalized terephthalate (BDC-CHO) at controlled ratios (e.g., 5–30% BDC-CHO) to introduce reactive sites without collapsing porosity.
1.2 Prepare capillary substrate: activate fused-silica inner wall (NaOH/HCl rinse), then deposit a catechol-silane adhesive primer (e.g., dopamine-derived silane or polydopamine + APTES) to provide (i) strong interfacial adhesion and (ii) surface amines for subsequent covalent anchoring.
1.3 Grow an open-tubular MOF film: perform solvothermal layer-by-layer (LbL) or modulated growth (benzoic acid/acetic acid as modulators) to form a 200–800 nm continuous UiO-type film on the inner wall; verify coverage by SEM (capillary cross-sections) and XRD (scraped film reference).

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Install dynamic covalent ‘pore gates’: diffuse bifunctional hydrazides or diamines into the MOF to form reversible hydrazone (with BDC-CHO) or imine linkages, producing a dynamic covalent network partially spanning pore windows. Tune gate density by BDC-CHO content and linker length (e.g., adipic dihydrazide vs aromatic dihydrazide) to target pore-aperture modulation in the 0.5–1.0 nm regime.
2.2 Create proton-conduction pathways: introduce a confined proton-carrier guest (e.g., 1H-1,2,4-triazole or imidazole) by vapor/solution infiltration; co-introduce small amounts of sulfonic acid (e.g., tethered sulfonate via mono-hydrazide bearing –SO3H) to create fixed acid sites while preserving dynamic exchange at other positions.
2.3 Covalent anchoring to prevent film delamination: couple a fraction of MOF aldehydes to capillary-wall amines (Schiff base) followed by mild reductive amination (NaBH3CN) ONLY at the interface to “lock” the MOF to the substrate, while leaving internal aldehydes reversible for gating.
2.4 Implement CEC operation and stimulus control: run CEC with controlled humidity/aqueous-organic mobile phases (e.g., 10–40% ACN, buffered pH 3–8). Apply electric field (e.g., 100–400 V/cm). Modulate pH and field polarity to shift imine/hydrazone equilibria and guest protonation state; optionally apply short high-field pulses to induce transient gate opening for release.
2.5 Drug loading/release demonstration: load model ionizable drugs (e.g., propranolol, lidocaine, diclofenac) into the MOF coating under low-field conditions, then trigger release by switching to a condition that (i) protonates carriers and increases proton conductivity and (ii) shifts dynamic covalent equilibrium to a more open-pore state (acidic pulse for hydrazones; basic pulse for certain imines).

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structural/chemical validation: confirm dynamic covalent formation by FTIR (C=N), solid-state NMR (if feasible), and derivatization assays on aldehyde consumption; quantify guest loading by TGA and solvent extraction/LC.
3.2 Proton conduction quantification: perform impedance spectroscopy on analogous MOF films on planar interdigitated electrodes under controlled RH to extract σH+ vs RH and vs gate density; correlate σH+ with CEC EOF stability.
3.3 CEC performance metrics: measure EOF (neutral marker), plate number, resolution, selectivity factors for drug panels across pH/field/RH; compare to (i) bare silica, (ii) static UiO-66 film without dynamic gates, (iii) conventional silica C18, and (iv) polymer monolith.
3.4 Mechanistic tests: (a) gate-density series (BDC-CHO %) to link pore gating with retention/selectivity; (b) isotope effect (H2O vs D2O mobile phase) to probe Grotthuss contribution; (c) competitive guest experiments (triazole present/absent) to decouple proton-carrier contribution from mere surface charge.
3.5 Durability/self-healing: perform 200–500 run cycling, including deliberate pH shocks; track performance recovery after “damage” (drying/rewetting) to evidence dynamic covalent self-repair; inspect film integrity post-cycling by SEM.
3.6 Drug-delivery relevance: quantify on-column controlled release kinetics (peak-area vs trigger protocol), and evaluate payload protection (stability of labile drugs) by comparing degradation products with/without MOF confinement.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: MOFs are established as high-surface-area solid stationary phases for CEC, and proton conduction in MOFs is known to be enhanced by heterocycles (e.g., triazole/imidazole) and hydration, consistent with Grotthuss/vehicular mechanisms. Dynamic covalent bonds (imine/hydrazone) provide reversible, stimulus-responsive functional reconfiguration under mild conditions compatible with organic/water mobile phases.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal uses a rational Zr-MOF (UiO-type) for hydrolytic stability, mixed-linker installation of aldehyde handles for post-synthetic dynamic covalent chemistry inside nanopores, and interfacial covalent anchoring to silica to satisfy capillary-format constraints (thin, adherent, low backpressure). The dynamic covalent network is deliberately confined to pore interiors (tunable gating) while the interface is locked, enabling a true ‘adaptive stationary phase’ rather than a degradable coating.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to static MOF/silica phases, the dynamic-gated MOF can be tuned in situ to optimize separations across diverse drug chemotypes without re-packing or re-coating. Coupling proton-conducting guests with fixed acid sites stabilizes EOF and adds an orthogonal control knob (σH+) to modulate retention and release. The self-healing dynamic covalent chemistry addresses a key limitation of MOF capillary coatings—microcracking/delamination and irreversible fouling—by allowing reversible bond exchange and functional re-equilibration after stress, improving lifetime and reproducibility.
final_critique: The proposal is ambitious and largely well engineered, with a rare level of mechanistic forethought for MOF-based CEC. Strengths include the mixed-linker UiO strategy, clear separation of interfacial vs internal chemistry, and a rigorous validation plan (gate-density series, isotope effects, impedance spectroscopy). However, several logical links are somewhat overstated: (i) the extent to which an applied electric field directly shifts imine/hydrazone equilibria inside UiO-66 pores is not quantitatively justified and may be secondary to pH/hydration effects; (ii) partial pore-spanning ‘gates’ in UiO-66 (≈6 Å windows) risk excessive permeability loss or kinetic trapping at higher BDC-CHO fractions; and (iii) translation of proton conductivity measured on planar films to stable, reproducible EOF modulation in a capillary under high fields is assumed rather than demonstrated. These are not fatal flaws but introduce uncertainty in the central coupling claim (gating ↔ σH+ ↔ selectivity).

original_chain: Light -> Solid-state reactivity -> Reactive vapours -> Light -> Coordination number -> Solvent -> Bridging organic ligand -> Catalysis
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A photoaddressable “coordination-number gate” can be engineered into a single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SCSC) MOF by (i) building 1D channels lined with switchable bridging ligands and (ii) deliberately installing a solvent-labile, high-coordination-number metal node that can reversibly drop coordination upon light-triggered ligand isomerization. Mechanistically, irradiation (UV/visible) toggles an azobenzene- or diarylethene-bearing bridging ligand between conformers that change donor orientation and steric crowding at the SBU, lowering the metal coordination number (e.g., 6→5 or 6→4) and creating a transient open metal site (OMS). The OMS then catalyzes reactions of reactive vapours (e.g., epoxides, aldehydes, isocyanates, CO2/propylene oxide) via Lewis-acid activation. Solvent molecules act as an orthogonal, competitive ligand that controls the baseline coordination saturation and stabilizes the SCSC pathway; thus, catalytic activity becomes a function of (light, solvent occupancy, vapour identity) with spatiotemporal control and minimized framework collapse.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select an exchangeable, solvent-labile SBU platform known to tolerate coordination-number ambiguity under solvent (Asset 2 logic): start from a Zn(II) or Cd(II) paddlewheel/chain node (labile) or Zr6 for backbone robustness plus appended labile sites; target a node environment that can access multiple coordination numbers without bond rupture.
1.2 Design a mixed-linker MOF: (A) a rigid ditopic backbone linker to ensure crystallinity/rigidity (e.g., 4,4′-biphenyldicarboxylate, BPDC, or 2,6-naphthalenedicarboxylate) and (B) a photoswitchable bridging N-donor linker (e.g., 4,4′-azobispyridine (AzoBPY) or a diarylethene-bis(pyridyl)) positioned as a pillar/bridge that directly defines the metal coordination sphere.
1.3 Grow single crystals under solvothermal conditions in coordinating solvents (DMF/DEF) containing a controlled fraction of stronger neutral ligands (MeCN, pyridine) to “pre-load” the high coordination number state.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Methodological adaptation—Light-gated coordination-number modulation under vapour flow (“photovapour operando SCSC”): build a custom operando cell enabling simultaneous (i) controlled reactive vapour dosing, (ii) solvent vapour co-dosing (to tune competitive coordination), and (iii) in situ irradiation while collecting single-crystal XRD (where feasible) or high-resolution PXRD.
2.2 Install a cation-exchange layer to tune lability without destroying topology (Asset 2): perform post-synthetic transmetallation at the labile node (e.g., partial Zn→Cu or Zn→Co exchange) to increase Lewis acidity while preserving crystallinity; quantify exchanged fraction via ICP-OES and anomalous XRD/PDF.
2.3 Calibrate coordination-number states: (i) solvent-saturated “OFF” state (maximally coordinated), (ii) partially desolvated “ARMED” state, (iii) photoisomerized “ON” state. Use variable-temperature/vacuum activation with controlled solvent backfilling to avoid amorphization.
2.4 Mechanism-focused spectroscopy: track OMS formation and ligand switching using in situ IR (ν(C=N)/ν(N=N) changes), diffuse reflectance UV–vis (photoswitch state), EPR/XAS (metal-site geometry/coordination), and microcalorimetry (vapour adsorption enthalpy shifts upon light).
2.5 Catalysis with reactive vapours: evaluate a vapour-phase model reaction sensitive to Lewis acidity and confinement, e.g., (a) cycloaddition of CO2 with epoxide vapours to cyclic carbonates (with/without a tethered halide cocatalyst), or (b) acetalization of aldehyde vapours with alcohol vapours. Measure conversion/selectivity by GC/MS of effluent; perform light OFF/ON cycling under identical flow.
2.6 Spatial control test: irradiate only part of a packed-bed or a single-crystal microreactor and map product gradients; correlate with local structural state by micro-XRD or Raman mapping.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structural validation: demonstrate reversible SCSC or at minimum topotactic transformations (Asset 1) via repeated PXRD patterns and (when possible) single-crystal refinement showing coordination-number change and altered metal–ligand metrics.
3.2 Causality: decouple effects of adsorption vs true catalytic OMS generation by comparing (i) photoswitchable ligand MOF vs (ii) non-switchable analog (replace AzoBPY with BPY) under identical solvent/vapour/light.
3.3 Kinetic signatures: obtain apparent activation parameters under OFF/ON; show rate enhancement correlates with OMS markers (XAS coordination, IR band shifts) rather than only uptake.
3.4 Solvent role: construct a “coordination competition” map (solvent vapour partial pressure vs light state) linking coordination number to activity; verify by controlled co-dosing of MeCN/EtOH/H2O vapours.
3.5 Stability metrics: quantify performance across ≥50 light/vapour cycles; check metal leaching (ICP of downstream traps), crystallinity retention, and photoswitch fatigue.
3.6 Comparative benchmark: compare to a conventional OMS MOF catalyst (e.g., HKUST-1-like or UiO-66 defect-engineered) under identical vapour-phase conditions to establish advantage in switchability and resistance to deactivation by competitive ligands.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 1 supports that coordination polymers/MOFs can undergo stimulus-driven solid-state transformations (including light and solvent removal/exchange) with coordination-number changes while retaining crystallinity/topology. Asset 2 supports that apparent coordination numbers can exceed static crystal-structure assignments due to solvent/ligand lability and that cation exchange/transmetallation can tune metal-site behavior in MOFs. Asset 3 supports that bridging N-donor ligands (pyridine/tetrazole families) and solvent-rich coordination networks can be tuned for catalytic function and stimulus responsiveness.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal adapts SCSC transformation methodology into an operando photovapour protocol explicitly designed to control coordination number in real time. It leverages MOF design principles (rigid backbone + functional pillar ligand) to couple a photoswitch to the first coordination sphere, turning coordination-number variability—often a nuisance—into a controllable catalytic gating element.
3. Comparative Advantage: Conventional OMS catalysts are either always-on (poor selectivity/control) or deactivate under competitive vapours/solvents. Here, solvent is used as a purposeful competitive ligand to stabilize an OFF state, while light triggers an ON state that transiently creates OMS only when needed. This should improve resistance to poisoning, enable spatiotemporal catalysis (patterned irradiation), and provide mechanistic traceability via direct coordination-number readouts (XAS/XRD) unavailable in many porous catalysts.
final_critique: This is an unusually sophisticated proposal with strong command of MOF chemistry, SCSC transformations, and operando characterization. The central mechanism—light-induced ligand isomerization perturbing the first coordination sphere to gate OMS formation—is logically consistent and well motivated. Engineering resolution is high, particularly in the design of mixed-linker architectures, solvent-labile coordination environments, and the integration of operando diffraction/spectroscopy under vapour flow. The main weaknesses are (i) optimistic assumptions about the magnitude and crystallographic resolvability of coordination-number changes (e.g., clean 6→4 or 6→5 transitions) under irradiation without introducing disorder, and (ii) the cumulative experimental burden: simultaneous SCSC integrity, photoswitch fatigue resistance, catalytic turnover, and spatial patterning may be difficult to achieve in a single system. The Zn/Cd vs Zr6 logic is somewhat underdeveloped mechanistically—Zr6 nodes rarely exhibit true coordination-number lability at catalytically relevant timescales, and appended labile sites may decouple the photoswitch from the active metal center. These issues slightly weaken logical inevitability rather than feasibility.

original_chain: Defect site -> UiO-66 -> Surface stabilization -> Nucleation -> Metal-organic framework -> Nonlinear optical material
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A UiO-66 thin film grown by substrate-anchored, diffusion-controlled heterogeneous nucleation under a rigorously maintained monotonic modulator gradient will exhibit a **true bulk second-order nonlinear susceptibility χ(2)** (not dominated by interfaces or EFISH) because a depth-coherent, optically phase-matched gradient of charged missing-linker Zr6-node defects generates (i) a macroscopic internal electric field that is uniform in sign over the optical coherence length and (ii) a statistically biased orientation of sub-nanometer dipolar pore residents and/or linker substituents. The key mechanistic advance over prior defect-engineered UiO-66 systems is that polarity is encoded *during nucleation and growth* by a one-dimensional reaction–diffusion process that kinetically locks in a non-centrosymmetric distribution of defect charge across hundreds of nanometers, exceeding both the SHG coherence length and the scale over which surface-only χ(2) contributions dominate. By explicitly quantifying (a) the defect-charge gradient, (b) the resulting internal field magnitude, and (c) the expected orientational order parameter of confined dipoles, the proposal closes the mechanistic gap between missing-linker chemistry and a measurable, thickness-scaling bulk χ(2).
Plan: Step 1: Reaction–diffusion architecture with monotonicity control.
1.1 Interfacial diffusion cell with quantified transport: Construct a vertical, sealed diffusion cell (gap 1.0 ± 0.1 mm) using a PTFE spacer and optical fused-silica windows. Both compartments contain DMF with identical viscosity modifiers (1.5 wt% PMMA, Mw ~120 kDa) to suppress convection at 60–80 °C. Solution A: ZrCl4 (20–40 mM), H2O (Zr:H2O = 1:6), mixed modulators AA:TFA (total modulator:Zr = 30:1). Solution B: H2BDC (20–40 mM), no modulator. Temperature ramp ≤1 °C/min to avoid density-driven flow.
1.2 Reaction–diffusion modeling: Prior to experiments, solve a 1D diffusion–reaction model (COMSOL or equivalent) with parameters: D_modulator ~ 5×10⁻⁶ cm²/s (gelled DMF), first-order modulator consumption coupled to Zr6 SBU incorporation, and surface reaction boundary conditions. Define operating windows where ∂C_mod/∂z < 0 for the full growth duration. Only conditions predicted to preserve monotonicity are executed experimentally.
1.3 Suppression of homogeneous nucleation: Operate below bulk supersaturation predicted by the microkinetic framework for UiO-66 (leveraging Asset 2). Continuously monitor mother liquor turbidity (in situ laser scattering) and ex situ DLS; abort runs showing particle formation. Periodically exchange Solution B to remove any incipient nuclei.

Step 2: Substrate-anchored nucleation and gradient locking.
2.1 Substrate programming: Use phosphonate-terminated silane SAMs (12-phosphonododecyltrichlorosilane) on fused silica to maximize Zr–O–P binding energy and enforce surface-confined nucleation. COOH-SAMs serve as secondary comparison; CH3-SAMs as non-nucleating controls. Verify SAM density and uniformity by XPS and ellipsometry.
2.2 Gradient encoding during growth: Initiate growth at 70 °C. Early-stage nuclei experience high TFA activity (higher charged missing-linker density). As growth proceeds and the diffusion front advances, local TFA activity decreases monotonically, yielding progressively lower defect charge density toward the film–air interface. Target thickness series: 100, 300, 800, 1500 nm to enable χ(2) thickness scaling tests.
2.3 Defect charge-state stabilization: Post-growth, perform controlled hydration (DMF with 0.2–0.5 vol% H2O) to generate Zr–OH/Zr–OH2 at under-coordinated sites. Avoid ionic post-synthetic exchange to preserve the frozen gradient.

Step 3: Independent quantification of defect gradient and internal field.
3.1 Chemical gradient mapping: Cross-sectional STEM-EDS/EELS targeting F-K edge (from TFA-derived residues) and O-K fine structure to map Zr–OH vs Zr–O–C environments with <20 nm resolution. Correlate with angle-resolved XPS core-level shifts (Zr 3d, O 1s) vs take-off angle.
3.2 Internal field measurement: Prepare cross-sections by FIB and map surface potential via Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM), extracting E(z) from potential gradients. As an orthogonal probe, load pores with a low-loading Stark reporter (e.g., nitrile-functionalized benzene, size <6 Å) and quantify vibrational Stark shifts by polarized IR microspectroscopy across the thickness.

Step 4: Guest or linker dipole strategy compatible with UiO-66 apertures.
4.1 Replace DR1 with verified-size dipoles: Use small, rigid dipolar guests (e.g., benzonitrile, 4-fluorobenzonitrile, or nitrobenzene; kinetic diameter <6 Å) whose hyperpolarizability is known and whose orientation can be inferred from polarized IR/Raman. As an alternative, introduce low-density linker substitution (e.g., 2-nitro-terephthalate at ≤5%) to embed dipoles while retaining chromophore-free controls.
4.2 Orientation quantification: Determine orientational order parameter ⟨P2(cosθ)⟩ from polarized IR dichroism and compare to predictions based on measured internal field strength vs kBT.

Step 5: Disentangling bulk χ(2), surface SHG, and EFISH.
5.1 Polarization-resolved SHG: Measure s- and p-in/p-out combinations and fit to tensor elements expected for a polar C∞v-like symmetry along the film normal. Surface-only SHG will show different polarization signatures.
5.2 Thickness scaling: Measure SHG intensity vs film thickness; true bulk χ(2) will scale ~t² (or linearly in effective χ(2)) until absorption/dephasing, whereas surface SHG remains constant.
5.3 EFISH test: Apply an external DC field across the film using transparent electrodes. If EFISH contributes, χ(2)_eff will vary linearly with applied field (χ(2)_eff = χ(2) + 3χ(3)E). A non-zero intercept at E = 0 confirms intrinsic bulk χ(2).
5.4 Phase-sensitive Maker fringes: Extract sign and phase of χ(2) relative to substrate; flip-film experiments must invert the phase for a genuine built-in polarity.

Step 6: Correlating nucleation kinetics, defect gradient, and NLO.
6.1 In situ GIXS/QCM-D during early growth to extract nucleation density and growth rates as functions of modulator gradient parameters.
6.2 Correlate kinetic regime → defect-gradient slope → internal field magnitude → orientational order → χ(2), establishing a closed mechanistic chain.
Feasibility: 1. Mechanistic soundness: UiO-66 defect chemistry is exquisitely sensitive to modulator acidity and concentration. By embedding this sensitivity in a diffusion-limited, surface-anchored growth regime, the proposal converts local defect control into a macroscopic, depth-coherent polarity that exceeds the optical coherence length—addressing the core reviewer concern that defects alone do not guarantee χ(2).
2. Quantitative de-risking: Independent measurements of defect distribution (STEM-EELS/XPS), internal field (KPFM/Stark shifts), and dipole orientation (polarized IR) provide numerical inputs for an order-of-magnitude χ(2) estimate, rather than relying on qualitative symmetry arguments.
3. Clear separation of χ(2) sources: Polarization-resolved SHG, thickness scaling, and EFISH modulation explicitly discriminate bulk χ(2) from surface and χ(3)·E artifacts, directly responding to reviewer mandates.
4. Controlled gradient formation: Reaction–diffusion modeling, viscosity-matched compartments, and in situ turbidity/DLS monitoring address the risk of gradient scrambling and homogeneous nucleation highlighted by the reviewers.
5. Guest accessibility and interpretability: Replacing DR1 with aperture-compatible dipoles or dilute dipolar linker substitution ensures pore accessibility, measurable orientation, and clean mechanistic attribution.
6. Transferability and impact: If successful, the strategy establishes a general paradigm for encoding polarity and NLO activity into intrinsically centrosymmetric MOFs via nucleation physics rather than chromophore-heavy chemistry, enabling integration with photonic and optoelectronic platforms.
final_critique: The proposal is unusually well-instrumented and shows strong methodological resolution: controlled diffusion-cell architecture, precomputed monotonicity windows, and multiple orthogonal readouts for (i) defect gradient, (ii) internal field, and (iii) orientational order, followed by rigorous SHG deconvolution (polarization tensors, thickness scaling, EFISH test, phase-sensitive Maker fringes). The main scientific risk is not execution detail but physical identifiability: (1) the link between a modulator gradient and a *net, signed* space-charge/field over hundreds of nm is under-justified for UiO-66 in DMF because defect compensation, proton mobility, and adventitious ionic screening can neutralize or localize charge, collapsing the purported uniform-sign E(z) over the optical coherence length. (2) The proposed defect proxies (F mapping from TFA residues; O-K fine structure; ARXPS shifts) do not uniquely quantify *charged* missing-linker density versus neutral defect motifs, adsorbed species, or residual modulator; therefore the key mechanistic variable (ρ(z), not just defect concentration) may remain ambiguous. (3) KPFM on FIB cross-sections in an insulating porous MOF is prone to beam damage, charging artifacts, and humidity-dependent surface conductivity; extracting a reliable internal electric field profile from surface potential is nontrivial without stringent calibration and controls. (4) The orientational-bias mechanism is plausible but not quantitatively closed: for small guests in UiO-66, the field required to overcome rotational entropy and host–guest interactions can be large; without a priori estimates showing E·μ/kBT is meaningfully >1 across a large fraction of pores, the expected ⟨P2⟩ and thus χ(2) may be too small to separate from surface SHG/EFISH, even with thickness scaling. These gaps reduce confidence that the measured SHG, if any, will be attributable to a true bulk χ(2) rather than residual EFISH/surface contributions or extrinsic charging.

original_chain: Solvothermal process -> Capacity retention rate -> Interface bonding -> Capacity retention rate -> Current density -> Co2+
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A Co2+-programmed, solvothermally assembled interpenetrating coordination interphase (ICI) formed *inside* a Si/C/binder electrode—by (a) growing a defect-engineered UiO-66-type Zr-MOF within electrode meso-/macropores and (b) covalently tethering a controlled fraction of MOF linkers into the polymeric binder/conductive-carbon phase—will sustain higher current-density operation with superior capacity retention because interface bonding is converted from a fragile 2D contact into a 3D load-bearing coordination/covalent network that simultaneously stabilizes mechanical integrity and preserves percolating ion/electron pathways.

Mechanistic refinement per critique (chemically defensible Co model): Co2+ will *not* be claimed as an isovalent Zr(IV) replacement in the Zr6O4(OH)4 node. Instead, Co2+ will be deliberately positioned in a *characterized, reversible coordination environment* associated with UiO-66 defect chemistry: (i) Co2+ binding at missing-linker defect sites through terminal node groups (Zr–OH/Zr–OH2) as inner-sphere Co–O(hydroxo/aqua) adducts and/or (ii) Co2+ chelated by pendant carboxylate/chelating groups on a minority functional linker population that is simultaneously covalently anchored to the binder (a “tethered Co-carboxylate coordination crosslinker”). During cycling-induced microcrack formation or interfacial separation, these Co2+–O coordination linkages can dissociate/reassociate (ligand exchange among –OH/–COO−/H2O) across newly created surfaces, providing a *re-formable* bridging interaction that increases interfacial fracture energy and suppresses electrical/ionic disconnection. This mechanism is explicitly testable by Co K-edge EXAFS/XANES and by correlating quantified Co coordination motifs to interfacial fracture energy (Gc), impedance growth, and high-current cycling retention.
Plan: Step 0 — Define materials and quantitative design constraints (pre-registered go/no-go metrics)
0.1 Electrode baseline formulation (constant across all arms): Si nanoparticles (80–150 nm, optional thin carbon shell) : conductive carbon (Super P or Ketjenblack) : binder = 60:20:20 wt% (adjustable after initial screening but fixed within each comparison). Areal capacity target 2.0–3.0 mAh cm−2; electrode thickness 35–60 µm; initial porosity 30–40% (mercury intrusion or FIB-SEM porosimetry surrogate).
0.2 Binder chemistry to tolerate infiltration and enable covalent tethering: choose a DMF-tolerant, crosslinkable, carboxyl-rich elastic binder (two candidates run in parallel until one passes solvent-only exposure):
  - Candidate A: crosslinkable PAA-based copolymer (PAA-co-allyl acrylate, 3–8 mol% allyl) neutralized to Li/PAA ~30–50% to reduce swelling; crosslink via thiol–ene.
  - Candidate B: CMC/SBR blend with added multifunctional thiol crosslinker and post-treatment UV/thermal thiol–ene onto MOF vinyl handles.
Go/no-go for binder compatibility: <10% loss in peel strength and <15% change in electronic conductivity after solvent-only thermal exposure (Step 3 control).

Step 1 — Pre-establish (outside electrodes) the *actual* Co speciation achievable under proposed synthesis conditions (Mandatory Directive #1)
1.1 Build a matrix of MOF syntheses (powder form) to map Co incorporation modes and exclude CoOx/Co-carboxylate precipitates:
  - Base framework: UiO-66 or UiO-66-X with mixed linkers (BDC + 5–15 mol% BDC-R).
  - Defect engineering: modulator (formic acid or acetic acid) varied to generate missing-linker sites; target 5–20% missing-linker fraction (quantified by TGA + 1H NMR of digested MOF).
  - Co introduction modes (run separately to disambiguate):
    (i) One-pot Co present during UiO formation (Co(NO3)2 or Co(OAc)2, 0–10 mol% vs Zr) under conditions that preserve UiO topology.
    (ii) Post-synthetic Co2+ coordination to defect sites: soak activated defective UiO in ethanol/water with Co2+ (10–50 mM) at 25–60 °C.
