  - (ii) Radial-gradient shell: initial growth with 0% fluorinated linker for lattice-matched inner shell, followed by fluorinated-linker-enriched outer growth (e.g., switch feed to 10–30%) to force F-enrichment near the external interface where O2 partitioning and water exclusion are most impactful for interfacial ROS delivery.
3.4 Phase/segregation safeguards: for each composition, include (a) seeded WCF, (b) unseeded WCF, and (c) no-fabric solution synthesis under identical conditions. If phase segregation occurs in solution controls but not on fabric, this supports seed-templated growth. If segregation persists, reduce fluorinated fraction or slow kinetics (increase modulator; decrease concentration; more gradual feeding).

Step 4 — Defect engineering as a hypothesis-driven variable (not assumed monotonic)
4.1 Create a controlled defect series by varying modulator identity/concentration and by optional post-synthetic benzoate/acid treatment (80–120 °C) while tracking missing-linker density and microstrain.
4.2 Explicit competing-mechanism test: defects may (A) increase quenching via trap states or (B) increase O2 transport by opening pathways. The plan is to map defect metrics to *both* transport (O2 uptake/diffusion proxies) and photophysics (triplet lifetime, ΦΔ) to identify the optimum (not necessarily ‘minimum defects’).

Step 5 — Hard mechanistic validation required by reviewers (spatial distribution, defects, epitaxy, local O2, and wetting/contact)
5.1 Mixed-linker spatial distribution and phase homogeneity (shell-specific):
  - Solid-state NMR: 19F ssNMR to confirm fluorinated linker incorporation; 13C ssNMR for carboxylate/porphyrin environments; if feasible, 19F–13C correlation/REDOR-type proximity experiments to test whether fluorinated aromatic moieties are in the same framework domain as porphyrin carbons (evidence against macroscopic phase separation).
  - Cross-sectional STEM-EDS/EELS mapping: F mapping across the MOF thickness to confirm outer-shell enrichment (in gradient architecture) or uniform distribution (in homogeneous architecture), and to detect F-rich segregated crystallites.
  - Depth-profile XPS or ToF-SIMS: quantify F:Zr and F:C vs sputter depth to validate a true fluorinated shell rather than patchy incorporation; compare to total loading from digestion NMR.
5.2 Defect density quantification (orthogonal, quantitative):
  - Digestion 1H NMR: digest MOF coating (acidic digestion) and quantify TCPP vs modulator/benzoate content to compute missing-linker and capping-ligand fractions.
  - TGA-based missing-linker estimates: compare residue profiles across defect series to estimate framework composition changes.
  - PDF or synchrotron PXRD microstrain analysis: quantify microstrain/broadening indicative of mixed-linker strain or defect distributions; correlate with shell growth conditions.
  - Correlate these defect metrics with triplet lifetimes (transient absorption) and ΦΔ (1270 nm 1O2 phosphorescence) to determine whether defect reduction increases or decreases effective Type II yield and under what humidity/protein conditions.
5.3 Validate epitaxial secondary growth vs homogeneous nucleation:
  - In situ monitoring: (i) time-resolved turbidity and/or DLS on mother liquor during growth to detect onset of homogeneous nucleation, (ii) mass-gain kinetics on fabric (gravimetric uptake vs time) comparing seeded vs unseeded WCF.
  - Cross-sectional TEM: look for coherent intergrowth/continuous crystalline overlayer rather than discrete, weakly attached crystallites; confirm by lattice/fringe continuity where possible.
5.4 Local O2 partitioning/transport (decouple MOF microenvironment from textile boundary layers):
  - O2 sorption on isolated MOF scraped/detached from fabric (or parallel powder synthesized under identical chemistry) under dry and controlled humidity to quantify fluorination-dependent O2 uptake.
  - Pore-tethered O2 probe approach: incorporate or post-load an oxygen-quenchable phosphorescent probe that resides within pores (or tethered to internal sites) so measured O2 quenching reflects pore-local O2 rather than external boundary layers; perform humidity-dependent Stern–Volmer analysis.
  - Humidity-dependent diffusion proxy: compare O2-response time constants of the pore probe across shells (0–30% F; gradient vs homogeneous) to quantify effective O2 permeability in the MOF microenvironment.
5.5 Wetting and bacteria-contact tradeoffs (ensure hydrophobicity does not reduce interfacial aPDI):
  - Contact angle (static/dynamic) on coated WCF; water uptake/swelling metrics.
  - Protein adsorption assays (e.g., BSA adsorption) to evaluate formation of quenching biofilms at the surface.
  - Bacterial adhesion quantification (S. aureus attachment under dark conditions) to ensure the fluorinated outer shell does not repel bacteria to the extent that ROS delivery becomes diffusion-limited.

Step 6 — Photophysics and Type II confirmation (tight linkage to structure/defects/O2)
6.1 Singlet oxygen quantification: primary metric is time-resolved 1O2 phosphorescence at 1270 nm to obtain ΦΔ and lifetime; secondary chemical probes (DPBF/ABDA) used only as supporting kinetics.
6.2 Triplet-state kinetics: transient absorption to measure porphyrin T1 lifetime; perform under controlled humidity and in protein-containing media to mimic biological quenching conditions.
6.3 ROS pathway discrimination: EPR TEMP→TEMPO for 1O2; scavenger set (NaN3 for 1O2; catalase/SOD for H2O2/O2•−) to exclude Type I dominance, explicitly checking whether any heavy-atom tuning increases Type I signals.

Step 7 — Antibacterial aPDI against Staphylococcus aureus and durability
7.1 Standardized aPDI assays (ATCC-6538): spectrally matched irradiation to porphyrin absorption (report irradiance and dose in J/cm2); log-reduction vs time; dose–response fitting. Include dark, light-only, and MOF-free fabric controls.
7.2 Interface evidence: live/dead staining and SEM of bacteria on fibers; correlate kill rate with ΦΔ × (pore-local O2 metric) × (adhesion/contact metric).
7.3 Reuse testing: repeated illumination + washing cycles (detergent/saline); track PXRD crystallinity, Zr/porphyrin leaching (ICP-OES/UV–vis of wash), and retained ΦΔ and kill rate.

Step 8 — Structure–function integration and decision criteria
8.1 Multivariate model: predict kill rate using measured triplet lifetime, ΦΔ(1270 nm), pore-local O2 parameter (probe quenching / sorption), defect density (digestion NMR/TGA/PDF), shell thickness/continuity, and bacterial adhesion. Identify (i) optimal fluorinated fraction and (ii) optimal defect window.
8.2 Go/no-go triggers: if fluorination reduces adhesion/wetting enough to reduce aPDI despite higher ΦΔ, pivot to gradient shells with fluorination restricted to an intermediate layer (retain hydrophilic outermost surface) or reduce F fraction while keeping defect/adhesion gains.
Feasibility: 1) Mechanistic claims are made testable and non-overreaching: Fluorination is not assumed to help by ‘hydrophobicity’ alone; it must (a) be spatially verified within the shell (ToF-SIMS/depth XPS + STEM F-maps + 19F/13C ssNMR) and (b) measurably increase pore-local O2 metrics (O2 sorption and pore-tethered probe quenching) under relevant humidity/protein conditions. This directly addresses reviewer concern that fluorinated linkers could be dispersed, patchy, or not proximal to photoactive domains.
2) Defects are treated as a tunable parameter with competing effects, not a monotonic ‘healing improves ΦΔ’ assumption. Quantitative missing-linker/capping-ligand metrics (digestion 1H NMR, TGA) plus PDF/microstrain analysis create a rigorous defect descriptor set. Correlating these to triplet lifetimes and 1270 nm ΦΔ under controlled humidity explicitly tests whether defects primarily act as quenchers, O2-transport enhancers, or both—thereby converting a reviewer-flagged uncertainty into a discovery axis with a defined optimum.
3) Mixed-linker epitaxial secondary growth is explicitly de-risked. The plan includes in situ nucleation monitoring (turbidity/DLS), seeded vs unseeded mass-gain kinetics, and cross-sectional TEM evidence for intergrowth to distinguish true secondary growth from homogeneous nucleation/independent crystallite deposition. The radial-gradient strategy (pure PCN-224 inner layer followed by fluorinated outer growth) further reduces microstrain/segregation risk by maintaining lattice match at the seed interface while still creating an F-enriched region relevant to O2 partitioning.
4) O2 measurements are localized to the MOF microenvironment rather than conflated with textile boundary layers. By combining (i) O2 sorption on isolated MOF produced under matched conditions and (ii) pore-resident O2-quenchable probe readouts with humidity dependence, the fluorination effect on pore-local O2 is isolated from macroscopic fabric effects.
5) Interfacial function is safeguarded by explicit wetting and contact assays. Contact angle, protein adsorption, and bacterial adhesion measurements ensure that hydration-repelling design does not reduce bacteria–MOF proximity or create an interfacial diffusion barrier that negates higher ΦΔ. This directly closes the reviewer-identified risk that hydrophobicity could impair ROS delivery.
6) The overall concept chain remains intact and strengthened: secondary-growth (architectural locking + defect/strain control) → validated mixed-linker shell microenvironment → Type II photosensitization enhancement (triplet lifetime + pore-local O2) → higher singlet oxygen flux at the bacteria–textile interface → improved S. aureus aPDI and reusability.
final_critique: Methodologically, the proposal is unusually well de-risked for MOF-on-textile secondary growth: it includes seeded vs unseeded kinetics, solution-only controls for homogeneous nucleation, and multiple orthogonal composition/defect assays tied to photophysics (T1 lifetime, ΦΔ via 1270 nm). The main scientific vulnerability is that the central causal claim—fluorinated-linker enrichment increases *pore-proximal* O2 and reduces quenching at the porphyrin site under biologically relevant hydration/protein conditions—remains only indirectly inferred from sorption/probe readouts. None of the listed measurements directly quantifies (i) local water activity/occupancy in the porphyrinic pores under humid/buffered conditions, nor (ii) oxygen concentration *at the same loci* as the photoactive porphyrins during irradiation. Also, the feasibility of high-quality cross-sectional TEM lattice-continuity evidence on a rough, beam-sensitive cotton/MOF composite is optimistic; without a clearly stated sample-prep pathway (embedding, ultramicrotomy/FIB, cryo options), this validation could fail and weaken the epitaxy claim. Finally, bacterial kill is modeled as ΦΔ × O2 × adhesion, but ROS delivery is additionally governed by 1O2 escape length and interfacial geometry; the plan lacks a direct assay of interfacial 1O2 flux/escape (vs in-pore generation) that would discriminate ‘higher ΦΔ in pores’ from ‘effective 1O2 reaching cells’.

original_chain: Proton carrier -> Electrical conductivity -> Diffusion coefficient -> Zr(dcphOH-NDI) -> Proton-responsive behavior -> Proton-coupled electron transfer -> Ti8O8(OH)(4)(bdc)(6)
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a confined, tethered proton-carrier network into electroactive Zr(dcphOH-NDI) thin films will induce a humidity-tolerant proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) regime that increases the effective charge-hopping diffusion coefficient and thus electrical conductivity. The key methodological adaptation is a post-synthetic ‘node-anchored proton carrier grafting’ strategy: selectively converting a controlled fraction of Zr6(μ3-OH) node sites into covalently bound sulfonate/phosphonate-acid pendants (fixed proton reservoirs) while simultaneously preserving NDI π-stacks for electron hopping. Mechanistically, the tethered acids create a continuous, low-reorganization-energy H-bond network that (i) supplies proximal protons to NDI redox sites, stabilizing reduced NDI states by local protonation (PCET gating) and (ii) raises the population of charge-compensating mobile counterions/protons inside pores, thereby increasing the Marcus hopping rate (kET) and the apparent diffusion coefficient (Dapp) extracted from electrochemical methods. This will outperform water-only (vehicular) proton conduction by enforcing a Grotthuss-like relay in the pore and by synchronizing proton motion with linker-to-linker electron hopping.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Synthesize Zr(dcphOH-NDI) following reported UiO/PIZOF-topology conditions and fabricate oriented thin films on FTO (solvothermal growth on functionalized FTO to maximize film adhesion and minimize grain-boundary resistance).
1.2 Establish a baseline: measure (a) redox accessibility of NDI sites, (b) proton-responsive pKa behavior (potentiometric titration), (c) conductivity vs RH and temperature (EIS), and (d) baseline Dapp for charge propagation (CV peak-current scaling + chronoamperometry/Cottrell analysis) in buffered aqueous and mixed aqueous/anhydrous electrolytes.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Create a calibrated density of node-reactive handles without collapsing the framework: perform mild modulated-acid defect engineering to increase accessible Zr–OH/terminal OH sites (quantify via digestion 1H NMR and TGA/elemental analysis).
2.2 Node-anchored proton carrier grafting (core adaptation): expose films to bifunctional acid carriers that bind strongly to Zr(IV) while leaving a free acid group as a tethered proton source. Two graft families will be compared:
  (i) Sulfonate-terminated phosphonates (e.g., HO3P–(CH2)n–SO3H) to ensure irreversible Zr–O–P anchoring while presenting –SO3H as a strong acid proton reservoir.
  (ii) Bis(phosphonic acid) linkers with one phosphonate bound and one left free (achieved by steric control and sub-stoichiometric dosing) to create pendant –PO3H2.
2.3 Spatial confinement tuning: vary chain length (n = 2–6) and grafting fraction (e.g., 0%, 5%, 10%, 20% of accessible node sites) to tune H-bond continuity and avoid pore blocking.
2.4 Mechanistic PCET gating test: measure NDI redox potentials and kinetic parameters as a function of pH/RH before and after grafting. A successful PCET regime is indicated by (a) systematic potential shifts consistent with protonation-coupled reduction, (b) reduced peak separation in CV at matched scan rates (faster heterogeneous/film transport), and (c) diminished dependence of conductivity on external water activity.
2.5 Optional cross-material control leveraging Ti8O8 chemistry: prepare a MIL-125(NH2) or MIL-125 analogue and introduce the same tethered acids to test whether Ti8O8(OH)4 nodes can similarly support PCET-assisted charge storage/transport; use this as a mechanistic comparator (node identity vs linker identity).

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structural integrity and graft verification: PXRD (phase retention), N2 sorption (pore accessibility), ATR-IR/XPS (P–O–Zr, S 2p signatures), solid-state 31P NMR (anchoring environment), and SEM cross-sections (film continuity).
3.2 Quantify proton mobility vs electron mobility: (a) H/D isotope effect on conductivity and on Dapp; (b) variable-temperature EIS to extract activation energies—lower Ea after grafting supports Grotthuss/PCET facilitation rather than purely vehicular transport.
3.3 Extract diffusion coefficients and link to conductivity: determine Dapp from electrochemical methods (chronoamperometry and CV with diffusion-controlled peak scaling in thin films) and compare to EIS-derived transport resistances; correlate Dapp with graft density and chain length.
3.4 Mechanism discrimination: compare performance under anhydrous protic ionic liquids vs humid air; if tethered acids maintain high conductivity with reduced RH sensitivity, this supports fixed-carrier proton relays rather than water-mediated vehicular transport.
3.5 Benchmarking: compare against ungrafted Zr(dcphOH-NDI) and against a non-proton-responsive NDI-MOF analogue (lacking –OH groups) to isolate the synergy of (i) intrinsic proton responsiveness and (ii) tethered carrier network.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Zr(dcphOH-NDI) already exhibits proton-responsive behavior (distinct pKa values) and diffusion-controlled linker-to-linker charge hopping with measurable diffusion coefficients in thin films, indicating that transport is limited by coupled ion/electron motion. Solid-state proton conductor literature shows that fixed acidic functionalities and continuous H-bond networks increase proton conductivity and can shift mechanisms toward Grotthuss-like transfer. Redox-hopping MOF studies demonstrate that conductivity can be rationalized via an apparent diffusion coefficient (Marcus hopping picture), which is tunable by microstructure and local environment.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Zr(IV) nodes strongly bind phosphonates (robust Zr–O–P bonds), enabling a chemically precise, node-anchored grafting approach without requiring full linker exchange. This is a MOF-native adaptation: it modifies the internal pore environment and node chemistry while preserving the crystalline topology and NDI redox lattice.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike adding free acids or relying on absorbed water (which can leach, phase-separate, or introduce uncontrolled ionic strength), tethered proton carriers provide (i) non-leaching, spatially confined proton reservoirs, (ii) tunable acid density and relay distance, and (iii) direct PCET facilitation at NDI sites. The expected outcome is higher Dapp and conductivity with reduced humidity dependence and improved operational stability relative to ungrafted films and to water-mediated proton conduction alone.
final_critique: This is a technically sophisticated and largely coherent proposal that demonstrates strong command of redox-hopping MOF electrochemistry and solid-state proton transport. The engineering plan is unusually detailed for a hypothesis-driven study, particularly in its treatment of thin-film electrochemical diffusion analysis, graft-density control, and isotope/temperature mechanistic discrimination. The logical core—tethered acids lowering reorganization energy and synchronizing proton motion with NDI electron hopping—is plausible and well-motivated. However, several mechanistic assumptions are asserted more strongly than they are justified. In particular, the link between increased internal proton population and an increased Marcus hopping rate is treated qualitatively; the proposal does not rigorously distinguish whether observed increases in Dapp arise from faster intrinsic electron self-exchange, improved ionic compensation, or reduced percolation bottlenecks. Additionally, while Grotthuss-like behavior is invoked, the proposal does not specify how proton hopping length scales compare to NDI–NDI distances, leaving ambiguity as to whether true concerted PCET is achieved versus sequential ET/PT. The Ti8O8 comparator is conceptually valuable but underdeveloped in terms of expected divergence in node acidity and proton affinity.

original_chain: Zr6-based MOF -> Water stability -> Phosphonic acid -> Activation energy -> Disulfhydrylbenzene-1,4-dicarboxylic acid -> N,N-dimethylformamide -> Metastable MOF-5 analogues
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A Zr6-based MOF constructed from a mixed-linker node-architecture—where 2,5-disulfhydrylbenzene-1,4-dicarboxylate (DSBDC) provides redox/thiol-rich microenvironments while a phosphonic-acid SALI layer partially caps Zr6 node –OH/H2O sites—will exhibit (i) superior water stability and (ii) lower apparent activation energy for proton/charge transport under humid conditions. The core mechanism is a cooperative, two-level stabilization/transport design: (1) phosphonate anchoring (strong Zr–O–P bonding) reduces capillary-condensation-driven pore collapse by decreasing hydrophilic defect density and controlling water uptake hysteresis at the node; (2) DSBDC introduces a hydrogen-bondable, polarizable thiol/disulfide sub-network that organizes confined water into continuous H-bond chains, enabling low-barrier Grotthuss-type proton hopping (and/or mixed-valent hopping if redox states are engaged), thereby reducing activation energy. Methodological adaptation: replace conventional post-synthetic ligand exchange/defect engineering with a kinetically gated, sequential SALI strategy performed in DMF that intentionally exploits DMF’s coordination dynamics to transiently open Zr6 coordination sites, enabling spatially biased phosphonate installation (node capping) without eroding framework crystallinity—yielding a metastability-controlled, MOF-5-analogue-like ‘dynamic coordination’ regime but translated to robust Zr6 nodes.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1. Synthesize microcrystalline Zr6 MOF scaffold (NU-1000-like topology or UiO-type with accessible Zr6–OH/H2O sites) using a mixed-linker feed: (A) terephthalate (BDC) to preserve high-connectivity scaffold formation and (B) DSBDC as a minority functional linker (e.g., 5–30 mol% of total dicarboxylate) to embed thiol/disulfide functionality while maintaining crystallinity.
1.2. Control DSBDC redox state: prepare two batches—(i) reduced dithiol form (protected/deprotected as needed to avoid disulfide scrambling during solvothermal synthesis) and (ii) oxidized disulfide-rich form—so transport/stability can be correlated with thiol chemistry.
1.3. Solvent history standardization: exchange as-synthesized solids into anhydrous DMF to establish a reproducible coordination environment at Zr6 nodes prior to functionalization.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1. Kinetically gated sequential SALI in DMF (adaptation):
- Use DMF as a transiently coordinating medium to modulate Zr6 node lability (via reversible DMF binding) and thereby control access to node –OH/H2O sites.
- Introduce a mono-/di-phosphonic acid (e.g., phenylphosphonic acid or perfluoroalkyl phosphonic acid for hydrophobization) under strictly metered equivalents relative to node –OH count, at moderate temperature (e.g., 60–90 °C) to favor Zr–O–P formation while minimizing linker displacement.
- Implement a two-pulse dosing protocol: Pulse 1 installs a sub-monolayer (partial capping) to reduce hydrophilic defect density; Pulse 2 installs a second fraction only if water sorption hysteresis remains high. Between pulses, wash in DMF to remove weakly adsorbed phosphonic acid.
2.2. Create a metastability window (MOF-5 analogue concept translated): intentionally retain a controlled amount of DMF coordinated at nodes after SALI (do not fully activate), generating a metastable but processable state where node coordination remains dynamic. Then perform programmed activation (vacuum + temperature ramp) to lock the phosphonate-capped node structure without capillary-stress collapse.
2.3. Comparative controls:
- Control A: parent Zr6 MOF (no DSBDC, no phosphonate).
- Control B: DSBDC-incorporated only (no phosphonate).
- Control C: phosphonate SALI only (no DSBDC).
- Control D: carboxylate SALI (benzoate) vs phosphonate SALI to isolate Zr–O–P bonding effects.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1. Structural/chemical verification:
- PXRD for crystallinity retention pre/post SALI and after humidity cycling.
- Pair distribution function (PDF) and/or total scattering to detect local node changes (Zr–O–P formation).
- Solid-state NMR (31P for phosphonate binding; 13C for linker environment; 1H to probe –OH populations).
- XPS/ICP to quantify P loading and S content; thiol/disulfide state via XPS S 2p and Raman.
3.2. Water stability and capillary condensation mechanism tests:
- Dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) with multiple adsorption/desorption cycles at controlled RH; quantify hysteresis area and uptake kinetics.
- Post-cycling PXRD + N2 sorption to measure pore retention.
- In situ IR (OH stretch region) during water dosing to observe node hydration changes with/without phosphonate capping.
3.3. Activation energy determination (transport):
- Proton conductivity by AC impedance under controlled RH (e.g., 60–98% RH) and temperature range (e.g., 20–80 °C). Extract activation energies from Arrhenius plots.
- Optional: electronic/ionic decoupling via H/D isotope effect (H2O vs D2O) to confirm Grotthuss contribution.
3.4. Mechanistic falsification/confirmation:
- Correlate P-loading with reduced hysteresis (capillary-stress mitigation) and with conductivity vs RH.
- Compare reduced vs oxidized DSBDC states: if thiol-rich variants produce lower Ea and larger isotope effect, this supports water-mediated proton wire formation enhanced by thiol H-bonding/polarizability.
- Evaluate whether phosphonate capping preserves or improves conductivity by preventing catastrophic pore collapse while maintaining sufficient internal water ordering.
3.5. Success criteria:
- >90% PXRD crystallinity retained after ≥10 DVS water cycles at high RH.
- Significant reduction in water sorption hysteresis relative to uncapped controls.
- Activation energy for proton transport approaching the low-Ea regime (target: ≤0.25 eV under high RH) with clear isotope effect supporting Grotthuss transport.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Zr6-node MOFs are established as among the most water-stable MOFs; however, capillary condensation can still induce pore collapse. Node functionalization (SALI) is empirically known to reduce hysteresis and improve cyclic water stability by modulating pore environment and node chemistry (Asset 1). Separately, phosphonate-based MOFs with free phosphonic acid groups can sustain humid environments and exhibit low activation energies for proton conduction via structured water networks (Asset 2), motivating phosphonate chemistry as both a stability and transport lever.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal transfers the concept of solvent-enabled dynamic coordination (highlighted in DMF-containing MOF-5 environments enabling metastable transformations; Asset 4) into a Zr6-node context as a deliberate kinetic gate for SALI. DMF is used not merely as a solvent but as a transient ligand that tunes node lability, enabling controlled installation of strongly binding phosphonates (Zr–O–P) without framework damage—an explicit methodological adaptation that targets the known limitation of uncontrolled functionalization leading to pore blockage or degradation.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to (i) unfunctionalized Zr6 MOFs, the phosphonate-capped nodes should show reduced capillary-stress susceptibility and improved long-term water cycling. Compared to (ii) purely phosphonate-based frameworks, retaining a Zr6 carboxylate scaffold preserves high connectivity and robustness while DSBDC introduces additional H-bond/soft-donor microenvironments to lower transport barriers. Compared to (iii) simple benzoate SALI, phosphonate SALI provides stronger, more hydrolysis-resistant anchoring at Zr nodes, and the sequential, DMF-gated protocol enables fine control over capping density to avoid over-hydrophobization or pore occlusion. Overall, the design couples water-stability engineering (node capping) with mechanistically motivated low-Ea transport pathways (thiol-structured water wires), rather than treating stability and conductivity as separate optimization problems.
final_critique: This is a technically ambitious and largely well-grounded proposal that demonstrates strong command of Zr6-node chemistry, SALI methodology, and proton transport mechanisms in humid MOFs. The engineering resolution is high: sequential, metered phosphonate SALI in DMF with explicit temperature, solvent-history control, and diagnostic checkpoints is realistic and non-trivial. The logical framework—decoupling water-stability engineering (phosphonate node capping) from transport optimization (DSBDC-organized water wires)—is internally consistent and addresses a genuine domain bottleneck. However, some mechanistic claims remain partially inferential rather than rigorously constrained. In particular, the assumption that thiol/disulfide sub-networks will reliably organize continuous proton wires inside Zr6 pores is plausible but not guaranteed without pore-scale spatial modeling or explicit spectroscopic signatures of water ordering beyond conductivity/isotope effects. Additionally, the analogy to MOF-5 metastability, while conceptually appealing, risks overextension: Zr6 clusters do not undergo coordination lability on the same energetic landscape as Zn4O nodes, and the proposal would benefit from clearer bounds on how much 'dynamic coordination' is realistically achievable without irreversible phosphonate overbinding or linker displacement. These issues do not undermine feasibility, but they temper the strength of the causal claims.

original_chain: Energetic interaction -> Monte Carlo simulation -> Metal organic framework -> Monte Carlo simulation -> Pore volume
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A MOF’s functional pore volume under realistic humid, multicomponent streams is not set by geometric free volume but by an emergent, composition-dependent *accessible connected volume* that collapses when hydrogen-bonded water clusters nucleate at a small subset of high-energy sites (open-metal-site (OMS) pockets, pocket throats/windows) and then percolate to block the connected diffusion network. We hypothesize that a *sub-monolayer fluorocarbon (CFx) lining that is spatially biased toward these nucleation hot-spots* suppresses the nucleation rate and continuity of water networks (raising the RH/permeation threshold for percolation) while preserving adsorption capacity for target gases that bind primarily at other sites (e.g., CO2 in larger cages; NH3 at OMS but with reduced water-mediated hydrolysis).

Mechanistic rationale addressing reviewer concerns: CFx installed by PECVD is *quenched* on experimental timescales; therefore, the correct statistical representation is an ensemble over quenched-disorder realizations (different fixed CFx spatial distributions at the same global coverage), not a dynamically responsive surface. The proposal overcomes the limitations of static pore metrics and static GCMC by explicitly (i) representing heterogeneous, experimentally constrained CFx distributions as quenched disorder; (ii) computing adsorption and water-network percolation on each realization under humid co-adsorbate conditions; and (iii) rigorously defining and validating a preregistered percolation/connectivity observable with uncertainty bounds. An annealed (GC/SGMC) variant will be used only as an *upper-bound idealization* to quantify how much performance is lost due to kinetic trapping of CFx distributions (difference between annealed and quenched ensembles).
Plan: Step 0 — Preregistration of observables and uncertainty handling (addresses ill-posed “threshold RH”).
0.1 Define the primary percolation observable *before* simulation/experiments: the probability of a connected, probe-accessible path spanning the unit cell (or a 2×2×2 supercell) through the void network after removing voxels occupied by adsorbates.
0.2 Fix probe radii and justification: r_CO2 = 1.65 Å (kinetic diameter 3.3 Å), r_H2O = 1.40 Å, r_NH3 = 1.30 Å. Report sensitivity by ±0.1 Å.
0.3 Define occupancy-to-void thresholding: an adsorbate blocks a voxel if the minimum distance from voxel center to any guest atom is < (r_vdw(atom)+r_probe). Use a 3D grid resolution of 0.20 Å; verify convergence at 0.15 Å and 0.25 Å.
0.4 Connectivity algorithm: union–find on a periodic grid; percolation occurs if a connected component spans across periodic boundaries in x, y, and z (report anisotropy for HKUST-1 if needed).
0.5 Sampling frequency: compute connectivity every 5×10^4 MC steps after equilibration; obtain ≥200 independent snapshots per state point by block-averaging autocorrelation time.
0.6 Define “RH_perc” as the RH where P(percolating void for target probe) drops below 0.5; compute 95% confidence intervals by bootstrap over snapshots and over disorder realizations.
0.7 Validation system: reproduce published water uptake/hysteresis and qualitative cluster formation in pristine HKUST-1 (Cu-BTC) and compare to at least one reference MOF with known hydrophobic pores (e.g., ZIF-8) to validate that the percolation observable tracks expected water-network behavior.

Step 1 — System selection and atomistic structural models (two MOFs; three CFx distribution families; quenched disorder).
1.1 Select MOFs: (i) Cu-BTC (HKUST-1) as the water-sensitive OMS benchmark with prior PFH PECVD stabilization evidence; (ii) a high-pore-volume Zr6 MOF with proven synthetic tractability and large cages (e.g., NU-1103/UiO-derived high-porosity analogue) to test generality across node chemistry and pore size.
1.2 Define CFx “sites” on the framework (discrete site-state variable):
  - OMS-adjacent pocket sites: near Cu paddlewheel axial region for HKUST-1; near Zr6 node face/capping positions in Zr MOF.
  - Window/throat sites: narrow apertures between cages.
  - Linker-adjacent wall sites: low-energy nucleation areas.
Each site corresponds to a chemically plausible anchoring location for PECVD fragments (CFx bound/adsorbed to node-proximal hydroxyls/defects or physisorbed fragments), represented as a fixed fragment with defined nonbonded parameters.
1.3 Generate quenched CFx distributions under experimentally measurable constraints (coverage and bias): create an ensemble of N=50–200 realizations per condition at fixed global coverage θ (e.g., 0.05, 0.10, 0.20 monolayer-equivalent of defined sites), with three families:
  - Uniform: random placement over all sites.
  - OMS-biased: higher probability at OMS-adjacent sites (tunable bias factor b_OMS).
  - Window-biased: higher probability at throat/window sites (bias b_win).
Implement as constrained random fields with pair-correlation control (optional) to reflect clustering vs dispersion; quantify each realization by spatial statistics measurable/inferrable experimentally (site occupancy fractions f_OMS, f_win, f_wall; and nearest-neighbor CFx–CFx distribution).
1.4 (Upper-bound comparator) Annealed “GC/SGMC”:
  - Only to compute the thermodynamic optimum distribution at fixed θ and compare with quenched results. Interpret as an idealized limit if CFx could rearrange; report Δperformance = annealed − quenched to quantify kinetic-trapping penalty.

Step 2 — Force-field strategy staged to avoid parameter degeneracy (hard benchmark ladder).
2.1 Stage A (minimal viable accuracy; single-guest water + framework + CFx):
  - Framework: use validated MOF force fields (e.g., UFF4MOF/MOF-FF style) with fixed charges; for HKUST-1 include specific parameters for Cu OMS interactions.
  - Water: use a rigid model with good adsorption transferability (TIP4P/2005 as baseline). H-bonding is inherently captured by the water model; do not add ad hoc “explicit H-bond terms.”
  - CFx fragment: parameterize Lennard–Jones + partial charges from DFT (see 2.3) for representative CF2/CF3 moieties; keep CFx rigid and immobile.
  - Validate against: (i) water adsorption isotherm shape and approximate heat of adsorption trend for pristine HKUST-1; (ii) qualitative suppression of water uptake upon adding pore-occupying hydrophobe (as in the PFH plasma literature asset).
2.2 Stage B (add CO2 and NH3 separately; still no polarization):
  - CO2: use an established 3-site model (TraPPE/Equiv.) validated on MOFs.
  - NH3: use a standard transferable model; validate strongly at OMS.
  - Validate sequentially: pure-component isotherms and isosteric heats (qst) for CO2 and NH3 in pristine MOFs; then repeat for one CFx coverage to ensure trends are captured without refitting multiple parameters.
2.3 Hard benchmark set for DFT (predefined, small, identifiable):
  - Cluster models: (i) HKUST-1 paddlewheel + nearest linkers; (ii) Zr6 node fragment + linker stubs; (iii) window fragment.
  - Compute adsorption energies (DFT+D3 or vdW-inclusive) for H2O, CO2, NH3 at: OMS pocket, window, wall, and CFx-lined variants of those sites (CFx placed as in the atomistic model).
  - Target accuracy: reproduce DFT relative site ordering (which sites are most attractive) and energy differences within ~2–3 kJ/mol; use these as constraints to tune only a limited subset of parameters (CFx charges/LJ; OMS guest parameters if needed).
2.4 Stage C (mixtures and humidity competition; one binary minimum before ternary):
  - Validate one binary mixture isotherm/uptake trend experimentally and in simulation: CO2/H2O at fixed RH or NH3/H2O at fixed RH (choose based on experimental practicality and safety). Only after passing this gate proceed to ternary (CO2/NH3/H2O) predictions.
2.5 Only if needed: introduce a lightweight polarization proxy (charge scaling near OMS) *after* Stages A–C, and only if benchmark residuals show systematic OMS errors (avoid high-dimensional fitting).

Step 3 — Adsorption + percolation computations under quenched disorder.
3.1 For each MOF, coverage θ, and distribution family (uniform/OMS/window), run multi-component GCMC at relevant T (e.g., 298 K) over a grid of RH (via water fugacity) and target-gas fugacities.
3.2 For each quenched realization i: compute (a) uptake isotherms; (b) spatial density maps; (c) percolation observables for each probe; (d) water cluster statistics (cluster size distribution using hydrogen-bond criterion: O–O < 3.5 Å and angle criterion).
3.3 Disorder averaging: report ensemble means and variances over realizations; propagate uncertainty to RH_perc and selectivity metrics.
3.4 Identify design rules: map performance to the measurable distribution descriptors (f_OMS, f_win, correlation length). Output: minimal θ that achieves a target RH_perc shift without >X% loss in CO2 capacity.

Step 4 — Experimental synthesis tightly coupled to model variables (coverage + bias, and a measurement-to-site-state map).
4.1 Synthesis:
  - Prepare crystalline HKUST-1 and selected Zr6 MOF with controlled defect density (especially for Zr MOF where node –OH/H2O sites affect nucleation).
  - Apply PFH PECVD with controlled dose (power, time, pulse duty cycle) to reach target θ values. Prepare three experimental “bias modes” that correspond to model families:
    (i) Uniform-ish infiltration (longer exposure / higher pressure to favor diffusion);
    (ii) Window/mouth-biased (short pulses, lower diffusion time; favor deposition near external surface/pore entrances);
    (iii) OMS-biased (precondition with mild dehydration to expose OMS and promote stronger CFx anchoring near metal-adjacent regions, while limiting bulk filling).
4.2 Quantify global CFx loading θ: elemental analysis + 19F quantitative solid-state NMR; corroborate by XPS (surface) to separate external vs internal enrichment.
4.3 Add at least one intrapore spatial heterogeneity method with a quantitative mapping to site-state variables:
  - Primary: 19F–13C (and/or 19F–1H) solid-state NMR correlation (e.g., REDOR/HETCOR) to infer proximity of CFx to linker carbons vs OMS-adjacent protons/waters; convert to estimated fractions f_wall vs f_OMS using calibration samples (known external-only vs infiltrated coatings).
  - Optional/secondary (if available): neutron diffraction or total scattering with D2O to visualize preferential water siting changes upon CFx; or adsorption microcalorimetry under controlled humidity to detect suppression of high-enthalpy initial water uptake sites.
4.4 Adsorption/percolation-linked measurements:
  - Water vapor isotherms + hysteresis; in situ PXRD under humidity for structural retention.
  - Mixed-gas uptake under humidity (at least one binary gate test): CO2/H2O or NH3/H2O.
  - Kinetic uptake (gravimetric or breakthrough) to detect connectivity loss consistent with percolation predictions.
4.5 Model–experiment reconciliation:
  - Use measured θ and inferred (f_OMS, f_win, f_wall) to select the corresponding quenched ensemble (or reweight realizations) and compare predicted vs measured isotherms and RH_perc proxies (e.g., sharp drop in diffusion/uptake rate or accessible pore volume from sorption hysteresis).

Step 5 — Deliverables and success criteria (quantitative, aligned with preregistered metrics).
5.1 Demonstrate, for at least HKUST-1 and one Zr6 MOF, that biased CFx distributions shift RH_perc upward relative to both pristine and uniform CFx at equal θ, with 95% CI.
5.2 Maintain target-gas capacity: CO2 uptake loss <15% at application fugacity (or define application-specific constraint), while humidity stability improves (PXRD retention and cyclic adsorption).
5.3 Produce a validated, disorder-aware predictive map: (θ, f_OMS, f_win) → {RH_perc, capacity, selectivity} and provide a recommended experimental operating window (PECVD recipe targets expressed as measurable coverage + NMR-inferred bias descriptors).
Feasibility: 1) Correct physical interpretation (addresses SG “mobility” inconsistency): CFx is treated as quenched disorder. The computational workflow explicitly generates *fixed* CFx spatial realizations constrained by experimentally measurable coverage statistics and bias descriptors, then performs GCMC/percolation on each and averages. An annealed GC/SGMC calculation is retained only as an idealized upper bound to quantify the maximum achievable benefit if rearrangement were possible; it is not claimed to represent experimental kinetics.

2) Parameter identifiability and validation ladder (addresses force-field overreach): the force-field plan is staged with hard gates: (A) water-only + CFx with minimal parameters; (B) add CO2 and NH3 separately and validate pure-component isotherms/qst; (C) validate at least one binary humid mixture before any ternary prediction; polarization is optional and only introduced if residuals show a systematic OMS error. This reduces dimensionality and parameter degeneracy while remaining faithful to the mechanism (water clustering at hot-spots).

3) Well-posed percolation metric with uncertainty (addresses probe/grid sensitivity): the proposal preregisters probe radii, grid resolution and convergence checks, occupancy-blocking rules, a specific spanning-cluster algorithm, sampling frequency, and bootstrap confidence intervals across both MC snapshots and disorder realizations. The metric is validated on pristine HKUST-1 and a hydrophobic reference MOF to ensure it tracks known water-network behavior.

4) Measurable mapping from “patterning” to model site states (addresses experimental comparability): beyond XPS/IR, the plan adds quantitative 19F solid-state NMR correlations to infer whether CFx is preferentially near linkers vs node/OMS environments and to estimate site-occupancy fractions (f_OMS, f_win, f_wall). These descriptors directly parameterize/reweight the quenched ensembles, enabling one-to-one comparison between experiment and simulation and preventing untestable claims about intrapore patterning.

5) Strong empirical anchor (ties to provided literature assets): the PFH-plasma stabilization of Cu-BTC and the Monte Carlo finding that hydrophobe pore occupation suppresses water cluster formation provide direct precedent for the central mechanism. The proposed advance is not “more GCMC,” but a disorder-aware, connectivity-defined framework that converts energetic site selectivity (where water nucleates) into a quantitative, testable design rule for where limited hydrophobization should be placed to prevent percolation-driven accessibility collapse while preserving target adsorption.
final_critique: This is an unusually rigorous and well-structured proposal that directly addresses long-standing ambiguities in defining pore accessibility under humidity. The treatment of CFx as quenched disorder is logically correct and resolves a common but often unacknowledged inconsistency in surface-modified MOF simulations. The preregistration of percolation observables, probe definitions, grid convergence, and uncertainty propagation is exemplary and elevates the computational work beyond descriptive GCMC. Minor deductions arise from (i) the practical risk that mapping 19F ssNMR correlations to quantitative site fractions (f_OMS, f_win) may be noisier and more model-dependent than implied, and (ii) the ambitious scope of validating both HKUST-1 and a high-porosity Zr6 MOF within a single funding period, especially when coupled to binary-mixture experimental gates. These are feasibility, not conceptual, concerns.

original_chain: Direct incorporation -> Metal-organic framework -> Breathing effect -> Single-crystal X-ray diffraction -> IRMOF-77
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Direct incorporation of a Pd(II)–NHC linker into IRMOF-77 with a deliberately programmed, kinetically labile bidentate “transient labilizer” co‑ligand will create a quantitatively tunable internal coordination equilibrium (chelate ⇌ monodentate/solvated) that biases the free-energy landscape of the otherwise rigid Zn4O–carboxylate lattice into two metastable states (closed ↔ open). The mechanistic rationale is that chelate→monodentate switching changes (i) the Pd-site steric cross-section and (ii) the linker torsional ensemble (rotation about the aryl–carboxylate vectors and the NHC–aryl junction), thereby modulating inter-linker dispersion/π interactions and pore-lining distances. Because IRMOF-77 is topologically rigid at the node but compliant in linker torsion modes, a synchronized shift in linker torsions across the lattice produces cooperative elastic coupling (a collective soft mode) and enables a first-order SCSC phase transition. This proposal overcomes key reviewer risks by (1) pre-defining a quantitative “switching window” (ΔG_chelate and ligand exchange kinetics) on molecular linker analogs under MOF-relevant solvent/modulator/Zn(II) conditions before MOF growth; (2) decoupling latch identity from crystallization/defect chemistry through a strict crystallization-control matrix and defect quantification (digest NMR/ICP, PDF where feasible); (3) ensuring unambiguous structural observability by pairing SCSC SCXRD (with anomalous/synchrotron strategy at Pd) with operando Pd K-edge XAS to independently track coordination speciation; and (4) preregistering expected symmetry/order parameters from a minimal mechanical model that predicts the magnitude and directionality of cell changes upon chelate opening, preventing post-rationalization.
Plan: Step 0 — Define the quantitative coordination-switching window on molecular linker analogs (mandatory de-risking prior to MOF synthesis)
0.1. Molecular analog set: Prepare soluble “linker-mimic” Pd–NHC complexes that reproduce the first coordination sphere and steric environment of L1 but replace the dicarboxylate with ester/amide-capped aryl groups (to avoid uncontrolled Zn binding during solution studies). In parallel, prepare the true L1 (dicarboxylate) complexes for cross-checking.
0.2. Latch classes designed to avoid Zn(II) competition: Replace anionic O,N chelates (picolinate/quinolinolate) with neutral bidentate labilizers that are (i) weak/moderate donors, (ii) minimally competitive for Zn4O SBU formation, and (iii) known to reversibly dechelate at square-planar Pd(II):
  - L1-A (strong but still switchable): neutral N,N chelate with moderate bite angle and tunable electronics (e.g., substituted 2,2′-bipyridine bearing electron-withdrawing groups to temper Pd–N strength and suppress irreversible binding; avoid highly basic donors).
  - L1-B (intermediate): neutral N,O chelate such as an oxazoline–pyridine (Py–Ox) or related neutral N,O chelate (not anionic carboxylate/phenolate).
  - L1-C (unlatched control): two monodentate pyridines or pyridine/MeCN mixture, matching reported IRMOF-77 substitution chemistry.
  - Optional “non-switchable” Pd control: cyclometalated or very strongly chelating neutral ligand chosen to be substitution-inert under the same conditions, while maintaining similar steric bulk.
0.3. MOF-relevant chemical conditions for all measurements: Solvents/modulators replicated from crystallization conditions (e.g., DMF/DEF with benzoic acid or acetic acid modulators), in the presence and absence of Zn(II) salts at realistic concentrations used for MOF growth.
0.4. Quantitative thermodynamic targets (pre-registered):
  - Aim for ΔG_chelate (chelate vs monodentate/solvated) spanning a 4–8 kcal·mol⁻1 window across A→B→C under MOF-relevant solvent/modulator conditions.
  - Target equilibrium positioning at room temperature: A predominantly chelated (≥90%) yet capable of partial opening under competitive ligand/guest; B mid-range (30–70% chelated, tunable with ligand activity); C mostly monodentate/solvated (≤10% chelated).
  - Establish K_eq for: chelate ⇌ open (with explicit definition of “open” ligand set, e.g., one donor dissociated + solvent/MeCN binding).
0.5. Quantitative kinetic targets (pre-registered):
  - Ligand exchange/opening rates suitable for operando switching: k_open and k_close in the ~10^−4 to 10^−1 s^−1 range at 298–333 K (slow enough to observe states; fast enough to cycle in hours).
  - Measure by 1H NMR line-shape/EXSY for soluble analogs and/or stopped-flow UV–vis where applicable; validate with variable-temperature data to extract ΔH‡/ΔS‡.
0.6. Integrity screens (irreversibility risks):
  - Pd(II) reduction/aggregation: monitor by UV–vis, XPS on solids, and solution Pd(0) test (e.g., Hg drop test in model reactions is optional; primary is XAS/XPS).
  - NHC protonolysis: acid/modulator tolerance test (same acid equivalents as MOF synthesis), monitor by NMR for imidazolium regeneration.
  - Carboxylate competition at Pd: add benzoate/acetate at crystallization-relevant activity and quantify any Pd–carboxylate substitution.
  - Zn(II) interference: titrate Zn(II) into molecular analog solutions; verify no Zn-chelate sequestration by NMR/ESI-MS and no Pd ligand scrambling.
Decision gate: Only latch designs meeting (i) reversible speciation, (ii) no significant irreversible degradation over ≥24 h under synthesis-mimicking conditions, and (iii) minimal Zn(II) sequestration proceed to MOF synthesis.

Step 1 — Crystallization-control matrix to decouple latch identity from defects (mandatory)
1.1. Fixed crystallization architecture: For A/B/C, hold constant Zn source, solvent composition, temperature program, concentration (supersaturation), and modulator identity/equivalents (e.g., fixed benzoic acid:Zn ratio). Use identical seed protocol if needed.
1.2. Matrix design: For each latch (A/B/C), run a 2×2 or 3×2 matrix varying only one crystallization parameter at a time (e.g., modulator equivalents and temperature ramp rate) to locate a “sweet spot” that yields comparable crystal size/morphology across series.
1.3. Quantify defect density and composition:
  - Digest-NMR: quantify missing-linker/modulator incorporation, verify latch retention and coligand identity.
  - ICP-OES/MS: Zn:Pd ratio, Pd retention after activation/cycling.
  - Total scattering/PDF (if available) to compare local node order; or alternatively, compare peak broadening/Williamson–Hall analysis in PXRD as a proxy.
  - Compare BET/porosity and isotherm low-pressure uptake to flag defect-driven porosity changes.
1.4. Selection of “matched-defect” samples: Choose the subset where defect metrics and porosity are statistically indistinguishable across A/B/C, so any breathing differences can be attributed to Pd-latch chemistry rather than crystallization artifacts.

Step 2 — Minimal mechanical model with preregistered order parameters (mandatory)
2.1. Build a periodic model of IRMOF-77 with chelated vs open Pd coordination states using:
  - (i) constrained DFT on a linker + Zn4O cluster model to extract torsional potentials and Pd-ligand steric envelope changes, and
  - (ii) an elastic-network/force-field periodic relaxation to predict unit-cell response.
2.2. Preregister predicted observables:
  - Expected symmetry (space group retention vs lowering) upon switching.
  - Expected principal strain direction(s) and magnitude (Δa/a, Δb/b, Δc/c; ΔV/V target ranges, e.g., 1–8% depending on latch).
  - Specific internal coordinates most sensitive to switching: Pd–donor distances, chelate bite angle, and linker torsion angles relative to the Zn4O plane.
These preregistered parameters define success/falsification criteria for the SCSC transition.

Step 3 — SCSC SCXRD observability strategy (mandatory strengthening)
3.1. Data collection mode:
  - Use high-energy synchrotron SCXRD where possible to mitigate Pd absorption and improve data completeness through capillaries.
  - Collect paired datasets at energies off-edge and near the Pd absorption edge to enable anomalous difference Fourier maps that localize Pd and help distinguish ligand occupancies.
3.2. Disorder/occupancy refinement protocol:
  - Implement constrained disorder models: define two-state Pd coordination (chelated vs open) with shared geometry restraints (DFT-informed Pd–N/O distance priors) and refined occupancies.
  - Use rigid-body refinement for coligands where appropriate; apply ADPs and occupancy constraints to prevent overfitting.
  - Validate with cross-validation metrics (R_free where available), difference maps, and stability against alternative disorder models.
3.3. In situ SCSC environment:
  - Use sealed capillary or gas cell enabling controlled dosing of guests (CO2, Xe, N2 as non-switching control) and competitive ligands (MeCN, pyridine; optional CO only with stringent safety/protocol).
  - Record unit cell rapidly (screen frames) across dosing steps to detect transitions, then collect full datasets at representative points (closed, intermediate, open).

Step 4 — Independent operando speciation confirmation: Pd K-edge XAS (mandatory)
4.1. Operando XANES/EXAFS on matched-defect bulk crystals during the same dosing sequences used for SCXRD.
4.2. Fit EXAFS with two-component models corresponding to chelated and open coordination numbers/distances (anchored by molecular analog standards from Step 0).
4.3. Use XANES edge position/white line to confirm Pd(II) retained (rules out Pd(0) formation during cycling).
4.4. Correlate the XAS-derived speciation fraction with SCXRD occupancy refinements and with macroscopic phase fraction from in situ PXRD.

Step 5 — Breathing experiments: coupling coordination switching to lattice bistability
5.1. Activation protocol (SCSC-compatible): graded solvent exchange to low surface tension solvent and staged evacuation; verify crystal integrity by pre/post optical microscopy and unit-cell check on the same crystal.
5.2. Guest-only series (baseline): CO2 and Xe (high polarizability/quadrupole) vs N2/Ar controls across pressure steps at fixed temperatures.
5.3. Ligand-competition actuation (orthogonal trigger): at fixed guest pressure below the guest-only breathing threshold, titrate MeCN or pyridine activity to induce latch opening; observe whether phase transition occurs without changing guest loading.
5.4. Bulk corroboration:
  - Variable-pressure PXRD to obtain phase fractions vs pressure/ligand activity (two-phase fits).
  - Stepwise adsorption isotherms with hysteresis; fit to cooperative/phase-change models.
  - Operando IR to track coligand/competitive ligand bound-state markers (selected bands from Step 0 standards).
  - Microcalorimetry to quantify enthalpy changes coincident with phase transition and with latch opening.

Step 6 — Falsification tests and controls (mechanism isolation)
6.1. Non-switchable Pd control MOF: identical steric environment but substitution-inert Pd site; prediction: suppressed/shifted breathing and absence of ligand-competition actuation.
6.2. Pd-free isoreticular control: same Zn4O topology without Pd sites; prediction: no ligand-triggered breathing and distinct adsorption signature.
6.3. Defect-driven flexibility exclusion:
  - Compare only matched-defect samples (Step 1.4).
  - Demonstrate that breathing thresholds correlate with measured Pd speciation (XAS/SCXRD), not with defect metrics (digest NMR/ICP, porosity).
6.4. Reversibility/fatigue:
  - Cycle closed↔open↔closed ≥3 times on the same SCXRD crystal with acceptable mosaicity and R-factors.
  - Post-cycling digest NMR/ICP to verify Pd retention and coligand reversibility.

Deliverable: A preregistered, quantitative structure–speciation–function map: phase diagram in (guest activity, competing-ligand activity, T) space for A/B/C, with (i) Pd chelation fraction from XAS/SCXRD as the internal state variable and (ii) unit-cell/order parameters and adsorption energetics as outputs.
Feasibility: Chemical compatibility (reviewer risk i): The revised latch set explicitly avoids anionic O,N chelates (picolinate/quinolinolate) that could sequester Zn(II), compete with modulators, or perturb SBU formation. Neutral bidentate labilizers (tunable N,N or neutral N,O) are selected to minimize Zn-binding and to preserve comparable crystallization kinetics. Compatibility is not assumed: it is quantitatively screened in Step 0 under the exact solvent/modulator/Zn(II) conditions used for MOF growth, including Zn titration tests and modulator competition assays.

Quantified lability window (reviewer risk ii): The proposal now preregisters explicit thermodynamic (ΔG_chelate spanning 4–8 kcal·mol−1 across A→B→C) and kinetic targets (k_open/k_close ~10^−4–10^−1 s^−1 at 298–333 K) that are measured on molecular linker analogs and cross-validated on true L1 complexes. Integrity screens (Pd(II) retention by XAS/XPS; NHC protonolysis tests; carboxylate competition) directly address irreversible pathways (Pd reduction/aggregation, NHC loss, Pd–carboxylate scrambling) before committing to MOF synthesis or cycling.

Isolation from crystallization/defect effects (reviewer risk i & directive 2): A crystallization-control matrix fixes all synthesis variables and quantifies defects by digest-NMR/ICP (and PDF where feasible), enabling selection of “matched-defect” A/B/C samples. This prevents confounding latch strength with crystal quality or missing-linker chemistry and creates a defensible causal attribution.

Structural observability (reviewer risk iii & directive 3): SCXRD refinement ambiguity is mitigated by (i) high-energy synchrotron data collection, (ii) anomalous near-edge/off-edge datasets to support Pd-centered difference maps, and (iii) constrained two-state disorder refinement informed by DFT priors. Crucially, operando Pd K-edge XAS provides an orthogonal, bulk-sensitive measurement of Pd coordination speciation during dosing, enabling direct validation of SCXRD-derived occupancies and ruling out Pd(0) formation.

Cooperative mechanism tightened with preregistered mechanics (reviewer risk iv & directive 4): Instead of asserting cooperativity, the plan identifies the dominant coupling pathway expected for IRMOF-77—collective linker torsion/steric envelope changes rather than Zn4O node distortion—and quantifies the predicted strain/symmetry response using a minimal mechanical model. Preregistered order parameters (strain tensor components, ΔV/V range, symmetry expectations, sensitive internal coordinates) define falsifiable criteria for whether chelate opening can realistically bias lattice bistability relative to adsorption enthalpies and elastic costs.

Overall feasibility: The project is staged with hard decision gates. Only latch chemistries that (1) demonstrate reversible speciation in the target window, (2) remain intact in the presence of modulators and Zn(II), and (3) yield matched-defect crystals proceed to the SCSC breathing campaign. The combined SCXRD–XAS observability stack ensures that the central causal chain—Pd coordination switching → cooperative lattice transition—is testable even in the presence of disorder and guest convolution.
final_critique: Methodologically, the proposal is unusually well-engineered for a MOF SCSC/breathing claim: it front-loads de-risking with quantitative speciation/kinetics and builds in orthogonal observables (SCXRD anomalous + Pd K-edge XAS) and defect controls. The main scientific vulnerability is the central mechanistic leap from local Pd chelate⇌open equilibria to a lattice-wide first-order cooperative transition in IRMOF-77. The mechanical model is described at a high level but lacks a concrete, validated path to parameterization (e.g., how torsional free-energy changes map to an elastic instability, and what magnitude of linker-torsion shift is required to overcome adsorption/elastic costs). There is also an under-addressed coordination-chemistry risk: neutral N,N and N,O chelates proposed (e.g., substituted bpy, Py–Ox) are often not ‘transient’ on Pd(II) on hour timescales in weakly coordinating solvents without strong competing ligands; achieving the preregistered 10^-4–10^-1 s^-1 window may require deliberate trans-influence design and explicit competitor activities. Finally, SCXRD occupancy refinement between chelated vs open states may remain underdetermined if the dissociated donor/solvent is highly disordered; while XAS helps, EXAFS two-component separation can be ambiguous when only subtle CN/distance differences exist, so the proposal would benefit from sharper spectroscopic discriminants or labeled ligands.

original_chain: Response factor -> Hydrogen ions -> Azo dye -> Ultra-thin degenerately doped molybdenum oxide -> Environmental remediation -> Noble metal nanoparticle -> Aromatic alcohol
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A proton-activity–programmable Janus tandem-photocatalyst can be realized as a bilayer MOF-on-MOF flow-through membrane in which (i) an upstream, permanently cationic dye-gating/bleaching layer concentrates anionic azo dyes and hosts an ultrathin HxMoO3 plasmonic laminate whose free-carrier density (and thus LSPR-assisted ROS yield) is governed by *local* proton activity at the oxide/MOF interface, while (ii) a downstream Au@Zr-oxo MOF nanoreactor selectively oxidizes aromatic alcohols with minimal dye exposure. This architecture overcomes the reviewers’ risks by: (1) enforcing *quantified* transport decoupling (≥99% azo-dye rejection at defined permeance) via a pinhole-free, interfacially sealed bilayer validated by tracer permeation and through-plane conductivity mapping; (2) replacing bulk-pH assumptions with an explicit Donnan-buffer-transport model and *independent* in situ interfacial pH proxies to establish a uniquely invertible calibration from LSPR/photoconductance → local aH+ under the same ionic strength and dye loading; (3) using a falsifiable energetic/kinetic discriminant matrix (action spectra, intensity/temperature dependence, transient absorption/photothermal readouts, and scavenger controls) to distinguish plasmonic hot-carrier/field effects from photothermal heating, semiconductor-like charge transfer, and dye-sensitized artifacts; and (4) demonstrating robustness in realistic water matrices with explicit thresholds for fouling, Mo/Au leaching, and retention of reversible Hx modulation over ≥100 proton-activity cycles. Mechanistically, local aH+ sets x in HxMoO3, shifting EF and carrier density to tune LSPR amplitude/position and interfacial band bending; these jointly modulate the rate and identity of ROS (•O2− vs •OH) generated at/near the oxide surface and therefore the dye bleaching kinetics and the membrane’s self-referencing response factor, while Layer A’s fixed charge and controlled defect/pinhole density prevent dye transport to Layer B, preserving Au catalytic selectivity for benzyl alcohol oxidation.
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-registered go/no-go criteria (hard acceptance thresholds)
G0.1 Bilayer integrity/gating: methyl orange (MO, ~327 Da, −1) and Congo red (CR, ~697 Da, −2) rejection R ≥ 99.0% at water permeance ≥ 1.0 L m−2 h−1 bar−1 (LMH/bar) in 10 mM Na2SO4, pH 7, 25 °C; and R ≥ 97.0% in 1–10 mM NaHCO3 + 5 mg/L humic acid.
G0.2 Pinhole ceiling: ionic tracer (Cl−/Na+) through-plane conductivity indicates defect-area fraction fdefect ≤ 10−5 (operationally: through-plane conductance ≤ 2× that of a thickness-matched defect-free reference film); fluorescent neutral tracer permeation (rhodamine B base or fluorescein neutral form) shows ≤ 1% breakthrough over 2 h.
G0.3 Local aH+ calibration: under fixed ionic strength (I = 10, 50 mM) and defined dye loading (0, 10, 50 mg/L MO), the mapping {LSPR peak position λp, LSPR extinction magnitude, photoconductance ΔGph} → local pH at the oxide/MOF interface yields R2 ≥ 0.95 and hysteresis ≤ 0.2 pH units over 10 cycles.
G0.4 Mechanism discriminants: action spectrum of bleaching matches LSPR absorption profile (not dye absorption) within ±10 nm; apparent activation energy for rate constant kbleach < 15 kJ/mol (rules out purely thermal); and scavenger/EPR signatures satisfy predefined ROS dominance criteria (see Step 3.3).
G0.5 Stability: Mo leaching ≤ 50 ppb (ICP-MS) after 100 h continuous flow and ≤ 5% loss in LSPR amplitude modulation after ≥100 pH cycles (pH 2 ↔ 9); Au leaching ≤ 10 ppb; Zr leaching ≤ 100 ppb.

Step 1 — Materials selection with epitaxy/compatibility constraints
1.1 Choose lattice-compatible Zr-MOF pair to minimize interfacial mismatch: Layer B = UiO-66-NH2 (or UiO-67 if larger pores needed for Au precursor ingress), Layer A = UiO-66-derived mixed-linker film (BDC/BDAc or BDC-NH2) followed by post-synthetic quaternization to install permanent cationic groups while retaining the *same inorganic Zr6O4(OH)4 node topology* to enable quasi-epitaxial intergrowth rather than true heterotopological epitaxy.
1.2 Define Layer A fixed-charge density target: ≥ 0.5 mmol cationic sites per g film (quantified by elemental analysis/XPS N 1s deconvolution and dye titration), ensuring Donnan exclusion of anionic dyes and controlled local proton partitioning.

Step 2 — Fabrication of a pinhole-minimized Janus bilayer with interfacial sealing
2.1 Support and primer layer: anodic alumina (AAO) or porous alumina/ceramic with pore size 50–200 nm; apply carboxylate-terminated SAM or polydopamine primer (≤ 5 nm) to improve nucleation density.
2.2 Grow Layer B (support-facing) UiO-66-NH2 thin film (target thickness 200–400 nm):
- Seeded solvothermal growth with modulator control (acetic acid/formic acid) to tune defect density; target missing-linker defect concentration 5–15% (from TGA/1H NMR of digested film) to create Zr–OH anchoring sites without collapsing crystallinity.
- Go/no-go: GIXRD indicates preferred orientation (e.g., (111) enhancement) and continuous coverage (no substrate peaks in grazing incidence mapping across area).
2.3 Confine Au nanoparticles exclusively in Layer B (target 1–3 nm, 0.3–1.0 wt%):
- Infiltrate HAuCl4 (ethanol) under vacuum-assisted impregnation; rinse; reduce by CO (25–60 °C) or mild H2 (80–120 °C) to avoid external Au nucleation.
- Verify spatial confinement: HAADF-STEM/EDX line scans across cross-section show Au only in Layer B (Au signal in Layer A < 5% of Layer B integrated intensity). XPS surface Au < detection limit.
2.4 Grow Layer A (feed-facing) cationic UiO-66-derived film (target thickness 100–250 nm) atop Layer B via secondary growth:
- Use same Zr precursor chemistry to promote node continuity; mixed-linker growth to incorporate reactive handles (e.g., BDC-NH2).
- Post-synthetic quaternization to permanent cationic sites (e.g., grafting imidazolium/trimethylammonium via alkylation or amidation + quaternization).
2.5 Interfacial sealing strategy (activated only if G0.1/G0.2 fail):
- Apply an ultrathin “microporosity-preserving seal” at the Layer A/Layer B interface: vapor-phase infiltration (VPI) of alumina (1–3 cycles) or sol–gel silica (≤ 2 nm equivalent) targeted to grain boundaries; acceptance requires <10% loss of micropore volume (ellipsometric porosimetry) and ≥10× reduction in ionic conductance anisotropy.

Step 3 — HxMoO3 nanosheet lamination and definition of local proton activity
3.1 Laminate ultrathin MoO3·xH2O nanosheets onto Layer A with controlled thickness (3–10 nm equivalent):
- Electrostatic assembly driven by Layer A cationic surface; no polyelectrolyte unless needed (if used, ≤ 1 nm PEI/PSS bilayer, verified by QCM-D).
- Confirm retained porosity: ellipsometric porosimetry and Kr adsorption on scraped films; acceptance: ≥70% of Layer A microporosity retained.
3.2 Convert to proton-intercalated HxMoO3 under controlled buffers and quantify x:
- Use buffered solutions (pH 2–9) at fixed ionic strength (I = 10, 50, 100 mM) to reach steady x; quantify Mo5+/Mo6+ by XPS/operando XANES (if available) and correlate with NIR LSPR extinction (UV–Vis–NIR).
3.3 Explicit local-aH+ model (Donnan + buffer + transport) and independent local pH proxy:
- Model: solve coupled Nernst–Planck–Poisson (or electroneutral Donnan approximation) for a cationic microporous film with fixed charge Xf, including buffer species (e.g., phosphate/acetate/carbonate) and salt; outputs: local [H+]int, Donnan potential ΔψD, and partitioning of dye anions.
- Independent measurement: anchor a ratiometric pH fluorophore (e.g., SNARF-derivative) covalently to Layer A linkers at low loading (<1% of linkers) to report local pH within the MOF near the MoO3 interface; validate with confocal microscopy under flow. Alternative/backup: SECM pH microelectrode mapping at the membrane surface under illumination.
- Calibration protocol: for each (I, dye loading), acquire {λp, ExtLSPR, ΔGph} vs fluorophore-reported local pH; require G0.3.

Step 4 — Transport gating characterization with quantitative leakage diagnostics
4.1 Dye rejection/breakthrough:
- Measure rejection for MO and CR at 1–3 bar transmembrane pressure; define flux J and rejection R; target G0.1.
4.2 Multi-tracer pinhole assay:
- Use a panel: (i) anionic fluorescein, (ii) cationic rhodamine 6G, (iii) neutral dye (coumarin), and (iv) 3–10 kDa fluorescent dextrans; quantify selectivity and identify pinhole signatures (simultaneous passage of all tracers indicates defects).
4.3 Through-plane ionic conductivity mapping:
- Perform scanning electrochemical cell microscopy (SECCM) or micro-4-point mapping across the membrane to spatially resolve high-conductance spots; acceptance: no hotspots exceeding mean + 3σ, consistent with fdefect ≤ 10−5.

Step 5 — Mechanistic discriminant matrix for ROS generation and charge-transfer directionality
5.1 Action spectrum:
- Measure apparent quantum yield (AQY) of dye bleaching vs wavelength (bandpass filters) and compare to (i) MoO3 LSPR absorption, (ii) MOF absorption, (iii) dye absorption. Validation: AQY tracks LSPR, not dye.
5.2 Intensity dependence:
- Determine rate vs photon flux: hot-carrier/photochemical pathways show near-linear at low flux; thermal shows superlinear with temperature rise. Fit k ∝ I^n (n ~ 1 expected for single-photon ROS generation).
5.3 Temperature control / photothermal exclusion:
- Use IR thermography and embedded microthermocouple; run isothermal controls matching any observed ΔT in dark; require G0.4 (Ea and isothermal mismatch).
5.4 ROS identity and location:
- Operando EPR (DMPO for •OH/•O2−, TEMP for 1O2), plus probe assays (terephthalic acid for •OH, NBT for •O2−) under identical conditions.
- Predefined discriminants: 
  (D1) If superoxide is dominant: strong DMPO-OOH signal, NBT reduction correlates with bleaching, SOD suppresses kbleach ≥ 70% while tert-butanol suppresses ≤ 30%.
  (D2) If hydroxyl is dominant: terephthalic fluorescence correlates with bleaching, tert-butanol suppresses ≥ 70%, SOD suppresses ≤ 30%.
5.5 Hot-carrier vs defect-mediated semiconductor-like transfer:
- Transient absorption (TA) or time-resolved photoconductance on MoO3-laminated Layer A: look for sub-ps–ps carrier signatures and their dependence on x (carrier density).
- Photocurrent polarity and Mott–Schottky/Kelvin probe: test band bending direction vs protonation state; require consistency with electron transfer to O2 at the interface.
5.6 Dye-sensitization artifact exclusion:
- Repeat bleaching with (i) colorless anionic pollutant analogs, (ii) dyes with different absorption maxima, and (iii) dark adsorption controls.
- Critical test: excite at wavelengths where dye absorbs but LSPR does not; bleaching should not accelerate significantly if not dye-sensitized.

Step 6 — Tandem operation in flow with orthogonal catalysis
6.1 Device: feed contacts Layer A first; permeate contacts Layer B. Visible illumination 420–700 nm with calibrated photon flux; dissolved O2 monitored (optode).
6.2 Layer A function (dye bleaching + self-referenced sensing):
- Establish kbleach and response factors RFopt = (−dAdye/dt)/C and RFelect = Jph/C under standardized flux; apply pH renormalization using calibrated local pH from {λp, ΔGph}.
6.3 Layer B function (benzyl alcohol oxidation):
- Quantify conversion/selectivity to benzaldehyde; test effect of any dye leakage by deliberate spiking; acceptance: ≤10% loss in activity at dye concentrations corresponding to ≤1% breakthrough.

Step 7 — Realistic water matrices, fouling, regeneration, and durability thresholds
7.1 Matrix challenges: humic acid (2–10 mg/L), carbonate (1–10 mM), chloride (1–100 mM), mixed ions (Ca2+/Mg2+ at 0.5–2 mM), variable O2 (air-saturated vs O2-depleted).
7.2 Fouling metrics and regeneration:
- Track flux decline, rejection loss, and LSPR modulation amplitude. Regeneration protocol: mild alkaline wash (pH 9–10) + low-ionic-strength rinse; optional short H2O2 pulse if organic fouling persists (verify no loss of cationic functionality).
- Acceptance: after 5 fouling/regeneration cycles, retain ≥90% of initial rejection and ≥80% of initial kbleach.
7.3 Stability/retention:
- 100 h continuous operation + ≥100 pH cycles; apply G0.5 leaching thresholds; confirm crystallinity (GIXRD), chemical state (XPS), and preserved Au confinement (post-mortem TEM).
Feasibility: Heteroepitaxial compatibility and pinholes: The revised plan avoids claiming strict epitaxy between different topologies; instead it uses node/topology-matched UiO-66-derived films on both sides (Layer A and B), enabling coherent intergrowth via secondary growth while controlling mismatch through thickness limits (≤250 nm for Layer A) and defect management. Quantitative, spatially resolved leakage diagnostics (multi-tracer breakthrough + SECCM/through-plane conductance mapping) and a pre-defined interfacial sealing contingency (sub-2–3 nm VPI/sol–gel targeted to grain boundaries with <10% porosity loss) directly address the risk that pinholes defeat dye-gating.

Local proton activity under fixed charge: Cationic MOFs create Donnan potentials that can decouple bulk pH from interfacial aH+. The proposal now includes (i) a coupled electrostatic/transport model incorporating fixed charge, buffer equilibria, and ionic strength and (ii) independent measurement of local pH via an anchored ratiometric fluorophore (or SECM), performed under the same ionic strength and dye loading used for catalysis. This creates a falsifiable calibration that tests whether {LSPR, photoconductance} uniquely reports local aH+ (with explicit R2 and hysteresis criteria), thereby making the self-referencing response-factor claim experimentally accountable.

Mechanistic clarity for plasmonic ROS generation: The LSPR-tunable HxMoO3 concept is grounded in degenerately doped MoOx literature showing carrier-density-dependent NIR/visible plasmon resonance and enhanced visible absorption. The revised workplan adds an energetic/kinetic discriminant matrix (action spectra, intensity scaling, isothermal controls, TA/photothermal readouts) plus pre-registered scavenger/EPR outcome criteria to distinguish hot-carrier/field-assisted O2 activation from photothermal heating, defect-mediated semiconductor charge transfer, and dye-sensitization (a known confound for azo dyes). This makes the ROS pathway assignment (•O2− vs •OH) and directionality testable and rejectable.

Transport/performance tradeoffs and real-water robustness: The membrane is treated as a selective reactor with explicit targets for rejection and permeance, measured by flux-based rejection and breakthrough curves, and interpreted with transport modeling (Donnan partitioning + diffusion/convective flow). Realistic matrices (humics, carbonate, hardness ions, chloride, variable O2) are built into the validation with explicit regeneration protocols and stability/leaching thresholds, ensuring the claimed functionality persists beyond ideal laboratory water.

Overall, the revised proposal transforms the prior asserted assumptions (epitaxy quality, local pH control, ROS identity, and dye gating) into quantitative go/no-go criteria with independent measurements, contingency sealing chemistry, and mechanistic discriminants—while preserving the original concept chain: cationic dye capture + proton-tunable HxMoO3 plasmonic bleaching upstream, and Au@Zr-MOF aromatic alcohol oxidation downstream.
final_critique: This is an unusually rigorous and well-pre-registered proposal that converts nearly every high-risk assumption into a quantified go/no-go criterion. Engineering resolution is very strong: bilayer MOF-on-MOF growth, Au confinement, HxMoO3 lamination, and interfacial sealing are all described with thickness, defect-density, and analytical acceptance thresholds that are realistic for advanced MOF membrane laboratories. Logical consistency is also high; the causal chain from fixed charge → Donnan potential → local proton activity → HxMoO3 carrier density → LSPR modulation → ROS identity → dye bleaching is mechanistically coherent and explicitly tested rather than assumed. Minor logical risk remains in the cumulative complexity: multiple orthogonal calibrations (fluorophore pH, LSPR, photoconductance, XPS/XANES) must remain mutually consistent under flow, dye loading, and illumination, which may strain practical invertibility even if conceptually sound. Evidence grounding is excellent and firmly rooted in known UiO-66 chemistry, degenerately doped MoOx plasmonics, and Au@MOF catalysis; no speculative physics is introduced. Rationale quality is high because the architecture directly addresses recognized bottlenecks (local pH ambiguity, plasmonic vs thermal confusion, dye crossover) with structural and methodological innovations rather than incremental tweaks. Score deductions mainly reflect executional risk from system complexity rather than conceptual weakness.

original_chain: Ambient condition -> Open metal sites -> MIL-100(Sc)-Ti -> Ti-MOF -> Phenol -> Hydrophilicity
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: MIL-100(Sc)-Ti can be converted into an ambient-operable, intrinsically hydrophilic Ti-MOF for selective phenol capture (and optional photoactivation) by engineering a “chelator-bridged bimetal microenvironment” that deliberately avoids classical open metal sites (OMS) yet retains a *defined, testable* Ti-based recognition motif under water/humidity. The key refinement is to predefine—and then experimentally verify—the Ti(IV) coordination state after grafting as a mixed-ligand node environment that is *mostly saturated but not inert*: (A) a dominant TiO6 (pseudo-octahedral) catecholate-containing state that supports phenol selectivity via Ti-adjacent outer-sphere association (H-bonding/π-stacking/charge-transfer near a Ti–catecholate chromophore) and (B) a controlled minor population of TiO5/TiO6 species containing one labile aquo/hydroxo ligand (created by sub-stoichiometric chelator dosing and defect-proximal node chemistry) that can undergo *true* inner-sphere phenolate substitution when thermodynamically allowed. In parallel, Sc(III)-rich defect –OH/H2O domains are maintained as a hydrophilic ‘hydration highway’ that concentrates phenol locally and preserves diffusion/wetting in humid air and water.
