This hypothesis directly addresses the reviewer’s concern: we no longer assume that a fully saturated Ti–catecholate must perform inner-sphere Ti–OPh binding; instead we (i) design for a quantifiable fraction of Ti sites with a labile ligand, and (ii) treat outer-sphere Ti-adjacent complexation and Sc–OH adsorption as explicit alternative (and potentially dominant) phenol-binding modes. Selectivity and water-tolerance arise from combining: (1) water-stable hard–hard Ti(IV)–O,O chelation (resisting hydrolytic deactivation typical of OMS motifs), (2) local hydrophilicity (Sc–OH/H2O, plus hydrophilic chelator substituents) to maintain pore wetting under ambient RH, and (3) a Ti-centered electronic/π surface that biases phenol over water through specific outer-sphere association and/or limited inner-sphere exchange at the designed labile subset. The proposal is therefore mechanistically falsifiable: phenol uptake must be partitionable among three modes—(i) inner-sphere Ti–OPh, (ii) Ti-adjacent outer-sphere association to the Ti–catecholate adduct, and (iii) Sc–OH adsorption—each discriminated by distance-sensitive EXAFS, isotope-labeled IR/ssNMR, and competitive displacement thermodynamics.
Plan: Step 0 — Define quantitative design space, targets, and go/no-go criteria (pre-registered to avoid underconstrained optimization)
0.1 Parameter matrix (3×3×3 core):
  • Defect fraction (missing-linker/node –OH density): low/med/high targeting ~2–5%, ~8–12%, ~15–20% missing-linker equivalents relative to ideal MIL-100(Sc) connectivity, generated by modulated synthesis.
  • Ti fraction installed by HVMO: ~5%, ~15%, ~30% of node metals as Ti (Ti:(Ti+Sc) by ICP), chosen to preserve MIL-100 topology while giving measurable Ti XAS signal.
  • Chelator equivalents relative to Ti: 0.25, 0.50, 0.75 eq (sub-stoichiometric by design to favor site-isolation and retain some labile ligation).
  Secondary screen (only after passing criteria): chelator identity (3,4-dihydroxybenzoate (DHBA), dopamine-derived catechol (DA-cat), tiron) at the best-performing loading.
0.2 Performance targets and go/no-go criteria:
  • Structural retention: PXRD similarity index ≥0.9 vs parent; N2 BET retention ≥70% of MIL-100(Sc)-Ti precursor after grafting; no macroscopic collapse after 24 h water immersion at pH 3, 7, 11.
  • Hydrophilicity window: water vapor uptake at 298 K reaching ≥10 wt% by 50% RH (or matched to MIL-100(Sc) baseline) while maintaining hysteresis consistent with stable wetting; differential enthalpy of water adsorption (microcalorimetry) not exceeding a threshold that indicates irreversible pore flooding (criterion: stable cycling with <10% loss water capacity over 10 cycles).
  • Phenol performance (ambient-relevant): aqueous phenol distribution coefficient Kd ≥ 10^4 mL g−1 at pH 6–7 in presence of 10 mM NaCl; vapor phenol uptake measurable at 30–70% RH with <30% capacity loss when RH increases from 30%→70%.

Step 1 — Build the defect lever with quantified –OH/H2O density (MIL-100(Sc) template)
1.1 Modulated synthesis to tune missing-linker defects: vary monocarboxylate modulators (formate/acetate/benzoate) and modulator:linker ratios to hit the three defect bins above.
1.2 Defect quantification (triangulated):
  • 1H NMR of digested MOF to quantify modulator incorporation and linker:modulator ratios.
  • TGA to cross-check organic content vs ideal.
  • Total scattering/PDF to detect local node disorder consistent with missing-linker creation.
1.3 Node hydroxylation readout: H/D exchange with D2O vapor + IR (O–D bands) to quantify exchangeable –OH populations vs defect bin.

Step 2 — Install Ti into MIL-100(Sc) nodes via HVMO with controlled Ti% and oxidation state
2.1 HVMO conditions: metal exchange using Ti(III) precursor (oxygen-free handling) into each defect-bin MIL-100(Sc), then gentle oxidation to Ti(IV) (controlled O2 exposure or chemical oxidant) to avoid framework damage.
2.2 Quantify Ti incorporation and distribution:
  • ICP-OES for bulk Ti:Sc.
  • STEM-EDS mapping for spatial heterogeneity; flag phase segregation.
  • PXRD + N2 sorption to verify topology/porosity retention.
2.3 Node speciation baseline (pre-grafting): Ti K-edge XANES/EXAFS to confirm Ti(IV) environment and average Ti–O distances; Sc K-edge XAS to monitor Sc environment stability.

Step 3 — Program Ti with catecholate chelation while *predefining* intended coordination states
3.1 Chelator selection rationale (screened but mechanistically mapped):
  • DHBA (catechol + carboxylate): can anchor spatially and add hydrophilicity.
  • Dopamine-derived catechol (catechol + amine): stronger H-bonding microenvironment; risk of nonselective adsorption mitigated by pH control.
  • Tiron (disulfonated catechol): maximizes hydrophilicity; may reduce π-stacking—used to test whether selectivity is electronic/π-driven vs purely hydrophilic.
3.2 Grafting conditions (Ti-selective window): buffered aqueous/ethanolic media with pH tuned to favor Ti–catecholate formation while minimizing Sc binding and framework hydrolysis; implement stepwise dosing (e.g., 2–3 aliquots) to avoid local overfunctionalization.
3.3 Intended Ti coordination-state outcomes (explicit):
  • Target dominant state: TiO6 with one bidentate catecholate + remaining oxo/hydroxo/aquo ligands (no classical OMS).
  • Target minor state: TiO5/TiO6 containing one labile H2O/OH− ligand (created by sub-stoichiometric catechol dosing and defect-proximal coordination), enabling possible inner-sphere phenolate substitution.
3.4 Verification of Ti–catecholate formation and loading:
  • UV–vis DRS for ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) bands diagnostic of Ti–catecholate.
  • XPS (Ti 2p, O 1s) for new Ti–O environments.
  • Elemental analysis + digestion NMR to quantify ligand loading and confirm sub-stoichiometry vs Ti.
  • Crucially: Ti K-edge EXAFS fitting (see Step 6) to quantify coordination number distribution and Ti–O distance components.

Step 4 — Hard control to prove Ti-selective grafting and rule out dominant Sc–catecholate binding
4.1 Sc-only binding control: apply identical chelator grafting protocol to defected MIL-100(Sc) (no Ti). Quantify uptake/loading and binding signatures (UV–vis DRS, digestion NMR, XPS). This establishes the non-Ti baseline for catechol immobilization.
4.2 Element-specific discrimination:
  • Acquire both Ti and Sc K-edge XAS on (i) MIL-100(Sc)-Ti, (ii) chelator@MIL-100(Sc)-Ti, (iii) chelator@MIL-100(Sc). Use difference spectra and EXAFS fitting to detect whether Sc coordination shell changes consistent with Sc–catecholate formation.
  • ToF-SIMS mapping (or nanoSIMS if available) targeting characteristic chelator fragments (and Ti-containing fragments) to spatially correlate ligand with Ti-rich microdomains vs uniform adsorption.
4.3 Decision rule: if Sc K-edge EXAFS shows significant new short Sc–O contributions attributable to catecholate beyond the Sc-only control, adjust grafting pH/solvent, reduce chelator equivalents, and/or switch to chelator with stronger Ti selectivity (e.g., sulfonated catechol vs carboxylated) until Sc perturbation is minimized.

Step 5 — Partition phenol adsorption into three explicit binding modes with decisive experiments
We will not infer mechanism from uptake alone; we will allocate uptake among: Mode I (inner-sphere Ti–OPh), Mode II (Ti-adjacent outer-sphere association to Ti–catecholate), Mode III (Sc–OH adsorption).
5.1 Competitive substituted-phenol thermodynamics + calorimetry (mode fingerprinting):
  • Measure adsorption isotherms and heats (microcalorimetry) for phenol series (phenol, p-cresol, 4-fluorophenol, 4-nitrophenol) in water at controlled pH where they remain largely neutral (and separately at pH where partial deprotonation occurs).
  • Interpret trends: strong sensitivity to phenol pKa/electronics suggests inner-sphere/acid–base driven exchange; sensitivity to hydrophobicity/π character suggests outer-sphere/π-stacking.
  • Perform competitive displacement: pre-load MOF with a weakly bound phenol then challenge with a stronger-binding substituted phenol; quantify displacement to infer relative binding free energies.
5.2 Isotopic labeling to localize binding and distinguish H-bonding vs coordination:
  • Phenol-18O (Ph-18OH) exposure in aqueous and humid vapor conditions. Track IR shifts of C–18O vs C–16O stretches and O–H/O–D exchange behavior.
  • Phenol-d6 for ssNMR proximity experiments (Step 6.3).
  • Decision logic: direct Ti–18O incorporation (detectable via Ti–O distance changes in EXAFS and characteristic IR shifts consistent with metal–phenolate) supports Mode I; absence of Ti–O changes but presence of strong aromatic proximity to catecholate supports Mode II; dominance of –OH spectral changes at Sc domains supports Mode III.
5.3 Site-blocking/poisoning controls to allocate Mode III:
  • Selectively cap Sc–OH sites (e.g., mild silylation or acetate capping under conditions that do not affect Ti–catecholate) and test phenol uptake changes; major loss indicates Sc–OH contribution.

Step 6 — Quantitative operando spectroscopy to resolve Ti–O(phenolate) vs Ti–O(catecholate)
6.1 Operando Ti K-edge EXAFS under wet phenol exposure:
  • Collect EXAFS for chelator@MIL-100(Sc)-Ti in (i) water, (ii) water+phenol, (iii) water+substituted phenols, (iv) humid phenol vapor.
  • Fit with multi-shell models allowing two distinct Ti–O distances: Ti–O(cat) (short, bidentate chelate) and a longer/variable Ti–O(aquo/phenolate). Quantify coordination numbers and distance shifts.
  • Mechanistic discriminator: emergence/increase of a Ti–O distance consistent with phenolate coordination and/or decrease in Ti–O(aquo) coordination upon phenol dosing supports Mode I; unchanged Ti first-shell but changes in higher-shell carbon backscattering consistent with nearby aromatics supports Mode II.
6.2 Complementary IR (ATR-FTIR/DRIFTS) under controlled hydration:
  • Monitor phenolate vs phenol signatures, and changes in catechol-related bands upon phenol exposure.
  • Use D2O to separate H-bonding networks (O–D shifts) from coordination effects.
6.3 ssNMR localization:
  • 1H–13C HETCOR using phenol-d6 (or 13C-labeled phenol if available) to locate phenol relative to catecholate aromatic carbons vs framework linkers.
  • If Mode I is significant, expect signatures consistent with constrained phenolate environment and altered chemical shifts; if Mode II, expect close contacts without clear phenolate formation.

Step 7 — Ambient-relevant performance testing (aqueous + vapor; competitive water)
7.1 Aqueous phenol adsorption:
  • Isotherms at 25 °C, pH 3–10, ionic strength series; quantify capacity, Kd, and selectivity vs natural organic matter surrogates.
  • Include phenolate-forming conditions (higher pH) specifically to test whether Mode I turns on with deprotonation.
7.2 Vapor-phase phenol capture under RH 30–90%:
  • Dynamic breakthrough (preferred) or gravimetric uptake under controlled RH.
  • Compare chelator@MIL-100(Sc)-Ti vs MIL-100(Sc)-Ti vs MIL-100(Sc) vs chelator@MIL-100(Sc) to isolate Ti-programming benefit.
  • Apply IAST (where appropriate) for phenol/water competitive sorption; report uncertainty and validate against binary experiments.

Step 8 — Durability, leaching, and stability boundaries tied to defect/Ti/chelator matrix
8.1 Cycling ≥30 cycles in both aqueous and humid vapor phenol capture:
  • Track PXRD, N2 BET, water vapor sorption retention, and ICP of digests.
  • Ligand leaching: UV–vis (LMCT bands) and LC/MS if needed in supernatants.
8.2 Identify stability design window:
  • From the matrix, map failure modes (pore blocking at high chelator eq; hydrolysis at high defect; Ti clustering at high Ti%) and define the feasible region meeting go/no-go criteria.

Step 9 — Optional catalytic extension (only after adsorption mechanism is resolved)
9.1 If pursued, test aerobic photo-oxidation of phenol under visible light using chelator@MIL-100(Sc)-Ti as a Ti–catecholate CT-active motif.
9.2 Mechanistic controls: ROS scavengers, H2^18O / ^18O2 labeling to identify oxygen source; ensure adsorption-mode conclusions are not conflated with solution-phase ROS chemistry.

Deliverables (explicit mechanistic outputs)
D1: Verified Ti coordination state distribution (TiO6 vs minor TiO5/aquo) as a function of chelator eq and defect level (EXAFS-derived CN and distances).
D2: Quantitative allocation of phenol uptake among Modes I–III using competitive substituted phenols + calorimetry + isotope-labeled IR/ssNMR + operando EXAFS.
D3: A validated parameter window (defect%, Ti%, chelator eq) meeting predefined stability and performance metrics under humidity/water.
Feasibility: 1) Mechanistic feasibility of phenol recognition without relying on classical OMS: Literature and empirical precedent show that high uptake/selectivity can be achieved under ambient conditions without OMS by engineering pore microenvironments and specific interactions (Asset 1). Here, Ti–catecholate chelation is used primarily to create a water-stable, electronically distinctive adsorption motif; we explicitly acknowledge that a fully saturated Ti–catecholate may not undergo facile inner-sphere exchange in water. Therefore, the plan is feasible because it does not hinge on inner-sphere binding alone: it designs for (i) a measurable minor population of Ti sites with a labile ligand (enabled by sub-stoichiometric chelator dosing and defect-proximal coordination) and (ii) robust Ti-adjacent outer-sphere association as a viable dominant pathway. The decisive experiments (operando EXAFS distance resolution, isotopic phenol-18O/phenol-d6 IR+ssNMR, competitive substituted phenols with calorimetry) are chosen specifically to validate or falsify inner-sphere claims rather than assume them.

2) Synthetic feasibility of MIL-100(Sc)-Ti and node-level Ti programming: HVMO has already demonstrated preservation of template topology while installing Ti into MIL-100(Sc)-Ti (Asset 2), directly de-risking the core scaffold. Post-synthetic catecholate coordination to Ti(IV) is chemically strong (hard–hard Ti–O) and typically accompanied by diagnostic LMCT bands, enabling straightforward confirmation and quantification. The proposal further de-risks by using sub-stoichiometric ligand dosing to avoid pore blockage and by predefining a matrix that explicitly searches for the stability/porosity/performance window.

3) Addressing Ti vs Sc grafting selectivity risk: Because catecholates can bind Sc(III), we include a hard Sc-only control under identical grafting conditions plus element-specific discrimination (Ti and Sc K-edge XAS difference analysis and ToF-SIMS mapping). This directly tests whether the intended ‘Ti-programmed / Sc-hydration’ separation holds. If Sc binding is significant, the decision rules specify how to adjust conditions/ligand identity to regain Ti selectivity.

4) Defect-density tradeoff managed by a predefined window and stability gates: Missing-linker defects are treated as a tunable but bounded variable with explicit defect bins and structural go/no-go criteria (PXRD similarity, BET retention, immersion stability, cycling). This prevents uncontrolled drift into high-defect regimes that compromise hydrolytic stability or accessibility, while still leveraging defects to tune –OH density and hydrophilicity relevant for ambient operation.

5) Alignment with phenol activation literature and ambient hydrophilicity needs: MOFs (including Ti-MOFs) are established as platforms for phenolic substrate oxidation/activation via photoinduced charge transfer and ROS pathways (Asset 3). Hydrophilicity and wetting under operating conditions are known to critically affect adsorption/transport and fouling resistance in water-relevant separations (Asset 4). Our design intentionally couples a hydrophilic Sc–OH domain (transport/wetting) with a Ti–catecholate motif (recognition/optional CT activity), maintaining coherence with the original concept chain while resolving the reviewer-identified mechanistic ambiguity through explicit, discriminating tests.
final_critique:
Methodologically, the workplan is unusually concrete for a MOF adsorption/mechanism proposal: defect binning with triangulated quantification, controlled HVMO Ti installation, explicit chelator dosing to tune Ti coordination statistics, and element-specific spectroscopy controls are all actionable and state-of-the-art. The strongest feature is mechanistic falsifiability—explicitly abandoning the earlier implicit assumption that saturated Ti–catecholate must bind phenolate inner-sphere, and instead designing experiments to allocate uptake among three modes.

Main deductions are due to (1) over-ambitious coordination-state resolution claims: extracting a reliable *population fraction* of TiO6(catecholate) vs TiO5/TiO6(aquo/hydroxo) from EXAFS in a heterogeneous node environment is possible but error-prone and often underdetermined (correlated CN/σ2, multiple scattering, disorder, mixed Ti siting). Without a clearly specified fitting strategy (constraints, standards, simulated EXAFS, uncertainty propagation, independent validation), the promised quantitative speciation (D1) risks being softer than implied. (2) The Mode I discriminator using phenol-18O is not fully convincing as written: inner-sphere Ti–OPh formation in water at pH 6–7 is thermodynamically disfavored for mostly neutral phenol; even if occurring at higher pH, EXAFS distance shifts from swapping H2O/OH−/phenolate may be subtle relative to disorder. You partly address this by pH-dependent studies, but the proposal still sets performance targets (Kd at pH 6–7) that likely reflect Mode II/III rather than Mode I; this is fine scientifically, but it weakens the centrality of the labile-Ti subset unless you specify what minimum Mode I fraction is required or why it matters for selectivity at neutral pH. (3) The hydrophilicity criterion (≥10 wt% by 50% RH) and the ‘irreversible flooding’ enthalpy threshold are not yet parameterized with realistic benchmarks for MIL-100-class pore volumes and defect chemistry; the stated target may be either too easy (MIL-100 can be very water-adsorptive) or too strict depending on activation state, and the enthalpy threshold is unspecified. (4) Selectivity benchmarking is under-defined: Kd ≥10^4 mL g−1 in 10 mM NaCl is a strong target, but the competing solutes relevant to real waters (humics, substituted phenols, cresols, anisole, chlorophenols) and the basis for “selective” vs hydrophilic nonspecific uptake are not quantitatively locked to a selectivity factor or competitive isotherm model.

Overall: very strong structure and controls, but the most difficult claim is the quantitative deconvolution of Ti speciation and binding modes with the stated spectroscopy set; it is plausible, yet needs tighter statistical/uncertainty treatment and sharper decision thresholds linking mechanism to performance.

original_chain: Zn-N coordination -> Mixed-matrix membranes -> Accessible porosity -> Mixed-matrix membranes -> Imidazole -> Proton conductivity -> Hydrogen-bonded water network
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a water-stable, defect-engineered Zn–imidazolate MOF as a continuous “proton highway phase” inside a polymer mixed-matrix membrane, then executing a post-casting, covalent imidazolium tethering reaction exclusively within the MOF pore system, will yield higher and more durable proton conductivity than conventional imidazole-doped MMMs. Methodological adaptation: instead of coordinating or physisorbing imidazole, we will (i) install pore-confined electrophilic handles on Zn–N linkers (via mixed-linker ZIF synthesis containing aldehyde- or chloromethyl-functionalized imidazoles), and (ii) perform a solvent-free, vapor-phase quaternization (Menshutkin-type) to convert infiltrated imidazole into covalently tethered imidazolium groups lining the accessible porosity. Mechanism: (a) the Zn–N coordination network provides rigid, connected micropores that template a percolating hydrogen-bonded water network at moderate RH; (b) tethered imidazolium sites create high local proton activity and strong hydration shells that stabilize continuous water wires and suppress imidazole leaching; (c) proton transport proceeds predominantly by Grotthuss hopping through coupled (H2O)n–H3O+ and imidazolium-associated water chains, with reduced interfacial resistance because the MOF phase itself becomes an internally ion-functionalized, water-structured conductor rather than a passive filler.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Choose a Zn–imidazolate MOF platform with proven hydrolytic stability and accessible porosity: ZIF-8-derived topology as baseline, then move to more hydrophilic analogs by mixed-linker substitution.
1.2 Synthesize a mixed-linker ZIF where a controlled fraction (5–30 mol%) of linkers carry an electrophile for post-synthetic quaternization:
- Option A: 2-(chloromethyl)imidazole (CMim) + 2-methylimidazole (mIm) to form Zn(mIm)2-x(CMim)x.
- Option B: imidazole-4-carbaldehyde (Im-CHO) + mIm to form Zn(mIm)2-x(Im-CHO)x, followed by aldehyde-to-leaving-group conversion (e.g., chlorination) if needed.
Target: retain crystallinity and pore accessibility while introducing a uniform internal density of reactive sites.
1.3 Create defects (missing-linker) in a controlled manner to increase water uptake without collapse (e.g., modulated synthesis with monodentate imidazole/amine modulators); quantify defect density by TGA/elemental analysis and positron annihilation lifetime spectroscopy (PALS).
1.4 Select polymer matrix emphasizing mechanical integrity and low intrinsic water swelling to isolate filler-driven conduction (e.g., PVDF-HFP or polysulfone as mechanically robust host). Prepare a secondary set with a mildly acidic polymer (low-IEC SPEEK) to test interfacial coupling while avoiding dominance by polymer conduction.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Form a percolated MOF microphase within MMM (structural novelty vs dispersed particles):
- Use shear-induced alignment + phase-inversion casting to bias MOF particles into a connected network (target near percolation threshold, typically 15–30 vol% depending on aspect ratio).
- Alternatively, grow a thin, continuous MOF “skeletal network” in situ on a sacrificial nanofiber template (electrospun polymer fibers), then embed the MOF network into the final polymer and remove the template if compatible (yielding an interpenetrating MOF/polymer architecture).
2.2 Preserve accessible porosity during embedding by using a pore-filling, removable neutral guest that does not coordinate Zn (e.g., cyclohexane or perfluorinated small molecules depending on MOF affinity), removed after casting by mild vacuum; verify no polymer intrusion by gas sorption and PALS.
2.3 Pore-confined, vapor-phase imidazolium tethering (core methodological adaptation):
- Load imidazole (Im) into the activated MMM by controlled vapor sorption (mass uptake target set by functional-site stoichiometry).
- Perform solvent-free quaternization inside pores: heat the membrane under Im vapor (or Im + mild base scavenger if required) to drive Menshutkin reaction between Im and –CH2Cl groups on CMim linkers, yielding tethered –CH2–Im+Cl− sites lining the pore walls.
- Optional anion exchange post-step to tune water structure and proton mobility (Cl− → HSO4− or H2PO4−) by exposing the membrane to vapor/solution of the corresponding acid, then drying to remove excess acid while retaining counterions in pores.
2.4 Condition the hydrogen-bonded water network: hydrate under precisely controlled RH steps (e.g., 30→60→90% RH at fixed T) to fill micropores and establish connected water wires around imidazolium sites; lock into operating state by equilibration at target RH.
2.5 Build mechanistic control series:
(A) polymer only; (B) MMM with nonfunctional ZIF (no electrophile) + no Im; (C) MMM with electrophile-ZIF but no Im treatment; (D) MMM with electrophile-ZIF + Im loading but no quaternization (low-T exposure only); (E) full quaternized (tethered imidazolium) MMM; (F) full quaternized MMM after anion exchange (HSO4− / H2PO4−). Keep filler fraction and processing identical.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Verify Zn–N framework integrity and accessible porosity after membrane processing and after quaternization:
- PXRD for crystallinity retention; N2/CO2 sorption on extracted filler and on microtomed MMM pieces; PALS for free-volume connectivity.
3.2 Confirm covalent tethering and quantify functional density (distinguish from coordination/physisorption):
- Solid-state 13C/15N NMR (use 15N-imidazole for unambiguous detection of quaternized N), FTIR/Raman for imidazolium signatures, XPS (N 1s chemical shifts; Cl 2p), and chloromethyl consumption (elemental analysis/ion chromatography of released Cl− during exchange).
- Chemical stability/leaching: exhaustive water soaking and accelerated humidity aging; quantify any released imidazole by HPLC/LC-MS (expect near-zero for tethered samples).
3.3 Map the hydrogen-bonded water network in pores:
- Dynamic vapor sorption (DVS) to obtain RH-dependent uptake and hysteresis; variable-temperature IR of OH stretch to infer H-bond strength distribution; DSC to separate confined vs bulk-like water; if available, quasi-elastic neutron scattering (QENS) for confined water mobility.
3.4 Proton conductivity and mechanism under relevant conditions:
- Through-plane and in-plane EIS from 20–120 °C and 20–95% RH; fit Arrhenius/VTF to extract activation energies.
- Isotope effect: repeat EIS under D2O humidity to quantify Grotthuss contribution (expect significant drop if hopping dominates).
- Transference number and electrode polarization analysis to confirm proton-dominant conduction.
3.5 Microstructure/percolation and interfacial resistance:
- FIB-SEM tomography or nano-CT to confirm connected MOF microphase; SAXS/WAXS to monitor dispersion.
- Spatially resolved conductivity (humid-state conductive AFM or scanning microwave impedance microscopy) to verify conduction localized along MOF network and across polymer–MOF interfaces.
3.6 Success criteria:
- Conductivity: ≥10× improvement over polymer-only and ≥3× over non-tethered Im-loaded MMM at 60–80 °C, 50–95% RH.
- Mechanism: activation energy ≤0.30 eV at high RH with strong H/D isotope effect, consistent with Grotthuss hopping through structured water.
- Durability: <1% loss of tethered Im content after leaching/aging; stable conductivity over ≥300 h at 80 °C/80% RH.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Imidazole enhances proton transport when immobilized/organized; literature shows large conductivity gains from imidazole inclusion in porous solids under anhydrous conditions, while hydrogen-bonded water networks enable low-barrier Grotthuss transport under humid conditions. Imidazolium groups are known to strongly hydrate and can nucleate continuous water wires in confined pores, increasing proton hopping rates. Zn–imidazolate frameworks provide robust Zn–N coordination backbones with tunable linker functionality and stable microporosity.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): MOF chemistry uniquely enables mixed-linker synthesis and pore-confined covalent functionalization without destroying the coordination network. Converting neutral imidazole into tethered imidazolium inside the MOF transforms accessible porosity into a chemically programmed proton-transport channel. This addresses MMM limitations (additive leaching, interfacial resistance, and uncontrolled water structuring) via molecular-level design rather than composition-only optimization.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to free-imidazole MMMs, covalent tethering eliminates volatility/leaching and prevents polymer plasticization. Compared to MOF-filled MMMs without internal ion functionalization, the imidazolium-lined pores actively template hydrogen-bonded water networks and increase local proton activity, lowering activation energy. Compared to approaches relying on reversible coordination, the permanently grafted sites provide reproducible, humidity-tolerant conduction while maintaining Zn–N framework stability and accessible porosity.
final_critique: This is an exceptionally detailed and technically mature proposal with strong command of MOF chemistry, MMM processing, and proton-transport physics. The engineering resolution is high: mixed-linker ZIF synthesis, defect control, vapor-phase quaternization, and percolation-engineered MMM architectures are all credible and actionable. The logical framework linking tethered imidazolium sites to stabilized water wires and reduced activation energy is sound and well-supported by contemporary understanding of confined proton transport. Minor deductions arise from two areas: (i) the chemical feasibility window of chloromethyl-functionalized imidazolates in Zn–N frameworks under vapor-phase Menshutkin conditions is narrow and may risk partial linker degradation or Zn–N lability, which is acknowledged only implicitly; and (ii) the percolated MOF microphase strategies, while innovative, approach the boundary between MMMs and composite ionomer networks and would benefit from clearer fallback paths if percolation proves irreproducible. Evidence grounding is strong and remains within the chemistry/MOF/proton-conduction domain without speculative excursions. The rationale is creative and directly addresses known MMM bottlenecks (leaching, interfacial resistance) via a nontrivial structural adaptation rather than incremental tuning.

original_chain: Cascade reactions -> Reactive oxidative species -> Maltose -> TMB -> Serum analysis
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A pore-partitioned, redox-stratified MIL-88(NH2) heterometal MOF nanozyme—engineered by (i) introducing TPY as a rigid internal pore-partition ligand to stabilize MIL-88 breathing under serum/ROS conditions and (ii) spatially segregating CeO2 nanodomains at the crystal periphery while embedding Fe/Co-TPY catalytic nodes in the interior—will enforce a directional ROS-mediated cascade (maltase/GOx-generated H2O2/ROS -> MOF-confined peroxidase-like oxidation of TMB) that yields higher colorimetric fidelity and serum tolerance for maltose quantification than conventional co-dispersed CeO2@MOF or unpartitioned Fe/Co-MIL-88(NH2). Mechanistically, TPY partitioning increases local coordination saturation and suppresses linker/cluster hydrolysis, while the core–shell redox gradient minimizes radical quenching by serum antioxidants (ascorbate/urates) by generating •OH/Fe(IV)=O equivalents within confined pores and consuming ROS rapidly at the MOF interior surface where TMB is preconcentrated via π–π/hydrogen-bond interactions with aminoterephthalate and TPY.
Plan: Step 1: System setup (materials + assay architecture).
1.1 Synthesize Fe/Co-TPY-MIL-88(NH2) with controlled TPY loading (e.g., 0, 5, 10, 20 mol% vs aminoterephthalate) to tune partition density; characterize by PXRD (phase), N2 sorption (pore evolution), FTIR/XPS (TPY coordination), ICP-MS (Fe/Co ratio), and in situ PXRD in PBS/serum-mimic to quantify breathing/stability.
1.2 Create a redox-stratified composite: grow a thin CeO2 nanolayer selectively on external MOF surface via seeded deposition (Ce(III) precursor adsorption followed by mild oxidation/precipitation) to form CeO2@Fe/Co-TPY-MIL-88(NH2) core–shell; confirm spatial segregation by STEM-EDS line scans and depth-profile XPS.
1.3 Assemble a maltose cascade: immobilize maltase (α-glucosidase) upstream and glucose oxidase (GOx) co-localized or downstream (paper microfluidic or well-plate) to convert maltose -> glucose -> H2O2; position the MOF nanozyme zone downstream to oxidize TMB.

Step 2: Implement the methodological adaptation (directional cascade + confinement control).
2.1 Engineer directional transport: in a 3D μPAD, design sequential zones (enzyme zone -> diffusion delay -> MOF/TMB zone) and compare against a co-mixed single-zone format to test whether spatial separation plus MOF confinement reduces serum quenching.
2.2 Tune partition/redox gradient parameters: screen TPY loading and CeO2 shell thickness to maximize (i) peroxidase-like kinetics (TMB + H2O2) and (ii) cascade efficiency (maltose -> TMBox). Extract Michaelis–Menten parameters (Km, Vmax) for TMB and H2O2; determine ROS identity using scavengers (tert-butanol for •OH, p-benzoquinone for O2•−) and EPR spin trapping (DMPO) to link performance to confined radical generation.
2.3 Quantify TMB preconcentration and anti-interference: measure TMB adsorption isotherms on TPY-partitioned vs non-partitioned MOF; evaluate signal retention in the presence of physiological interferents (ascorbate, urate, cysteine, bilirubin) to demonstrate that rapid intrapore ROS turnover outcompetes solution-phase quenching.

Step 3: Validation and analytical framework (serum analysis + benchmarking).
3.1 Analytical performance in buffer and serum: build calibration curves for maltose (e.g., 10 µM–5 mM) in PBS and 10–50% (v/v) human serum; compute LOD/LOQ, linear range, and time-to-read.
3.2 Specificity controls: test glucose, sucrose, fructose; include enzyme-free and heat-inactivated enzyme controls; confirm that maltose response requires maltase+GOx and is not driven by endogenous serum H2O2 by catalase spiking.
3.3 Comparative benchmarking: compare to (i) CeO2@NH2-MIL-88B(Fe) co-dispersed composite, (ii) Fe/Co-MIL-88(NH2) without TPY, (iii) HRP-based TMB assay. Use identical μPAD geometry and readout (RGB or absorbance at 652 nm) and report relative error vs HPLC for spiked and real serum samples.
3.4 Mechanistic structure–function proof: correlate stability metrics (PXRD retention, leached metal by ICP, activity after incubation in serum) with cascade output; validate that pore partitioning suppresses framework degradation and maintains catalytic turnover under repeated ROS exposure (cycling tests).
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 1 demonstrates CeO2@MOF synergistic mimic activity enabling sugar cascades with TMB readout; Asset 2 shows TPY pore partitioning stabilizes Fe/Co-MIL-88(NH2) and enhances peroxidase-like catalysis in bioassays. Combining these establishes a grounded route to both higher catalytic output and higher biological-matrix robustness.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The proposal uses rational MOF-level architectural control (pore partitioning + heterometal nodes + core–shell redox stratification) to address a domain-specific limitation: MIL-88 instability/breathing and radical quenching in serum that degrade cascade fidelity. TPY acts as an internal coordination strut and pore modulator; CeO2 is positioned as a surface ROS modulator to shape ROS flux into the MOF.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike co-mixed nanozyme/enzyme systems where ROS are generated and quenched in bulk solution, the redox-stratified, partitioned MOF forces ROS generation/consumption into confined catalytic volumes, preconcentrates TMB, and resists serum-induced deactivation/leaching. This should deliver (i) lower LOD in serum, (ii) improved color uniformity and reduced background, and (iii) higher operational stability than CeO2@NH2-MIL-88B(Fe) and unpartitioned Fe/Co-MIL-88(NH2).
final_critique: This is a technically ambitious and largely well-constructed proposal that demonstrates strong command of MOF chemistry, nanozyme catalysis, and bioanalytical assay design. The engineering plan is unusually detailed for a concept-stage proposal, with appropriate structural, spectroscopic, and kinetic characterization aligned to the hypothesis. The logic connecting pore partitioning to breathing suppression and TMB preconcentration is sound, and the redox-gradient argument for mitigating serum antioxidant quenching is plausible. However, several deductions are warranted. First, selective external growth of CeO2 on MIL-88 without partial pore blockage or Ce diffusion into defects is assumed rather than rigorously de-risked; the proposal would benefit from contingency strategies or quantitative shell-thickness control limits. Second, while ROS confinement is invoked, the proposal occasionally overstates mechanistic certainty (e.g., Fe(IV)=O equivalents in MOF pores) without specifying how these short-lived species will be distinguished experimentally beyond generic scavenger/EPR assays. Third, the maltase–GOx–MOF spatial cascade is well motivated, but enzyme immobilization stability and mass-transport limitations in μPAD formats under serum conditions are underdeveloped relative to the MOF chemistry. These issues do not undermine feasibility but slightly weaken logical closure and translational clarity.

original_chain: RE6 cluster -> Mixed-linker strategy -> Mesopore -> Citric acid -> Hydrogen bonding -> Selenate
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A rare-earth RE6-cluster MOF can be made simultaneously mesoporous and highly selective for selenate (SeO4^2−) by a methodological adaptation of the mixed-linker strategy: co-assembling (i) a dominant rigid aromatic polycarboxylate that enforces an RE6-node topology and (ii) a minor, citrate-derived multidentate modulator/linker that (a) kinetically caps a subset of RE–OH/H2O sites to bias RE6 (vs RE9) formation and (b) introduces dense, proton-responsive –COOH/–OH arrays that act as directional hydrogen-bond donors/acceptors. Upon activation in humid conditions, these citrate-rich patches in expanded (mesopore-adjacent) cavities create multivalent inner-sphere/outer-sphere binding motifs—RE···O(SeO4) coordination complemented by cooperative hydrogen bonding—that preferentially stabilize tetrahedral oxoanions over competing anions, thereby increasing uptake and selectivity without collapsing framework crystallinity.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select an RE6-cluster-forming platform: choose RE(III) = Y, Tb, or Eu and a tritopic aromatic linker family known to support high-connectivity RE6 nodes (e.g., a benzene- or triazine-cored tricarboxylate with controlled steric bulk).
1.2 Define the citrate role as an "asymmetric multidentate defect-linker/modulator": use citric acid (H3Cit) and partially esterified citrate (e.g., mono-methyl citrate) to tune denticity and steric demand; pre-determine pH window where citrate is 1–2× deprotonated to avoid full chelation shutdown of SBUs.
1.3 Establish mixed-linker feed ratios (e.g., 95:5 to 70:30 aromatic:citrate-equivalent by carboxylate) and a constant total carboxylate:RE ratio to control defect density.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Citrate-assisted mixed-linker solvothermal synthesis: run parallel solvothermal reactions (DMF/H2O with controlled water fraction) where citrate is introduced after an initial 30–60 min nucleation period (“delayed modulator addition”) to bias RE6 SBU locking while allowing the primary topology to form.
2.2 Mesopore engineering via "cluster-proximal defect zoning": implement a two-stage thermal profile (low-T nucleation, higher-T growth) to spatially concentrate citrate at growth fronts, producing correlated missing-linker regions that merge into mesopore domains (2–20 nm) while retaining an RE6-connected backbone.
2.3 Post-synthetic re-protonation and hydrogen-bond activation: exchange DMF to ethanol/water, then mild acid wash (pH 3–4) to regenerate –COOH/–OH groups on citrate patches; activate under dynamic vacuum at temperatures that preserve RE–O integrity.
2.4 Mechanism-targeted selenate loading: perform vapor/humidity-conditioned adsorption (0–95% RH) to preserve H-bond networks; compare to dry conditions to isolate hydrogen-bond contribution.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Node/topology confirmation: SCXRD/3D ED where possible; otherwise PXRD + Rietveld/Le Bail to confirm RE6-node phase and exclude RE9 phases; pair distribution function (PDF) analysis to verify RE6 local structure.
3.2 Quantify mixed-linker incorporation and zoning: digest-NMR/IC for linker ratios; XPS and ToF-SIMS depth profiling to detect citrate-enriched regions; IR (ν(C=O), ν(OH)) to confirm –COOH regeneration.
3.3 Mesoporosity verification: N2 sorption (BET), NLDFT pore-size distribution, and mercury intrusion or SAXS for 2–50 nm regime; TEM/SEM for mesopore domains.
3.4 Selenate binding mechanism: (i) batch isotherms and selectivity vs sulfate/phosphate/nitrate/chloride; (ii) in situ ATR-FTIR/Raman to track Se–O environment shifts; (iii) EXAFS at RE edge to detect inner-sphere RE–O(Se) contributions; (iv) solid-state 77Se NMR (if feasible) to differentiate bound vs free selenate.
3.5 Performance metrics: kinetics (pseudo-second-order vs intraparticle diffusion to assess mesopore benefit), cycling stability (10–50 cycles), and tolerance to ionic strength; compare to non-citrate mixed-linker controls and to a purely microporous RE6 analogue.
3.6 Computational corroboration: DFT cluster models of RE6–(citrate patch) binding sites to compute adsorption energies and hydrogen-bond cooperativity; GCMC with heterogeneous binding-site distributions to connect mesoporosity + site density to observed isotherms.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Rare-earth clusters exhibit adaptable coordination environments, and mixed-linker strategies are empirically proven to steer RE-cluster connectivity/topology via sterics and linker symmetry; citrate is a known multicarboxylate chelator that can partially cap RE sites while retaining framework growth when dosage and deprotonation are controlled. Hydrogen bonding is a demonstrated driver of guest-dependent responses in MOFs, and oxoanion recognition commonly benefits from multivalent H-bonding coupled with Lewis-acidic metal nodes.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The adaptation is not a generic multivariate MOF; it is a topology-preserving RE6 framework where citrate is intentionally deployed as a defect-linker/modulator to (i) lock RE6 SBUs (preventing RE9 rearrangements) and (ii) create mesopore-adjacent, hydrogen-bond-rich microenvironments. This directly leverages RE-cluster flexibility (Asset 1) and mixed-linker/mesopore synergy (Asset 2) while mechanistically connecting citrate-driven hydrogen-bonding (Asset 4) to oxoanion capture.
3. Comparative Advantage: Conventional RE-MOF anion sorbents often trade capacity for diffusion limits (micropores) or lose selectivity in high ionic strength. Here, mesopores accelerate transport and expose more RE sites, while citrate patches provide cooperative H-bonding that differentiates tetrahedral oxoanions by geometry and hydration-shell disruption. The RE6 backbone maintains crystallinity and hydrolytic robustness, and the humidity-gated binding mode targets environmentally relevant aqueous selenate conditions.
final_critique: This is a technically ambitious and largely well-reasoned proposal that demonstrates deep familiarity with rare-earth MOF chemistry, defect engineering, and oxoanion adsorption mechanisms. The strongest aspects are the explicit control logic for RE6 versus RE9 cluster formation, the nontrivial use of citrate as an asymmetric defect-linker rather than a generic modulator, and the multi-modal validation plan (PDF, EXAFS, ToF-SIMS) that directly targets the hypothesized mechanism. However, several assumptions remain insufficiently constrained. First, the spatial 'zoning' of citrate at growth fronts is asserted but not convincingly justified kinetically; no quantitative model or precedent is cited showing that delayed modulator addition can yield mesoscale-correlated defects rather than stochastic linker dilution. Second, the coexistence of mesoporosity (2–20 nm) with retained long-range crystallinity in an RE6 framework at citrate loadings up to 30% is optimistic and risks framework amorphization or RE–citrate phase separation. Third, the selectivity argument for selenate over sulfate/phosphate relies heavily on hydrogen-bond cooperativity but does not adequately address competing hydration energies or the known strong affinity of RE(III) for phosphate, which may overwhelm subtle H-bond effects. These gaps slightly weaken the logical closure between design intent and expected selectivity outcomes.

original_chain: Conditioning of the inverse problem -> CH4/CO2 sensor array -> Measurement error -> Sensor array -> Gas sensor -> Acetone -> [Rh(dppe)(COD)]BF4 -> Rh
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A reaction-enabled MOF sensor array that immobilizes site-isolated [Rh(dppe)(COD)]+ within an anionic, large-pore framework will convert acetone from a cross-sensitive adsorptive interferent into a kinetically amplified, orthogonal sensing channel via selective, low-temperature acetone→isopropanol hydrogenation under a fixed trace H2 co-feed. Mechanistically, acetone (polar, Lewis-basic C=O) is uniquely activated at Rh(I) through reversible η2(C=O) coordination followed by heterolytic H2 activation (enabled by the confined, polar counterion environment) and hydride transfer to form a Rh–alkoxide intermediate that releases isopropanol; CH4 and CO2 remain non-reactive and contribute only reversible physisorption. This creates two independent observables per pixel: (i) a time-resolved gravimetric signature with a reaction-specific induction/initial-rate term distinct from instantaneous adsorption, and (ii) an in-pore vibrational signature (C=O depletion near 1710 cm−1 and C–O growth near 1050–1150 cm−1) that reports chemical conversion rather than uptake. By designing operation in a demonstrably reaction-limited regime (Da << 1 across the thin film) and by constraining catalyst site density to preserve true site isolation (prevent bimolecular deactivation/aggregation), the array’s feature sensitivity matrix becomes full-rank and less collinear across (yCH4, yCO2, yAce) space. Consequently, the inverse problem for CH4/CO2 composition inference in the presence of acetone is better conditioned (lower κ(J)) against realistic measurement noise compared to adsorption-only arrays, because catalysis-derived kinetic/spectral features provide orthogonal information that cannot be replicated by static adsorption correlations.
Plan: Step 1 — Commit to a single dual-readout architecture with quantified noise/LOD.
1.1 Architecture: QCM-ATR-IR integrated pixel. Each pixel is a 5 MHz (or 10 MHz) AT-cut QCM crystal coated with (a) a thin, continuous MOF film (target thickness L = 0.5–2.0 µm) and (b) an adjacent planar IR internal-reflection element (IRE) in the same flow cell enabling ATR collection through/along the MOF-coated surface. The flow cell is thermostatted (T = 298–333 K) and operated at 1.0 bar total pressure with mass-flow-controlled gas mixing.
1.2 Target detection limits/noise budget (pre-registered):
- QCM: frequency noise ≤ 0.2 Hz RMS at 1 Hz sampling after Allan variance optimization; mass LOD ≤ 5 ng (pixel-dependent). Baseline drift target ≤ 10 ng h−1 via temperature control (±0.02 K) and blank referencing.
- ATR-IR: spectral resolution 4 cm−1; averaging to achieve absorbance noise ≤ 2×10−4 AU in the 1000–1800 cm−1 window. LOD target for acetone C=O depletion: equivalent to ≤ 0.5 ppm acetone conversion in the film for a 2 µm coating (calibrated by known acetone adsorption bands).
1.3 Committed spectral observables: integrated band areas A(C=O, 1685–1740 cm−1) and A(C–O, 1020–1180 cm−1), plus their ratio R = A(C–O)/A(C=O) and time-derivatives dA/dt over the first 60–180 s after a step.

Step 2 — MOF and catalyst immobilization with operationally defined site-isolation and homogeneity metrics.
2.1 MOF selection criteria (must meet all): (i) anionic framework enabling cation exchange without ligand substitution at Rh; (ii) pore aperture ≥ 10 Å to admit acetone/isopropanol with minimal steric trapping; (iii) hydrothermal and CO2 tolerance; (iv) stable thin-film growth on QCM substrates. Primary candidate class: anionic, sulfonate-lined or polyoxometalate-containing MOFs with 1D channels (selected based on demonstrated cation exchange and robustness). Down-select by: PXRD stability after 24 h exposure to 10% CO2 + 1% H2O at 323 K; and retention of crystallinity/porosity.
2.2 Immobilization protocol (cation exchange): exchange native charge-balancing cations with [Rh(dppe)(COD)]+ in acetone under inert atmosphere, followed by extensive solvent exchange and mild activation (≤ 333 K, vacuum). Maintain constant Rh oxidation/ligand sphere.
2.3 Site-isolation definition and maximum loading criterion (pre-registered):
- Define “site-isolated” as mean Rh–Rh separation ≥ 2.5 nm (framework-dependent) and no detectable Rh–Rh clustering signature by microscopy/spectroscopy.
- Operational loading ceiling: ≤ 0.15 Rh per framework cavity (or ≤ 10% of exchangeable anionic sites, whichever is lower) to minimize bimolecular deactivation pathways. Prepare a controlled series (e.g., 2%, 5%, 10% of sites exchanged) to validate the ceiling.
2.4 Quantification and spatial uniformity measurements:
- Bulk Rh loading: ICP-OES/ICP-MS after complete digestion; cross-check with charge-balance-derived theoretical capacity.
- Ligand integrity/coordination: solid-state 31P MAS NMR (single dominant 31P environment; no broad/extra peaks consistent with decomposition), and XPS for Rh(I) signatures.
- Spatial homogeneity across films: micro-XRF mapping (Rh distribution uniformity criterion: coefficient of variation CV < 10% across the active area) and ToF-SIMS depth profiling (no surface-enriched Rh layer > 20% relative to bulk).

Step 3 — Quantitatively bound operating regime: H2 partial pressure, temperature window, and catalytic performance targets.
3.1 Operating window (bounded):
- Temperature: 298–333 K (to preserve low-temperature selectivity and suppress non-specific thermally activated processes).
- H2 co-feed: pH2 = 0.5–5.0 mbar (500–5000 ppm at 1 bar), fixed during inference; chosen to remain far below flammability in typical CH4/CO2-diluted streams and to keep H2 adsorption minor but kinetically relevant.
- Acetone: 0.5–50 ppm (stepwise), CH4/CO2 spanning composition simplex at fixed total pressure.
- Water challenge (realistic): 0–1% H2O; CO2: 0–50%; optional O2: 0–1% (screening only).
3.2 Performance targets to validate feasibility of “kinetic amplification”:
- Minimum apparent acetone hydrogenation activity in-film: TOFapp ≥ 0.01 s−1 per Rh at 323 K and pH2 = 1 mbar for acetone ≥ 5 ppm (sufficient to produce measurable band evolution within 1–3 min).
- Stability: TON ≥ 10^3 over ≥ 100 cycles with <20% activity loss; Rh leaching < 1% of initial Rh by ICP of effluent/condensate.

Step 4 — Demonstrate reaction-limited kinetics (transport identifiability) using Damköhler-based experiments.
4.1 Reaction–diffusion model and criterion: treat acetone transport through the MOF film with effective diffusivity Deff and intrinsic pseudo-first-order rate constant kobs (at fixed pH2). Define film Damköhler number Da = kobs L^2 / Deff.
- Goal regime: Da ≤ 0.1 during sensing so that observed initial rates and induction behavior reflect intrinsic kinetics, not diffusion limitation.
4.2 Experimental plan to quantify Deff and kobs separately:
- Measure Deff for acetone and isopropanol by uptake transients under zero H2 (reaction off) at several film thicknesses (L = 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 µm) and temperatures; fit to Fickian diffusion-in-film models.
- Measure kobs under reaction-on conditions (fixed pH2) using initial ATR-IR C=O depletion rate and early-time QCM slope; repeat across thickness series. Reaction-limited confirmation requires: (i) initial ATR-IR rate independent of L, (ii) normalized QCM initial slope scales with Rh loading and acetone partial pressure but not with L, and (iii) Da computed from measured Deff and fitted kobs stays ≤ 0.1.
4.3 Hydrodynamic/film-external transport checks: vary total flow rate (e.g., 20–200 sccm) and confirm invariance of kinetic descriptors; if dependence appears, redesign cell geometry or reduce L.
4.4 Heat effects: bound adiabatic temperature rise by calculating reaction enthalpy × conversion vs gas/film heat capacity; verify no QCM temperature artifacts by blank crystal control.

Step 5 — Pre-registered optimal experimental design (OED) and identifiability to prevent an underdetermined forward model.
5.1 Forward model (minimal identifiable form):
- Adsorption: competitive Langmuir with at most one site class for CH4/CO2 and one for polar VOCs (acetone/isopropanol), or virial truncated to second order if better supported by data; prohibit unconstrained multi-parameter dual-site forms unless FIM supports it.
- Reaction: microkinetic reduced to a small parameter set identifiable from transients: r = k0 exp(−Ea/RT)·f(pAce, pH2) with inhibition term only if statistically required (e.g., CO2 competitive adsorption decreasing local acetone activity). Enforce parameter priors from independent calibration where possible.
5.2 OED dataset (fixed sequence, pre-registered):
- Stage A (adsorption-only): single-component isotherms for CH4, CO2, acetone, isopropanol at 298/323 K on each pixel; plus binary CH4/CO2 and CH4/acetone at select points to validate competitive assumptions.
- Stage B (reaction transients): step acetone (0→5→20 ppm) at fixed pH2 (1 mbar) and fixed CH4/CO2 backgrounds (e.g., 100/0, 50/50, 0/100) at 298/323 K; collect synchronized QCM and ATR-IR at 1 Hz for 15 min per step.
- Stage C (H2 dependence): repeat a subset at pH2 = 0.5, 1, 5 mbar to identify H2 order without overparameterizing.
5.3 Structural identifiability + Fisher information: perform (i) local structural identifiability checks on the chosen model, and (ii) FIM-based ranking of which transients and which features (m(t) points, dm/dt, A(C=O), A(C–O), R) maximize parameter identifiability. If rank deficiency is detected, reduce model order (e.g., remove inhibition term or collapse adsorption sites) before proceeding to inversion studies.

Step 6 — Inverse-problem conditioning and array design (conditioning-driven pixel/feature selection).
6.1 Feature vector per pixel: [m(t1..tn), dm/dt|t0–t60s, A(C=O,t*), A(C–O,t*), R(t*)], with t* chosen by OED to maximize Fisher information (typically early-time for kinetics, mid-time for conversion extent).
6.2 Compute sensitivity matrix J = ∂features/∂(yCH4, yCO2, yAce) under measured noise covariance Σ (from blank runs and baseline drift characterization). Use κ(J) and predicted posterior covariance as design criteria.
6.3 Select minimal array (target 3–6 pixels) by combinatorial search over pixels and feature subsets to minimize κ(J) subject to practical constraints (acquisition time ≤ 3 min per inference update).
6.4 Bayesian inversion: constrained (non-negativity, sum-to-one), using the calibrated forward model with priors from OED. Compare against adsorption-only controls (Rh poisoned or absent) using identical MOF films.

Step 7 — Real-stream poisons and guard-bed strategy to preserve catalysis-derived orthogonality over >100 cycles.
7.1 Poison panel and stress conditions:
- H2O: 0.1–1% (humidity), CO: 0.5–10 ppm, H2S: 50–200 ppb.
- Protocol: 100-cycle acetone pulsing (e.g., 5 ppm, 2 min on/5 min off) under representative CH4/CO2 mixtures; monitor loss of kinetic/spectral orthogonality (decline of early-time C=O depletion rate and R(t*) contrast).
7.2 Mitigation/guard-bed integration (upstream, replaceable):
- Moisture control: Nafion dryer or desiccant micro-bed to fixed dew point for baseline studies; then reintroduce humidity intentionally.
- CO/H2S scrubbing: disposable metal-oxide or impregnated activated carbon micro-guard bed; quantify breakthrough by inline electrochemical CO/H2S indicator.
7.3 Deactivation diagnostics: post-mortem 31P MAS NMR/XPS to detect ligand loss or Rh oxidation; ICP to detect leaching; PXRD/IR to detect framework degradation.

Step 8 — Falsification controls (mechanism-linked) aligned to conditioning claim.
8.1 Reaction-off control: pH2 = 0 (or D2 substitution tests) to demonstrate loss of kinetic/spectral features and degraded κ(J) to adsorption-only levels.
8.2 Inert-cation control: replace [Rh(dppe)(COD)]+ with isostructural non-catalytic cation of similar size/charge; confirm that adsorption changes alone do not reproduce time-dependent C=O depletion/C–O growth.
8.3 Selective Rh poisoning: introduce trace CO (ppm) to suppress hydrogenation while retaining adsorption; show orthogonality and conditioning improvements disappear in tandem with catalytic signatures.

Milestones (go/no-go):
- M1 (Month 1–3): stable MOF thin film on QCM-ATR with defined spectral LOD; stable PXRD after CO2/H2O exposure.
- M2 (Month 3–6): Rh loading quantified; site-isolation criteria met (CV < 10% by micro-XRF; no clustering by ToF-SIMS depth profiles).
- M3 (Month 6–9): reaction observed at pH2 ≤ 5 mbar, 298–333 K with TOFapp ≥ 0.01 s−1 and TON ≥ 10^2 in preliminary cycling.
- M4 (Month 9–12): Da ≤ 0.1 demonstrated via thickness/flow invariance; minimal identifiable model validated by FIM.
- M5 (Month 12–18): κ(J) reduced and posterior composition uncertainty shrinkage demonstrated versus adsorption-only arrays; robustness shown over >100 cycles including poison/humidity protocols (with/without guard beds).
Feasibility: 1) Catalysis at trace H2 and low temperature: The proposal no longer assumes “any Rh will work”; it bounds a specific window (298–333 K; pH2 = 0.5–5 mbar) and sets quantitative go/no-go targets (TOFapp ≥ 0.01 s−1; TON ≥ 10^3 over 100 cycles). The Rh complex choice is grounded in MOF cation-exchange precedent that preserves the ligand sphere, while confinement and local polarity (tuned by co-exchanged spectator cations) are explicitly used to promote heterolytic H2 activation and carbonyl hydrogenation under mild conditions. If activity fails to meet M3, the project pivots by increasing pH2 within the bounded window or by tuning microenvironment (counterion polarity) before expanding model/inversion work.

2) Transport/identifiability risk is actively controlled: Reaction-limited behavior is not asserted; it is enforced by design (thin films L = 0.5–2 µm) and verified quantitatively using a measured Deff and a Damköhler criterion (Da ≤ 0.1) plus invariance tests against thickness and flow rate. This directly addresses the concern that QCM time traces could conflate diffusion and reaction.

3) Site isolation/uniformity are operationally defined and measurable: The plan sets a maximum loading ceiling (≤10% of exchangeable sites or ≤0.15 Rh per cavity) to avoid bimolecular deactivation, and it specifies orthogonal quantification methods (ICP for total loading; micro-XRF/ToF-SIMS for spatial homogeneity; 31P MAS NMR/XPS for chemical integrity). These metrics convert “site isolated” from a claim into an acceptance criterion.

4) Forward model complexity is constrained by pre-registered OED and identifiability analysis: Instead of a potentially non-identifiable dual-site + detailed microkinetics model, the plan commits to a minimal parameterization unless Fisher-information analysis justifies extra terms. The transients/isotherms and step sequences are specified a priori, ensuring the model is supported by data rather than fit flexibility.

5) Dual-readout feasibility is engineered rather than optional: The proposal commits to a QCM-ATR-IR geometry with explicit SNR, baseline drift, and LOD targets for both mass and vibrational features. The spectral features are pre-defined and tied to conversion chemistry (C=O depletion/C–O growth), reducing ambiguity in interpretation.

6) Real-stream poisons are addressed as a first-class test of the core claim: Water/CO/H2S are incorporated into cycling protocols with diagnostics and an upstream guard-bed strategy. Because the conditioning advantage depends on sustained catalytic orthogonality, the proposal explicitly measures whether poisoning collapses κ(J) improvements, thereby directly validating or falsifying the central premise under realistic contaminants.
final_critique: Methodologically, the proposal is unusually well resolved: dual-readout architecture with pre-registered noise/LOD, quantified site-isolation metrics (ICP, 31P MAS NMR, XPS, micro-XRF/ToF-SIMS), and explicit transport identifiability via a Damköhler criterion with thickness/flow invariance tests. The main technical risk is the central catalytic premise: [Rh(dppe)(COD)]+ is not, by itself, a canonical low-temperature acetone hydrogenation catalyst at ppm acetone and mbar H2 without an established metal–ligand cooperative handle; the proposal asserts heterolytic H2 activation aided by a polar counterion environment but does not specify a concrete base/acceptor functionality (framework node, anion, or co-cation) that would close the mechanistic loop, nor does it define how to distinguish true hydrogenation from (i) acetone adsorption-induced band shifts/intensity changes, (ii) formation of a bound alkoxide that does not desorb, or (iii) slow ligand hydrogenation/complex speciation as the source of time dependence. The chosen IR markers (1710 cm−1 depletion; 1050–1150 cm−1 growth) can be confounded by overlapping MOF lattice modes and concentration-pathlength changes in ATR; without isotope labeling (D2) and quantitative product accounting, spectral “conversion” could be over-interpreted. Finally, the conditioning claim relies on sustained orthogonality; yet poisoning/humidity are only screened after significant build-out, and CO/H2S binding to Rh(I) is likely catastrophic at very low levels, potentially collapsing the kinetic channel and reducing the array back to adsorption-only performance.

original_chain: Linker ratio -> Surface area -> Thermal stability -> CPM-26-Co -> Framework topology
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: By implementing a continuously variable mixed-linker strategy inside the CPM-26-Co (BCT zeotype) architecture—specifically, co-assembling BTC with a sterically matched, more rigid/less decarboxylation-prone trigonal linker at controlled ratios while preserving the 4-2-1 metal-hook motif—we can decouple pore size/surface area tuning from topology loss and thereby raise thermal stability at a given (or higher) BET surface area. Mechanistically, the rigid co-linker increases the energetic penalty for hook cleavage and carboxylate decarboxylation at elevated temperature, while the mixed-linker distribution introduces controlled elastic strain that suppresses cooperative bond-rupture pathways; simultaneously, maintaining BCT connectivity prevents the surface-cage ‘opening’ modes that typically reduce apparent surface area upon activation. The methodological adaptation is a topology-preserving “CVMOF-on-a-zeotype” approach: instead of isoreticular expansion (discrete) or additive-controlled surface changes, we impose continuous linker-ratio control within a fixed zeotype CPM-26-Co framework to tune surface area and stabilize the thermal response without phase transformation.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select co-linker candidates that are trigonal and size/angle-compatible with BTC to preserve BCT net formation while altering rigidity/rotational freedom: examples include 1,3,5-tris(4-carboxyphenyl)benzene (TCPB) (rigid, extended) and 1,3,5-triazine-2,4,6-tricarboxylic acid (TTCA) (electron-poor core, reduced propensity for decarboxylation), alongside BTC as the baseline.
1.2 Define a linker-ratio library (BTC:co-linker = 1:0, 0.9:0.1, 0.75:0.25, 0.5:0.5, 0.25:0.75) and keep metal sources constant to target CPM-26-Co-like node chemistry (Co-based, with optional secondary metal in the ‘hook’ position to mirror the dual-metal capture feature).
1.3 Pre-screen linker solubility/acid–base speciation by in situ 1H NMR of synthesis solutions (deuterated analog solvents) to ensure comparable deprotonation kinetics across ratios; adjust modulator identity/dose accordingly (formic acid vs acetic acid) to normalize nucleation rates.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Topology-preserving mixed-linker synthesis (adaptation): run solvothermal reactions under CPM-26-Co-forming conditions, but introduce a staged dosing protocol for linkers: (i) form a BTC-rich pre-nucleus to lock in BCT connectivity; (ii) slowly dose the rigid co-linker during crystal growth to favor statistical incorporation rather than separate nucleation. This is a deliberate adaptation to prevent phase separation typical of mixed-linker attempts in zeotype MOFs.
2.2 Enforce “hook integrity” via coordination environment control: add a competing monodentate ligand (e.g., low equivalents of pyridine-N-oxide) only during growth to bias the third carboxylate ‘hook’ into the desired immobilization geometry, then remove it by post-synthetic solvent exchange. This functional modification targets the covalent metal-hook interactions reported for CPM-26-Co while enabling mixed-linker incorporation.
2.3 Activation and thermal-stress protocol designed to diagnose surface vs bulk failure: (i) solvent exchange to low-surface-tension solvent (MeOH then acetone); (ii) supercritical CO2 drying or very slow vacuum ramping; (iii) stepwise thermal holds (100, 150, 200, 250, 300 °C) under dynamic vacuum to map onset of surface-cage opening and bulk collapse separately.
2.4 Optional heterometal ‘hook’ stabilization: prepare a second series where the immobilized cluster metal (hook-captured species) is varied (e.g., Co-only vs Co/Fe or Co/Ni in the captured site) to test whether stronger M–O bonds in the hook region synergize with rigid co-linkers to increase thermal stability without sacrificing topology.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Confirm mixed-linker homogeneity (avoid phase separation): digest-NMR quantification of linker ratios in the final solid; spatial mapping by confocal fluorescence quenching (using a trace fluorescent analog of one linker) to verify uniform distribution across single crystals; PXRD pattern fitting/Rietveld refinement to confirm BCT topology retention and continuous lattice-parameter shifts with ratio.
3.2 Quantify porosity and surface area: N2 sorption (77 K) to obtain BET and pore-size distributions; compare to parent CPM-26-Co and evaluate continuous tunability vs discrete jumps. Track any hysteresis indicative of surface-cage alteration.
3.3 Thermal stability metrics tied to mechanism: TGA coupled to MS/FTIR to identify decarboxylation/ligand loss; variable-temperature PXRD to determine the temperature of topology loss; in situ IR/Raman to monitor carboxylate coordination modes and “hook” bond persistence; low-dose HRTEM on crystal edges pre/post heating to directly observe surface-cage completeness/opening analogous to MIL-101 surface phenomena.
3.4 Structure–property modeling: build a quantitative map linking linker ratio → lattice metric/elastic strain proxy (from SCXRD/PXRD) → surface area (BET) → thermal stability onset (VT-PXRD, TGA) to test the proposed suppression of cooperative bond rupture and surface-cage opening. Use simple elastic-network/phonon proxy calculations (DFT or force-field) on representative mixed-linker supercells to correlate increased rigidity with higher decomposition barriers.
3.5 Performance-relevant stress tests: repeat activation/thermal cycling (e.g., 5 cycles to 250 °C) and measure retained BET and PXRD crystallinity; benchmark against unmixed CPM-26-Co and a high-surface-area mixed-linker control that does not preserve BCT topology.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Mixed-linker “continuously variable” strategies have already demonstrated smooth, ratio-controlled tuning of BET surface area and lattice dimensions without phase separation when linker distribution is controlled (Asset 1). Separately, thermal treatment can selectively alter surface structure while leaving bulk intact, and additive/synthetic history governs whether surface cages open or phase transformations occur (Asset 2). CPM-26-Co specifically demonstrates topology-directed immobilization via a 4-2-1 strategy and covalent metal-hook interactions, providing a clear structural handle to preserve connectivity while modifying ligand composition (Asset 3).
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The adaptation explicitly keeps CPM-26-Co’s BCT zeotype topology and metal-hook motif as the invariant scaffold while importing CVMOF-style continuous linker-ratio control as the variable. The staged dosing and hook-environment bias are MOF-native synthetic controls aimed at a known limitation: mixed-linker systems often phase-separate or shift topology; zeotype frameworks can be particularly sensitive. The thermal protocol is designed to separate surface degradation from bulk collapse, directly integrating insights from surface-cage completeness studies.
3. Comparative Advantage: Relative to single-linker CPM-26-Co, the mixed-linker CPM-26-Co series should offer (i) continuously tunable surface area at fixed topology (rather than discrete isoreticular analogs), (ii) higher thermal stability at comparable surface area by increasing linker rigidity and stabilizing hook bonds, and (iii) reduced surface-cage opening/porosity loss upon activation through suppression of cooperative failure pathways. Compared to additive-only approaches, linker-ratio tuning provides a persistent, built-in molecular control knob rather than a synthesis-history-dependent surface effect.
final_critique: This is a technically strong and unusually detailed proposal with clear awareness of known failure modes in mixed-linker zeotype MOFs. The staged dosing strategy and hook-environment biasing are well-motivated and plausibly address phase separation and topology drift, which elevates the engineering resolution above standard mixed-linker approaches. The mechanistic logic—rigidity-induced suppression of cooperative bond rupture and surface-cage opening—is coherent and largely consistent with known thermal degradation pathways in carboxylate MOFs. However, the proposal occasionally overstates mechanistic certainty: elastic strain suppression and energetic penalties for decarboxylation are asserted more confidently than the proposed measurements can strictly prove, particularly given the complexity of mixed-linker disorder. While the evidence grounding is solid, some validation tools (e.g., low-dose HRTEM for surface-cage integrity, phonon/elastic proxies on disordered supercells) may be challenging to interpret unambiguously and risk producing correlational rather than causal support. Overall, the work is ambitious but remains within the bounds of credible, expert-level MOF research.

original_chain: trans-2-butene -> Selectivity -> Molecular solubility -> Dianin's compound -> Molecular solubility -> Extrinsic porosity -> Dianin's compound
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a Dianin’s-compound-derived, soluble, cleavable pendant (“transient covalent porogen”) onto a controlled fraction of dobdc phenoxide sites in M2(m-dobdc) (M = Co2+, Ni2+) will generate *quantifiable, connected* extrinsic mesoporosity after on-demand cleavage, while preserving the crystallographic backbone and the open-metal-site (OMS) adsorption thermodynamics that govern C4 olefin discrimination. Mechanistic rationale (addressing reviewer risks): (1) **Thermodynamic selectivity remains OMS-governed**: charge-dense Co2+/Ni2+ OMS in m-dobdc preferentially stabilize 1-butene over cis-/trans-2-butene; trans-2-butene remains the weakest binder due to steric/geometric mismatch at OMS. The pendant strategy is designed to be *orthogonal* to OMS by reacting at linker –OH (phenoxide) rather than coordinating/poisoning the metal site; therefore, equilibrium selectivity and ΔQst(1-butene)–ΔQst(trans-2-butene) should remain within a predefined drift window. (2) **Connected mesoporosity is created by a falsifiable structure–process–property chain**: pendant installation generates local steric strain and packing frustration during secondary crystal aging/pellet consolidation. Upon cleavage, these strained regions become mesopore segments. *Connectivity* emerges only when pendant-modified regions percolate (above a critical functionalization-dependent threshold) and when the modification is spatially distributed (uniform or engineered core–shell) such that mesopore segments intersect intrinsic micropore channels. This predicts a measurable percolation-like transition in 3D connectivity metrics and a corresponding increase in effective diffusivity/mass-transfer coefficients with minimal change in Henry constants and Qst. (3) **Molecular solubility is an evidentiary driver**: the Dianin-derived reagent’s solubility and partitioning into the MOF solvent-filled pore volume control reaction kinetics and functionalization gradients (core–shell vs uniform). By tuning solvent/reagent solubility (and thus diffusion and local concentration), we can intentionally program spatial distributions that, after cleavage, program mesopore connectivity/tortuosity and thereby reduce the mass-transfer zone (MTZ) in multicomponent breakthrough without inducing missing-linker defects typical of etching/modulator routes.
Plan: Step 0 — Predefine quantitative acceptance criteria and statistical power (mandatory windows).
0.1 OMS retention window: post-cleavage accessible OMS ≥ 95% of pristine as measured by CO and CD3CN probe-IR (integrated band areas normalized by mass and confirmed by elemental analysis). Fail if OMS loss > 5%.
0.2 Thermodynamic drift window: |ΔQst shift| ≤ 2.0 kJ/mol for both 1-butene and trans-2-butene relative to pristine; Henry constant ratio K_H(1-butene)/K_H(trans-2-butene) must remain within ±10% of pristine. Fail if exceeded.
0.3 Connectivity requirement: mesoporosity must be *connected* with a percolating pathway across a representative crystallite/pellet subvolume; quantified as (i) connected mesopore volume fraction ≥ 60% of total mesopore volume from 3D segmentation, and (ii) tortuosity τ decreases by ≥ 25% vs pristine pellets (defined below). If only macroscopic interparticle gaps increase with no intracrystal connectivity, hypothesis fails.
0.4 Power: replicate synthesis/processing n ≥ 3 per condition; breakthrough MTZ and fitted LDF mass-transfer coefficients must show ≥ 20% improvement with p < 0.05 to claim transport benefit.

Step 1 — Baseline platform + controls (pristine and ‘sham’).
1.1 Synthesize phase-pure Co2(m-dobdc) and Ni2(m-dobdc) in two size regimes: (A) microcrystals 1–3 µm; (B) larger crystals 10–30 µm to resolve spatial gradients. Activate to expose OMS (validated by probe-IR and PXRD).
1.2 Controls: (i) pristine activated MOF; (ii) solvent/base exposure without electrophile; (iii) exposure to electrophile analog lacking leaving group (nonreactive) to control for physisorbed organics.
1.3 Baseline adsorption/transport: multitemperature single-component isotherms for 1-butene/cis-2-butene/trans-2-butene to extract K_H and Qst; multicomponent breakthrough at industrially relevant C4 compositions to obtain MTZ and productivity; ZLC or gravimetric uptake for effective diffusivities (De,eff) of 1-butene and trans-2-butene.

Step 2 — Dianin-derived pendant library with *orthogonality-by-design* and spatial tag for mapping.
2.1 Reagent architecture: Dianin’s-compound-derived rigid scaffold bearing (i) a cleavable linker (carbonate *or* acetal) and (ii) a terminal electrophile selective for phenoxide O-alkylation/O-carbonylation (activated carbonate or chloroformate class), designed to avoid strong Lewis basic donors that would bind OMS.
2.2 Spectroscopic/elemental tag (mandatory): incorporate a single-atom tag for spatial mapping and quantification (choose one primary):
  • Br-tag: para-bromophenyl substituent on pendant (R–C6H4–Br) for X-ray contrast and EDS; or
  • F-tag: trifluoromethyl group for 19F solid-state NMR and ToF-SIMS mapping.
2.3 Pendant size/rigidity series: at least three pendants spanning excluded volumes (V_p) and contour lengths (L_p): short/compact, medium, and long/rigid. Compute approximate V_p from molecular modeling (e.g., Connolly surface volume) to use as an input to the structure–process model.

Step 3 — Solubility- and diffusion-governed installation to program spatial gradients (tie-in to ‘molecular solubility’).
3.1 Solvent selection logic: choose two solvent systems with contrasting (i) Dianin-reagent solubility S (g/L) and (ii) MOF pore wetting/partitioning (estimated by uptake of solvent and Hansen solubility parameters). Example screening set: THF, 2-MeTHF, CH2Cl2, toluene, acetonitrile. Select:
  • Solvent U (uniform-loading candidate): high S and high pore partitioning (fast diffusion).
  • Solvent G (gradient/core–shell candidate): moderate S and/or lower pore partitioning (diffusion-limited).
3.2 Reaction–diffusion design rule (quantitative): use a Thiele-modulus-type criterion for functionalization uniformity across a crystallite radius R:
  φ = R * sqrt(k_obs * C_reagent / D_reagent,eff).
Target φ < 0.3 for uniform functionalization; target φ > 1 for core–shell gradients. Estimate D_reagent,eff via uptake/transport of tagged reagent analog (or pulsed-field gradient NMR in solvent where feasible) and/or from time-dependent mass uptake and crystal size dependence.
3.3 Installation protocol (orthogonal to OMS):
  • Pre-fill pores with chosen solvent (U or G) under inert atmosphere to avoid water.
  • Use a noncoordinating base (sterically hindered) at controlled equivalents to deprotonate a fraction of phenols without generating strongly coordinating anions.
  • Add tagged Dianin-electrophile at fixed C_reagent; react at low temperature initially to reduce side reactions.
3.4 Degree-of-functionalization (DoF) grid: 0%, 5%, 10%, 15%, 20%, 25% (molar % of linker OH modified, quantified by digestion NMR + tag quantification). This DoF grid is an explicit independent variable in the structure–process–property model.

Step 4 — Mandatory orthogonality controls at each stage (before cleavage).
4.1 Probe-IR staged comparison (mandatory): measure CO and CD3CN adsorption IR spectra for pristine → installed (pre-cleavage) → cleaved → reactivated. Acceptance: pre-cleavage OMS signal may decrease due to steric blockage, but post-cleavage must recover to ≥95% of pristine.
4.2 Competitive adsorption check for residual fragments: collect 1-butene and trans-2-butene isotherms at one temperature pre-cleavage and post-cleavage; any anomalous strengthening/weakening beyond the ΔQst/K_H windows flags OMS poisoning or altered site distribution.
4.3 Metal-site integrity: XANES/EXAFS at Co/Ni for pristine vs installed vs cleaved to confirm unchanged first-shell coordination; ICP-OES on supernatants to quantify metal leaching (<0.5% of total metal acceptable).

Step 5 — Cleavage chemistry with node-protection logic (avoid hydrolysis/ligand exchange).
5.1 Carbonate route: transcarbonation in anhydrous alcohol with a mild catalyst/base that does not promote linker displacement; strictly controlled water content (Karl Fischer). Time/temperature minimized. Monitor by FTIR loss of carbonate C=O.
5.2 Acetal route: mild, buffered acid cleavage under conditions demonstrated not to attack M–O nodes (short contact time, controlled pH, low water activity via mixed solvent). Monitor by FTIR/Raman disappearance of acetal bands.
5.3 Post-cleavage cleanup: exhaustive washing with solvent sequence chosen to dissolve cleavage fragments (guided by Dianin-fragment solubility) followed by activation. Confirm fragment removal by LC-MS of washings until below detection and by absence of tag signal in supernatant.
5.4 No ‘vague healing’: disallow any post-treatment that changes linker stoichiometry. Only permitted “reconstitution” is solvent exchange/activation; any attempt to add linker or modulator is treated as a separate condition and must be defect-quantified.
