Step 6 — Spatially resolved mapping of pendant distribution (mandatory evidence).
6.1 Confocal Raman mapping: use a pendant-specific vibrational band (and/or tag band) to map cross-sections of single crystals (10–30 µm) prepared by microtoming; generate radial intensity profiles to distinguish uniform vs core–shell functionalization.
6.2 FIB-SEM-EDS or ToF-SIMS: if Br-tag used, perform FIB cross-sections with EDS Br maps; quantify Br signal vs radius. If F-tag used, perform ToF-SIMS/19F mapping. Output: spatial distribution function f(r) used as model input.

Step 7 — Demonstrate *connected* mesoporosity creation (not just PSD).
7.1 3D nano-CT (mandatory): perform nano-CT on representative crystals and pellets pre-cleavage and post-cleavage. Segment pore/solid phases and compute:
  • connected mesopore volume fraction (C_M),
  • connectivity (e.g., Euler characteristic / percolation probability across the volume),
  • tortuosity τ (random-walk or diffusion-simulation-based),
  • pore-throat size distribution (to verify access from external surface).
7.2 Corroborate with gas sorption: Ar (87 K) for micropores; N2 (77 K) plus BJH/DFT only as supportive (not primary for connectivity). Use mercury intrusion or advanced methods only if compatible; report hysteresis interpretation carefully.
7.3 Distinguish interparticle vs intracrystal mesoporosity: analyze pellets and single crystals separately. If mesoporosity appears only in pellets, classify as interparticle; hypothesis requires measurable intracrystal component for at least one programmed-gradient condition.

Step 8 — Quantitative structure–process–property model (falsifiable; links DoF/pendant to connectivity and transport).
8.1 Inputs: DoF, pendant excluded volume V_p, rigidity descriptor (e.g., number of rotatable bonds), solvent-defined uniformity parameter φ, and measured spatial distribution f(r).
8.2 Mesopore generation model: define a “modified-zone” volume fraction in the crystal from f(r) and DoF; assume mesopore segments form upon cleavage with local void probability p proportional to DoF×V_p and modulated by rigidity. Predict a percolation threshold p_c for connectivity.
8.3 Outputs to test: predicted connected mesopore fraction C_M(DoF,V_p,φ) and tortuosity τ(DoF,V_p,φ). Validate against nano-CT metrics.
8.4 Transport link: fit breakthrough curves with an LDF model to extract k_LDF; relate k_LDF to De,eff and τ using De,eff ∝ ε/τ (ε = accessible porosity including connected mesopores). Test whether k_LDF increases monotonically with decreasing τ while K_H and Qst remain within windows.

Step 9 — Separation demonstrations under realistic conditions.
9.1 Multicomponent breakthrough: measure MTZ and productivity for industrial C4 mixtures across flow rates and pellet sizes. Success criterion: ≥20% MTZ reduction at unchanged selectivity order (1-butene > cis-2-butene > trans-2-butene) and within thermodynamic drift windows.
9.2 ZLC/uptake kinetics: extract De,eff for 1-butene and trans-2-butene; confirm that both increase with connected mesoporosity, while the ratio of equilibrium uptakes remains governed by OMS binding.

Step 10 — Stability/regenerability and cleanliness.
10.1 Cyclic operation: ≥100 cycles under TSA/VSA-like protocols; track PXRD, probe-IR OMS, nano-CT connectivity (subset), and breakthrough performance drift.
10.2 Desorbate cleanliness: online GC-MS during regeneration to confirm absence (or quantified trace) of Dianin fragments; any persistent release indicates incomplete cleavage/washing and fails the “operational cleanliness” requirement.

Mechanistic falsification tests (explicit).
F1 If nano-CT shows non-percolating voids (C_M below threshold) despite DoF and pendant size increases, then pendant removal does not generate connected mesoporosity—reject the architectural premise.
F2 If OMS probe-IR and ΔQst drift exceed windows post-cleavage, then chemistry is not orthogonal to OMS—reject the claim of preserved thermodynamic selectivity.
F3 If MTZ improvement occurs without changes in τ/C_M, then performance is not due to the proposed connectivity mechanism (must be reattributed; hypothesis not supported).
Feasibility: 1) Chemical feasibility with orthogonality controls: The proposal treats the key risk—competitive coordination/poisoning at OMS—as a primary experimental axis, not an afterthought. Orthogonality is tested by staged probe-IR (CO/CD3CN), XAS, competitive olefin adsorption, and strict OMS/Qst acceptance windows. Tagged pendants plus digestion analytics decouple “covalent attachment” from “mere physisorption,” and LC-MS of washings + GC-MS of desorbates enforce cleanliness.

2) Physical feasibility of creating *connected* mesoporosity: Rather than assuming void creation, the plan enforces 3D connectivity evidence (nano-CT segmentation, percolation/connectivity metrics, tortuosity) and separates intracrystal from interparticle contributions. The percolation-style model is falsifiable: varying DoF, pendant V_p, and spatial gradients (via solvent/solubility and reaction–diffusion control) must produce a measurable connectivity transition that correlates with k_LDF/MTZ.

3) Solubility as a causal control knob (addressing the reviewer gap): The Dianin-derived reagent’s molecular solubility and partitioning are used to program functionalization gradients through a quantitative reaction–diffusion criterion (φ). Crystal-size-dependent kinetics and spatial tag mapping directly validate whether solubility-controlled loading produces uniform vs core–shell modification—closing the evidence chain from “molecular solubility” to spatial distribution to connected mesoporosity to mass transfer.

4) Alignment with literature assets and separation mechanism: The C4 selectivity logic remains anchored in Co2/Ni2(m-dobdc) charge-dense OMS that favor 1-butene and disfavor trans-2-butene (thermodynamic discrimination). The Dianin’s compound asset is used not only as a bulky scaffold but as a soluble, derivatizable platform enabling controlled infiltration and spatial programming. The approach is deliberately positioned as a non-etching, non-defect-randomizing route to hierarchical porosity, with quantitative guardrails to ensure OMS density and binding energetics are preserved.
final_critique: The proposal is unusually well engineered: it predefines acceptance windows, includes appropriate staged orthogonality controls (CO/CD3CN probe-IR, XAS, leaching limits), and—critically—treats “connected mesoporosity” as a 3D, falsifiable metric rather than a PSD claim. The primary score deductions are feasibility and mechanistic gaps at two points. (i) Chemical selectivity/orthogonality risk remains nontrivial: achieving selective O-alkylation/O-carbonylation of m-dobdc phenoxides inside Co/Ni(m-dobdc) without concurrent coordination to OMS, local hydrolysis, or partial node perturbation is plausible but not yet de-risked by precedent or kinetic selectivity arguments (e.g., rate of phenoxide substitution vs competitive OMS adsorption of reagent/base/cleavage intermediates). (ii) The mesopore-creation mechanism relies on “steric strain/packing frustration during aging/pellet consolidation” that is not yet tied to a quantitative mechanical/structural model of where voids originate (intra-crystal vs grain boundaries) and may collapse into an interparticle-void explanation despite the planned controls. Nano-CT is appropriate, but typical voxel sizes may not resolve the most relevant 10–100 nm mesopores; without complementary SAXS/FIB-SEM tomography, the connectivity claim could be underdetermined. Finally, the structure–process–property model is directionally correct but currently parameter-rich (p ∝ DoF×Vp×rigidity) without an independent way to estimate p or p_c, risking post hoc fitting rather than prediction.

original_chain: Laser-flash time-resolved microwave conductivity -> Mesoporous TiO2 -> Band gap -> SU-101 -> Drug adsorption capacity -> Ciprofloxacin -> Fe-TCPP-2
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Fe‑TCPP‑2 can be engineered to combine (a) high ciprofloxacin (CIP) uptake via cooperative binding at Fe(III) open metal sites (OMS) plus porphyrin second-sphere H‑bond/π interactions and (b) a reproducible, light-modulated adsorption/desorption window, but the causal link between optoelectronics and binding must be established with a falsifiable transport/kinetic model that explicitly separates TiO2, MOF, and interfacial contributions to the TRMC signal. We hypothesize that in a MOF@meso‑TiO2 core–shell architecture with a thickness series and wavelength-selective excitation, TRMC transients can be decomposed into at least two resolvable kinetic components: (i) a TiO2-dominated component (fast rise, trap-limited decay) and (ii) an interface/MOF-associated component (slower rise and/or distinct decay) that is selectively perturbed by CIP coordination at Fe‑OMS. Illumination near the MOF absorption edge will alter the population of Fe–porphyrin charge-transfer states (ligand→metal / metal→ligand / interfacial electron transfer), producing a measurable change in the Fe local electronic environment (detectable by independent excited-state probes and light–dark core-level shifts) that reduces the stability of *outer-sphere* Fe···O(CIP) interactions and weakens H‑bonding, while *inner-sphere* Fe–O chelation—if present—will be directly tested and, if dominant, will be rendered photo-labile only upon deliberate tuning to more labile Fe coordination (controlled axial-ligand lability and OMS density). Therefore, the central, testable claim is not that “Δσ directly equals binding enthalpy,” but that a specific TRMC-extracted kinetic component assigned to Fe‑site/interfacial charge-transfer correlates with (a) independently measured changes in Fe–CIP bonding descriptors (IR/EXAFS/Mössbauer) and (b) photoinduced changes in those descriptors during release; dielectric loading/trap-filling artifacts are ruled out by inert-adsorbate controls and by site-blocking producing matched changes in adsorption thermodynamics and the same kinetic component.
Plan: Step 0 — Predefine the quantitative TRMC/transport model (mandatory falsifiability framework)
0.1 Equivalent-circuit/kinetic scheme: Model the composite as parallel photoconductive channels with interfacial charge transfer: σ_total(t)=σ_TiO2(t)+σ_MOF(t)+σ_int(t). Operationally, fit TRMC transients with a minimal set of components justified by controls: Δσ(t)=A1·f1(t;τ1,…)+A2·f2(t;τ2,…) where (Component 1) is TiO2-like (validated on bare meso‑TiO2) and (Component 2) is MOF/interface-like (emerges only when MOF is present and is wavelength-selective). Use global fitting across thickness series + excitation wavelengths to constrain shared parameters (e.g., τ1 fixed/limited to TiO2 control range).
0.2 Optical/electromagnetic constraints to justify MOF shell thickness: Choose MOF thickness range such that (i) optical absorption in MOF is significant under MOF-selective excitation yet (ii) TRMC still detects mobile carriers without complete TiO2 dominance. Implement a thickness series of 5–20–50–100 nm (mandatory) and include a “thick MOF” limit (≥200 nm) only as a diagnostic to show signal collapse or MOF-only behavior. Validate thickness by cross-sectional TEM/SEM and ellipsometry/profilometry.
0.3 Wavelength selectivity (mandatory): Select at least two excitation wavelengths: λ_TiO2 (e.g., 355 nm) where TiO2 absorbs strongly; λ_MOF (e.g., 532 nm or 450–650 nm depending on porphyrin Q/Soret band) where TiO2 absorption is negligible and Fe‑porphyrin absorbs. Confirm selectivity by diffuse reflectance/absorbance of each layer. The model is falsified if MOF-selective excitation produces the same kinetic fingerprint as bare TiO2 or if thickness scaling cannot separate components.

Step 1 — Materials and architecture with metrological control
1.1 Mesoporous anatase TiO2 scaffold: Prepare optically transparent, electrically insulating-supported (quartz) meso‑TiO2 films/monoliths with pore sizes 10–30 nm (target) and thickness 1–10 µm to ensure high internal area while remaining TRMC-compatible. Characterize: BET, pore size distribution, UV–Vis, SEM.
1.2 Fe‑TCPP‑2 baseline MOF: Synthesize Fe‑TCPP‑2 under conditions that minimize defect variability (fixed modulator/metal:linker ratio, solvent, time). Quantify defect/Fe site density by digestion NMR (linker quant), ICP-OES (Fe), and missing-linker proxies (thermogravimetric + elemental analysis).
1.3 Two rational variants with normalization safeguards:
  (A) OMS-enriched Fe(III): Create OMS by controlled activation and axial-ligand removal. Quantify OMS density via probe-molecule titration (e.g., pyridine adsorption + IR/XPS) and/or CO/NO binding where applicable. Ensure Fe remains Fe(III) via Mössbauer/XPS.
  (B) Second-sphere H-bond pocket with minimal crystallinity loss: Use low-degree post-synthetic modification (PSM) capped at predefined substitution (e.g., ≤10–20% of peripheral sites) to avoid pore collapse. Implement a statistically controlled PSM (time/stoichiometry series) and select the highest-crystallinity sample meeting a target functionality density (measured by digestion NMR/IR). Reject variants that reduce BET area by >20% relative to baseline unless porosity is restored and normalized in analysis.
1.4 Conformal MOF@TiO2 shells (mandatory thickness series): Grow Fe‑TCPP‑2 on TiO2 by surface-anchored growth using robust anchors (phosphonate or carboxylate) preinstalled on TiO2 to nucleate uniform films. Prepare shells of 5, 20, 50, 100 nm (and optional ≥200 nm diagnostic). Confirm continuity, thickness, and pore accessibility by FIB-SEM/TEM cross-sections, grazing-incidence XRD/PXRD, and N2 sorption (or Kr sorption for thin films).

Step 2 — Adsorption thermodynamics and binding-mode assignment (before any TRMC claims)
2.1 Dark adsorption isotherms: Measure CIP adsorption on (i) MOF powders and (ii) MOF@TiO2 composites using batch adsorption (controlled ionic strength, pH) to extract qmax and affinity (Langmuir/Freundlich). Normalize capacities by accessible MOF mass and surface area; independently quantify MOF loading on TiO2 (TGA/ICP).
2.2 Microcalorimetry / isosteric heat: Determine ΔH_ads (dark) to decouple capacity from binding strength.
2.3 Inner-sphere vs outer-sphere Fe–CIP binding (mandatory):
  - IR/Raman: Track Δν(C=O) and Δν(COO−) of CIP; identify chelation signatures vs H-bond/electrostatic shifts.
  - EXAFS at Fe K-edge: Look for Fe–O(CIP) scattering contributions and changes in Fe coordination number upon CIP loading.
  - Mössbauer (57Fe): Identify changes in quadrupole splitting/isomer shift consistent with altered Fe ligand field.
Decision point: If strong inner-sphere chelation dominates and is photostable, pivot to (i) controlling axial lability/coordination saturation or (ii) targeting outer-sphere/H-bond dominated binding for photomodulation while retaining high capacity.

Step 3 — TRMC with decisive origin controls and falsifiable decomposition
3.1 Baselines and controls (mandatory): Perform TRMC on bare meso‑TiO2, MOF film/powder (where measurable), and each MOF@TiO2 thickness under λ_TiO2 and λ_MOF. Establish the TiO2 kinetic fingerprint (A1, τ1 distribution) and the MOF/interface fingerprint (A2, τ2) via emergence only under MOF-selective excitation and/or thickness dependence.
3.2 Thickness scaling test (mandatory): Under λ_MOF, require monotonic increase of MOF/interface component amplitude with MOF thickness up to an optimum (then saturate), while TiO2 component remains minimal. Under λ_TiO2, require TiO2 component dominance at thin MOF shells and systematic modulation by MOF thickness only through interfacial transfer (fit parameter changes). Failure to separate components invalidates the TRMC–binding mechanistic pathway.
3.3 CIP loading series + inert-adsorbate control (mandatory criterion): Generate a TRMC “loading curve” for CIP (multiple loadings quantified gravimetrically/HPLC). In parallel, load an inert adsorbate matched for polarity/size but lacking Fe-chelating functionality (e.g., a fluoroquinolone analog with blocked chelation or a zwitterion of similar dipole) to diagnose dielectric/trap-filling effects. Mechanistic criterion: the Fe-site/interfacial TRMC component (A2 and/or τ2) must change significantly for CIP but not for inert adsorbate at comparable mass uptake.
3.4 Site-blocking concordance test (mandatory criterion): Block Fe‑OMS with pyridine/imidazole. Measure (i) ΔH_ads and qmax changes and (ii) TRMC component changes. Required concordance: the same TRMC component assigned to Fe-site/interfacial transfer must be altered in the same direction as Fe-site adsorption metrics (e.g., reduced ΔH_ads magnitude and reduced CIP-induced perturbation of A2/τ2). If TRMC changes persist without adsorption changes, infer dielectric/percolation effects and revise model.

Step 4 — Independent excited-state localization probes (mandatory concordance)
4.1 Transient absorption spectroscopy (TAS) or time-resolved photoluminescence (TRPL): Under λ_MOF, measure excited-state lifetimes and quenching upon CIP loading; distinguish interfacial charge separation from simple optical filtering. Require that the CIP-sensitive TAS/TRPL component corresponds to the TRMC-assigned MOF/interface component (shared trend with loading and site-blocking).
4.2 Operando/light–dark spectroscopy tied to Fe environment:
  - Light–dark XPS (Fe 2p, N 1s, O 1s) on thin films to detect reproducible photopotential/core-level shifts attributable to charge redistribution; compare with and without CIP and with Fe-blocking.
  - Operando EPR (if feasible) to detect Fe-centered or porphyrin radical signatures under illumination and their modulation by CIP.
Concordance requirement: at least one independent probe must show CIP-dependent changes in charge localization consistent with the TRMC component assignment.

Step 5 — Demonstrate illumination perturbs binding signatures (mandatory)
5.1 Operando IR/EXAFS under illumination: Monitor CIP coordination markers (IR Δν bands; EXAFS Fe–O contributions) during light exposure at λ_MOF and correlate with release kinetics. Even subtle reversible shifts count if statistically significant and absent in inert-adsorbate control.
5.2 Photomodulated adsorption/desorption cycles: Quantify reversible release (HPLC/UV–Vis) under dark vs illuminated conditions, matching excitation to MOF absorption edge and controlling temperature to exclude photothermal artifacts. Require cycling stability with preserved PXRD/porosity.

Step 6 — Data integration and decision rules
6.1 Multivariate regression/causal consistency: Relate qmax and ΔH_ads to OMS density, functionality density, and binding-mode classification (inner/outer sphere). Separately relate TRMC component parameters (A2, τ2) to TAS/TRPL and light–dark XPS/EPR metrics. The mechanistic claim is accepted only if (i) Fe-site blocking and inert-adsorbate controls behave as predicted, (ii) TRMC component assignment is validated by thickness/wavelength selectivity, and (iii) illumination measurably perturbs binding signatures concurrent with release.
6.2 Benchmarking vs SU‑101: Run identical adsorption thermodynamics and (where possible) optical/excited-state probes; TRMC may be limited if conductivity is too low, but TAS/TRPL + operando IR under illumination should be directly comparable to establish whether Fe‑TCPP‑2 provides a uniquely quantifiable optoelectronic–binding linkage.
Feasibility: This revision directly addresses the reviewers’ underdetermination concerns by making TRMC an origin-resolved, model-tested measurement rather than a standalone proxy for binding. (1) Signal origin is isolated by a mandatory shell thickness series (5–20–50–100 nm) and wavelength selectivity (TiO2-only vs MOF-only absorption), enabling falsifiable decomposition into TiO2 and MOF/interface kinetic components; if decomposition fails, the central TRMC-based mechanism is rejected rather than overinterpreted. (2) The optoelectronic-to-bonding link is independently localized using TAS/TRPL plus light–dark XPS and/or operando EPR, with required concordance to the TRMC-assigned component, preventing misassignment to trap filling, dielectric loading, or percolation artifacts. (3) Decisive controls distinguish dielectric/trap effects from true binding modulation: an inert adsorbate of similar polarity/size, and Fe-site blocking with pyridine/imidazole, must shift adsorption thermodynamics and the same TRMC kinetic component in tandem. (4) The strongest reviewer concern—whether Fe(III)–fluoroquinolone binding is too strong to be photo-labile—is handled by explicitly classifying inner-sphere vs outer-sphere binding via EXAFS/Mössbauer/IR and then requiring operando light-induced changes in those signatures during release; if binding is dominantly inner-sphere and photostable, the design space pivots toward more labile Fe coordination or toward second-sphere dominated photomodulation, preserving the original concept chain while preventing unsupported claims. (5) Potential PSM-induced crystallinity/porosity confounds are controlled by limiting substitution degree, enforcing BET/crystallinity acceptance criteria, and normalizing adsorption to accessible MOF mass and site density. The use of mesoporous TiO2 as a scaffold remains essential (as established in TRMC literature for separating mobility/recombination and interfacial effects), but the revised plan prevents TiO2 dominance from masquerading as MOF-driven behavior by construction.
final_critique: This is an unusually rigorous and well-specified proposal that directly addresses the canonical failure modes of TRMC-based MOF–adsorption studies (signal underdetermination, TiO2 dominance, dielectric artifacts, and overinterpretation of conductivity as binding strength). The engineering plan is exceptionally detailed, with mandatory thickness series, wavelength selectivity, global fitting constraints, and decisive controls that render the central hypothesis falsifiable rather than rhetorical. Logical consistency is strong: the proposal explicitly separates inner- vs outer-sphere Fe–CIP interactions and correctly anticipates the risk that strong Fe(III) chelation may be photostable, providing a pre-defined pivot strategy. Minor deductions arise from practical feasibility risk: the full integration of TRMC, TAS/TRPL, operando EXAFS/IR, light–dark XPS, and Mössbauer within a single project is extremely resource-intensive and may strain timelines or sample comparability. Additionally, while SU‑101 benchmarking is mentioned, its role in the optoelectronic mechanism is largely comparative rather than mechanistically integrated. These are scope, not logic, limitations.

original_chain: Interlayer space -> Bu-MnCr -> Ambient conditions -> Thermogravimetric analysis -> Pesticide -> Water pollutant -> Plasticizer
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Bu–MnCr can be converted into an ambient-condition, regenerable co-adsorbent for hydrophobic plasticizers and moderately polar pesticides by mechanically stabilizing its layered galleries with *chemically explicit, carboxyl-preserving interlayer straps* that (a) covalently bridge adjacent organic-ammonium layers to suppress humidity-driven breathing/collapse while maintaining open slit-access under 30–65% RH, and (b) introduce *unconsumed pendant –CO2H/–CO2− sites* to sustain a persistent H-bond/ion–dipole network for pesticide anchoring. The refined strap architecture is a bifunctional aromatic ‘pillar’ comprising: (i) a rigid π-rich aromatic core (dispersion/π capture plane for phthalates), (ii) two terminal coupling groups that react selectively with interlayer nucleophiles (diol/diamine handles) to form stable amide/urethane/carbonate linkages under controlled water activity, and (iii) at least one additional pendant carboxyl group intentionally left unreacted (trimellitic/pyromellitic-derived motifs or protected/deprotected carboxyl strategies) to preserve polar binding sites post-installation. Mechanistically, the straps impose a fixed interlayer registry and reduce the free-energy penalty of guest intercalation under ambient humidity by preventing gallery collapse and by stabilizing a confined water population; simultaneously, the aromatic strap faces create a low-polarity adsorption plane that concentrates plasticizers, while pendant –CO2H/–CO2− plus structured interlayer water cooperatively bind pesticide heteroatoms (e.g., triazine N, phosphoryl/sulfide motifs) through H-bonding and ion–dipole interactions. TGA is retained as a central tool but is repositioned from ‘DTG feature assignment’ to a *calibrated desorption/decomposition framework*: evolved-gas signatures will be validated against standards and intact-guest evolution will be independently quantified (TGA–GC/MS and stepwise isothermal desorption with analytical recovery), enabling defensible confinement-strength distributions and regeneration windows that avoid strap/framework damage.
Plan: Step 1 — Baseline material, stability envelope, and pollutant panel
1.1 Synthesize phase-pure layered Bu–MnCr ({Bu3NH}[MnCr(ox)3]·nH2O or the closest reported Bu–MnCr analogue) and confirm: (i) low-angle PXRD interlayer reflections, (ii) composition by ICP-OES (Mn/Cr) + CHN, (iii) interlayer water by DVS (30–90% RH) and TGA (under N2). Establish baseline ‘humidity-breathing’ by variable-RH PXRD (30/50/65/80% RH) to quantify Δd-spacing and reversibility.
1.2 Define adsorbate set spanning hydrophobicity/polarity and distinct MS fragments: plasticizers (DBP, DEHP), pesticides (atrazine, chlorpyrifos), optional polarity controls (2,4-D acid and 2,4-D ester). Prepare aqueous matrices at pH 6–8, ionic strength 1–10 mM, ±5–10 mg/L humic acid; concentrations μg–mg/L.

Step 2 — Chemically defensible strap architecture that preserves pendant acids
2.1 Install *interlayer nucleophile handles* by co-templated growth (not cation exchange) using a minor fraction (5–20 mol%) of functional ammonium templators that are (a) gallery-compatible and (b) provide high-yield coupling in confined media:
- Option A (diol handle): HO–(CH2)3–NH2+R2 (secondary/tertiary ammonium), providing terminal –OH.
- Option B (diamine handle): H2N–(CH2)3–NH3+R2 (one free –NH2 plus one protonated –NH3+), providing a faster acylation site than –OH.
Quantify incorporation by solid-state 13C CPMAS NMR (handle carbons), FTIR (O–H/N–H), and elemental analysis (N/C change vs parent).

2.2 Strap-linker selection explicitly preserving polar sites (reviewer directive)
Design strap molecules where only two positions are coupling-competent and ≥1 carboxyl remains pendant/unreacted after bridging:
- Primary strap motif: 1,2,4-benzenetricarboxylic (trimellitic) platform converted to *di-activated + one free acid*.
  • Route 2.2a (protected acid strategy): Start from trimellitic anhydride; selectively open/derive a mono-protected carboxyl (e.g., tert-butyl ester) leaving two carboxyls activatable. Convert the two to acid chlorides (SOCl2/oxalyl chloride) or activated esters (NHS/EDC) for coupling; after grafting, deprotect to regenerate –CO2H.
  • Route 2.2b (intrinsically mono-acid pendant): Use a pre-made di-functional coupling reagent bearing a pendant carboxyl (e.g., bis(NHS-ester) of trimellitic acid with one acid left free).
- Secondary strap motif (higher density of pendant acids): pyromellitic core where two opposite positions are used for bridging and remaining two remain as acids (via orthogonal protection/activation).
Explicit functional-group map for each strap type will be included in the synthetic plan (before/after coupling), documenting which –CO2H are consumed and which are preserved.

2.3 Diffusion- and selectivity-controlled post-synthetic strap installation (de-risking water/acylation)
2.3.1 Pre-conditioning to control water activity (aw): equilibrate crystals at defined RH (e.g., 30% RH) then solvent-exchange with dry acetonitrile or dry ethyl acetate to reduce free water while retaining structural water required for lattice integrity (verified by mass balance and DVS).
2.3.2 Compare two functionalization modes side-by-side:
- Vapor-phase (preferred for diffusion and low aw): expose crystals to strap reagent vapor (or sublimable activated ester) with catalytic base scavenger in a separated reservoir, minimizing hydrolysis.
- Low-water solution route: dry aprotic solvent with controlled ppm-water (Karl Fischer monitored); add base (2,6-lutidine) and catalytic DMAP for –OH coupling, or mild base for –NH2 coupling.
2.3.3 Use coupling chemistries that are less water-sensitive than acid chlorides when needed:
- For –NH2 handles: activated esters (NHS-esters) to form amides cleanly at low aw.
- For –OH handles: carbonate/urethane formation using di-activated carbonates/isocyanates bearing pendant acid (protected), avoiding direct acid chloride hydrolysis.
2.3.4 Control strap density by stoichiometry relative to quantified handle content (from CHN/NMR). Target low/med/high strap densities (e.g., 10/30/60% of handles reacted), anticipating that sparse bridging can already lock mechanics.

2.4 Removal of residuals and re-generation of pendant acids
Extensive washing (dry solvent) and vacuum activation at mild temperature below any strap cleavage threshold (set by model-compound TGA). If protection was used, deprotect under conditions compatible with Bu–MnCr (e.g., mild acidolysis for tert-butyl esters with minimal water exposure, or catalytic methods in organic media), then re-equilibrate at 30–65% RH.

Step 3 — Decisive structural proof of *covalent interlayer bridging* and functionalization depth
3.1 Structural proof beyond low-angle PXRD (mandatory)
3.1.1 Total scattering/PDF: Collect synchrotron total scattering for parent, handle-bearing, and strapped materials. Fit/compare real-space correlations expected for aromatic strap C–C distances and new interlayer correlations (e.g., handle–strap–handle vectors). A true bridge should introduce reproducible new pair correlations absent in (i) parent and (ii) physically intercalated aromatic controls.
3.1.2 Advanced SSNMR connectivity/distance constraints:
- Prepare 15N-labeled amine handle (for Option B) in a subset.
- Use 13C{15N} REDOR (or related dipolar recoupling) to measure distances between strap carbonyl/aromatic 13C signals and 15N sites. Interlayer bridging predicts consistent short-range 13C–15N proximities not achievable by surface-only adsorption.
- 1H–13C HETCOR to detect spatial proximity between aromatic strap carbons and interlayer water/protons.
3.1.3 Depth profiling to rule out surface-only grafting:
- ToF-SIMS depth profiling (strap-specific fragments, e.g., aromatic + carboxyl fragments) across particle cross-section.
- Complement with microtomed cross-sections + confocal Raman mapping (aromatic band intensity vs depth) and/or XPS depth profiling (gentle sputter) tracking O=C–O components.
Go/no-go for ‘true interlayer’ modification: strap signature must be present through ≥70% of particle thickness (normalized), and REDOR/PDF must support covalent proximity rather than mere intercalation.

3.2 Controls critical for interpretation
- Physical intercalation control: expose parent Bu–MnCr to nonreactive aromatic acids (no coupling group) under identical conditions to quantify mere adsorption/intercalation signatures.
- Intralayer tethering control: handle-bearing material treated with mono-functional acylating agent to form ‘dangling’ groups without bridging; compare mechanics and spectroscopy.

Step 4 — Adsorption performance with humidity-mechanics coupling
4.1 Ambient-condition uptake: kinetics and isotherms for single solutes and mixtures at 30–65% RH-equilibrated solids. Quantify by GC–MS (DBP/DEHP/chlorpyrifos) and LC–MS (atrazine/2,4-D). Report capacity, distribution coefficient (Kd), and selectivity factors in mixed matrices.
4.2 In situ variable-RH PXRD during adsorption to confirm: strapped materials show minimal Δd-spacing across RH and during loading (mechanical lock), whereas parent/control exhibits measurable breathing/collapse.
4.3 Verify pendant acid availability post-strap: titration of accessible acid sites (e.g., vapor-phase base uptake, or potentiometric titration on dispersions where framework is stable), FTIR of –CO2H/–CO2−, and XPS carboxyl speciation.

Step 5 — Mechanism dissection of dual binding physics
5.1 Separate contributions:
- Plasticizers: dependence on aromatic strap identity (tere-/naphthalene-based) and slit size; expect enhanced uptake correlated with aromatic content and constant spacing.
- Pesticides: dependence on pendant acid density and RH; expect maximum uptake at intermediate RH where structured water + –CO2H cooperate.
5.2 Competitive sorption under controlled RH and ionic strength to test ‘stabilized interlayer water’ hypothesis (asset-1 logic extended): compare uptake as a function of pre-equilibrated water content (from DVS) and measure whether strapped materials maintain uptake where parent collapses or excludes.
5.3 Spectroscopic evidence of binding:
- FTIR shifts: atrazine ring modes; chlorpyrifos P–O/P=S region; carboxylate changes upon guest binding.
- SSNMR (where feasible): observe guest-induced perturbations; 1H signatures for H-bonded water.

Step 6 — TGA-centered confinement quantification, calibrated and orthogonal (mandatory)
6.1 Build evolved-gas libraries and separate desorption from decomposition
- Run TGA–MS/FTIR on pure pollutants and on pollutants physically mixed with inert matrix to establish fragmentation vs intact volatilization signatures.
- Add TGA–GC/MS (or interface to trap evolved organics followed by GC/MS) to confirm whether intact DBP/DEHP/chlorpyrifos evolves at specific temperature windows.
- Implement stepwise isothermal desorption (e.g., hold at 40/60/80/100/120 °C under N2) and quantify desorbed intact guests by solvent trapping + GC/LC, generating direct desorption curves independent of DTG peak overlap.
6.2 Apply kinetic analysis only to validated ‘desorption-only’ regions
- Use modulated TGA (MTGA) or multi-rate TGA with isoconversional methods (Friedman/OFW) only on regions proven (by TGA–GC/MS + isothermal trapping) to correspond to intact guest release rather than decomposition.
6.3 Define regeneration windows
- Select regeneration temperature/time where (i) ≥95% guest is recovered/desorbed intact, (ii) strap bands (FTIR/NMR) remain unchanged, and (iii) interlayer spacing/mechanics remain constant (PXRD/DVS).

Step 7 — Environmental robustness, mitigation criteria, and contingency
7.1 Define acceptance thresholds (go/no-go)
- Humidity-mechanical stability: Δd-spacing ≤2% between 30–80% RH over 3 cycles; DVS hysteresis reduced vs parent.
- Adsorption performance targets (initial): Kd ≥10^3–10^4 L/kg for DBP/DEHP and ≥10^3 L/kg for atrazine in mixed matrices; selectivity vs humics maintained within 50% of clean-water performance.
- Leaching thresholds: Mn and Cr each <10 µg/L under pH 6–8 after 24 h contact (or aligned to local regulatory/WHO limits as applicable); TOC leachables from straps below method detection after washing.
7.2 Stress tests
- pH window mapping (pH 5–9), oxidant sensitivity (e.g., residual chlorine), and ionic strength. Track structural retention (PXRD), performance, and leaching (ICP–MS).
7.3 Contingency route if covalent bridging is nonuniform (mandatory)
If ToF-SIMS depth profiling/REDOR indicates surface-only grafting or insufficient penetration:
- Pivot to *noncovalent aromatic pillaring* using dicarboxylate salt-bridges: introduce aromatic dicarboxylates as dianions that ion-pair with interlayer ammonium (Bu3NH+) and/or mixed ammonium handles, creating reversible ‘ionic straps’ that still lock spacing. Validate via variable-RH PXRD (mechanical stabilization) and leaching/robustness tests. This preserves pendant carboxylates inherently and reduces synthetic water-sensitivity.

Deliverables
(i) Strap library with explicit pendant-acid density; (ii) decisive proof of interlayer covalent bridges (PDF + REDOR + depth profiling); (iii) calibrated desorption/decomposition model (TGA–GC/MS + isothermal trapping) with regeneration windows; (iv) adsorption/selectivity maps vs RH and strap parameters; (v) robustness/leaching acceptance report + contingency outcome if needed.
Feasibility: Addresses Reviewer Risk (i): chemistry selectivity/kinetics in hydrated, ion-rich galleries
- The strap architecture is redesigned so that *polar binding sites are not sacrificed*: pendant –CO2H/–CO2− groups remain after coupling via trimellitic/pyromellitic-derived motifs and/or protection/deprotection. Coupling is shifted toward less hydrolysis-prone activated esters (for –NH2 handles) and carbonate/urethane strategies (for –OH handles), with explicit water-activity control (RH pre-equilibration + dry solvent exchange + Karl Fischer monitoring). Vapor-phase functionalization is directly compared to low-water solution routes to maximize penetration and minimize acylation by adventitious water.

Addresses Reviewer Risk (ii): proving true interlayer bridging vs intercalation
- The plan adds *decisive structural proof*: total scattering/PDF to detect new real-space correlations; 15N-enabled SSNMR distance constraints (13C–15N REDOR) to demonstrate covalent proximity; and ToF-SIMS/confocal Raman/XPS depth profiling to confirm modification throughout particles and rule out surface-only grafting. Controls (nonreactive aromatic intercalation; mono-functional dangling graft) isolate mere adsorption effects.

Addresses Reviewer Risk (iii): TGA mechanistic fragility for complex organics
- The TGA approach is upgraded into a calibrated framework: evolved-gas assignments are benchmarked using pure standards and validated by TGA–GC/MS (intact parent detection) plus stepwise isothermal desorption with analytical recovery. Kinetic/isoconversional analysis is restricted to verified desorption-only regimes, explicitly separating desorption from decomposition/oxidation.

Addresses Reviewer Risk (iv): availability/orientation of carboxyl groups after coupling
- Functional-group accounting is built into the strap design: at least one carboxyl per strap is preserved (or regenerated by deprotection), and its accessibility is verified experimentally (carboxyl speciation by FTIR/XPS; acid-site titration/uptake tests). Thus, the pesticide-binding hypothesis remains chemically coherent post-reaction.

Addresses Reviewer Risk (v): environmental robustness and leaching
- The proposal defines explicit go/no-go acceptance criteria for humidity stability, adsorption/selectivity, and Mn/Cr leaching, and includes stress testing across pH/oxidant/ionic strength. A contingency pathway (ionic/noncovalent aromatic pillaring via dicarboxylate salt bridges) is pre-specified if covalent straps are nonuniform, preserving the central concept (mechanically stabilized π-rich slit + pendant acids) while reducing synthetic risk.

Anchor to provided assets
- Asset 1 supports the central role of interlayer water/hydrophilicity under ambient RH and the diagnostic value of TGA for retained volatiles; the revised plan uses this while enforcing structural locking.
- Asset 2 validates the lamellar-spacing control concept and the use of diffraction/TGA to quantify organic content and stability.
- Asset 3 supports dual-interaction adsorption (hydrophobic/π plus H-bonding) for plasticizers/pesticides; the revised architecture explicitly encodes these interactions with preserved pendant acids.
final_critique: This is an unusually deep and carefully de-risked proposal that demonstrates strong command of layered MOF/coordination polymer chemistry, confined-space reactivity, and adsorption thermodynamics under ambient humidity. The engineering plan is detailed down to coupling chemistry choice, water-activity control, and quantitative strap-density targeting, which significantly reduces feasibility risk. Logical consistency is strong: mechanical stabilization, π-rich concentration planes, pendant carboxyl sites, and structured interlayer water are coherently integrated into a dual-mode adsorption mechanism. The upgrade of TGA from qualitative DTG assignment to a calibrated desorption/decomposition framework is particularly rigorous and directly addresses a known weakness in adsorption studies of complex organics. Minor score deductions arise from (i) the cumulative synthetic and characterization burden, which may strain timeline/resources even with contingency routes, and (ii) reliance on multiple high-end techniques (synchrotron PDF, REDOR, ToF-SIMS) whose access and integration could become a bottleneck rather than a scientific flaw. Overall, the proposal is scientifically sound, innovative, and unusually well-defended against reviewer risks.

original_chain: Fe/Co molar ratio -> Surface area -> Channel collapse -> Solvent exchange -> Framework decomposition -> Porous framework -> CH4
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A solvent-filled, heterometallic Fe/Co rod-SBU “chain–pillar” MOF can be made intrinsically collapse-resistant if (i) topochemical constraints (pendant-group proximity and orientation) are verified crystallographically in the solvated state, (ii) open metal sites are deliberately capped to prevent catalyst poisoning and uncontrolled coordination chemistry, and (iii) an intrapore covalent crosslinking reaction is selected that is (a) Cu-free / metathesis-free or uses a protected catalyst and (b) sufficiently strain-tolerant to proceed via a programmed single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SCSC) transformation. Mechanistically, solvent-exchange collapse in rod-MOFs is initiated by capillary-pressure-driven linker hinging and node shear; adding a sparse, percolating covalent ‘brace network’ converts the lattice from purely coordinative connectivity to a coordinative–covalent hybrid, raising the shear modulus (G) and increasing the collapse pressure threshold. The Fe/Co ratio is not assumed to monotonically control stiffness; rather, it is treated as a coupled control variable that modulates (1) node Lewis acidity and ligand-exchange kinetics (thereby controlling how strongly temporary capping ligands protect the node and how readily the node tolerates crosslinking reagents), (2) defect chemistry (missing-linker/terminal ligand populations that soften the lattice), and (3) breathing amplitude that perturbs pendant-group distances. By staging (a) structure-guided crosslinker selection/redesign, (b) a minimal chemistry screen in homometal parents under capped-node conditions, and (c) direct mechanical readouts (nanoindentation/Brillouin) before expanding the full Fe/Co matrix, we de-risk the two highest-failure modes identified by reviewers: (i) catalyst deactivation/poisoning or framework damage, and (ii) insufficient topochemical alignment for high-yield inter-linker coupling. After ‘locking’, CH4 pressure-swing cycling will be performed under explicitly controlled dry vs humid conditions, enabling separation of adsorption-strain-driven damage from hydrolysis/impurity-driven decomposition; the resulting composition–structure–mechanics–stability map will identify the Fe/Co window that maximizes (crosslink density × modulus gain × surface-area retention) while preserving crystallinity and CH4 working capacity.
Plan: Stage 0 (Go/No-Go gate design; weeks 1–10): determine whether topochemistry + benign intrapore coupling + SCSC retention is achievable in at least one parent composition before any full Fe/Co matrix.

0.1 Select an implementable rod-MOF family and define node-capping strategy up front.
- Target topology: MIL-53/MIL-68-like 1D channels built from infinite M–O–C rods (carboxylate chains) + pillar/linker.
- Metals: Fe(III) and Co(II/III) in mixed-metal rods; initial de-risking uses homometal Fe-only and Co-only analogues.
- Node-site protection (mandatory): install labile, monodentate capping ligands to occupy open metal sites during crosslinking to prevent catalyst sequestration and uncontrolled coordination. Two orthogonal caps will be screened:
  (A) pyridine-N-oxide (PNO, weakly coordinating, displaceable) or DMF retained at nodes (baseline), and
  (B) acetate/benzoate terminal ligands introduced via modulated synthesis to pre-saturate labile sites.
- Verification of capping: quantify terminal ligands/defects by quantitative digest NMR (linker:cap ratio) and thermogravimetric titration (mass loss assignment to caps/solvent), supported by XPS (N 1s for PNO) and EXAFS for coordination-number changes.
- Go/No-Go criterion G0: capped-node samples must show no significant loss of crystallinity after 72 h soak in the intended reaction solvent at reaction temperature (≤60 °C), judged by PXRD peak integrity (≥90% relative intensity retained) and unchanged unit cell within ±0.5%.

Stage 1 (Topochemical feasibility; weeks 4–14): crystallographically prove pendant-group geometry in the solvent-filled state and under solvent swaps.

1.1 Solve at least one solvent-filled crystal structure (as-synthesized) for one composition.
- Choose the composition that yields the largest, highest-quality crystals first (anticipated: homometal Co-MOF often crystallizes better; if not, use Fe-MOF).
- Crystal size/quality window for SCXRD: target 50–150 µm single crystals, low mosaicity (<0.5° preferred). Establish growth conditions by modulated solvothermal synthesis (acid modulator equivalents varied 5–50 eq) to tune size.
- Data: SCXRD structure with resolved pendant groups (or partially occupied disorder model) and channel solvent.

1.2 Quantify the ‘reactive distance distribution’ and breathing sensitivity.
- Extract across-channel pendant–pendant distances (d) and relative approach angles (θ) for the intended coupling reaction (e.g., S···C for thiol–ene preorganization, azide–alkyne proximity for click-like, alkene–alkene proximity for [2+2]/metathesis).
- Perform solvent-dependent unit-cell + geometry mapping by sequential, gentle solvent replacement while keeping crystals solvated (e.g., mother liquor → DMF → MeCN → acetone), collecting SCXRD where possible or high-resolution PXRD + Pawley/Rietveld to track cell changes.
- Go/No-Go criterion G1: identify at least one solvent condition in which a majority population of pendant pairs satisfy d ≤ 6.5 Å (for flexible bis-thiol bridging/thiol–ene proximity) or d ≤ 7–10 Å (for a designed bifunctional crosslinker length), and where breathing does not broaden d beyond a bimodal distribution that would preclude percolation (operationally: standard deviation of d across symmetry-unique pairs ≤ 1.5 Å).

1.3 Crosslinker-length selection/redesign based on measured geometry.
- If pendant pairs are too far: redesign linker to enforce proximity (e.g., move pendant group from meta to ortho relative to carboxylate to bias inward projection; incorporate a rigid spacer to reduce conformational freedom).
- If pendant pairs are too close and risk pore blocking: select a shorter, more flexible crosslinker to avoid dense network formation.

Stage 2 (Minimal chemistry screen in homometal parents; weeks 10–26): demonstrate intrapore coupling under capped-node conditions with SCSC/PXRD retention before expanding to Fe/Co series.

2.1 Replace high-risk CuAAC and Grubbs metathesis with a staged reaction screen that prioritizes catalyst-tolerant, strain-tolerant, Cu-free pathways.
- Primary route (Cu-free, node-benign): photoinitiated thiol–ene coupling.
  • Linker pendant group: terminal alkene preferred for thiol–ene.
  • Diffuse a dithiol crosslinker (HS–(CH2)n–SH; n chosen from Stage 1 geometry; start n=2,4,6) into solvent-filled crystals.
  • Initiation: 365–405 nm LED irradiation with a pore-diffusible photoinitiator (e.g., DMPA at low mM) in MeCN or acetone; temperature 25–35 °C.
  • Rationale: radical thiol–ene is tolerant of carboxylates and avoids strong metal-binding catalysts; often proceeds with low strain penalty and high functional-group tolerance.
- Secondary route (latent crosslinker, thermal trigger): incorporate pendant groups that undergo thermally activated cycloaddition without metal catalysts.
  • Example: furan–maleimide Diels–Alder (DA) pair split across linkers (requires dual-linker strategy) or a masked nitrile imine precursor for photoinduced 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition.
  • Trigger at 40–80 °C (DA) or UV (photo-click), all under capped-node conditions.
- Tertiary route (only if needed, and only after soak-stability is proven): Cu-free strain-promoted azide–alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC).
  • Use cyclooctyne-bearing pendant groups (linker redesign) + difunctional azide crosslinker; eliminates Cu entirely.
  • This is retained as a contingency due to synthetic overhead.

2.2 Diffusion timescale and reaction uniformity control.
- Measure reagent uptake kinetics using gravimetry or UV–vis depletion (for initiator) and/or confocal Raman mapping (alkene band intensity vs position) across a single crystal.
- Establish diffusion time t90 (time to reach 90% uptake) for each crystal size; restrict SCSC experiments to crystals where t90 ≤ 12 h to avoid gradients.
- Go/No-Go criterion G2: post-reaction crystals must retain sharp PXRD peaks (FWHM increase ≤ 20%), maintain unit cell within ±1%, and show ≥30% conversion of pendant groups (digest NMR) without evidence of linker cleavage (LC-MS of digests: no new low-mass fragments above 5% relative abundance).

2.3 SCSC monitoring strategy that does not rely solely on in situ SCXRD.
- In situ: high-resolution PXRD during reaction (capillary setup, solvent-saturated) to monitor phase purity/unit-cell drift.
- Ex situ: SCXRD on a subset of crystals that survive (not mandatory for every condition).
- Spectroscopy: Raman/IR (loss of C=C or appearance of thioether C–S band); solid-state 13C NMR confirming new bond formation.

Stage 3 (Mechanical hardening validation; weeks 18–36): directly measure modulus gain and tie it to stitch density and collapse threshold.

3.1 Mechanical proxies.
- Nanoindentation on oriented single crystals (if size permits): measure reduced modulus (Er) pre/post crosslinking; target ≥25% increase as meaningful hardening.
- If crystals are too small: Brillouin light scattering on crystal aggregates to extract longitudinal/transverse sound velocities and estimate elastic constants; complement with AFM modulus mapping on microcrystals embedded in epoxy.

3.2 Collapse threshold mapping.
- Variable-pressure in situ PXRD during controlled drying (stepwise reduction of solvent vapor pressure) to detect gate-closure/collapse onset.
- Surface area retention: N2 (77 K) and Ar (87 K) BET; compare to non-stitched controls.
- Go/No-Go criterion G3: crosslinked sample must retain ≥80% of the parent’s solvated-porosity-derived accessible volume (operationally: ≥80% of BET area of the best-activated control using the same drying protocol) and shift collapse onset to lower vapor pressure (or higher applied capillary stress) by ≥30% relative to non-stitched analog.

Stage 4 (Only after passing G1–G3): expand to Fe/Co composition matrix with defect and node-chemistry covariates explicitly measured (weeks 28–60).

4.1 Composition set and synthesis.
- Ratios: Fe/Co = 0/1, 1/9, 1/4, 1/2, 1/1, 2/1, 1/0 (as originally proposed), but synthesized in two waves:
  • Wave A (3 compositions): Co-only, Fe/Co=1/4, Fe-only.
  • Wave B (remaining): fill in after identifying the ‘safe’ crosslinking window.
- Control defect density via modulator equivalents; track missing-linker populations via quantitative digest NMR and TGA-based cap quantification.
- Metal distribution/speciation: ICP-OES for bulk; STEM-EDS for homogeneity; 57Fe Mössbauer + Co K-edge XANES/EXAFS to assign oxidation/spin states and coordination.

4.2 Crosslinking under the validated chemistry and capped-node condition.
- Apply the best-performing route from Stage 2; keep reaction conditions fixed to isolate composition effects.
- Quantify stitch density (digest NMR, solid-state NMR, XPS) and correlate with mechanical and sorption outcomes.

Stage 5 (CH4 adsorption/cycling with dry vs humid separation; weeks 40–72): isolate strain-driven effects from hydrolysis/impurities.

5.1 Gas quality and water control.
- Dry CH4 spec: use 6.0-grade CH4; pass through additional purifier; continuously monitor H2O with an online hygrometer at the instrument inlet/outlet.
- Define conditions:
  • “Dry”: H2O ≤ 1 ppm.
  • “Humid”: controlled 200–500 ppm H2O (and a higher-stress condition at ~1000 ppm) using a calibrated humidification loop.
- Analyze impurities (O2/CO2) by inline GC if possible; otherwise batch certificate + purifier performance logs.

5.2 Cycling protocol.
- CH4 isotherms at 273 and 298 K up to 65 bar.
- Pressure-swing cycling: 65→5 bar, ≥50 cycles dry and ≥50 cycles humid, identical ramp rates and dwell times.
- In situ PXRD under CH4 pressure for representative samples to monitor reversible breathing vs irreversible collapse.

5.3 Decomposition/defect propagation diagnostics.
- Post-cycling: BET area, pore-size distribution, PXRD.
- Chemical stability: TGA-DSC (inert/air), TGA-MS for fragments, LC-MS of digested linkers, EXAFS for node rearrangement, ICP of leached metals after humid exposure.
- Model includes defect density and capping-ligand population as covariates to avoid attributing all effects to Fe/Co ratio.

Deliverable: a composition–structure–stitch density–elastic modulus–collapse threshold–CH4 working capacity map identifying an Fe/Co window where (i) stitch conversion is high without SCSC loss, (ii) modulus gain is measurable, (iii) activation without supercritical CO2 yields high retained surface area, and (iv) CH4 cycling stability is limited by strain rather than hydrolysis (quantified by dry vs humid divergence).
Feasibility: This revision explicitly addresses the review board’s feasibility gaps by adding staged de-risking gates, chemistry alternatives, node-protection, quantitative mechanics, and humidity-controlled CH4 testing.

(1) Topochemical constraints are no longer assumed: Stage 1 requires solving a solvent-filled crystal structure and quantifying pendant-pair distances/angles under multiple solvent states. Crosslinker length (or linker redesign) is chosen from measured geometry, directly satisfying the directive to prove inter-linker proximity in breathing rod-MOFs before committing to a composition matrix.

(2) Stitching chemistry is de-risked away from the two highest-risk catalytic assumptions (in-node CuAAC and ppm Grubbs metathesis). The primary screen uses photoinitiated thiol–ene (Cu-free, tolerant of carboxylates), while latent thermally/photochemically triggered options and SPAAC remain as contingencies. This directly mitigates risks of Cu sequestration/poisoning, uncontrolled metal-mediated nucleation, and metathesis catalyst deactivation by Fe/Co carboxylate environments.

(3) Open-metal-site poisoning and framework damage are proactively controlled via deliberate, quantified node capping (PNO or carboxylate terminals) plus mandatory soak-stability tests with PXRD/XANES/EXAFS validation, aligning with the directive to demonstrate catalyst/structure compatibility rather than assuming it.

(4) Mechanical hardening is made quantitative: modulus gain is measured (nanoindentation or Brillouin) and explicitly correlated with stitch density and collapse threshold (variable-pressure in situ PXRD during drying). This supplies the missing mechanical proxy for the shear-modulus premise and ties it to the functional outcome (surface-area retention) rather than relying on qualitative arguments.

(5) CH4-induced effects are separated from hydrolysis/impurity-driven degradation by explicit gas specs, online water-ppm monitoring, and parallel dry vs humid cycling under identical pressure swings, with defect density and terminal-ligand populations treated as covariates. This directly addresses the reviewer’s concern that “CH4-induced decomposition” can be confounded by moisture.

Integration with provided literature assets: Asset 2 motivates that activation protocol improvements alone cannot reliably prevent collapse; therefore, the proposal shifts the locus of control to pre-activation internal mechanical reinforcement. Asset 3 supports the premise that solvent-handling and post-synthetic transformations can preserve porosity and stability when designed to avoid decomposition pathways; here, SCSC-compatible intrapore locking is explicitly engineered with strain-tolerant chemistry and capped nodes. Asset 4 underscores that oxidative/hydrolytic environment changes can catastrophically reduce surface area and adsorption; accordingly, we incorporate humidity-controlled cycling and chemical-state diagnostics. Asset 1 establishes that Fe/Co ratio can strongly modulate morphology/porosity; in this proposal, Fe/Co is treated mechanistically and quantitatively through its effects on node chemistry, defect populations, breathing, and ultimately stitch yield and modulus gain—validated experimentally rather than assumed.

Overall, the concept chain remains identical (Fe/Co rod-MOF → solvent-filled intrapore covalent ‘locking’ → activation without collapse → CH4 cycling stability), but the highest-risk elements are now front-loaded into minimal go/no-go experiments with explicit quantitative criteria before expanding scope.
final_critique: Methodologically, the staged de-risking with quantitative gates is strong and addresses the two dominant failure modes (misalignment and node/catalyst incompatibility). However, several key chemical/structural uncertainties remain under-specified for a rod-SBU Fe/Co system: (i) the actual identity/stoichiometry/charge balance of the heterometallic rod node and where “open metal sites” exist in the solvated structure is not pinned down, yet capping strategy, defect accounting, and crosslinking compatibility all depend on it; (ii) the primary thiol–ene route introduces plausible side reactions in redox-active Fe/Co carboxylate environments (thiyl radical quenching at metals, thiol coordination/displacement of caps, oxidative disulfide formation, radical damage to linkers), but the plan lacks explicit control experiments/analytics to distinguish true inter-linker stitching from thiol adsorption, chain transfer, or pore-filling; (iii) the percolation/‘sparse brace network’ premise is asserted but not quantitatively connected to a required conversion threshold, crosslink topology, and expected modulus gain—without a minimal mechanical model, the ≥25% modulus target and ≥30% conversion gate risk being arbitrary; (iv) SCSC is treated as a major objective, but rod-MOF breathing/disorder may preclude reliable pendant-pair statistics from SCXRD in many realistic cases (partial occupancy, dynamic disorder), so the proposal should define what “success” looks like if only high-resolution PXRD + spectroscopic constraints are achievable. Overall the concept chain is preserved and the engineering plan is credible, but the mechanistic link from chemistry → verified covalent network architecture → quantified modulus/collapse improvement needs tighter, falsifiable structure–property predictions.

original_chain: Radical stability -> Spin localization -> Aryl ring twist angle -> Dihedral angle -> 6-c hexagonal zirconium cluster
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding persistent triarylmethyl (TAM/PTM-derived) radical centers as pendant groups within a zirconium MOF built from a 6-connected hexagonal Zr6 node will enable *quantitative, deterministic control* of spin localization and radical stability **only if** the aryl-ring dihedral angles are constrained by an intramolecularly registered, node-proximal clamp rather than stochastic defect modulation. We hypothesize that a bifunctional linker architecture—combining (i) a TAM/PTM radical pendant and (ii) a secondary, weakly coordinating docking motif (e.g., pyridyl, phenoxy, or amide) positioned at a defined vector and distance from the radical ipso carbon—will reversibly bind to a specific open Zr6 coordination site and act as a spatially defined torsional clamp. This intramolecular docking converts the Zr6 node into a deterministic dihedral reference frame, enforcing a narrow aryl twist-angle distribution (target σ < 10°) independent of global defect density. Mechanistically, the clamp fixes the balance between steric repulsion and π-conjugation at the TAM center: increased enforced twist localizes spin density on the central carbon (or designated aryl ring), enlarges the SOMO–SUMO gap (ΔESO–SU analogue), suppresses bimolecular coupling and oxygen-mediated decay, and enhances radical persistence; reduced enforced twist increases through-bond delocalization, narrows ΔESO–SU, and strengthens exchange coupling without conflating effects from radical loading, pore polarity, or defect heterogeneity. By anchoring the ‘wedge’ intramolecularly and quantifying defect populations a priori, dihedral angle becomes an independently addressable design variable rather than an emergent, ill-defined average.
Plan: Step 1: Clamp-registered linker and node architecture.
1.1 Select a pbz or pbz-derivative Zr-MOF topology with a well-defined 6-connected hexagonal Zr6 node that tolerates a controlled population of open coordination sites (μ3-OH/H2O). Build periodic and cluster DFT models explicitly including one open Zr site per node.
1.2 Design a hexatopic linker bearing: (a) a protected TAM/PTM precursor pendant (e.g., trityl alcohol, PTM–H) and (b) an intramolecular docking arm (pyridyl-N, phenoxy-O, or amide-O) tethered via a rigid spacer (phenylene or ethynylene) whose length and orientation predefine the radical–node geometry. Spacer lengths will be discretized (e.g., 6.5, 8.0, 9.5 Å) to target distinct dihedral windows (ca. 45–60°, 60–75°, 80–90°).
1.3 Incorporate ortho-buttress substituents on the TAM aryl rings (Me, iPr, F/Cl) as a secondary, static bias; these are held constant across docking-arm variants to isolate the clamp effect.

Step 2: Defect-controlled MOF synthesis.
2.1 Synthesize the Zr-MOF under modulated solvothermal conditions using a single, calibrated monocarboxylate modulator (e.g., formate) to establish a fixed missing-linker fraction. Defect density will be predefined and matched across all samples using TGA, ICP-OES, and quantitative modulator analysis.
2.2 Verify framework topology and node connectivity by SCXRD where possible; otherwise, use high-resolution PXRD with Rietveld refinement benchmarked against simulated defect models.

Step 3: Intramolecular clamp engagement (deterministic wedge).
3.1 Activate the MOF to expose Zr–OH/H2O sites, then induce reversible intramolecular docking by mild heating or solvent exchange that promotes coordination of the tethered docking arm to the Zr6 open site.
3.2 Confirm clamp engagement by IR (shifted ν(C=O)/ν(C–O) or ν(C–N)), solid-state 15N or 13C NMR (coordination-induced shifts), and DFT-calculated binding energies. Importantly, no additional external modulators are introduced at this stage.

Step 4: Radical generation with chemical compatibility mapping.
4.1 Establish a redox/chemical compatibility map: screen radical precursor stability against solvothermal solvents, modulators, and Zr–OH sites using solution and cluster tests.
4.2 Convert precursors to radicals post-synthetically under non-protic, non-coordinating conditions (e.g., mild oxidants for trityl alcohols; electrochemical or outer-sphere redox for PTM analogues).
4.3 Implement a go/no-go decision tree: if EPR indicates quenching by Zr–OH, cap residual protic sites with inert silylating agents prior to radical generation.

Step 5: Dihedral-angle metrology (deterministic criterion).
5.1 Structural: extract mean dihedral angles from SCXRD where ordered; otherwise refine against PDF data constrained by DFT/MD libraries generated for known torsion standards.
5.2 Local probe: introduce site-specific isotopic labeling (e.g., 13C at the TAM ipso carbon or deuterated ortho positions) and perform ENDOR/ESEEM to extract hyperfine tensors sensitive to torsion; correlate with calibrated DFT hyperfine–dihedral maps.
5.3 Variable-frequency EPR (X/Q/W-band) to separate g-strain from exchange and confirm σ(dihedral) < 10° as the operational definition of determinism.

Step 6: Causal deconvolution and validation.
6.1 Hold constant: radical loading, defect density, and radical–radical distance distribution (verified by spin counting and DEER where applicable).
6.2 Vary independently: docking-arm length (dihedral control) while keeping all other parameters fixed.
6.3 Correlate dihedral metrics with (i) spin localization, (ii) ΔESO–SU from periodic DOS projections, (iii) radical decay kinetics, and (iv) magnetic exchange (χT vs T).

Step 7: Secondary tuning and falsification.
7.1 Apply small, reversible mechanical strain to oriented films only after deterministic dihedral control is established; monitor for amorphization by in situ PXRD.
7.2 Demonstrate falsification: show that in linkers lacking the docking arm, identical defect densities and radical loadings do *not* yield narrow dihedral distributions or predictable spin behavior.
Feasibility: The refined approach directly addresses the reviewers’ concerns by replacing stochastic modulator wedges with an intramolecularly registered clamp whose geometry is encoded at the linker level and read out at the node. Zr6 clusters are uniquely suited because their open coordination sites bind weak N/O donors reversibly without altering node connectivity, enabling controlled second-sphere interactions. By predefining and holding defect density constant, changes in EPR or stability can be causally assigned to dihedral control rather than framework heterogeneity. Chemical compatibility is ensured by decoupling MOF synthesis from radical generation and by implementing a go/no-go redox decision tree that avoids Zr-bound protic quenchers. Determinism is operationalized quantitatively (σ(dihedral) < 10° with invariant inter-radical distances), and validated using orthogonal local probes (ENDOR/ESEEM + variable-frequency EPR) that are explicitly sensitive to torsion. This architecture thus overcomes the intrinsic disorder limitations of pendant radicals in MOFs and translates the dihedral–spin logic established in 2D-COFs into a chemically robust, three-dimensional Zr-MOF platform with falsifiable, quantitative structure–property control.
final_critique: This is an unusually rigorous and technically mature proposal that demonstrates deep command of both Zr-MOF defect chemistry and organic radical spin physics. The central mechanistic claim—that deterministic dihedral control cannot be achieved via stochastic defect modulation but can be imposed via an intramolecularly registered clamp—is logically consistent and well supported by a detailed experimental plan. Strengths include explicit defect matching, a priori falsification criteria, and sophisticated dihedral metrology (ENDOR/ESEEM calibrated by DFT). Minor deductions arise from practical risk rather than conceptual weakness: (i) the assumption that weak N/O donors will selectively and uniformly occupy a single open Zr site per node across a bulk material may be optimistic given competitive solvent binding and dynamic disorder, and (ii) the feasibility of extracting σ(dihedral) < 10° from PDF-constrained refinements in the absence of long-range order remains challenging, even with DFT libraries. These concerns do not undermine the logic but introduce execution risk.

original_chain: Water stable metal-organic framework -> Water adsorption -> Ambient conditions -> Bu-FeCr -> Water adsorption -> Environmental transmission electron microscopy
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Bu-FeCr layered oxalate MOFs can be converted into a water-stable, ambient-condition water adsorbent by installing a crystallographically testable “coordination-latched interlayer” motif that is distinct from (and experimentally separable from) simple intralayer strengthening or dissolution–reprecipitation. The latch will be created by partial substitution of oxalate with a mono-phosphonate/mono-carboxylate heterolinker (phosphonoacetate-type, abbreviated PA2−) that binds one metal center through a bidentate O–P–O chelate and a second metal center through a bidentate carboxylate/oxalate-like chelate. The key, falsifiable structural claim is that PA2− can adopt an out-of-plane bridging conformation in which the phosphonate binds a labile Fe(III) site on one layer while the carboxylate binds a facing Fe(III) site on the adjacent layer (Fe–O–P(O)–O···(interlayer gap)···O–C(O)–O–Fe), creating a discrete interlayer ‘pillar’ that increases the effective interlayer shear modulus and suppresses humidity-driven registry loss/delamination.

Mechanistic rationale (addressing reviewer points): (i) Cr(III) kinetic inertness is treated as a feature: latch formation is designed to occur predominantly at Fe(III) sites (fast ligand exchange) while Cr(III) remains as a topology-preserving anchor, preventing wholesale reconstruction. This creates a built-in kinetic constraint against dissolution–reprecipitation and provides a handle for attributing effects specifically to Fe-centered latching. (ii) The interlayer latch hypothesis yields two diagnostic signatures that are not expected for mere intralayer strengthening: (a) an RH-dependent but reversible change in interlayer (00l) spacing and stacking coherence length with reduced broadening under cycling, and (b) a substitution-dependent emergence/shift of low-angle (00l) reflections consistent with a reduced layer–layer repeat distance distribution (narrower microstrain) rather than only in-plane peak shifts. (iii) Increased hydrophilicity from phosphonate introduction is explicitly decoupled from mechanical stabilization by normalizing adsorption to independently measured accessible pore volume and by comparing isosteric heats and hysteresis at matched water loading; true latching predicts reduced hysteresis/cycling decay at comparable heats (thermodynamics) and comparable pore volume (capacity). (iv) ETEM is used only after a non-beam, structure-resolved latch decision is made; beam-driven artifacts are controlled through dose budgets, RH calibration at the specimen, mandatory no-beam trajectories, and post-mortem speciation/leaching checks.

Falsifiable outcomes: If PA2− incorporation results only in intralayer chelation strengthening (non-latched), then spatial P mapping will show uniform P but (00l) coherence will not improve and PXRD signatures will match an in-plane distorted model; if changes arise from dissolution–reprecipitation/phase segregation, then P will be heterogeneous (core–shell or separate phosphonate-rich domains), isotope tracers will show exchange/mass transport, and PDF will require multiple local environments inconsistent with the parent lattice. Only true latching should simultaneously produce: (1) uniform P distribution, (2) a latch-consistent PDF component (Fe–O–P and Fe···Fe interlayer distances), (3) a distinct low-angle (00l) signature/microstrain narrowing, and (4) improved RH cycling stability at matched adsorption thermodynamics.
Plan: Step 0 — Define the parent lattice, locate plausible latchable sites, and generate testable structural models (mandatory structure-resolved latch model).
0.1 Parent structure acquisition and indexing: Synthesize Bu-FeCr {NR3(CH2COOH)}[FeCr(ox)3]·nH2O (Bu = tributylammonium-derived cation as in Asset 2 family) and collect high-resolution PXRD (synchrotron if available) plus Rietveld/Le Bail fits to extract unit cell and specifically the interlayer repeat (c parameter or analogous stacking vector). Confirm layered nature and identify (00l) reflections.
0.2 Identify out-of-plane coordination availability: Use PDF (high-energy X-ray total scattering) and EXAFS at Fe K-edge/Cr K-edge to determine whether Fe sites exhibit any labile coordination (aqua/terminal oxalate oxygen environment) relative to Cr. The latch design proceeds only if Fe shows greater disorder/longer M–O distribution consistent with lability.
0.3 Explicit latch motif + simulated PXRD signature: Build two atomistic candidate models:
  Model L (latched): PA2− bridges adjacent layers with phosphonate bound to Fe(III) in layer n and carboxylate bound to Fe(III) in layer n+1, yielding a discrete interlayer Fe···Fe distance constraint and reduced stacking microstrain. Predict (i) modest contraction or tighter distribution of interlayer spacing (Δd00l), (ii) sharpening of (00l) peaks upon RH cycling compared to parent, and (iii) a new weak superstructure feature at low angle if latch periodicity is partially ordered.
  Model S (strengthened-only): PA2− binds intralayer (both donors chelate metals within same layer) or acts as a terminal chelator, increasing local rigidity but not creating interlayer constraints; predicted signature: primarily in-plane peak shifts/broadening changes with no systematic (00l) coherence improvement.
Simulate PXRD for both using Debye scattering (finite-crystal platelets) to include stacking disorder; define discriminating metrics: FWHM(00l), Williamson–Hall microstrain along stacking direction, and Δq for first (00l) peak.

Step 1 — Heterolinker selection and chemical constraints tuned to Fe(III) vs Cr(III).
1.1 Heterolinker choice (architectural parameterization): Use phosphonoacetic acid (H3PO3CH2CO2H) or closely related rigid mono-phosphonate/mono-carboxylate ligands that can present (a) bidentate phosphonate O–P–O to Fe(III) and (b) bidentate carboxylate to Fe(III). Select 1–2 derivatives with minimal extra rotatable bonds to reduce conformational entropy penalty for interlayer bridging.
1.2 Speciation window and kinetics plan (Fe vs Cr): Perform pH-dependent speciation calculations (Fe(III) and Cr(III) with oxalate and PA2−) and validate by UV–vis titration for Fe(III) complexation and by time-dependent measurements for Cr(III) (expected slow). Lock synthesis and post-synthetic steps into a window where Fe(III) exchange occurs but Cr(III) exchange is negligible:
  • Target pH 2.5–4.0 (suppress Fe(OH)3, keep phosphonate partially deprotonated for binding).
  • Control water activity (aw) using water/ethanol mixtures (e.g., 30–70% EtOH) to slow dissolution of oxalate framework while permitting local ligand exchange at Fe.
  • Time constraints: Fe exchange minutes–hours; Cr exchange days–weeks—use this to ensure ‘re-clamping’ does not rely on Cr.

Step 2 — Mixed-linker synthesis with controls for phase segregation and gradients.
2.1 Composition series with tight substitution targets: Prepare 0, 2.5, 5, 10, 15, 20 mol% PA2− relative to total linker equivalents (keep below amorphization threshold). Use modulated solvothermal conditions with acetate/formate modulator; explicitly maintain constant ionic strength and metal:linker ratio to prevent uncontrolled nucleation.
2.2 Anti-segregation protocol: Employ slow-diffusion or temperature-ramped solvothermal synthesis (e.g., 80→120 °C ramp) to promote equilibrium incorporation rather than kinetic core–shell growth.
2.3 Primary decision gate (bulk crystallography): Accept only batches whose PXRD retains the parent layered pattern with continuous, monotonic peak shifts and without extra crystalline phosphonate phases. Any extra reflections trigger segregation pathway (Decision Tree branch C).

Step 3 — Post-synthetic ‘Fe-selective reclamping’ with isotope tracing to exclude dissolution–reprecipitation.
3.1 Reclamping chemistry (explicit constraints): Treat mixed-linker crystals in Fe(III) salt solution (e.g., Fe(ClO4)3) in water/ethanol (aw reduced), buffered pH 3.0–3.5, at 25–40 °C, for 0.5, 2, 8, 24 h. Maintain low total metal concentration to minimize reprecipitation; quantify dissolved species continuously.
3.2 Isotope-labelled tracer experiments (mass-transport discriminator):
  • Linker tracer: use 13C-labelled phosphonoacetate (13CH2) or 18O-labelled phosphonate to track incorporation without requiring bulk recrystallization. Monitor incorporation by solid-state NMR (13C) and ToF-SIMS (18O/13C maps).
  • Metal tracer: perform reclamping with 57Fe-enriched Fe(III) and detect whether new Fe enters the lattice (57Fe Mössbauer / ICP mass balance). True ‘reclamping’ should show minimal net metal uptake (local coordination completion) versus dissolution–reprecipitation which would show significant metal exchange and composition drift.
3.3 Solution mass balance: Collect supernatants over time and quantify Fe/Cr leaching (ICP-OES) and linker release (LC-MS). A latch formation pathway must satisfy: leaching rate ≪ incorporation rate; otherwise classify as branch C.

Step 4 — Spatially resolved composition/coordination mapping (mandatory heterogeneity controls).
4.1 STEM-EDS/EELS mapping: Map P, Fe, Cr across individual platelets (cross-sectional lamellae via FIB if needed). Quantify P/Fe ratio as a function of radius and thickness; acceptance criterion for ‘uniform incorporation’: no systematic core–shell gradient exceeding, e.g., ±10–15% relative variation across thickness.
4.2 ToF-SIMS depth profiling: Quantify phosphonate fragments (POx−) and organic fragments (CH2CO2−) vs sputter time to detect surface-enriched phosphonate layers or buried domains.
4.3 Nano-FTIR (or IR s-SNOM) for coordination state mapping: Spatially map P–O stretching frequencies; chelated phosphonate should show characteristic shifts relative to free phosphonic acid. Compare edges vs basal planes to see whether latches preferentially form at interlayer interfaces.

Step 5 — PDF/EXAFS model discrimination (latch vs strengthened-only local structure).
5.1 Total scattering/PDF fitting: Fit PDFs against a two-model library (Model L vs Model S) focusing on:
  • Fe–O–P distance signatures,
  • Fe···Fe distances consistent with interlayer bridging constraint,
  • Changes in distribution width along stacking direction.
Require that Model L improves fit quality specifically in r-ranges sensitive to interlayer correlations, not just local Fe–O.
5.2 Fe/Cr-edge EXAFS: Look for increased Fe coordination number/changed scatterer identity consistent with phosphonate binding at Fe; Cr EXAFS should remain essentially unchanged if latch formation is Fe-selective.

Step 6 — Water sorption: decouple mechanical stabilization from altered sorption energetics.
6.1 Accessible pore volume normalization: Measure N2/Ar sorption (where applicable) and/or use water intrusion/He pycnometry to estimate accessible pore volume. Report water uptake normalized per accessible pore volume (gH2O per cm3 pore) to separate capacity changes from structural collapse/pore blocking.
6.2 Matched-loading thermodynamic comparison: Acquire water isotherms at ≥2 temperatures (e.g., 20 and 30 °C) to compute isosteric heat (Qst). Compare hysteresis area and cycling decay at matched loading (same mmol g−1 H2O) and similar Qst. True latching predicts: reduced hysteresis/cycling degradation without requiring substantially lower Qst (i.e., not merely making the material less hydrophilic).
6.3 Cycling and stability metrics: 100–200 RH swing cycles (e.g., 10%↔70% RH) with periodic PXRD and mass uptake retention; define a combined stability metric: retained (00l) intensity/coherence + leaching constant (from ICP of condensate or washings).

Step 7 — ETEM with explicit dose budgets, RH calibration, and mandatory no-beam controls.
7.1 RH calibration at sample: Use an in-holder humidity sensor or calibrate via known deliquescence standards positioned near the grid; verify local RH by observing a reference material transition. Record temperature and gas composition continuously.
7.2 Dose budgeting: Establish maximum cumulative dose per trajectory (e.g., keep below a pre-determined threshold from a dose series where no chemical change is detected by post-mortem 31P NMR/ICP). Use nanobeam diffraction with minimal exposure; HRTEM only sparsely for defect localization.
